title: GOP chairman says WNBA response on Caitlin Clark ‘falls short,’ keeps ‘every option on the table’
excerpt: Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, speaks with OutKick about his congressional letter questioning the WNBA’s handling of Caitlin Clark and player safety, one day before Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sent th...
body_text:
Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, speaks with OutKick about his congressional letter questioning the WNBA’s handling of Caitlin Clark and player safety, one day before Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sent the league’s formal response to lawmakers.

Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, chairman of the Republican Study Committee, says the WNBA’s response to congressional concerns about Caitlin Clark’s treatment "falls short" and warned that lawmakers will keep "every option on the table" as they continue pressing the league for answers.

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert responded on July 24 to a letter from Pfluger and 10 other House Republicans who questioned whether the league had adequately protected Clark and held opposing players accountable for overly physical conduct.

In the two-page response obtained exclusively by OutKick, Engelbert said the WNBA’s "top priority is the health, safety, and well-being of every player in our league, including Caitlin Clark."

REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS PRESS WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT TO PROTECT CAITLIN CLARK

Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark tries to defend herself during a loose ball scramble while Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas stands over her. (Grace Smith/IndyStar / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

In the response, the commissioner outlined the league’s standard procedures for reviewing officiating and potentially dangerous play but did not address any of the Clark-related incidents cited by the lawmakers individually.

"The WNBA’s response falls short of what we asked for, unsurprisingly," Pfluger told OutKick in a statement. "We didn’t request a description of the league’s general officiating and disciplinary procedures, we asked how those procedures have actually been applied in the specific incidents we raised involving Caitlin Clark, and the league chose not to answer that."

Engelbert wrote that WNBA Basketball Operations and Referee Operations conduct separate reviews after every game. One review examines "atypical or overly physical plays," while the other evaluates the overall performance of the officials.

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert addresses reporters before the WNBA All-Star Game. (TNS)

WNBA MEDIA PREDICTABLY EMBARRASSES ITSELF AGAIN BY IGNORING SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM STORY OVER ALL-STAR WEEKEND

Those reviews can result in fouls being upgraded after a game, as well as fines, suspensions or other disciplinary measures. The league also uses the reviews to inform future officiating evaluations, training and guidance, Engelbert wrote.

"In all instances, the League seeks to apply the WNBA rulebook and applicable disciplinary processes consistently across all games and for all players," the commissioner said.

Pfluger said the league offered no supporting information to demonstrate that its rules had been applied evenly.

"Saying you apply your rules ‘consistently across all games and for all players’ is an assertion, not evidence, and it’s the league’s burden to show that, not ours to assume it," Pfluger said.

"Until the WNBA is willing to engage with the specifics of our information requests instead of simply restating their own policies back to us, our concerns remain unaddressed. We will continue to press for real answers and keep every option on the table until players are actually getting the protection the league claims they already provide."

Pfluger and the other lawmakers initially wrote to Engelbert on July 7, following several highly publicized incidents involving Clark. Their letter cited instances in which the Indiana Fever star had been hip-checked, poked in the eye and struck in the throat. The WNBA later assessed Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas a Flagrant Foul 2 and one-game suspension for the June 24 throat-contact incident.

The lawmakers argued that the incidents went "far beyond routine physical play" and accused the league and its officials of too often failing to address the conduct or hold opposing players accountable.

They asked Engelbert to explain the WNBA’s process for reviewing physical hostility and violence during games, how the league holds players accountable for overly aggressive actions, including conduct directed at Clark, and what it is doing to protect players from online harassment and off-court threats.

CAITLIN CLARK IS MISSING FROM ESPN'S NEW WNBA DOCUMENTARY AND THE FILMMAKERS WON'T SAY WHY

The letter also said lawmakers were concerned by reports suggesting some of Clark’s treatment could be racially motivated and warned that a failure to prevent discrimination, retaliation or a hostile work environment could raise questions under federal workplace and civil rights laws. The lawmakers requested a response by July 24.

Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark reacts after a flagrant foul by Chicago Sky player Diamond DeShields. (Getty Images)

Engelbert met the deadline, but her response did not address the alleged racial motivation, discuss any specific play involving Clark or provide comparative information about how the league’s officiating and disciplinary procedures had been applied to different players.

The response also did not say whether the WNBA conducted a separate review in response to the congressional inquiry.

Engelbert devoted part of the response to the league’s efforts to protect players from harassment away from games.

The commissioner pointed to enhanced arena and travel security, full-time charter flights, technology used to identify and report online threats, stronger fan conduct policies and expanded mental health resources. She also said the WNBA regularly communicates with teams, players and security personnel about player safety.

"The WNBA will continue its efforts to ensure all of our players are able to compete in a safe, respectful, and professional environment," Engelbert wrote.

The league’s emphasis on off-court harassment followed a July 22 joint statement from the WNBA and the Women’s National Basketball Players Association addressing an increase in racist, hateful and abusive messages directed at players.

During a July 23 interview with OutKick, conducted one day before Engelbert sent her response, Pfluger called that issue separate from the questions raised in the lawmakers’ letter.

"I’m sure there are plenty of other issues that the league needs to address, and they can do that as they see fit, but our questions are pretty pointed," Pfluger said. "The only way to clear up our questions is to actually answer them."

Rep. August Pfluger speaks during a House Committee on Homeland Security hearing. (Getty Images)

During the interview, Pfluger said the burden was on the WNBA to provide information demonstrating that its standards were enforced fairly. He argued that allowing a perception of unequal treatment to persist would damage confidence in the league’s ability to govern itself.

When asked during the interview to identify specific evidence supporting the original letter’s suggestion of racial motivation, Pfluger did not cite an example. He instead broadened his argument to whether every WNBA player receives equal protection under league rules.

"It is about everybody," Pfluger said. "The burden of proof should be on the commissioner, should be on the league, to provide evidence of how players on different teams and from different areas are treated."

Pfluger’s latest statement did not identify a specific congressional action he intends to pursue next, but his pledge to keep "every option on the table" leaves open the possibility of additional information requests, hearings or other scrutiny.

The WNBA did not respond to additional questions from OutKick and Fox News Digital prior to publication.

"Women’s sports are at a turning point," Pfluger said. "How the WNBA treats its own biggest star will show whether the league is actually committed to protecting the players carrying it forward."

title: Pedro Sánchez says next 12 hours will be ‘decisive’ in battle to contain wildfires – Europe live
excerpt:
Authorities fear progress in containing the fires in the Gironde and Madrid regions may be set back by temperatures expected to hit the low 40s

The European Union’s crisis-management team is expectin...
body_text:
Authorities fear progress in containing the fires in the Gironde and Madrid regions may be set back by temperatures expected to hit the low 40s

The European Union’s crisis-management team is expecting difficult weeks ahead, fearing a further outbreak of wildfires in Italy and Greece as the summer goes on.

Maria Zuber, a senior official at the EU’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre in Brussels, said the next few days will be “very difficult” for France, where firefighters are battling to contain the massive fire in the Gironde region near Bordeaux amid a spike in temperatures on Wednesday.

The ERCC is the EU’s crisis-management centre, which monitors disasters around the world and coordinates the dispatch of firefighting planes, equipment and teams to countries that have asked for help.

Speaking to reporters, Zuber said Greece had so far been spared, but “now we see it will go to Greece” and forecast an intensification of fires in Italy from early August. Her colleague, ERCC wildfires expert Moises Galan Santano, also raised concerns about Portugal.

One “new” and “worrying” factor, the ERCC sees uniting the massive fires in France and Spain is their proximity to major cities. Around 220,000 people have been evacuated in the Bordeaux region alone. Over the weekend residents in eight towns near Toledo were forced to leave their homes.

That means firefighters cannot put all their energies into extinguishing the flames, because they have to protect people and property.

“A firefighter will focus on protecting people. They will focus on protecting houses, protecting a business, a company, because this is something that matters for all our society. And indeed, sometimes by focusing on that, they cannot extinguish fire, [as] they would do it if it would be just forest.

So this is new, this is worrying. And of course also, this means that we need to adapt our methods of fighting the fires.”

Authorities in the Gironde region said the blaze had not spread overnight, but rising heat and afternoon winds could revive smoldering hotspots, carry embers across firebreaks and open new fronts beyond crews’ reach, AP reported.

At the command center in Lège, firefighters bent over maps spread across a car hood, tracking three danger zones: northern Cap-Ferret; the wooded corridor around Marcheprime, Cestas and Saint-Jean-d’Illac; and a military site near Martignas, where a major outbreak forced a large deployment.

PA said that nore than 2,200 firefighters and over 20 aircraft remained mobilized, backed by crews from across France and European partners.

“We strike quickly and strike hard at any new smoke emissions,” Gironde fire commander Matthieu Jomain said.

The advance of major fires in the Landes and Var regions have been halted. That left Gironde as France’s biggest remaining wildfire battle, interior minister Laurent Nuñez said.

We are getting some heartbreaking pictures showing people returning to their homes near Madrid and finding their homes completely destroyed by the blaze.

While the situation near Madrid is gradually improving, the Spanish media are reporting that a separate fire near The Vall d’Uixó in the Castellón province is still spreading uncontrollably.

RTVE reported that it remains out of control after burning nearly 10,000 hectares across 81 kilometers, forcing authorities to evacuate some 10,000 people.

Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez has been speaking in the last ten minutes on his visit to a command post in Navalcarnero.

He said the current situation remains “favourable,” but the next 12 hours will be “decisive” in consolidating and securing the progress made by the firefighters as temperatures rise and create new risks.

Sánchez also asked those displaced by fires for trust and patience, as he said these decisions are not political, but taken on scientific advice as to when these returns are safe.

As is customary in the last few days, he also warned people against believing hoaxes and conspiracy theories spread on social media.

In Spain, thousands of people have been allowed back to their homes last night near Madrid, even as emergency services still continue to fight the blazes.

24,000 evacuees returned to the area, with another 20,000 released from stay at home orders.

More progress have been made overnight too, but local authorities urged caution as the new heatwave is set to hit the area.

“Efforts will focus on securing the perimeter, monitoring for new hotspots and cooling the areas to keep control of the fire,” a statement said.

Météo-France’s weather forecast shows temperatures up to 39C near Bordeaux – just where the largest wildfire continues to blaze – 38C in Lyon, 37C in Paris and Toulouse.

Over in Spain, it will be even hotter, with Aemet expecting 42C in Pamplona, 41C in Cordova and Saragossa, 40C in Ciudad-Real and Toledo, and 37C in Madrid.

The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has delayed going on holiday and stays in Paris to manage the wildfire crisis, BFMTV reported.

Despite clear progress made in tackling the blazes, there are continuing concerns over the potential impact of the latest heatwave, starting today.

France and Spain are braced for the fourth heatwave of the summer to hit just as they were making progress battling destructive wildfires, with temperatures once again expected to cross into high 30s and low 40s celsius later today.

Sophie Brocas, the ⁠prefect of Gironde and the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, said overnight that the fire remained contained this morning, with several flare-ups quickly brought under control.

“We will win this war,” the communications director for the French Firefighters Federation, Éric Brocardi, told broadcaster BFMTV.

But the return of high temperatures puts authorities on high alert for new potential fires. Sixty-five French departments were put on a high fire risk warning.

Over in Spain, the government’s regional representatives in Madrid are warning of “extreme” fire danger in parts of the region. But, encouragingly, the main forest fire near the capital remained stable overnight, with no significant flare-ups.

It’s Wednesday, 29 July 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

title: 'I thought I would die': Survivors describe shock and horror of powerful Japan earthquake
excerpt:
The ramifications of the earthquake have been widely felt

Business was winding down for the day at Sendan Shokudo, a diner in Japan's south-western city of Yatsushiro, when the whole building suddenl...
body_text:
The ramifications of the earthquake have been widely felt

Business was winding down for the day at Sendan Shokudo, a diner in Japan's south-western city of Yatsushiro, when the whole building suddenly lurched.

Everything on the kitchen shelves cascaded to the floor; bowls and glasses shattered.

The restaurant's co-owner, 75-year-old Hiroko Ogata, had just walked in.

"I was surprised, and scared," she told BBC News. "I went under one of the tables right away, but the table moved sharply towards the right, left, right, left, with me."

There's a reason Ogata knew how to react so swiftly: she has lived in Yatsushiro, in central Kumamoto prefecture, her whole life.

The area is located on an active tectonic fault system and is no stranger to tremors. In 2016, a pair of earthquakes killed 277 people and injured 2,800 others.

But Ogata has "never experienced this big of a jolt".

"The last quake 10 years ago was nothing like this one," she said. "I thought I would die."

At least 13 people have been killed in the wake of the 6.8-magnitude earthquake that hit Kumamoto late on Tuesday.

Of that number, three died in the Aeon shopping mall in Kumamoto city, where a number of people remain unaccounted for.

Rescue efforts are under way, but Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has warned that emergency services are in a "race against time".

Just a few hundred metres away from the Aeon mall, Yui - who preferred not to use her real name for this report - was sitting in the back office of her cake shop when the quake hit.

"I couldn't tell which was the sound of the earthquake and which was the sound of the explosion," she told the BBC.

"All I could do was hold the chair I was sitting in as big jolts came one after another," she added, appearing to still be in shock.

"I didn't know what to feel; I couldn't even feel scared in such a situation. Even now I don't know what to feel, and I don't know how to explain."

Authorities and emergency responders mobilised quickly. Shortly after the tremor struck, Takaichi put 4,600 personnel on the ground to assist with recovery, and said that teams would work "tirelessly through the night" to assess and monitor the damage in affected areas.

Tens of thousands of people have experienced power and water outages across Kumamoto City and at least 45 medical facilities have been damaged.

The exterior walls of the 17th century Kumamoto Castle, in the city's centre, came toppling down in a plume of dust. The worship hall of the 19th Century Yatshushiro Shrine completely collapsed.

Kumamoto is no stranger to earthquakes - but locals have described this one as particularly strong

One local resident Michal Posan said there is "no water or food left in the stores".

Posan, 25, has been living in Kumamoto for two years, and was at home at the time of the quake.

"My TV fell on me, my mirror smashed and the roads around me were damaged," she told the BBC – adding that she had started preparing evacuation bags amid the "constant aftershocks".

Another resident said aftershocks were still rattling the city hours after the initial tremor.

"People are wary of another earthquake on the way," he said. "The 2016 earthquake [was] followed by a second days later."

Experts are also concerned. Shinji Kiyomoto of Japan's Meteorological Agency has asked the public to "remain vigilant" for further earthquakes. He too referenced 2016's deadly series of earthquakes, which struck days apart.

"We cannot rule out the possibility that an even larger quake could follow this time as well," he said. "We urge people to remain on alert."

Kyushu island, where Kumamoto prefecture is located, is a spiderweb of active fault zones. These include the Hinagu fault, which runs about 81km through the island's heartland.

That fault zone was partially activated in the 2016 quakes – but experts have long warned that its remaining, unruptured sections could generate a major earthquake.

Assessments by the government's earthquake research committee suggest that tremors with magnitudes as high as 7.5 could strike along the inland section of the zone. If the whole Hinagu fault were to rupture, the magnitude could reach 8.

Many people are left with no choice but to pick up the pieces, even as fear of another earthquake lingers

In the meantime, locals like Ogata and Yui are having to pick up the pieces and try to restore some kind of normality – even as the shockwaves, both geological and psychological, continue to occur.

"The whole of my place is messy, and I don't know where to stand – but we have to earn our living by restarting our restaurant as soon as possible, so I am cleaning the place today," Ogata said on Wednesday.

"But when I try to work for a bit, an aftershock occurs and I have to stop – then I do some work and we have another aftershock… So it is going so slowly.

"If we keep having this many aftershocks it will be very stressful."

Yui's cake shop remains closed, as she assesses the extent of the damage.

"I haven't checked whether the machines such as the oven are working," she said. "After I check those, I will have an idea whether I can go back to business or not."

title: The bedrock of American liberty was laid in Jerusalem
excerpt: U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee introduced Guatemala at the City of David, declaring that "just as the U.S. has discovered that we have roots here, so Guatemala has discovered." (Credit: Barak Meir Xmed...
body_text:
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee introduced Guatemala at the City of David, declaring that "just as the U.S. has discovered that we have roots here, so Guatemala has discovered." (Credit: Barak Meir Xmedia & City of David Archives.)

When considering the sites upon which the foundations of the United States were established, Plymouth Rock, Valley Forge and Independence Hall come to mind. Yet America's Founding Fathers looked far beyond them for the inspiration to build a nation.

In October 2020, the United States formally recognized the City of David — the historic site of biblical Jerusalem — as a heritage site. Not as a Jewish heritage site, nor as an Israeli one, but as an American heritage site.

Why would the United States recognize a site more than six thousand miles beyond its borders as part of its own national heritage? Why, in 2025, would Argentina's President Javier Milei do the same, calling the City of David a source of inspiration for his republic? And why, this past week, would Guatemala become the third nation to do so?

THE WAR ON AMERICA’S JUDEO-CHRISTIAN ROOTS THREATENS EVERYTHING WE SHARE

Overview of the excavation site in the City of David National Park in Jerusalem. (Israel Nature and Parks Authority)

The answer is something Americans are in danger of forgetting.

The moral bedrock on which the United States was built — and on which it endures — traces back to Jerusalem's biblical heritage. Equality before the law. Inherent human dignity. The right to speak truth to power. These revolutionary ideas didn't come from Athens, and they didn't originate in Rome. They came from Jerusalem.

Consider what they replaced: rulers who sat above the law, accountable to no one, in societies where only a select few were deemed worthy of rights at all.

RARE AMERICAN BIBLE AND FOUNDERS’ LETTERS TRACE FAITH’S ROLE IN BIRTH OF THE NATION

Yet in Jerusalem, three thousand years ago, when King David was confronted by the prophet Nathan over a moral failing, rather than execute the man who dared challenge a king, David took ownership — acknowledging his own accountability to the law, declaring that he had sinned before God and vowing to make amends.

Thomas Paine knew the source of that ideal. In Common Sense, the pamphlet that inspired the American Revolution, he pointed to the Book of Samuel and declared that in America, the law is king.

Four centuries later, in the same city, a young man named Jeremiah challenged a throne whose courts were corrupt and under which the poor were being crushed. Officials, unwilling to heed his call to change their ways, threw him into a cistern to sink in the mud and die.

A U.S. plaque in the City of David recognizing its significance to America's heritage and founding principles. The proclamation says:                                 "The City of David brings Biblical Jerusalem to life at the very place where the kings and prophets of the Bible walked. It is the site where internationally acclaimed archeological discoveries have been unearthed, including the Pool of Siloam, the Pilgrimage Road, the Gihon Spring and Hezekiah’s Tunnel.     As the prophet Isaiah said, "Out of Zion shall go forth the law and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." The spiritual bedrock of our values as a nation comes from Jerusalem. It is upon these ideals that the American republic was founded, and the unbreakable bond between the United States and Israel was formed. The City of David serves as a proud reminder of the glorious heritage of the United States of America.                                                            "I REJOICED WITH THOSE WHO SAID TO ME, ‘LET US GO TO THE HOUSE OF THE LORD.’OUR FEET ARE STANDING IN YOUR GATES, JERUSALEM."— PSALM 122:1–2                                                                                               David Friedman U.S. Ambassador to Israel Paul Packer Chairman, U.S. Commission for the Preservation of America’s Heritage Abroad. (City of David Archive/Kobi Harati)

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

The personal seals of two of those officials — Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur, the men named in the Book of Jeremiah as plotting to put the prophet to death for the crime of speaking truth to power — were unearthed in the City of David by the archaeologist Dr. Eilat Mazar. The names in the ground match the names on the page. The First Amendment's protections of speech and dissent didn't begin in America. Their roots run back to Jerusalem.

Athens executed Socrates for asking too many questions. Jerusalem made holding truth above human power a sacred duty. Benjamin Franklin proposed seven words as the motto for the Great Seal of the United States: Rebellion to tyrants is obedience to God.

A bulla — a clay seal impressed with an official seal stamp— bearing the name of Gedaliah son of Pashhur. (Courtesy: Eilat Mazar/Gabi Laron, Institute of Archaeology, The Hebrew University & City of David Archives)

And Thomas Jefferson wrote in the Declaration of Independence that all men are created equal, endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights.

Not endowed by the king, nor by the government. By the Creator.

Panoramic view of the Old City of Jerusalem, Israel , viewed from Haas Avenue in late afternoon. (Planet One Images/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The idea that every person carries inherent worth, simply by being made in the image of God, begins in Genesis — and found its first national expression in Jerusalem.

This was no secret to America's Founders. Of some 15,000 political writings of the founding era, the most-cited source was not Locke or Montesquieu. It was the Bible — cited more than both combined. They told us exactly where they got it.

These nations did not come to honor Israel and the Jewish people specifically. They came to connect themselves to Jerusalem and her story — to the ideals, rooted in this city, on which they were founded and on which they hope to endure.

In September 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood on the newly unearthed Pilgrimage Road at the City of David — the half mile that carried pilgrims from the Pool of Siloam up toward the Temple — and echoed the same sentiment: "The United States was founded… on the very powerful principle that the rights of mankind come from their Creator… But that idea did not come from the ether. It did not come from someone's imagination. It was deeply rooted in the teachings of ancient words, thousands and thousands of years old, that find their genesis here, literally on the very spot on which I stand."

As America enters her 251st year, what is the source of the ideals from which she will draw her sense of national purpose, meaning and destiny? Jerusalem offers an answer — the same inheritance it has offered for millennia, and one as relevant today as it was three thousand years ago.

Ze'ev Orenstein is the Director of International Affairs for the City of David Foundation in Jerusalem, Israel.

title: US schools are struggling to keep the yellow bus running amid shortages and cuts
excerpt:
Districts are reducing routes and exploring new ways to get students to class as transportation costs climb

Education officials across the United States are increasingly facing a fundamental challeng...
body_text:
Districts are reducing routes and exploring new ways to get students to class as transportation costs climb

Education officials across the United States are increasingly facing a fundamental challenge: how do they ensure that school students can actually get to their classrooms?

The bright yellow school bus might be a visual icon of US education famous around the world, but in reality it is becoming harder for districts to steer.

Student transportation has become more difficult for districts in the US in recent years due to factors such as a shortage of bus drivers, budget constraints, and the growth of the school choice movement.

This year, school officials in states such as Arizona; Connecticut; Florida; Idaho; New Jersey; New York; Ohio; Oregon; and Virginia have either reduced, or proposed reducing, student transportation services.

District leaders are trying to solve the transportation issues, which not only make life harder for parents but can lead to worse academic outcomes for students.

“It’s an especially important thing for families who don’t have reliable forms of transportation or others who they can regularly turn to for help,” said Jeremy Singer, assistant professor of education at University of Michigan-Flint, who has studied school transportation and absenteeism. “If schools reduce their school bus offerings, that means more families driving, which means more money on gas, more traffic and more emissions.”

Eighty percent of US districts have seen their transportation operations impacted by bus driver shortages, and 73% have seen such operations impacted by budget shortages, according to a 2025 report from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. The study was conducted in partnership with HopSkipDrive, a school rideshare company.

Experts trace many of the problems to the Covid-19 pandemic, when most schools shifted to remote learning, which, of course, meant there was less need for bus drivers. They then had to find other employment, and when schools reopened, some didn’t return. In August 2019, there were more than 223,000 US school bus drivers, according to the Economic Policy Institute, a left-leaning research group; in August 2025, there were only 202,000, a 9.5% decrease.

“If you want to drive to make money, it’s a lot easier to drive for Uber or Lyft than it is to drive a school bus,” said Sarah Cordes, a Temple University associate professor who studies education and urban policy. “Driving a school bus requires all kinds of training,” and “it’s not an easy job if you are dealing with a vehicle full of children.”

Public education systems, like the rest of the economy, have also been affected by inflation and more recently, increased gas prices. During the 2025-26 school year, more than half of school district leaders said their diesel fuel costs exceeded what they had budgeted, according to a survey from the School Superintendents Association. A quarter said they had to cover the overruns by transferring funds from other programs, and 19% said they had used reserve funding.

Districts also have less money to cover expenses because enrollment has decreased due to declining birth rates and parents increasingly sending their children to private or charter schools or homeschooling them, Singer said.

That enrollment decline has meant districts get less tax money.

But unlike some other expenditures, like elective class educators or technologies, districts have a harder time reducing the number of bus routes because students are still dispersed the same way throughout a district, Cordes said. Cutting buses would then require existing drivers to expand their routes, and students would spend more time in transit.

“Theoretically you could reduce routes but then depending on where kids live relative to each other and relative to school, that could mean that you have kids on the bus for an hour, an hour and a half, two hours,” Cordes said. “If kids are on the bus for more than an hour, that is not good for their attendance.”

Districts are now experimenting with other ways to get kids to school besides the yellow buses, including rideshare companies focused on students, like HopSkipDrive, that use small vehicles.

But regulations pose a challenge, Singer said. The federal School Bus Safety Amendments passed in 1974 require that new vehicles that carry 11 or more persons meet the same motor vehicle safety standards as school buses.

The Heritage Foundation, a conservative thinktank, called for the repeal of the law, arguing that states need “more tools in their transportation toolbox than yellow buses to meet the modern challenge”.

The National Association of State Directors of Pupil Transportation Services, a trade association of government officials overseeing school bus services, disagreed, stating that the law improved safety for students and that “using vehicles other than school buses compromises student safety and heightens the potential for disastrous crashes.”

But such a regulation creates additional costs because of the safety features needed to comply and limits flexibility on which vehicles districts can use, Singer said.

Ohio is among the states grappling with a significant bus driver shortage. In 34 districts, fewer than 10% of vacant bus driver positions were filled, according to a report published in June from the Ohio pupil transportation workgroup, which the state tasked with solving the school busing challenges.

Transportation cost Ohio districts an average of $1,273 per student during fiscal year 2026, an almost 5% increase over the previous year.

Meanwhile, the state’s public school district enrollment decreased by almost 100,000 students between 2016 and 2025, and 124 districts projected negative cash balances by 2029, the worst rate since the Great Recession, the Columbus Dispatch reported.

The state also still requires public schools to transport students who attend charter and private schools.

During the most recent school year, Ohio districts labeled more than 22,000 students “impractical to transport”, which allowed them to pay families in lieu of actually transporting their students, according to the transportation workgroup.

The group recommended that the state phase out the “impractical to transport” designation. Instead, Ohio “should establish a clear statewide policy that every transportation-eligible student receives safe and reliable transportation”.

The state could accomplish that by allowing “districts to coordinate with families of community and chartered nonpublic school students to identify centralized locations to serve as initial collection and drop-off points” and reviewing the “bus driver training model for opportunities to compress the timeline”, among other measures, the report stated.

Columbus City Schools transports 20,000 students to its schools and 8,000 to private and religious schools, according to Michael Brown, the district’s chief of communications and engagement.

School officials are considering reducing service to high school students because of the high costs, Brown stated. Eliminating the impracticality option would create a new unfunded mandate, he added.

Meanwhile, Ohio’s governor, Mike DeWine, a Republican, in 2025 approved legislation that caps how much funding school districts receive when property values increase, a measure aimed at reducing property tax increases not approved by voters. It will reduce revenue for schools by at least $1.7bn over the next three years, Ideastream Public Media reported.

“We continue to be concerned about the state’s lack of full, fair funding to meet the actual costs” of transportation, Brown stated in an email to the Guardian.

Cordes, of Temple University, said districts in Ohio and elsewhere must “weigh the costs and benefits of expanding access”.

“You may be getting more kids to school”, she said but “that might take away from the district’s ability to spend money on other important things that have to happen in the classroom”.

title: King Charles sends 'defiance' message to Prince William with Buckingham Palace room offer to Harry: expert
excerpt:
Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, discusses Prince Harry's expected UK return, his relationship with King Charles, and why a meeting with Prince William remains unlikely.

King Charles ...
body_text:
Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, discusses Prince Harry's expected UK return, his relationship with King Charles, and why a meeting with Prince William remains unlikely.

King Charles and his heir are said to be at odds over how to handle Prince Harry.

Multiple royal experts echoed the sentiment to Fox News Digital after royal author Robert Jobson told Page Six that Prince William and his estranged brother have "different agendas" and maintain very different relationships with their father.

Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.

KING CHARLES KEPT PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON IN THE DARK ABOUT SECRET HARRY AND MEGHAN REUNION: REPORT

The Sun reported that Prince Harry is expected to visit the U.K. in September and his father, King Charles (center), will offer his son a room at Buckingham Palace in London. (Aaron Chown - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"When it comes to Harry, William drew a line in the sand after the publication of Harry's memoir, 'Spare,' and he is disappointed that his father is not standing up for him," Christopher Andersen, author of "The King," told Fox News Digital.

"William loves his father and appreciates better than anyone how underestimated Charles has been over the years. He wants the king to leave his mark on history. But deep down, he knows he and his family — particularly his wife, Kate — are the future of the monarchy."

WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

While Charles and William are described as being "perfectly civil to each other," sources told Page Six there are ongoing disagreements about how the monarchy should be led.

"The problem with William is that he thinks he knows best," royal biographer Hugo Vickers told the outlet.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, meets young people and volunteers in the Common Room at Eagle House on July 9, 2026, in Hastings, England. (WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"King Charles is tired," Andersen stressed to Fox News Digital. "He would like to have everything as it was before Megxit. But he knows how willful William is. Queen Elizabeth's cousin Margaret Rhodes told me more than once that the relationship between Charles and his late mother wasn't cozy. But what people don't know is that the royal family isn't set up to be 'cozy.' Well, it still isn't. It's 'The Firm,' remember?"

Prince William, Prince of Wales and King Charles III walk behind Queen Elizabeth II's coffin as it is transported on a gun carriage from Buckingham Palace to Westminster Hall ahead of her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. William is heir to the British throne. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

People magazine reported Harry is expected to visit his home country again in September. The Sun also reported that the king plans to offer him a room at Buckingham Palace in London for his stay. Buckingham Palace and Harry's representatives had no comment on the report when reached by People magazine.

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that Charles' reported offer to accommodate Harry in September is "a potential lifeline" that also sends a message of "defiance" to William, who reportedly wants "no further contact with his estranged brother."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex departs from The Invictus Games Foundation Conversation: From Policy to Practice at Chatham House on July 7, 2026, in London. Multiple royal experts told Fox News Digital that there's no doubt King Charles' younger son misses his life in the U.K. (Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images)

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that William is known for being stubborn behind palace doors and is not one to forgive easily.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father, King Charles III, at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"Megxit forced William to grow up fast as the future king," she said.

"Prince Harry’s potential lifeline return to the United Kingdom in September and being offered accommodation at Buckingham Palace by King Charles is, to me, a major sign of defiance to William’s wishes of no future contact with his erstwhile brother," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"He had to protect the institution while his brother walked away. William believes the monarchy must be seen to do the right thing, even when it's painful. From what I understand, he felt his father didn't handle that firmly enough. He also believes in protecting it by drawing hard lines. But he's not the king yet."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, known as the Duke of Rothesay and Catherine, Princess of Wales, known as the Duchess of Rothesay when in Scotland, smile to well-wishers as they arrive for a visit to Aros Hall, a local community hub on April 29, 2025, in Tobermory, Scotland. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"Where Charles may want to smooth things over, to play peacemaker with Harry, William and Catherine are determined to set boundaries. Charles is reigning, but William and Catherine are planning. And that planning is starting to look a lot like leading. Charles wants healing. William and Catherine want survival and stability. William is not doing this to be difficult. He’s doing it because he believes it’s right."

Since marrying in 2018 and making their royal exit in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been attempting to carve out their own independent roles outside of the monarchy. (Joshua Sammer/Getty Images)

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that William and Harry have remained estranged since the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior working royals in 2020 and relocated to California. Harry and Meghan have maintained that relentless tabloid scrutiny and what they describe as a lack of support from the palace drove their decision to leave royal life.

Prince William, Prince of Wales and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex attend the Committal Service for Queen Elizabeth II at St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle on Sept. 19, 2022, in Windsor, England. (Getty Images)

Since stepping away from royal life, Harry and Meghan have publicly aired their grievances in high-profile interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further deepened the fallout within the royal family.

Prince Harry's book "Spare" is displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)

On July 10, the king hosted his younger son and his family for the first time in years in what royal observers viewed as an effort to repair the longstanding rift. The Sussexes secretly met with the king and Queen Camilla at Highgrove House, a country estate west of London, Buckingham Palace confirmed.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, relocated to California in 2020. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl reported that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware that the meeting was taking place." A source close to Charles also told Nicholl the hour-long meeting was "completely cloak-and-dagger, orchestrated by the king."

Meanwhile, William and Kate attended the DMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026 at Guards Polo Club in Windsor. The brothers did not see each other.

Kate Middleton kisses Prince William as she presents the prizes after the DMMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Obviously, King Charles and Prince William are very different characters, sometimes with conflicting temperaments," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "What no one can alter is that William, Kate, and their family are the future of the monarchy. And it is natural for the king, who is battling cancer, to want to see his grandchildren."

British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital there's no feud between Prince William and his father, King Charles. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Fitzwilliams argued that William made his disapproval clear on the day the king and queen saw the Sussexes by being absent from the reunion.

"William is making it clear that he has his own set of principles, his own set of rules about what is right and wrong," Andersen said.

A general view of Buckingham Palace in London, England, on July 6, 2026. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

"He feels Harry has violated those rules one too many times. It's not entirely personal. William has a strong sense of duty when it comes not only to his family but also to his country and his family's place in history. He feels Harry has shot the royal family's reputation full of holes. And for what? To become a SoCal influencer?"

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the last time the brothers spoke was in 2022 during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral. (Dominic Lipinski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"William feels Harry has betrayed not only the current generation of royals but also past generations, including their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, and future generations," Andersen added.

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that while reports of a fracture between Charles and William are overstated, the two are far from aligned on how to deal with Harry. Whether father and son can find common ground on Harry remains to be seen.

From left: Prince William, Prince of Wales, King Charles III and Queen Camilla attend the Thistle Service at St. Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, Scotland on July 1, 2026. (Aaron Chown/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"Prince William is no fool," Fordwich said. "Every time his zero-tolerance approach is proven correct, his influence increases."

Prince Harry attends the Time100 Sports Gala at Pier Sixty on July 16, 2026, in New York City. (WWD via Getty Images)

In May 2025, Harry told the BBC he would like to reconcile with his family.

"There's no point in continuing to fight anymore."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Carly Simon reveals the common condition that masked her Parkinson's diagnosis
excerpt:
Dr. Guy Schwartz, a neurologist with Stony Brook Medicine in New York, describes how symptoms can overlap across the two conditions.

Singer Carly Simon has revealed that her Parkinson's disease was i...
body_text:
Dr. Guy Schwartz, a neurologist with Stony Brook Medicine in New York, describes how symptoms can overlap across the two conditions.

Singer Carly Simon has revealed that her Parkinson's disease was initially mistaken for arthritis, highlighting how the two conditions can share similar symptoms, particularly in the early stages.

"My health issues began with arthritis in both knees and one hip. I had all three joints replaced, and at first, I thought the difficulty I was having walking was simply part of the long recovery process," Simon said in a statement shared with multiple media outlets on July 27.

"Eventually, there were periods when I could not walk without considerable help. My family and I knew that something more was going on. After an extensive evaluation at Mayo Clinic, I was diagnosed with Parkinson's."

'YOU'RE SO VAIN' SINGER CARLY SIMON SAYS PARKINSON'S AND CANCER DIAGNOSES KEPT HER FROM PUBLIC EYE

Arthritis is far more common than Parkinson's disease, affecting nearly 60 million U.S. adults compared with about 1.1 million Americans living with Parkinson's, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Even so, about 90,000 Americans are diagnosed with Parkinson's disease each year, making it a relatively common neurological disorder despite being far less prevalent than arthritis.

Singer Carly Simon (pictured in 2019) has revealed that her Parkinson's disease was initially mistaken for arthritis, highlighting how the two conditions can share similar symptoms, particularly in the early stages. (Getty Images)

Arthritis primarily affects the joints and connective tissues, causing pain, inflammation, stiffness and structural damage, per the CDC. The most common types are osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear of cartilage) and rheumatoid arthritis (an autoimmune disease).

Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disorder that mainly affects the brain and nervous system, according to the National Institute on Aging (NIA). Dopamine-producing nerve cells in the brain gradually die or become impaired, affecting movement.

HOW EATING HABITS COULD INFLUENCE PARKINSON’S DISEASE RISK, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

Although the conditions can share mobility problems, arthritis is typically driven by painful joint inflammation, while Parkinson's primarily affects movement through changes in the brain, according to Dr. Guy Schwartz, a neurologist with Stony Brook Medicine in New York.

"Parkinson's disease can sometimes be misdiagnosed as arthritis, and vice versa," Schwartz, who specializes in Parkinson's disease, told Fox News Digital. "The one main symptom that they share is difficulty with walking — some kind of impediment, limitation or disability."

Arthritis is far more common than Parkinson's disease, affecting nearly 60 million U.S. adults compared with about 1.1 million Americans living with Parkinson's, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (iStock)

While arthritis and Parkinson's are fundamentally different diseases, health experts say they can share the following symptoms that can make diagnosis difficult.

EARLY PARKINSON’S WARNING SIGNS MAY BE HIDING IN THE GUT, STUDY FINDS

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The two conditions can also occur in the same person, Schwartz noted, since both become more common with age. "I've definitely been challenged by individuals who come to me with these symptoms," he said. "Sometimes the examination is confounded by significant arthritis."

The two conditions can be especially difficult to distinguish because both are largely diagnosed based on a patient's symptoms and physical examination rather than one definitive test. (iStock)

While many people may connect Parkinson’s with tremors, early signs of the disease usually include stiffness, slowness and changes in gait.

In older adults who have been diagnosed with arthritis or have had joint replacements, those same symptoms can easily be attributed to joint disease or surgical recovery.

Some Parkinson’s symptoms are not typically seen in arthritis cases. People who experience the following signs should consult a neurologist, according to the Parkinson's Foundation.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"It's not unusual for there to be misdiagnoses."

While tremor is often considered a hallmark symptom, Schwartz cautioned that it isn't always present. "About a third of individuals with Parkinson's disease do not have a tremor," he said. "That's when the diagnosis becomes more challenging."

"In Parkinson's disease, dexterity becomes compromised because of slowness and stiffness," the expert added. "In arthritis, it's more of a mechanical issue, where the joints don't allow full range of motion."

The two conditions can be especially difficult to distinguish because both are largely diagnosed based on a patient's symptoms and physical examination rather than one definitive test, according to Schwartz.

There is no single blood test or imaging scan that can definitively confirm Parkinson’s, as "very few things in medicine are 100%," he said.

However, newer diagnostic tools have emerged, including specialized imaging and skin biopsy testing. "We're still learning," the neurologist said, adding that a blood test may be on the horizon.

While many people may connect Parkinson’s with tremors, early signs of the disease usually include stiffness, slowness and changes in gait. (iStock)

For now, diagnoses are made based on the following factors, per the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS).

Schwartz emphasized that early diagnostic uncertainty is not uncommon. "It's not unusual for there to be misdiagnoses," he said. "Sometimes seeing a patient over time helps — eventually the disease declares itself, and then it's easier to make the diagnosis."

Anyone experiencing persistent walking difficulties, stiffness or other symptoms that don't seem fully explained by arthritis should discuss them with a healthcare provider, who can determine whether a neurological evaluation is appropriate.

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: NEWT GINGRICH: Want to reform Medicaid? Accountability is the way forward
excerpt: CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz spoke about Medicaid fraud, saying some blue states have made it a "feature" and criticizing California Gov. Gavin Newsom over his handling of fraud in his state. (Cred...
body_text:
CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz spoke about Medicaid fraud, saying some blue states have made it a "feature" and criticizing California Gov. Gavin Newsom over his handling of fraud in his state. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Thirty years ago this summer, Congress passed the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act. Welfare reform succeeded because it recognized a simple but powerful truth: Public programs work best when they reward responsibility, accountability, and innovation.

States make better decisions when they have both authority and responsibility for the results. By giving governors greater flexibility while also making them more accountable for the outcomes, we encouraged states to rethink old assumptions, experiment with new approaches, and become better stewards of taxpayer dollars. Good intentions alone do not produce good government. Incentives matter.

TRUMP'S WAR ON FRAUD EXPANDS AS TREASURY LAUNCHES NEW SITE WITH WHISTLEBLOWER INCENTIVES

Since returning to office, President Donald Trump has made rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse a hallmark of his administration. Early in that effort, Elon Musk remarked that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) was "where the big money fraud is happening." He was right. Few areas deserve more scrutiny than Medicaid, which involves hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars and the nation’s largest federal-state partnership.

CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz has made strengthening Medicaid program integrity a national priority, launching a 50-state initiative to improve provider oversight while expanding efforts to combat waste, fraud, and abuse across a range of healthcare services.

Those investigations deserve praise. But they also reveal something much larger than misconduct by a handful of providers.

TRUMP TRIES TO CUT BLUE-STATE MEDICAID FRAUD AND SAVE MORE GREEN

The real challenge is not simply fraud. It is that Medicaid's current financing structure often creates incentives that make waste, fraud, and abuse more likely while making sustained, effective oversight more difficult.

Human nature is predictable. Whenever government creates a system involving hundreds of billions of dollars, services that are difficult to measure, and payment models that reward volume, some people will exploit it. But the larger problem is program design. Unlike welfare after the 1996 reforms, Medicaid remains a joint federal-state program in which Washington pays a substantial share of additional dollars states spend. States therefore do not bear the full fiscal consequences of program growth, even while facing intense political pressure from provider organizations, advocacy groups, and local employers whenever stronger oversight is proposed.

The result is a predictable imbalance. Everyone supports eliminating fraud in theory. The political incentives to aggressively pursue it are often much weaker in practice.

MEDICAID FRAUD FEARS GROW AMID MASSIVE RED STATE BILLING SPIKE IN SECTOR THAT ALSO PLAGUED MINNESOTA

Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) therapy illustrates how this plays out in practice.

Federal law required Medicaid coverage of ABA beginning in 2014, and spending has grown dramatically across the country. Most providers are dedicated professionals who are helping children with autism develop critical skills and lead more independent lives. Families deserve access to these services.

But the combination of rapidly growing spending, payment based on billable hours, and inconsistent oversight has also made ABA vulnerable to waste, fraud, and abuse. Federal investigators have uncovered improper billing. Whistleblowers have described business practices that rewarded maximizing billable services rather than improving patient outcomes. In some cases, investigators have even uncovered disturbing allegations of abuse against vulnerable children.

This does not mean ABA is the problem. It means incentives matter.

The goal is not to spend less on children with autism. It is to make sure every dollar intended to help those children reaches them.

The same incentive problems have surfaced in other parts of Medicaid as well, including hospice care, home health services, and medical equipment. These are different providers, different services, but the same underlying lesson: When accountability fails to keep pace with spending, bad actors eventually find ways to exploit the system.

Georgia illustrates another dimension of the challenge. The Department of Community Health and the state’s Medicaid-managed care organizations have moved to strengthen oversight of ABA services. Yet, those efforts have faced significant political resistance from legislators and provider groups concerned about funding and access. Protecting access and protecting accountability, however, are not competing goals. Families deserve both.

State legislatures should support — not undermine — the efforts of Medicaid agencies, managed care organizations, and the Trump administration to strengthen program integrity. Honest providers should welcome stronger oversight because it protects both vulnerable families and the reputation of those delivering high-quality care.

Thirty years ago, welfare reform demonstrated that lasting public policy improvements begin by aligning incentives with the public interest. Medicaid needs the same lesson today.

Government works best when its rules reward responsibility rather than dependency, accountability rather than complacency, and results rather than spending for its own sake. Thirty years after welfare reform, this lesson remains every bit as important as it was in 1996. If we want to reduce Medicaid waste, fraud, and abuse, we must build a system with incentives that make integrity the easiest path — not the hardest.

Gingrich 360 consults with various organizations in the healthcare industry which would be impacted by the policy reforms described in this column.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM NEWT GINGRICH

Newt Gingrich was Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives from 1995-1999 and a candidate for the 2012 Republican presidential nomination. He is chairman of Gingrich 360.

title: 'Son of Sam' Berkowitz doesn't 'trust the media' 50 years after terrorizing city with letters to newspaper
excerpt: Jonathan Fahey, former DHS deputy assistant secretary, weighs in on anti-ICE protests in Brooklyn that blocked hospital entrances, condemning NYC Mayor Mamdani's reaction. Fahey also blasts proposed N...
body_text:
Jonathan Fahey, former DHS deputy assistant secretary, weighs in on anti-ICE protests in Brooklyn that blocked hospital entrances, condemning NYC Mayor Mamdani's reaction. Fahey also blasts proposed New York bills that could release violent criminals, including serial killers like David Berkowitz, the "Son of Sam," due to the "elder parole bill" for individuals aged 55+. These controversial bills raise serious public safety concerns statewide.

"Son of Sam" David Berkowitz, New York's infamous .44-caliber killer who taunted the public with letters to the legendary columnist Jimmy Breslin, says he no longer trusts the media 50 years after kicking off his killing spree.

Berkowitz's first victim, 18-year-old Donna Lauria, was shot and killed while getting out of an Oldsmobile in the Bronx on July 29, 1976.

Through an intermediary, "Lighter Side of True Crime" podcaster Keith Rovere, Berkowitz declined an interview request for this story.

UNEARTHED 'SON OF SAM' PRISON TAPES REVEAL CHILLING DETAILS ABOUT SERIAL KILLER DAVID BERKOWITZ

Police mugshot showing the front view and profile of convicted New York City serial killer David Berkowitz, known as the "Son of Sam." (Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

"I don't trust the media," he wrote to Rovere in a letter shared with Fox News Digital. "They will twist and distort whatever I say. Even recently they twisted my words concerning some changes in New York's parole law which, in this instant, had nothing to do with me."

New York lawmakers are mulling over bills that would create an elder parole system and abolish life without parole.

"They riled up a victim with a false information and a distortion, thus creating the victim needless grief and pain, and more," he wrote. "This was not the first time. If the media wishes to know what I've been doing with my life, all they have to do is visit the website which has probably over a thousand pages of my prison writings and various videos, interviews and more, which viewers could easily access. Ariseandshine.org."

Police officers escort American accused (and ultimately convicted) serial killer David Berkowitz (left), known as the Son of Sam, into the 84th precinct station, New York, New York, Aug. 10, 1977.  (Robert R. McElroy/Getty Images)

NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN

In May, Berkowitz skipped a parole hearing and wrote in a letter to the New York Post that he wasn't trying to get out.

"The only place I’m looking forward to going, is to heaven to be with the Lord," the outlet quoted him as writing.

The Post asked "Son of Sam" survivor Robert Violante, 68, for a reaction:

"I sincerely doubt he is going to heaven," he said. "He is lucky he is not already in hell."

FAMILY OF SHOOTING SURVIVOR SAYS 'DEFAMATORY' TRUE-CRIME DOC PAINTED OLYMPIC EQUESTRIAN SHOOTER AS REAL VICTIM

Donna Lauria, first victim of David Berkowitz. (NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)

Violente survived a gunshot wound to the head on July 31, 1977. His date, 20-year-old Stacy Moskowitz, did not. She was Berkowitz's final victim.

That was a year and two days after the first murder — Lauria's.

Her friend and the car's owner, 19-year-old Jody Valenti, was wounded but survived.

New York City saw a cool night, with lows in the 60s, after clouds and rain rolled in to break up scorching temperatures from the day before, according to Almanac.com. The Mets lost in extra innings to the Pittsburgh Pirates, 2-1. The Yankees had a day off after toppling the Boston Red Sox, 6-4.

LUIGI MANGIONE'S EMOTIONAL DISTURBANCE DEFENSE MAY HAVE HUGE IMPACT IN HIS OTHER CASE: LAWYER

A police officer leans over in the front seat of Robert Violante's car on service road of Shore Parkway across the street from a park between Bay 14th and 16th streets in Brooklyn. Violante and his date, Stacy Moskowitz, both 20, became the 12th and 13h victims of the "Son of Sam" as they sat in a car at 2:35 a.m. Moskowitz later died from her injuries. Violante lost an eye but survived. (Dan Godfrey/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)

The shooting would become known as the first of what police initially called the .44-caliber killings. They terrified New Yorkers for a year. Young couples shied away from sitting in parked cars. Young women cut and dyed their hair, believing that the killer was targeting people with long, dark locks.

Valenti provided a crucial description of her attacker — a White male in his 30s with curly dark hair.

Marielena Maddalena studies sketch of "Son of Sam" at Sheepshead photo store in Brooklyn. (Charles Frattini/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)

Still, it took months before police pieced together a pattern now known as the "Son of Sam" murders, when ballistic evidence linked the same gun to the July shooting and four more.

At that point, it was March 8, 1977, and Berkowitz had killed three and injured four.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

In the lead-up to the one-year mark, he sent a note to the former New York columnist Jimmy Breslin, whom he had been taunting with letters signed, "Son of Sam."

"Tell me, Jim, what will you have for July Twenty-Ninth?" he wrote to Breslin, according to one of his 1977 Daily News columns. "You can forget about me if you like because I don’t care for publicity. However, you must not forget Donna Lauria and you cannot let the people forget her, either. She was a very sweet girl but Sam’s a thirsty lad and he won’t let me stop killing until he gets his fill of blood."

This note was found by police in the 1970 Ford Galaxy owned by David Berkowitz when they arrested him, late Aug. 10, 1977, as he sat in the car in front of his Yonkers, New York home. It is written in the style of the .44 caliber killer.  (Getty Images)

He went on to warn that while he'd been quiet, he hadn't been inactive.

"I am still here," he wrote. "Like a spirit roaming in the night. Thirsty, hungry, seldom stopping to rest; anxious to please Sam. I love my work."

Berkowitz's letters showed the killer was following news coverage of the case, mocked police and cemented the "Son of Sam" moniker in place of the .44-caliber killer.

"I believe Berkowitz was focused on revenge, jealousy and attention, along with the feeling of power," said John Kelly, a criminal profiler and the president of STALK Inc. "He felt he was unlovable and acted out his rage on couples who could share a romantic emotional moment. Something he felt he could never have."

Still crying in rage, Danny Carrique leaves court in Brooklyn, New York, with his friend, Neysa Moskowitz, the mother of David Berkowitz murder victim, Stacy Moskowitz, on May 23, 1978. (Dan Jacino / New York Daily News via Getty Images)

Though the night of July 29 came and went without a new victim, another shooting two days later proved key to Berkowitz's arrest. Investigators, looking for suspicious vehicles in the area, found a parking ticket issued nearby. That led police to his door in Yonkers. He was arrested on Aug. 10, 1977.

By then, the shootings had killed six and injured seven.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

When searching his house, detectives found evidence that he had been closely following other crimes as well.

According to an FBI publication from July 1980, Berkowitz kept notes on hundreds of fires near New York City in the years before his arrest. Police found handwritten notes about 1,411 incidents, with details including the weather, street name and firefighters' response.

"He's one of the few serial killers that I know that I believe has completely changed his ways," said Rovere, a former prison pastor and the host of the "Lighter Side of True Crime" podcast who has been trading letters with Berkowitz for years.

Serving a life prison sentence, Berkowitz now claims to be a born-again Christian and calls himself the "Son of Hope." His letters are now signed "Bro[ther] David" or, occasionally, with his full name. Most are typed, no longer handwritten.

He spends some of his time producing illustrated religious pamphlets and posts content on his website and working on his prison ministry.

title: 'They fed him his own ears': Top Republican shares horrifying stories of gang rule in Haiti
excerpt:
Bill Hemmer and Chad Wolf analyze ICE plans to surge arrests of Haitian migrants, focusing on temporary protected status.

Walls full of bullet holes and police in "full armor" were among the sights t...
body_text:
Bill Hemmer and Chad Wolf analyze ICE plans to surge arrests of Haitian migrants, focusing on temporary protected status.

Walls full of bullet holes and police in "full armor" were among the sights that greeted a group of U.S. House lawmakers who recently traveled to Port-au-Prince, Haiti, a city that has been ravaged by gang rule since the July 2021 assassination of its former president.

"The gangs will essentially block the streets with rubble, with debris, they'll dig giant ditches in the road, and so these military and police units can't traverse," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. "Some of these areas are like Afghanistan, and it is probably the poorest place I've ever been through in my life."

Mast led a group of bipartisan members of Congress on a trip to Venezuela and Haiti recently, which he said was the first congressional delegation in either country in a decade.

In Haiti, they were hosted by the country's prime minister, whose palace "a year ago, would have been a war zone," Mast said. "They have been actively working to take back land across the breadth of Port-au-Prince."

REPUBLICAN REP MARÍA ELVIRA SALAZAR DECLARES, 'AFTER CUBA, NICARAGUA IS NEXT'

Police officers patrol a neighborhood amid gang-related violence in downtown Port-au-Prince on April 25, 2023. (Richard Pierrin/AFP via Getty Images)

But while he saw signs of slow improvement thanks to an international coalition of forces as well as a U.S. paramilitary group run by Erik Prince, Mast said the realities of gang violence were ever-present.

A video he was shown, for example, depicted Haitian gang torture of a heavy machinery operator helping police clear gang-made blockages in the city streets.

FIRST TREN DE ARAGUA GANG MEMBER EXTRADITED TO US ON HISTORIC TERRORISM CHARGES APPEARS BEFORE HOUSTON JUDGE

"They took this guy who was this equipment operator, and for working with the police, they kidnapped his family. And then they told him they'll trade his family for him. He turned himself over," Mast said.

"They brutally killed him. I mean it's all on video. They cut off his ears, fed him his own ears...Then they hacked at him for probably at least five minutes with machetes. His limbs looked like a Christmas tree afterwards, with just bone and skin and other things coming off of him, until ultimately they killed him. That is who these gangs are."

And it's not just adult allies of the local police forces suffering from gang violence, according to the Florida Republican. Another chilling incident Mast said he became aware of while in Haiti was the kidnapping of a 6-year-old U.S. citizen by a local gang who he said may have committed sexual crimes against her.

Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., speaks on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on May 21, 2025. (Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters)

MIKE WALTZ, TIM TEBOW LAUNCH EFFORT TO COMBAT ONLINE CHILD EXPLOITATION: 'IT'S HAPPENING IN THEIR BACKYARD'

"There was a 6-year-old American citizen girl. I don't want to say that she was raped, but there were health issues that led to believe that she was also raped, as a 6-year-old girl, by these gangs," Mast said. "It appears as though we were able to secure the release yesterday."

He said there was ultimately an "agreement" on the ransom money the girl's family would pay after she had been held hostage for at least 46 days.

"It appears as though we were able to get an exchange finally made yesterday. But again, it's just another example of who these gangs are and the forces that are being brought to bear, to bring them to heel," Mast said.

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans, and that it was aware of reports of an American child kidnapped for ransom in Haiti but would not provide further details out of respect for the family's privacy.

Beyond the current level of assistance, however, Mast said he doubted there was more the U.S. could do to help the country as a whole.

"This started with political people starting gangs there for their own benefit. And most of the politicians there are beyond guilty of pillaging their own country instead of doing something good for their country. That's how Haiti is in the state that it's in," he said.

Members of the U.S. Congressional Delegation (CODEL) welcomed by Haitian officials during their assessment of the security situation in Haiti. (Courtesy of House Committee on Foreign Affairs)

It comes as thousands of Haitians in the U.S. are facing a potential return to their home country after the Trump administration ended their temporary protected status (TPS) that was first granted after an earthquake in 2010.

Mast argued, however, that the return of those Haitians who did not get permanent residency in those 16 years could potentially help bolster security there.

"One of the big things would be to take the able-bodied males and put them into the police and military, which are actively recruiting, which were so decimated by the TPS taking place in the first place," he said. "All of these people took the chance to say 'Okay, I'm leaving,' and it left their forces that are supposed to protect the country essentially with no forces, which is one of the other parts of how the gangs came to be."

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com
