title: White House teleprompter operator accused over Trump bets no longer in job, official says
excerpt:
Official declines to say whether Gabriel Perez, who allegedly bet on prediction market Kalshi, resigned or was fired

A White House teleprompter operator who reportedly used inside knowledge to make b...
body_text:
Official declines to say whether Gabriel Perez, who allegedly bet on prediction market Kalshi, resigned or was fired

A White House teleprompter operator who reportedly used inside knowledge to make bets about Donald Trump’s speeches on the online prediction market Kalshi is no longer in his post, according to a White House official.

The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly about the personnel matter and spoke on condition of anonymity, said on Tuesday that Gabriel Perez “no longer works in the federal government”.

The official would not say whether Perez resigned or was fired.

The White House confirmed earlier this month that Perez had been placed on unpaid leave after ABC News reported he had used his inside knowledge to win more than $100,000 betting on what the president would say in big speeches, including his State of the Union address earlier this year.

That figure is more than half the $175,000 salary he earned for his teleprompter work, according to White House personnel records.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt had described the reports of the insider trading as “deeply unfortunate and, frankly, a disgrace”.

Robert Denault, Kalshi’s lawyer and head of enforcement, said on X following the ABC News report that the “Kalshi surveillance team promptly flagged, investigated and referred these trades” to the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the body that has regulatory authority over such matters.

His statement did not name Perez, who has operated Trump’s teleprompter since 2016.

The ABC report described suspicious activity on Kalshi’s “Mentions” market, in which users can place bets on phrases and specific words that might be used in public speeches. Kalshi recently began requiring users to disclose their place of employment, and the platform’s policy prohibits betting based on information that users gain because of their job.

Prediction markets, which allow users to place speculative bets on a seemingly endless list of public events and trends, have exploded recently. Trading volume on Kalshi, one of the two largest prediction market trading platforms, soared from $100m last year to $3bn today, according to an estimate cited by CNBC.

Kalshi recently said it would allow users to bet on drug trial results.

The rise in prediction markets has created a major new incentive for insider trading. In April, federal prosecutors indicted Gannon Ken Van Dyke for allegedly betting on the whether former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro would be deposed. Prosecutors say Van Dyke, a US soldier who worked on the operation to remove and extradite Maduro, walked away with $400,000 in earnings.

That same month, Kalshi said it had fined three political candidates who placed bets on their own races. In one case, Mark Moran placed a small bet on whether he would run for office before announcing his bid for a US Senate seat in Virginia as an independent.

The industry’s proponents describe prediction markets as a form of derivatives, a type of contract that allows parties to make bets on the future value of an asset or commodity.

Critics, however, have raised concerns from state authorities who view the industry as little more than unregulated gambling. Minnesota became the first state to ban them entirely in May, but a federal judge temporarily blocked the law before it went into effect.

Trump has defended the prediction markets industry, saying that states should avoid regulating them, leaving the job instead to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

title: Senate confirms Trump ally Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence
excerpt:
At confirmation hearing, Clayton sidestepped questions about 2020 election and declined to say Trump lost

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

The US Senate voted to confirm Jay Clayton...
body_text:
At confirmation hearing, Clayton sidestepped questions about 2020 election and declined to say Trump lost

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

The US Senate voted to confirm Jay Clayton as the director of national intelligence on Tuesday, giving Trump another key ally directing the nation’s intelligence apparatus.

The tally, 51-47, fell along party lines, with all Republicans supporting his nomination and all Democrats opposing it.

Clayton, currently the US attorney for the southern district of New York, will replace Bill Pulte, a staunch Trump loyalist who had been temporarily serving in the role since June. Trump’s first director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned earlier this year. Clayton served as the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) during Trump’s first term.

During his confirmation hearing on 15 July, Clayton sidestepped several questions about the 2020 election and declined to say that Trump lost it.

During an interview on CNBC in June, Clayton also suggested there was something amiss about the long period California takes to count ballots. “We had a problem, a deep problem with voting in America,” he said on the network. “On the integrity side, we’re doing an absolutely terrible job, and the American people are right to question it.” Clayton also would not say during his confirmation hearing whether voter fraud was a problem in American elections, even though several studies have shown it is exceedingly rare.

His office also issued widely-criticized subpoenas to New York Times journalists over their reporting on security concerns around Trump’s Air Force One airplane that was a gift from Qatar. The government abruptly withdrew those subpoenas during a court hearing in which a federal judge pressed an attorney from Clayton’s office about errors and irregularities in the subpoenas.

While Democrats saw Clayton as a more preferable pick than Pulte, who has assisted in executing some of Trump’s sloppy and ugly acts of political retribution, including the criminal prosecution of Letitia James and a ham-handed effort to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve board of governors. Pulte was also leading the office of the director of national intelligence earlier this month when Trump declassified and released intelligence in support of false claims about the 2020 election. Pulte oversaw several rounds of layoffs at the agency.

But Clayton’s contentious hearing earlier this month cost him bipartisan backing. Before the vote, the senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, spoke in opposition to the nomination, warning that Clayton was unqualified and would act as the president’s “election conspiracy win”.

title: FCC bans humanoid robots from China, citing ‘unacceptable risks’
excerpt:
Move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US

The Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on humanoid robots from China on Tuesday,...
body_text:
Move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US

The Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on humanoid robots from China on Tuesday, saying that the technology poses “unacceptable risks” to the country’s national security. The move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US.

The FCC defines the banned robots as “advanced robotic devices”, which include humanoids and animal-like quadrupeds.

“Advanced robotic devices collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots,” FCC officials wrote in their determination of the threat posed by robots.

In addition to the humanoid robots, the FCC also barred connected power inverters, which enable renewable energy sources and batteries to connect to grids and datacenter equipment.

The restrictions point to the Trump administration’s goal of elevating technology made in the US, along with driving firms to shift manufacturing to be done locally.

“The President has made clear that the United States must have independent and secure supply chains for critical and emerging technologies like robotic devices and power inverters,” an ⁠administration official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

“Economic security is national security, and the Trump administration continues to implement a nuanced and multi-faceted policy agenda to reindustrialize America,” he added.

The restrictions apply only to robot and inverter models that have not yet been released. However, the FCC has the authority to ‌revoke authorizations for sales of models that have already been authorized for purchase in the US.

Humanoid robots, topped with ‌AI-enabled “brains”, are forecast by some analysts for broad adoption in ‌consumer and industrial arenas, while explosive datacenter construction in the US will depend on reliable sources of inverters.

China is the world’s largest maker of inverters, led by Sungrow Power Supply and Huawei, which are already heavily sanctioned by the US.

The Chinese ​embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Yemen’s Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia oil tanker
excerpt:
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group says it has fired ballistic missiles at a Saudi oil tanker, more than a week after imposing a naval blockade on Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.

In a post on X, Yahya S...
body_text:
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group says it has fired ballistic missiles at a Saudi oil tanker, more than a week after imposing a naval blockade on Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.

In a post on X, Yahya Saree, the Houthi military spokesman, said the group had “carried out a military operation targeting the Saudi oil tanker (NCC GHAZAL) for violating the maritime navigation ban” that the group had imposed on Saudi vessels.

He added that the group had used several ballistic missiles and forced the vessel to retreat.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a maritime security monitor, said a tanker reported an explosion while transiting the Red Sea, adding that the crew is safe and no environmental damage was reported.

The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014 and have fought the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which Saudi Arabia backs, for more than a decade.

On July 20, the Houthis announced their maritime blockade, accusing Saudi leaders of imposing “an unjust and oppressive siege” on Yemen for nearly 12 years, “plundering our resources and imposing a comprehensive blockade”.

It went on to affirm “the right of our great people to respond to the blockade with a blockade”.

The Houthis have also claimed an attack on two Saudi oil tankers transiting the Red Sea last week.

“We targeted two Saudi oil tankers, named Encelia and Layla, for their violation of the blockade decision issued by the armed forces,” Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on July 22.

The Saudi Press Agency reported that the Encelia had been hit, citing an official source at Saudi Arabia’s Transport General Authority who said all crew members were safe.

The Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden is one of the world’s most important shipping routes, including for oil exports.

Between Yemen to the northeast and Djibouti and Eritrea in the Horn of Africa to the southwest, the strait is just 29km (18 miles) at its narrowest point, limiting traffic to two channels for inbound and outbound vessels heading to the Suez Canal.

In 2024, about 4.1 billion barrels of crude oil and refined petroleum products passed through the strait – about 5 percent of the global total.

title: Dems reject Trump’s top spy pick after demanding replacement, leaving counter-terror tool in air
excerpt: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Jay Clayton's Senate confirmation hearing as he looks to become the next director of national intelligence. Pergram also reports Hous...
body_text:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Jay Clayton's Senate confirmation hearing as he looks to become the next director of national intelligence. Pergram also reports House Republicans are linking the SAVE America Act to a State Department funding bill following the expiration of the FISA program.

Senate Democrats demanded a new, experienced person to lead the nation’s spy agencies, but when given the chance, they rejected President Donald Trump’s latest pick.

Still, their resistance was not enough to stop Republicans from confirming Jay Clayton to be the next Director of National Intelligence (DNI) to replace former DNI Tulsi Gabbard. Clayton, who was tapped to be the top prosecutor in Manhattan last year, was confirmed on a party line vote Tuesday.

He will replace acting DNI and Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte, whose interim appointment prompted Senate Democrats to demand an immediate, permanent replacement over fears that Pulte would weaponize the nation’s 18 intelligence agencies or try to dismantle them.

SENATE CLEARS WAY FOR TRUMP'S TOP SPY AS KEY ANTI-TERROR PROGRAM REMAINS IN LIMBO

Jay Clayton, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), during the Bloomberg Global Credit Forum in New York, US, on Wednesday, June 3, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Clayton’s confirmation was thought to be a means to an end for the ongoing standoff over Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), a tool that has been used to thwart several terror plots, including a planned mass-casualty event at a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna, Austria.

However, they changed their tune when it came time to vote, and after a contentious confirmation hearing where only Republicans voted to send him to the Senate floor.

"As Senate Republicans move to once again confirm an inexperienced and unqualified nominee to a position of massive national security consequence for years to come, one thing remains clear — this type of politicized leadership will only make Americans less safe," Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., said in a statement.

Boiled down, the Section 702 program allows the U.S. government to collect intelligence on foreigners abroad who are using U.S. communication systems, and it serves as a major part of Trump’s daily intelligence briefing.

LAWMAKERS SCRAMBLE AFTER TRUMP DERAILS BID TO REVIVE KEY COUNTERTERRORISM TOOL DAYS AFTER FBI THWARTS UFC PLOT

But it also sweeps up communications from Americans who are talking to foreign suspects — a key issue that threatened reauthorization among privacy hawks in both parties well before Pulte’s appointment and Clayton’s subsequent nomination.

The program expired, however, last month in response to Pulte’s appointment, despite warnings from Republicans that allowing Section 702 to go dark could have dire national security consequences.

And Clayton’s confirmation, for now, does not appear to be breaking through the partisan logjam. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., and the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, told Fox News Digital that the pressure wasn’t on to reauthorize FISA.

"Democrats have refused to pass a bipartisan FISA bill until a new DNI is confirmed," a spokesperson for Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told Fox News Digital. "Now that Jay Clayton is confirmed, it’s time for them to stop playing politics with national security and put up the votes to give our intelligence community the tools it needs to keep this country safe."

TRUMP'S DNI PICK CLEARS KEY HURDLE, REVIVING PATH FOR NATION'S TOP ANTI-TERROR SURVEILLANCE PROGRAM

Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., arrives to the Capitol Visitor Center for a briefing about Iran on Tuesday, February 24, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"You know … we don't have the immediate time pressure because the communication providers are still cooperating," Warner said.

Before the deadline to reauthorize, lawmakers had differing trains of thought on what would exactly happen should it go completely dark. Some argued that it would slowly draw down, given that FISA courts had already authorized continued intelligence gathering until 2027.

Others worried that telecommunications giants, like Google, would ignore agreements without explicit authorization from Congress.

But, as Warner noted, the latter isn’t happening.

Still, it leaves Clayton and the intelligence community on a murky path forward in the months ahead. And there’s not much time left on the Senate’s calendar to tackle the issue. The upper chamber is slated to leave Washington after the first week of August, and won’t return until early September. From there, keeping the government open will be a top priority for Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: UK faces ‘very difficult trade-offs’ in budget because of Iran war, say analysts
excerpt:
Leading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’

Andy Burnham has been warned by a leading thinktank of “very difficult trade-offs in the next...
body_text:
Leading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’

Andy Burnham has been warned by a leading thinktank of “very difficult trade-offs in the next autumn budget” if the Iran war keeps oil prices and inflation high.

The National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) said the new prime minister faced a “challenging inheritance” and his plans to revamp public services would meet severe pressure from persistently higher prices.

With oil prices having briefly gone back above $100 a barrel, and the strait of Hormuz all but closed since March, the thinktank said it expected inflation to rise to 3.8% over the next seven months, forcing the chancellor, John Healey, to find an extra £24bn by the end of the decade to maintain services and real-terms welfare payments.

The thinktank said it had cut its forecast for the chancellor’s spending headroom in the budget from just over £7bn to nearer £3bn. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the government’s independent forecaster, estimated in March that the Treasury had about £22bn of spare capacity above existing spending commitments.

Underscoring the cost of the Middle East conflict to the UK, the NIESR said the economy would grow at a slower pace this year and in 2027 as a result of higher energy prices and the spillover effects from uncertainty created by the on-off war.

It said a downgrade of growth to 1.1% this year and the same slow pace next year meant the UK would suffer £28bn in lost growth over two years compared with forecasts in January.

David Aikman, the institute’s director, said Burnham faced “a challenging inheritance” with spending “eroded by inflation”, coupled with the highest borrowing costs in the G7, new spending demands and cost-of-living pressures.

He said there would be a temptation to ease the strain on the public finances and pay for new initiatives by raising the level of borrowing.

Aikman said this would be a mistake and only cause further strife in later years, especially when another health or economic shock happened.

He added: “New commitments on defence or household support should be funded through taxation or savings elsewhere, not through further borrowing. Rebuilding the capacity to absorb future shocks will require a determined attempt to bring debt down.”

Burnham has made several announcements since becoming PM last week, including a pledge to improve adult social care, with an estimated £18.5bn bill for providing an NHS-style system free at the point of use by 2035.

He has also singled out for support the 1 million young people classified as not in education, employment or training (Neets), with more extensive mental health services and a revamp of the education system.

The NIESR said the government’s total debt, which has reached almost £3tn, or 95% of annual national income, was likely to rise again if the chancellor used borrowing to boost public spending.

The institute has proved to be one of the gloomier forecasters, predicting significant economic shocks that proved more muted.

Stephen Millard, the head of the thinktank’s macroeconomic forecasting, said the UK economy had proved to be “surprisingly resilient” in the first half of this year “but a slowdown is still to come”.

He added: “Even if peace is restored relatively quickly in the Middle East, inflation will still rise and the new chancellor will need to make some difficult decisions with respect to how to fund the latest policy announcements, from cuts to VAT on electricity and business rates for pubs, to the £2 bus fare cap.”

Millard said tax changes should be given priority over increases in existing taxes.

He said he supported the introduction of a land value tax to replace council tax and stamp duty on home sales. He said the government should also phase out the many exemptions and discounts that affect VAT, including those on energy and children’s clothes.

There was further scope to tackle tax avoidance by wealthy individuals and companies, he added.

Millard said the latest quarterly economic outlook showed the chancellor would need to cope with a 4% real spending squeeze by the end of the decade – equating to about £24bn in 2023 prices.

He said higher and more persistent inflation would create “very difficult trade-offs in the next autumn budget”.

The NIESR expects inflation to average 3.1% in 2026, peaking at 3.8% in February 2027 after energy price cap adjustments.

It said it would take until early 2029 to fall back to the Bank of England’s 2% target, rather than 2028 as previously forecast.

Bank of England officials meet on Thursday. Financial markets expect them to hold interest rates steady before raising them to 4% later in the year.

title: Polls close in Georgia as voters decide successor in special election
excerpt:
Fox News anchor Bill Hemmer reports on Georgia’s 2026 gubernatorial primary and Trump-backed candidate Ed Gallrein's defeat of Thomas Massie in Kentucky on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

The polls have c...
body_text:
Fox News anchor Bill Hemmer reports on Georgia’s 2026 gubernatorial primary and Trump-backed candidate Ed Gallrein's defeat of Thomas Massie in Kentucky on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

The polls have closed in Georgia as two races in politically disparate parts of the country set the stage for one of the most unusual split-screen election days of the year on Tuesday.

Rep. David Scott’s death in April at age 80 created a vacancy in a heavily blue district encompassing the southern and eastern Atlanta suburbs of Stockbridge, Conyers and Snellville.

With the general election ballot already decided, Tuesday’s contest will determine who will finish out Scott’s term. Scott was notably related by marriage to Braves slugger Hank Aaron.

Across the country in South Dakota, Republicans vying for the Mount Rushmore State’s safely red governor’s seat have created the state's first gubernatorial runoff between incumbent Gov. Larry Rhoden and self-made millionaire bitcoin investor Toby Doeden.

TRUMP’S GOP CLOUT FACES ARIZONA TEST WITH HOUSE MAJORITY, GOVERNOR’S RACE AT STAKE

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, left; the late Rep. David Scott, D-Ga., right. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images; Bill Clark/Getty Images)

Rhoden originally took the reins in Pierre after President Donald Trump chose former Gov. Kristi Noem to be Homeland Security secretary in his second term. He was unable to garner enough support in the June primary to secure the nomination outright in his first statewide election as governor.

South Dakota’s runoff is expected to be a classic establishment-versus-outsider race, with Rhoden heavily favored in the polls but Doeden hoping for a Sioux Falls-fueled upset.

Minnehaha County, home to Sioux Falls, is a key county to watch Tuesday after helping propel Doeden to a first-place finish in the June primary.

WATCH: LAWMAKERS REVEAL WHERE THEY STAND ON CONGRESSIONAL TERM LIMITS AFTER RECENT HEALTH SCARES

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks with the press during Education Secretary Linda McMahon’s "Returning Education to the States" tour on April 8, 2026, at McCrossan Boys Ranch in Sioux Falls, S.D. (Samantha Laurey / Argus Leader / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

Pennington County, on the state’s western side, will also be closely watched after contributing to Doeden’s top finish in June.

In contrast to what is expected in Scott’s district in November, Republicans are heavily favored because South Dakota has not elected a Democratic governor since the 1970s.

Then-Gov. Richard Kneip served nearly two terms before President Jimmy Carter nominated him as ambassador to Singapore. Gov. Harvey Wollman completed the final six months of Kneip’s term, and is the state’s last Democrat to hold the office.

EX-NFL LINEBACKER POISED TO RETURN TO CONGRESS AFTER TEXAS RUNOFF WIN WITH JASMINE CROCKETT ENDORSEMENT

Shifting back to the Deep South, Georgia Democrats are expected to hold Scott’s seat in the fall by a wide margin.

Efforts to replace Scott grew in recent months, particularly among the party's progressive wing, as the 12-term, often-combative lawmaker drew increasing frustration from Democrats.

FROM LOCKER ROOMS TO CONGRESS, JAY FEELY THE LATEST ATHLETE SEEKING TO TAKE LESSONS ON LEADERSHIP TO CAPITOL HILL

A sign welcomes travelers to the Peach State at the I-20 East Welcome Center near Tallapoosa, Georgia, on October 3, 2022. (Charlie Creitz)

Last year, Scott made waves in Washington media when he shouted expletives at a Politico photographer as he was wheeled through the Capitol by staff.

"Who gave you the right to take my picture, a--hole," Scott shouted at photographer Francis Chung in late 2025.

That demeanor was similar to what led Everton Blair to launch his primary bid against Scott, in what his campaign page calls a "voice for a new generation."

Blair previously told Fox News Digital it was a run-in with Scott at a Gwinnett County town hall, where the lawmaker gave insufficient answers to questions and then reportedly became confrontational, that led him to explore a bid.

Blair had said he would "love to just hear a little bit more of the congressional and legislative strategy, congressman, that you have for this administration, particularly as it pertains to safeguarding federal funds," according to Semafor, when Scott replied "hold on," before becoming agitated:

"I don’t know who sent y’all, but we got these folks here who are providing answers. And I’m doing this. That’s what I’m doing," Scott said, according to the outlet.

Blair responded by launching a primary bid, while remarking to Fox News Digital at the time that two other elderly Democratic members had recently died in office "at a time when every vote counts."

The wave of millennial candidates seeking to replace aging Democrats was at the time dubbed the "Biden effect" — Democratic lawmakers retiring or facing potential primary challenges following the octogenarian Delawarean’s disastrous debate performance, which led to his decision to step aside for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

"Change can’t wait, and Democrats need a new bench of leaders who are committed to solving real problems for working people," Blair said in a previous press release.

Meanwhile, Scott’s daughter is hoping to replace her late father in Congress, remarking that she wants to continue his legacy.

"That is my thing, is to finish out his year strongly, make sure that this money gets down to the district, and just make sure the 13th district is taken care of, constituency-wise, and making sure the projects go into finalization," she told the Georgia Recorder, while adding she would retain her father’s staff locally and at the Capitol for added stability.

"[W]hen he first got into politics, I wasn’t even born, so I ran for some type of office or campaign every two years of my life, so this is just my norm, I’m just picking up where we left off with him," she told the outlet.

A third candidate, former Mississippi judge Carlos Moore, also criticized Rep. Scott’s tenure, telling the Mississippi Free Press he wants to be a "leader who actually shows up."

Moore had been suspended from the bench for one year in 2024 after a bar tribunal found he mishandled a wrongful death settlement, according to the outlet.

When asked by the press about the infraction, he pointed to Trump’s 34-count indictment in New York. He also pledged, if elected, to be a leader who understands "how to defend our democracy and Constitution" from the president.

The winner of Tuesday’s special elections will serve only until January.

Georgia state Rep. Jasmine Clark, D-Tucker, won the Democratic nomination for the full term earlier this year and is heavily favored against Republican Air Force veteran Jonathan Chavez in November. Trump lost the district by about 43 points in 2024.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Raiders new head coach Klint Kubiak names Kirk Cousins starting QB over No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza
excerpt: Patrick Mahomes was cleared to fully participate in Kansas City Chiefs training camp. Danny Parkins, Eric Mangini, and Greg Jennings discuss the expectations for the Chiefs and Mahomes this season, an...
body_text:
Patrick Mahomes was cleared to fully participate in Kansas City Chiefs training camp. Danny Parkins, Eric Mangini, and Greg Jennings discuss the expectations for the Chiefs and Mahomes this season, and if Fernando Mendoza should start for the Las Vegas Raiders week 1.

It may have been his plan all along heading into his first year as the Las Vegas Raiders head coach, but Klint Kubiak confirmed who his starting quarterback will be to begin training camp this week.

It’s veteran Kirk Cousins – not Fernando Mendoza, the Raiders’ No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft.

"When we go out to practice tomorrow, Kirk Cousins in the starting quarterback. He’s the guy, and he’s going to get a ton of reps. He deserves them because he’s played really good football," Kubiak told the press, via NFL.com. "But I want Fernando and I want Aidan [O’Connell] to push him."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Kirk Cousins of the Las Vegas Raiders practices during an OTA offseason workout at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on June 3, 2026, in Henderson, Nev. (Getty Images)

Fans and media weren’t waiting anxiously for Kubiak’s decision, as he’s been straightforward with his thoughts after taking over as head coach following a Super Bowl-winning season as the Seattle Seahawks’ offensive coordinator last year. But this solidifies the plan, at least to begin training camp.

While coaches can lead training camp with players in starting roles, nothing is final until players walk on the gridiron Week 1. And that’s exactly Kubiak’s thought process.

TOM BRADY SENDS CLEAR MESSAGE TO RAIDERS ROOKIE FERNANDO MENDOZA: EARN YOUR OPPORTUNITY

"For every position, there’s gotta be competition, right?" he added. "The best player has to play, and that’s not just what I’m gonna see. You guys are gonna see it in the preseason games. We as coaches, we’re gonna see who the best guard is, the best quarterback, across the board.

"There’s battles everywhere on the roster. It’s important for me to be fair to the players to put the best player out there."

Kubiak has noted in the past that the ideal scenario for the Raiders is Cousins starting and Mendoza developing and learning from the 14-year signal-caller ahead of him on the depth chart.

Fernando Mendoza and Kirk Cousins of the Las Vegas Raiders walk on a field during an OTA offseason workout at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center in Henderson, Nev., on June 3, 2026. (Getty Images)

But could things change if Mendoza is outperforming Cousins in training camp? As a first-year head coach, there isn’t a track record of a similar scenario with Kubiak, but he seems to be ready to evaluate every position no matter who’s in place.

Cousins was signed by the Raiders just days after Mendoza, who won a national championship with Indiana this past season, finally heard his name called first overall after months of speculation it was going to happen.

And while Cousins may be the man atop the depth chart, this will be Mendoza’s team at some point in the future. Kubiak wouldn’t want it to be right away, but if the time feels right for himself, his staff and the organization, they will hand the keys to their top draft choice.

Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza warm up during mandatory minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center in Henderson, Nev., on June 9, 2026. (Getty Images)

In the meantime, all three quarterbacks will be working hard to build chemistry with their teammates and get after it as training camp begins across the league this week.

The Raiders’ first preseason contest will be against the Arizona Cardinals on Aug. 13. They will open the season against the Miami Dolphins on Sept. 13 at home.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump pausing Iran attacks shows US military power is not enough on its own
excerpt:
Tehran has not been bombed into submission, leaving America unable to enforce its demands without a ground war that it does not want

Has Iran won a war it didn’t start against the United States? It i...
body_text:
Tehran has not been bombed into submission, leaving America unable to enforce its demands without a ground war that it does not want

Has Iran won a war it didn’t start against the United States? It is not a victory in any conventional military sense: about 3,500 Iranians have been reported killed and the US-led bombing has caused anywhere between $150bn and $270bn of damage.

Yet Donald Trump’s decision to pause, rather than intensify, the 13-night summer bombing campaign in effect represents a degree of recognition that the US cannot achieve its stated goals by military power alone.

“Iran’s initial standard for victory was simply to survive,” said HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute. “If anything, that’s been raised. The regime has demonstrated it is not going anywhere, and Tehran has changed the calculus on the strait of Hormuz”.

The past five months are a clear demonstration of how an asymmetric conflict can flip the tables. All Iran, helped by its extensive and mountainous geography, has needed to do is maintain enough of a missile and drone capability to scare merchant shipping from using the strait of Hormuz. It is a low bar Iran’s military is still clearing.

Two tankers were attacked sailing north of Oman last week. One of them caught fire in the engine room and had to be evacuated, before being towed to Oman, one of a handful of serious attacks on merchant shipping that took place during the nearly two-week July escalation of fighting.

The US, meanwhile, has spent at least $38bn and used more than 1,000 Tomahawk and 1,100 Jassm $2.6m cruise missiles, according to estimates by the CSIS thinktank, to bomb targets in Iran, a third and a quarter of total stockpiles. The Tomahawks, which cost up to $3.6m each, might not be replaced until 2031.

It is surprising that the US has allowed key munitions to be run down at such speed. On Monday, Trump tried in part to blame Ukraine, arguing that “so much was given” to Kyiv in military aid – though the reality is that Ukraine was never given long-range cruise missiles, only Patriot air defence systems.

Patriot missile interceptors were more heavily depleted, by 1,000 or so, or 50% of the total US stockpile, raising questions as to how well the US can continue to defend its bases in the Gulf. More were used during the 38 days of heavy fighting in the spring than the 600 or so that Ukraine has said it had received during four years of war.

A fresh escalation in the Red Sea by the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen, complicates the picture further. The rebel group kept out of the first phase of the US-Iran war in the spring but, as Saudi Arabia seeks to redirect oil traffic through the Red Sea, they have stepped up attacks, targeting a refinery in the Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday.

The US’s stated central war aim, meanwhile, may have repeatedly shifted but it has always been maximalist – whether it was regime change (as demonstrated by the killing of Ali Khamenei), destroying Iran’s entire missile programme or, as most frequently stated, preventing the country from having a nuclear weapon.

Yet the US has no means of enforcing this level of demand without committing ground forces in numbers to occupy Tehran – an unlikely move that the US has not shown signs of preparing for. Donald Trump’s previous threats to bomb Iranian power plants to try to force the regime’s capitulation have raised concerns they would amount to war crimes, and he dropped them in April and again last week.

“I don’t think the Iranians can be bombed into accepting US terms,” said Peter Ricketts, a former UK national security adviser. “Until the US accepts it can’t get its way by bombing, Iran has effective leverage. Tehran can absorb the pain, and they know they can close the strait with the economic impact it has on the US.”

The resulting situation is what Ricketts calls an “escalation dominance” that he says favours Iran. Tehran, faced with US pressure to abandon its nuclear programme, can string out peace negotiations, wait for the White House to get impatient and restart bombing, then close Hormuz until the US has to stop attacking because the oil price is tto high for too long.

The question then becomes who gains as unstable equilibrium endures. Tehran may well believe it has leverage as the US heads towards midterm elections in November, given how unpopular the war is. Just a third of all Americans support the war, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey out on Tuesday, though that rises to 71% of Republicans.

Laurel Rapp, from the Chatham House thinktank, said that “a resumed ceasefire and promise of future talks is the least bad option for Washington” – though whether that is attractive to US ally Israel, whose prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu has his own election to fight in October, is another source of uncertainty.

But if Tehran may have short or medium-term leverage, any idea that it has won the war is exaggerated. Hellyer argues that Iran, long struggling under western sanctions, cannot afford to rebuild without an agreement with the US: “Ultimately this isn’t sustainable for Iran, because its economy isn’t going to be able to survive”.

title: Tom Cruise, Katie Holmes' daughter Suri legally changes her famous last name
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes' daughter Suri legally dropped her last name.

Suri, a 20-year-old college student, legally changed her ...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes' daughter Suri legally dropped her last name.

Suri, a 20-year-old college student, legally changed her last name from Cruise to Noelle, according to records obtained by Fox News Digital.

The voter registration report noted that Suri, a student at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, is registered to vote in Allegheny County, Pa.

Her registration is under Suri Noelle, an homage to her mother's middle name. Suri previously used the name during her high school graduation in 2024.

TOM CRUISE SAVED SAMANTHA HARRIS FROM GETTING CRUSHED BY A '500-POUND' MOTORCYCLE

Tom and Katie Holmes were married in Italy in 2006, and divorced in 2012. (KMazur/WireImage)

Cruise and Holmes' representatives did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

Monica Mazzei, Chair of Buchalter’s Family Law Group, exclusively told Fox News Digital that Suri, as an adult, can change her name herself.

"Katie Holmes has had sole legal custody of her daughter, which means up until Suri’s 18th birthday, she could make all legal decisions without needing Tom’s permission and could have consented to the name change prior if there was a desire," Mazzei said. "You can legally change your name to anything you want."

Katie Holmes has been fiercely private about her daughter Suri's life following the star's split from Tom Cruise. (Robert Kamau)

The "Dawson's Creek" actress previously admitted she was looking forward to seeing how her daughter would embrace college.

"I’m proud of my daughter. Of course, I will miss the close proximity, but I’m really proud of her, and I’m happy," Holmes shared with Town & Country.

"I remember being this age, this time of beginnings. It’s exciting to learn about yourself, and I loved that time, so it makes me happy to think about it like that."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

In a rare move later that year, Holmes publicly spoke about her daughter after a report suggested Suri inherited millions of dollars from her famous father when she turned 18.

The actress wrote "completely false" over a screenshot of an article shared on social media.

Holmes admitted she feels a mix of emotions watching Suri grow older. (Amy Sussman)

The image alluded to Holmes also having set aside a designated amount of money for her daughter, in addition to funds allegedly saved by her father.

title: Baker Mayfield's self-imposed contract deadline arrives as Buccaneers and quarterback fail to agree on deal
excerpt: Lamar Jackson expressed his desire to have confetti rain down on him and the Baltimore Ravens this season, hoping for a Super Bowl win. Danny Parkins determines how open the Ravens’ Super Bowl window ...
body_text:
Lamar Jackson expressed his desire to have confetti rain down on him and the Baltimore Ravens this season, hoping for a Super Bowl win. Danny Parkins determines how open the Ravens’ Super Bowl window is, how close the Los Angeles Rams are to the Seattle Seahawks, and if Baker Mayfield will re-sign with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Baker Mayfield's relationship with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers has reached a defining moment and how it goes after Wednesday could determine whether this is the quarterback's final year with the club.

Mayfield reported to training camp Tuesday, as all Bucs veterans were scheduled to do. But for Mayfield, this day might have signaled the end of his desire to engage with the team about a new contract.

The Bucs and Mayfield do not practice until Wednesday but they may be already past the deadline Mayfield imposed for getting a new deal done before turning his attention to football.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers Quarterbacks Baker Mayfield (6) and Kyle Trask (2) go thru a drill during the Tampa Bay Buccaneers OTA Offseason Workouts on May 30, 2023 at the AdventHealth Training Center at One Buccaneer Place in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

PRO BOWL PLAYER REQUESTS TRADE FROM TAMPA BAY BUCCANEERS ON EVE OF TRAINING CAMP AMID CONTRACT DISPUTE

"Obviously, yes, I would love to have a long-term deal done, but they know my deadline," Mayfield told reporters weeks ago. "As soon as training camp starts, we're not doing any contract stuff. It's all ball. It's not up to me when that gets done by. Hopefully before that, but if not – still going to have a good year."

Multiple reports citing unnamed sources said Mayfield reporting to training camp without a new deal was his red line. It means he intends to play out the final year of his contract before becoming an unrestricted free agent.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers' Baker Mayfield responds to questions during a news conference after the team's NFL football game against the Houston Texans Monday, Sept. 15, 2025, in Houston, Texas. (AP Photo/Eric Gay)

It means Mayfield is now figuratively betting on himself in the coming season, letting his performance determine what sort of contract he gets after the season. This could reward him with the kind of deal he's been trying to convince Buccaneers general manager Jason Licht to offer – a deal that pays in the mid-to-high $50 million per year on an annual average basis.

Or this could penalize Mayfield with a mid-tier sort of deal, averaging in the $35-$38 million per year, that Mayfield has already rejected and the Bucs see as more fair.

For the team, meanwhile, this is a gamble. It has clearly declined to meet Mayfield's asking price over the months of negotiations and that has spoken loudly that it really likes Mayfield but doesn't love him on par with other franchise quarterbacks.

If Mayfield proves the Bucs right, it's bad news because it means he didn't play well enough this coming season.

If Mayfield proves the Bucs wrong, it's potentially still bad news because he's going to be a very hot commodity in free agency next offseason and the Bucs might not be able to pay him what he wants.

(That's to say nothing of the fact Mayfield may be a little irritated with the club for not believing in him now.)

Mike Evans of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers looks on during the second quarter of the NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Raymond James Stadium on Dec. 11, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. (Logan Bowles/Getty Images)

So everybody's opinion of Mayfield is riding on what happens this season and what's at stake is both the player's and the franchise's future.

The Buccaneers, by the way, are at something of a crossroads.

They didn't move quickly to extend receiver Mike Evans before the 2025 season, so he played out his contract and left as an unrestricted free agent to San Francisco this offseason.

Nose tackle Vita Vea, meanwhile, has asked for a trade because he is unhappy the team has not given him an extension offer he believes fair before the final year of his current deal.

Vea, like Mayfield, is in the final year of his deal.

That's a lot of talent the Bucs have either let leave their building or put at risk of leaving.

And here's a Hail Mary idea: The team will practice for the first time Wednesday. So, technically, training camp doesn't begin until then.

Maybe the Bucs try one last time to get a deal done with Mayfield before that moment he steps on the field and his self-imposed deadline becomes concrete.

It's hard to believe the impasse of the previous few months can be overcome in one day. But that's why it's a Hail Mary.

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

title: Seattle police recover machine gun and ghost gun from scene of mass shooting
excerpt:
Three people died, including one of the suspects, and at least five more were wounded, including two-year-old boy

Seattle police recovered a modified machine gun and an untraceable “ghost gun” from t...
body_text:
Three people died, including one of the suspects, and at least five more were wounded, including two-year-old boy

Seattle police recovered a modified machine gun and an untraceable “ghost gun” from the scene of a mass shooting at a food festival this weekend that left three people dead – including one of the suspects – and at least five more wounded, the police chief, Shon Barnes, said on Tuesday.

Sunday’s shooting appeared to involve at least three suspects, Barnes said at a televised news conference. One of those three, 19-year-old Junior Cee Niko Semo, died at the scene. A second, 15-year-old suspect was disarmed and arrested at the scene. At least one more suspect remains at large, Barnes said.

The shooting broke out in the middle of a three-day food festival at Seattle Center, a park located near the city’s Space Needle.

Two people whom Seattle police say were uninvolved in the shooting were killed: Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56. People wounded by crossfire included a two-year-old boy. Others were trampled as the crowd rushed to safety.

Casings from fired cartridges and three pistols were recovered from the scene, police say.

Police seized a 9mm ghost gun produced from a parts kit made by the now-defunct company Polymer80 from the 15-year-old suspect at the scene. They also recovered a Glock pistol modified with an auto sear, or “switch”, allowing it to be fired as a fully automatic machine gun.

Both of those pistols had extended magazines, with the Glock holding 40 rounds and the ghost gun holding 33. The state of Washington generally bans firearms from carrying more than 10 rounds.

Both types of weapon have raised concerns among law enforcement officials in recent years, for different reasons. Illegal machine guns increase a firearm’s rate of fire while reducing the shooter’s accuracy. Ghost guns make it easier for prohibited persons to acquire firearms and harder for law enforcement officials to trace weapons used in crimes.

The third gun, a .45-caliber pistol, was not used in the crime. Police did not so far believe that any of the recovered firearms had been stolen, though authorities were still working on tracing the two serialized guns.

Cheap, user-installed auto sears or switches that allow shooters to convert semiautomatic pistols into fully automatic machine guns have proliferated in the age of 3D printing and internet shopping. Unserialized “ghost guns” were legal to buy and assemble under federal law from parts kit manufacturers like Polymer80, until the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives started regulating them as firearms in 2022.

The advent of 3D printing, however, has made it easier for private individuals to produce ghost guns illegally.

Police were still trying to locate a person who showed up at a nearby hospital with what may have been a gunshot wound, but had not been confirmed as a victim of Sunday’s shooting, Barnes said.

Authorities are continuing to review physical evidence, digital recordings and camera footage from the shooting scene to reconstruct what happened and locate at least one suspect who remains at large. There may be more than one at-large suspect involved in the shooting, Barnes said.

The shooting was probably linked to gang violence, according to Seattle police. “We’re working to determine the groups involved and what their relationship may be,” Barnes said.

body_text:
Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., is blaming President Donald Trump for the surge of socialist victories after a new poll revealed Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., as Democrats top 2028 candidate. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., argued that President Donald Trump is driving Democratic voters toward far-left candidates like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez after the New York Democrat topped a recent 2028 presidential primary poll.

A recent New Hampshire poll found Ocasio-Cortez was the top choice among likely Democratic voters for the party's 2028 presidential nomination. Kelly placed third with 9% support, behind Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, while ahead of California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. The poll comes as several self-described Democratic Socialists have defeated more moderate Democrats in recent primary elections, showing the growing influence of the party's progressive wing.

Kelly has teased a run for president in 2028, recently saying in an NBC interview that it is part of an ongoing discussion with his family that he has "plenty of time" to decide on.

HASAN PIKER MAKES AOC HIS 2028 PICK FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS IT'S 'NOT EVEN A QUESTION’

Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, is seen during a news conference ahead of the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I don't know about her message, but people are really struggling," Kelly told Fox News Digital about why Ocasio-Cortez was Democrats top 2028 pick.

Fox News Digital asked Kelly why Ocasio-Cortez and other candidates associated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are resonating with the Democratic voters ahead of upcoming election seasons.

"The policies of this president — supporting billionaires over hardworking people," Kelly said. "1% of the country now owns more wealth than the middle class, and I think it's a response to that."

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., speaks during a campaign rally for Democratic congressional candidate State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, Friday, July 17, 2026, in Memphis, Tenn. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)

In 2021, Federal Reserve data showed the top 1% of households now hold more wealth than the bottom 60% combined for the first time since the central bank began tracking the data in 1989.

Trump has defended his economic agenda as aimed at boosting middle-class Americans through tax relief and lower costs, pointing to efforts to extend the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, eliminate taxes on tips and overtime pay and lower energy costs.

Kelly said voters' frustration with Trump's policies is driving support for candidates like Ocasio-Cortez, while also criticizing the president more broadly.

LIZ PEEK: TRUMP IS STARVING THE MACHINE THAT CREATES AMERICA'S SOCIALIST REVOLUTIONARIES

"It's unfortunate we have people like this running the government and I think people are really frustrated," Kelly said about Trump to Fox News Digital.

"I mean this president doesn't prioritize anybody but him and his family," Kelly said. "The corruption is just off the charts. "

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Reds get majorly hosed by winning a challenge that leads directly to a Guardians grand slam
excerpt:
ESPN host Monica McNutt is under EXTREME heat after claiming Indiana Fever superstar Caitlin Clark needs to show more "accountability and self-awareness."

With challenges becoming a bigger and bigger...
body_text:
ESPN host Monica McNutt is under EXTREME heat after claiming Indiana Fever superstar Caitlin Clark needs to show more "accountability and self-awareness."

With challenges becoming a bigger and bigger part of more sports, including Major League Baseball, we're going to see lots and lots of ways that they can backfire.

However, you'll be hard-pressed to find a way that hoses the team that won the challenge more than what happened on Tuesday to the Cincinnati Reds.

Tuesday saw the two Ohio-based teams meeting for a day-night doubleheader, and it was in the first game that the Reds had a big challenge win, followed by a big loss.

It's too often that you see a team celebrating two pitches after an opponent's successful challenge, but that's what we got from the Cleveland Guardians on Tuesday, (Photo by Dylan Buell/Getty Images)

In the top of the first inning, the Guardians managed to load the bases with Kyle Manzardo at the plate.

With a 1-2 count, Manzardo took a pitch from Reds righty Chase Burns high and inside.

It was certainly in on his forearms, and Manzardo did his best to let the home plate umpire know that the pitch clipped him.

REDS FANS GO BERSERK AFTER CATCHER TYLER STEPHENSON'S ABS CHALLENGE WINS THEM FREE PIZZA

It was ruled that he had been hit by a pitch, which brought in a run.

However, the Reds challenged and won, so the at-bat resumed with Manzardo facing a 2-2 count.

He fouled off one pitch and then blasted the next into the outfield bleachers for a grand slam that wouldn't have ever happened just a few years ago.

I'll be honest: I'm just shocked this sort of thing didn't happen to the Mets.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

First of all, top-notch acting from Manzardo on that one. I thought it did hit him in real time, but when you slow it down, it wasn't even close. He'd have gotten away with it too if it wasn't for video review.

Kyle Manzardo of the Cleveland Guardians celebrates a grand slam (and one heck of an acting job earlier in the same at-bat). (Photo by Dylan Buell/Getty Images)

But then, what are the odds that the Reds feel like they had another chance to end the inning, and Manzardo does the worst possible thing in that situation and goes yard?

What's worse is that the Reds did manage to battle back, but that early grand slam was the difference-maker. The Guardians took the first game of the doubleheader 6-5.

title: Rescuers pick through wreckage after ‘devastating’ Wisconsin tornado
excerpt:
No deaths reported after twister leveled homes and topples trees and power lines in north-east of state

First responders searched homes and buildings on Tuesday for possible victims of a powerful tor...
body_text:
No deaths reported after twister leveled homes and topples trees and power lines in north-east of state

First responders searched homes and buildings on Tuesday for possible victims of a powerful tornado that ravaged several north-eastern Wisconsin communities.

The Fox Cities region, which is home to more than 100,000 people in the cities of Appleton, Menasha and Neenah, was left in shambles by Monday’s twister, with homes leveled, cars flipped and power lines and trees toppled.

“The depth of the tornado and its impact is incredible, devastating. We’re really still at the assessment stage,” the Winnebago county executive, Gordon Hintz, said at a news conference on Tuesday.

David Chew, 55, said a tree smashed through his roof in Menasha, and he still hadn’t located an outdoor patio lounger swept away by the storm. But he is better off than a neighbor: a portion of her roof was ripped clean, with furniture and drywall “sucked out”.

“It was just a shocker,” said Chew, who had rushed to the basement with his wife and son.

Despite widespread damage, the timing of the storm could be why there have been no reported deaths. The tornado arrived in the early afternoon, authorities noted, when most people were awake and after warnings had been issued.

“Everybody was at work. It was the middle of the day,” Menasha’s police chief, Matt Albrecht, said. “Most people were not at home and at their place of employment.”

Dozens of people were injured, and officers were still going door-to-door a day later in search of possible victims.

The tornado touched down around 1pm and remained on the ground for more than 20 minutes, cutting a roughly 12-mile (19km) path of destruction, the National Weather Service reported. The area is about 100 miles north-west of Milwaukee.

Governor Tony Evers declared a state of emergency for the affected areas. Shelters were opened for displaced residents.

As chainsaws roared in the background, Appleton’s mayor, Jake Woodford, said a number of neighborhoods were “truly devastated”. Like elsewhere in the region, electricity lines were tangled around broken trees, making power restoration a slow, risky process.

More than 10,000 customers in Winnebago and Outagamie counties were still without power, according to utilities that serve them. It could be several days before power is fully restored.

The twister was spun off by a large storm system that moved through the Great Lakes and was fueled by a buildup of heat and humidity, the weather service said.

title: Children's YouTube star 'Ms. Rachel' stirs controversy with racial claim about Nolan Wells investigation
excerpt: Former state attorney Dave Aronberg tells Fox News Digital that YouTube star "Ms. Rachel's" comments surrounding race in the case of Nolan Wells' mysterious death "is not helping" the investigation an...
body_text:
Former state attorney Dave Aronberg tells Fox News Digital that YouTube star "Ms. Rachel's" comments surrounding race in the case of Nolan Wells' mysterious death "is not helping" the investigation and public perception of the investigation.

A controversial children’s educator and YouTube star is weighing in on the investigation into Nolan Wells’ mysterious death, with a now-viral social media post pointing to unsupported allegations that race played a role in law enforcement’s handling of the case.

In a post shared on Instagram, Ms. Rachel — a popular content creator whose real name is Rachel Accurso — appeared to question the case surrounding Wells’ death, suggesting the investigation would have played out differently had the races been reversed.

"We know the investigation and everything that followed would have been different if Nolan Wells were white and his friends were Black," Accurso wrote in a post on Monday. "Nolan and his family deserve justice."

SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST

Ms. Rachel is pictured during an appearance on the "TODAY" show on Tuesday, Sept. 24, 2024. (Nathan Congleton/NBC via Getty Images)

Wells, 18, vanished while on a July 4 boat trip with a group of high school friends to Horn Island, a barrier island located roughly eight miles offshore from Mississippi's Gulf Coast.

His remains were found on the northwestern tip of the island by a National Park Service ranger just two days later, with his friends returning to shore on the evening of his disappearance without him.

An independent autopsy later commissioned by Wells’ family labeled his manner of death to be "undetermined" pending further investigation.

NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS

Nolan Wells, 18, disappeared July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. His body was found two days later by a National Park Service ranger. (Christine Wonsley/Facebook and Jackson County Sheriff's Department)

Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who was hired to represent the Wells family, revealed the findings last week at the annual NAACP National Convention in Chicago, according to the Associated Press.

Crump reportedly pointed out that the autopsy report showed no evidence of fractures or deep tissue injuries, and labeled a "red discoloration" located on the back of Wells’ skull as "inconclusive" — meriting further investigation.

Forensic pathologist Dr. Roger Mitchell reportedly wrote that, without the additional information, he was unable to rule out the possibility that "non-accidental factors contributed to or caused the death."

CHILDREN'S YOUTUBE STAR 'MS. RACHEL' TALKS TO ANTI-ISRAEL REPORTER ABOUT GAZA POSTS

The United Cajun Navy shared a video of the search Monday morning on Facebook. (United Cajun Navy via Facebook)

The results of a second autopsy, commissioned by the Mississippi medical examiner, have yet to be released. Additionally, authorities have not announced charges stemming from the case.

The case has sparked questions surrounding the circumstances of the 18-year-old’s death, with rampant online speculation pointing to the fact that Wells was Black and his friends are white.

Following Accurso’s Instagram post, hundreds of her followers took to the comments to echo their support for her suggestion that the investigation into Wells’ death would have played out differently had the group’s races been reversed.

"If Nolan was white, the friends would have been arrested the day of, no questions asked," one commenter wrote. "Now all these ‘friends’ and their parents have had more than enough time to destroy and hide any potential evidence that would have proved that Nolan was murdered."

Another follower shared the same sentiment, commenting, "The stuff coming out about the case is so crazy, but it all sounds about white also. I just hope they are actually held accountable for once."

However, former Palm Beach County, Fla., State Attorney Dave Aronberg cautioned against online personalities, such as Accurso, jumping to conclusions surrounding race in such sensitive — and ongoing — investigations.

CONSERVATIVE PARENTS CALL TO BOYCOTT 'MS. RACHEL' OVER LATEST PRIDE MONTH VIDEO: 'KIDS LOOK UP TO' HER

"I'll be the first to tell you that the investigation into the tragic death of Nolan Wells needs more transparency," Aronberg told Fox News Digital. "His family deserves answers."

"But jumping on social media to race bait — without a shred of evidence — that law enforcement is covering up a murder is not helping," Aronberg continued. "But she always has to throw gas on a fire."

"Ms. Rachel is at it again. Whether it's injecting division into domestic tragedies or spreading toxic, antisemitic rhetoric in her posts about the Middle East, she constantly pushes narrative over facts," Aronberg told Fox News Digital, adding, "We need real investigative transparency [in the Wells case], not popular children's creators using tragic deaths and foreign policy to divide us."

MS. RACHEL POSTS SUPPORT FOR HIJAB-WEARING KINDERGARTNERS AFTER TRUMP POST

Accurso’s comments come on the heels of similar posts made to her Instagram account, in which the viral children’s educator fired back at critics who suggested she "stay in [her] lane" when speaking on hot-button political issues.

In one recent post, Accurso shared a carousel of images showing her response to criticism she has received surrounding her decision to be politically outspoken.

"I liked you better when you just sang on YouTube," one slide read.

"Ok. I never just sang on YouTube though. I’ve always cared about how children around the world are treated," Accurso responded.

She also recently made headlines after she posted a video to Instagram pushing back against President Donald Trump for sharing a viral video showing several children wearing hijabs at a Minnesota kindergarten graduation.

Fox News Digital reached out to Accurso, Crump and the Mississippi Department of Public Safety for comment.

Fox News Digital's Madison Columbo and Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.
