title: What are Trump’s military options?
excerpt: Last week, it was reported that US President Donald Trump placed massive attacks on Iran on hold after a meeting with advisers at the White House. Clearly, domestic political pressure on him and on th...
body_text:
Last week, it was reported that US President Donald Trump placed massive attacks on Iran on hold after a meeting with advisers at the White House. Clearly, domestic political pressure on him and on the Republican Party over rising economic costs is fierce. Current polls suggest nearly 70 percent of Americans oppose the war.

Despite assertions, notably by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, that Iran’s military has reached “its lowest point ever”, Iran is still able to conduct massive drone and missile strikes. Some intelligence suggests Iran has reconstituted and increased its capacity to build these weapons.

Meanwhile, the US has moved more aircraft and missile defence units in preparation for what may be a campaign to target staging points for Iranian forces. Two Marine Expeditionary Units (MEUs) and components of the 82nd or 101st Airborne are currently stationed in the region.

Yet, reports that the US and its Gulf allies have exhausted defensive missile magazines, as well as Tomahawk land-attack missiles, may be a powerful constraint.

While Trump appears not to have made a decision yet, he has several options on how to move forward.

The first option is ramping up air and missile strikes. One of the challenges of this strategy is that the list of military targets may have been exhausted. If so, expanding the aerial campaign would mean attacking largely civilian infrastructure, including energy production facilities, electricity and power grids, bridges and roads, and television and phone networks. The likely outcomes are all bad.

Trump would be accused of war crimes. The Iranian public would coalesce in their resentment against the US. Iran’s ability to strike back would not be significantly curbed and it may strike Gulf desalination and energy infrastructure. The result would be a humanitarian catastrophe. No plans exist to deal with this contingency. And of course, oil could soar to $150 or even $200 a barrel, triggering an international economic disaster.

Another option is a ground invasion of some sort. The forces currently deployed in the region are too small to achieve any realistic military objectives. A MEU numbers about 2,500 marines and only 800 of them are infantry, able to conduct very limited ground operations. Airborne units deploy with only a few days worth of bullets, beans and batteries. Resupply is essential for these units.

As retired US Army General Barry McCaffery has pointed out, even 150,000 troops may not be enough to secure control of the Strait of Hormuz along the Iranian coast.

Attacking Kharg Island requires a long and dangerous transit from the western end of the Strait of Hormuz. That would create conditions for a high number of casualties among US troops.

The third option is for Trump to employ a nuclear weapon, at least as a demonstration shot. That would open a catastrophic Pandora’s box of consequences. Trump would be declared a war criminal. Wherever and however the weapon is detonated—an air or surface burst—it would have destructive outcomes.

If exploded exoatmospherically, the nuclear bomb would emit an electromagnetic pulse (EMP) which would destroy virtually all chip-installed systems for hundreds of miles beyond Iran. Few modern militaries, including in the Gulf, are protected from EMP due to costs. A surface burst would form a radioactive cloud that would travel east given the winds and affect populations well beyond Iran.

A major geopolitical consequence would be that such an attack could change the way Russia’s President Vladimir Putin sees the possibility of using nuclear weapons in the war in Ukraine.

Given this list of unpalatable options, the most promising is to claim victory and pursue negotiations. Trump will say he has brought Iran to the negotiating table even though talks between Washington and Tehran have not stopped despite the escalation. The first issue would be reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb. Oil prices would drop. Stock markets would rebound.

Trump would take the credit. And a devastating war and economic crisis would be sensibly avoided. This is his best and only sensible option.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to US in 2025 after Trump’s return to office
excerpt:
Data shows Canadians have replaced US vacations with other international trips in apparent rebuke to Trump

Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to the US in 2025 than in the previous year, as Donald...
body_text:
Data shows Canadians have replaced US vacations with other international trips in apparent rebuke to Trump

Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to the US in 2025 than in the previous year, as Donald Trump’s hostile policies towards his northern neighbour continue to incur an economic cost, new government data shows.

The research also indicates that Canadians are not bucking travel overall and instead have replaced US vacations with other international destinations, in a rebuke to Trump’s tariff regime and the president’s continued musings on annexing Canada.

“Following the change in the US administration in early 2025 and the implementation of America First policies, Canadian travel sentiment shifted abruptly,” said authors of the report published by Statistics Canada, the country’s national statistics agency.

Total US travel spending in 2025 amounted to $18.8bn, down from $22.1bn in 2024.

In contrast, Canadian spending on travel abroad, excluding the US, grew by $3.6bn in 2025, to a total of $22.8bn.

Canadian visits to Europe increased by nearly 14% compared to 2024, while visits to Asia increased by almost 17%.

Those increases offered a stark contrast to the dwindling US visits. Overall in 2025, return trips to Canada from the US by vehicle and by plane dropped by about one quarter compared to 2024. The highest travel declines were recorded in July 2025, when border crossings fell by about one-third from the previous year.

Those plummeting border crossings through nearly the entire year were “the deepest and most sustained on record”, the agency said. Since digital record-keeping began in 1972, declines of more than 30% have only ever been seen in September 2001, after the 9/11 World Trade Center attacks.

Looking at 2026 data so far, Statistics Canada said the drop in leisure travel to the US is continuing. Return trips to Canada from the US this year are at similar levels seen at the end of 2025, which saw a 27% decline between October and December, it reported.

The data signals “a persistent shift away from the United States by Canadian residents in their travel preferences”.

title: Pakistan accused of firing on unarmed protesters in Kashmir leaving 30 dead
excerpt:
Local civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackout

At least 30 people are alleged to have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in the past ...
body_text:
Local civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackout

At least 30 people are alleged to have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in the past two days as part of what has been claimed is a brutal state crackdown that has engulfed the disputed region for weeks.

According to a local civil society group, Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the Pakistani security services fired on tens of thousands of peaceful protesters, killing 25 people on Monday and five more on Tuesday.

Protests and violence have been erupting in Pakistani Kashmir since June. The state has in response imposed a severe communication shutdown, including an internet blackout that cut the region off from the rest of Pakistan, and began carrying out mass arrests.

Amnesty International on Tuesday called for Pakistani authorities to lift the communications blackout.

JAAC and their supporters had taken to the streets to call for electoral reform in the heavily-militarised region. Monday marked the first phase of an election disputed by local groups who say a system of reserved seats for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir now living across Pakistan gives outsiders too much control over the region.

SA Khan, a spokesperson for JAAC, accused Pakistan’s security agencies of firing on unarmed protesters in Mirpur on Tuesday and then removing the evidence.

“Security forces have taken away the dead bodies and locked away the hospital in Mirpur,” he said. “We have the photos and video evidence of dead bodies lying on streets in a pool of blood. The security forces abducted the dead bodies to erase the evidence.”

A local resident in Mirpur, requesting anonymity for fear of retribution by the authorities, said that the violence had erupted early Tuesday afternoon when people gathered to protest against killings the previous day. “The bodies were shifted to hospital and then they went missing. Now, all shops nearby have been closed after the violence,” they said.

The Guardian could not independently verify the death toll as media were prevented from accessing the area and the internet blackout remained in place, making it hard to reach local communities. Pakistani media has largely ignored the protests and alleged killings.

Pakistani authorities have rejected the accusation of state involvement in killing of civilian protesters. In a press conference over the weekend, information minister Atta Tarar alleged that the protests in Pakistani-administered Kashmir were receiving “funds and instructions” from India.

JAAC spokesperson Khan rejected the accusations that the unrest was sponsored by India. “It is nothing new: people asking for political or economic rights are termed India-sponsored or anti-state in Pakistan, same goes in India,” he said.

The protests, led by JAAC, have been ongoing for a year, demanding political and economic rights for local people, as well as electoral reforms.

Pakistan-administered Kashmir has been rocked by bouts of deadly violence in recent years. The protests that began in June, calling for the abolition of 12 reserved seats for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir, have prompted the deadliest crackdown in years. Locals say the reserved seats are used by the central government to retain control over the region and destabilise regional politics.

About 40 people were alleged to have been killed when violence erupted in June and the government accused protesters of killing police. The local government responded by proscribing JAAC as a terrorist organisation, arresting and detaining its political workers en masse and responding to protests with force.

It prompted the UN rights chief, Volker Türk, to call for an investigation into the deadly violence.

Isabelle Lassée, Amnesty International’s action regional director for south Asia, said: “The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities’ long history of unlawful violence against protesters in Jammu and Kashmir. A prompt, independent, and transparent investigation must be ordered into the security forces’ use of force against protesters.

“So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area.”

title: Mets broadcaster admits being 'sick to my stomach' over Braves pitcher’s brutal outing
excerpt:
An Atlanta Braves fan blew a kiss to The Freeze, but his taunt went awry as he got a taste of his own medicine. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

Atlanta Braves reliever Connor Thomas had abo...
body_text:
An Atlanta Braves fan blew a kiss to The Freeze, but his taunt went awry as he got a taste of his own medicine. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

Atlanta Braves reliever Connor Thomas had about as bad a day at the office as possible on Monday night against the New York Mets. In fact, it was so bad that MLB legend Keith Hernandez could barely watch what was taking place at Citi Field.

Hernandez, who has been a commentator on Mets broadcasts for nearly 30 years, was in a unique spot in the booth on Monday.

Witnessing the mightily struggling team pound Atlanta 14-3 had to have been a nice change of pace for Hernandez given the team's many inconsistencies this season, but he didn't exactly love how the team eventually got to its dominating victory.

"I'm sorry, I just think that's criminal what we just witnessed," Hernandez said during the bottom of the eighth inning.

Keith Hernandez speaks on stage as Stephen A. Smith and Christopher Russo host SiriusXM shows live from Fanatics Fest at Javits Center on July 17, 2026 in New York City. (Jason Mendez/Getty Images for SiriusXM)

TRUMP CAN'T HELP BUT TAKE JAB AT METS IN SPEECH WHILE PRAISING BRAVES CEO: 'THEY LOSE ALL THE TIME'

"Poor kid, you just want to give him a hug," Hernandez continued while the broadcast panned to Thomas in the Braves dugout. "Literally, I'm sick to my stomach. I'm not a happy camper."

"Criminal" may be too harsh a word to describe Thomas' outing against New York, but Hernandez feeling bad for the relief pitcher is certainly understandable.

Connor Thomas of the Atlanta Braves pitches during the game between the Atlanta Braves and the Pittsburgh Pirates at PNC Park on Tuesday, July 7, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Rayni Shiring/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

Thomas entered the contest with things knotted up at 3-3 before giving up 10 hits, 11 earned runs, three home runs, and walking five batters in just 2.2 innings of work.

It was very much a situation that we see quite often in today's game where relievers have to stay in contests far longer than they should to preserve other arms in the bullpen.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Francisco Lindor #12 of the New York Mets rounds the bases after hitting a three-run home run in the eighth inning during the game between the Atlanta Braves and the New York Mets at Citi Field on Monday, July 27, 2026 in New York, New York. (Evan Yu/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

Thomas, who retired just eight of the 23 batters he faced, was eventually replaced by a position player on the bump.

Monday night's rough go marked Thomas' second appearance on the mound for Atlanta this season. The 28-year-old came on in relief against the Pittsburgh Pirates on July 7 and allowed four runs, including one long ball, in 3.2 innings of action.

title: Mysterious deaths of 14 elephants in Kenya prompts urgent inquiry
excerpt:
It is estimated that more than 2,000 elephants roam in and around Amboseli National Park

An urgent investigation has been launched into the mysterious deaths of 14 elephants in southern Kenya near th...
body_text:
It is estimated that more than 2,000 elephants roam in and around Amboseli National Park

An urgent investigation has been launched into the mysterious deaths of 14 elephants in southern Kenya near the Amboseli National Park.

The Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) told the BBC that experts were examining the carcasses and said that tissue samples had been sent to laboratories to determine whether the deaths were caused by disease, poisoning or another factor.

The park and its surrounds are known as the Amboseli ecosystem, a vast area that straddles the border with Tanzania, which is famous for its wildlife.

Officials say this is the first time in decades that elephant mortalities on this scale have been recorded in the region where they have successfully cracked down on poaching.

KWS says there is currently no evidence pointing to a single cause of death.

The carcasses include elephants of different ages and sexes, suggesting the deaths are not limited to a single family or demographic.

The wildlife agency's head of communication, Duncan Wanyama, told local media the bodies had been found at different locations surrounding the Amboseli National Park, around 15km (nine miles) to 30km from its boundaries.

According to figures from the Amboseli Trust for Elephants, which monitors the movements of the animals, there were more than 2,000 elephants in the Amboseli ecosystem as of 2025.

body_text:
After MLB owners offered a salary cap for the first time since 1994, NFL star Saquon Barkley recently spoke to Fox News Digital and shared his full support for the players.

Saquon Barkley knows exactly what it's like to be stiffed in a salary cap sport.

The Philadelphia Eagles running back rushed for 2,000 yards and won an Offensive Player of the Year Award just one season after the New York Giants decided not to pay him.

Running backs were getting the short end of the stick before a recent resurgence, as general managers felt that the position was hardly that valuable. The best are still getting paid, but there was a lot of recycling throughout the league.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley (26) carries during the second half of the NFL Super Bowl 59 football game against the Kansas City Chiefs, Sunday, Feb. 9, 2025, in New Orleans. (AP Photo/Matt Slocum)

In any case, lots of difficult decisions are made in football, whereas baseball remains a non-capped sport, resulting in $700 million contracts and no cap casualties.

However, MLB owners have officially proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994 - and we all know how that turned out. The players have remained steadfast in saying that a salary cap is not negotiable, and Barkley is supporting them.

"Whatever is best for the players, I’m with that. Whatever is for the players," Barkley told Fox News Digital.

"I get how the owners have the power and stuff like this, but we go out there and sacrifice our bodies. Athletes go out there and sacrifice their bodies. I’m not under the pressure of, ‘Oh, you’re an athlete. Go out there and do what you’re told.’ I don’t get with that at all. You should be compensated for what you’re doing, and however way you should be, that’s how it should be. If that’s what they believe over there, that they should have that, and that’s going to benefit them and help them provide for their families even more, then why not? It should happen."

Commissioner of Major League Baseball Robert D. Manfred speaks during the 2026 All-Star Legacy Veterans Multi-Service Center renovation at Veterans Multi-Service Center on Monday, July 13, 2026, in Philadelphia, Pennsvlvania. (Daniel Shirey/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

INSIDE MLB CBA NEGOTIATIONS AS MANFRED, PLAYERS UNION EXEC DISCUSS ISSUES AS SIDES ATTEMPT TO SAVE 2027 SEASON

Surely, Barkley and other athletes are probably a bit jealous, and he admitted he feels some responsibility as "quote-unquote, one of the faces of the league."

"I don’t know if that’s going to happen for us. I think we’ve got a little more work to do for that. We’ve got to continue to be more vocal. We’ve got to continue to educate ourselves on it. ... I need to do that. I actually had this conversation the other day with my family. But yeah, I’m all for the players, and what the players think is great for them, I agree with it," Barkley added.

Saquon Barkley of the Philadelphia Eagles takes the field prior to the NFC Wild Card playoff game against the San Francisco 49ers at Lincoln Financial Field on Jan. 11, 2026, in Philadelphia. (Getty Images)

MLB is likely headed to an owners' lockout if the two sides cannot agree to a new collective bargaining agreement by Dec. 1, but the salary cap is each side's top priority, and they could not be further apart on the issue.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X, and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

title: Miami Secret Service agent charged in near-deadly fraternity hazing, officials say
excerpt: A man whose son died during a 2017 fraternity hazing ritual at Penn State University warned students and parents of the ills of the practice in an interview with Fox News Digital, saying anyone could ...
body_text:
A man whose son died during a 2017 fraternity hazing ritual at Penn State University warned students and parents of the ills of the practice in an interview with Fox News Digital, saying anyone could become a victim.

A U.S. Secret Service agent has been arrested and charged with five felony counts, including attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon, after allegedly being involved with hazing "rituals" that left two victims with life-threatening injuries.

Marquez Pinder, a 29-year-old special agent with the Miami Field Office, was ordered to be put on house arrest with a GPS tracking device.

Pinder held the title of "dean of pledges" during four, hours-long hazing sessions for a Miami chapter of the Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity, according to an affidavit filed with the Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit of Florida. In that role, Pinder was allegedly involved in the hazing of two prospective members of the fraternity.

SECRET SERVICE AGENT ON JD VANCE'S DETAIL INVESTIGATED FOR ALLEGEDLY LEAKING OPERATIONAL SECURITY INFO

Marquez Pinder was arrested by the Sweetwater Police Department after allegedly being involved in a near-deadly hazing. (Miami-Dade Corrections)

According to court records, the two victims were "paddled" and struck with "canes" by Pinder and two other fraternity members. One victim’s concern was "dismissed" by the fraternity when he reported "urinating blood" during the first hazing session, records show.

Days later, the man had to be intubated at a hospital while receiving "critical care to prevent further physical deterioration and death," a law enforcement officer reported in a sworn statement.

The other victim was treated for "blackened" and "necrotic" tissue on his buttocks from the beating, court records show. "Substantial portions of skin and soft tissue" needed to be surgically removed, and he received "extensive skin grafts to cover the areas," according to an affidavit.

A drone view shows the downtown skyline in Miami, April 16, 2025. Marquez Pinder is a special agent with the Secret Service's Miami Field Office. (REUTERS/Marco Bello)

AMERICA'S TOP PARTY COLLEGE HIT BY ANOTHER SEX ATTACK WEEKS AFTER BRUTAL CAMPUS RAPE CASE

His "mobility and quality of life have been significantly impacted," a law enforcement officer wrote. And without emergency medical care, "his injuries would have resulted in renal failure leading to death."

The alleged hazing occurred every day April 1-4 at two different residences in Miami-Dade County, court records show.

During the meetings, the two victims were tested with questions about the fraternity and its history, according to the affidavit. Victims told law enforcement officers that when they failed to answer a question correctly, they were placed in what they called a "stress position," the affidavit shows.

RIDESHARE DRIVER ARRESTED IN ALLEGED SCHEME TARGETING IVY LEAGUE STUDENTS FOR SEX: PROSECUTORS

They described the "stress position" as a half-squat with one arm pointed forward. While in that position, the victims said they were "struck on their buttocks with a paddle." One of the victims said that, before the hazing, he was told that "if he ever felt that he was reaching his physical limit," he should tell Pinder, his "dean of pledges," officers reported. He said he was told that indications of reaching that limit might include urinating blood or feeling that he was going to pass out, according to the affidavit.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Investigators reported they’d reviewed messages between fraternity members about the need for cleaning supplies to "mop up sweat and blood" from the hazing. After four days of "testing" to become members of the fraternity, one victim sought emergency medical treatment because his "health continued to deteriorate, and he began to suffer from vomiting, fevers, and immense pain on his buttocks," officers reported.

Marquez Pinder, who works in the Miami Field Office, has been employed with the U.S. Secret Service since September 2023, an agency spokesperson told Fox News Digital. Pinder is currently on administrative leave. (Matias J. Ocner/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service)

Pinder now faces five felony charges, including two counts of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, two counts of attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon and one count of hazing with a deadly weapon.

Jared James and Elijah Dyous, who allegedly helped in the hazing, face the same charges, court records show.

Jared James faces five felony charges after allegedly hazing two prospective fraternity members. (Miami-Dade Corrections)

The three men could not be reached for comment. An attorney reportedly representing Pinder did not respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.

Elijah Dyous was arrested in an alleged Miami hazing incident. (Broward County Sheriff's Office)

Pinder has been employed with the U.S. Secret Service since September 2023, an agency spokesperson told Fox News Digital. Pinder is currently on administrative leave.

"The United States Secret Service takes seriously any criminal misconduct allegations involving one of our employees," said Michael Townsend, special agent in charge of the Secret Service Miami Field Office. "We are fully cooperating with the investigation."

"The Secret Service remains committed to accountability, professionalism, and integrity, and any misconduct will be addressed swiftly and appropriately upon completion of the investigative and judicial process."

The Secret Servie said it is "fully cooperating with the investigation." (AP Photo/Julia Nikhinson, File)

Kappa Alpha Psi is described on the organization's website as a "historically African-American fraternity." The national organization was founded in 1911.

The Richmond-Perrine Alumni Chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi is not affiliated with the University of Miami, Megan Afkham, assistant vice president of university communications, told Fox News Digital in an email.

One of the victims is a University of Miami School of Law student, Afkham said, but the chapter is not connected to the university or its undergraduate chapter.

In a written statement issued by the national Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity, Jimmy McMikle, the organization’s national president, said the organization "maintains a strict zero-tolerance policy on hazing."

title: One of these eight college football teams will be hoisting the national championship trophy in 2026
excerpt: Joel Klatt revealed his way-too-early top 10 for 2026. He explained why the Ohio State Buckeyes landed on this list, and why they will be back on the top end of college football with QB Julian Sayin a...
body_text:
Joel Klatt revealed his way-too-early top 10 for 2026. He explained why the Ohio State Buckeyes landed on this list, and why they will be back on the top end of college football with QB Julian Sayin and WR Jeremiah Smith returning.

At the beginning of every college football season, the age-old adage of "hope springs eternal" rings true for every fanbase.

Every team is 0-0 and all their goals for the coming year are in front of them.

Many programs, coaches, and fanbases all believe they have a chance to win a national title, and in a mathematical sense they aren't wrong.

I'm here to tell you, however, that it's rarely that wide open and, during any given year, only a handful of teams can actually win the whole thing.

This year, I've identified eight teams who I believe can hoist a national championship trophy.

MISSOURI'S ELI DRINKWITZ BECOMES LATEST SEC COACH TO MAKE RIDICULOUS COMPLAINTS ABOUT BIG TEN SCHEDULES

Through some combination of returning production, transfer portal talent, and elite coaching, one of these eight teams will more than likely be the last one standing next January.

Jeremiah Smith #4 of the Ohio State Buckeyes attempts a catch in front of OJ Frederique Jr. #29 of the Miami Hurricanes in the second quarter during the 2025 College Football Playoff Quarterfinal at the 90th Goodyear Cotton Bowl Classic at AT&T Stadium on Dec. 31, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Alex Slitz/Getty Images)

The Ohio State Buckeyes could probably get penciled into this list every year while Ryan Day is their head coach and their talent acquisition stays at the level it's currently at, but this year in particular feels like a big one in Columbus.

Coach Day has assembled a staff consisting largely of former NFL coaches and coordinators, and the addition of offensive coordinator Arthur Smith feels like a particularly noteworthy one to keep an eye on.

The Buckeyes have been recruiting at a top-five level for the past several cycles, and have supplemented that with a small but elite transfer portal class, including bolstering their defense with the likes of Alabama defensive linemen Qua Russaw and James Smith as well as Florida State safety Earl Little Jr.

On offense, Ohio State returns what may end up being the best quarterback-wide receiver tandem in the country, as Julian Sayin looks to build on a quietly brilliant 2025 while Jeremiah Smith could be argued as the best overall player in college football.

An early test on the road against Texas as well as a rematch of the Big Ten Championship in Bloomington against the Hoosiers will tell us everything we need to know about how real the Buckeyes are in 2026.

Texas Longhorns head coach Steve Sarkisian walks into Camping World Stadium ahead of the Citrus Bowl against the Michigan Wolverines in Orlando, Fla., on Dec. 31, 2025. (aAustin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

Speaking of those Longhorns, Texas will be looking to right the wrongs from a disappointing 2025 heading into this year.

Last season, the Horns were a popular preseason national championship pick, but a less than ideal start had them on the outside looking in by season's end.

Texas will likely be near the top of the preseason polls again this year, but unlike in 2025, they know what they have in signal caller Arch Manning.

Manning's first half of last season was forgettable, but by November, you could argue he blossomed into one of the best quarterbacks in the country.

He has the weapons he needs to be truly elite, with receiver Ryan Wingo returning and wideout Cam Coleman coming over from Auburn, so there won't be any excuses for another sputtering start out of the gate in '26.

Texas' defense will be among the best in the country, and veteran leaders like edge rusher Colin Simmons and linebacker Rasheem Biles (both preseason All-Americans) will bolster a fearsome unit.

There has never been a dearth of talent in Austin, but coach Steve Sarkisian may finally have his most complete team since stepping foot on the 40 Acres, and that alone has people starting to feel like it's 2005 in Central Texas again.

Mohamed Toure of the Miami Hurricanes reacts after a stop in the second quarter against the Ohio State Buckeyes during the 2025 College Football Playoff Quarterfinal at the 90th Goodyear Cotton Bowl Classic at AT&T Stadium on Dec. 31, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Stacy Revere/Getty Images)

The Miami Hurricanes were a fourth quarter Carson Beck interception away from winning the national championship in January, but the scary thing is they might be even more dangerous in 2026.

Head coach Mario Cristobal has built a machine in Coral Gables, and the Canes have the most talented roster they've had since the early 2000s.

That's not to say they don't have to replace some absolute studs, particularly along the lines of scrimmage, but Cristobal and co. have recruited well enough in the trenches that this may be a matter of reloading rather than rebuilding.

On the offensive side of the ball, Miami has an embarrassment of riches for offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson to tinker with.

The Canes return wide receiver Malachi Toney and running back Mark Fletcher Jr. from their CFP runner-up squad last season, and they added Duke wide receiver Cooper Barkate, who was one of the most coveted pass catchers in the portal from this past offseason.

The real prize, though, was Duke quarterback Darian Mensah.

Miami will be paying Mensah a pretty penny, but he will be worth every cent of his exorbitant paycheck, as the redshirt junior may end up being the most talented signal caller Cristobal has had while in South Florida.

The schedule is forgivable, even by ACC standards, but a rematch on the road against Notre Dame will separate the Canes as contenders or pretenders.

Indiana Hoosiers head coach Curt Cignetti looks on before the 2025 Big Ten Championship Game against the Ohio State Buckeyes at Lucas Oil Stadium on Dec. 6, 2025. (Robert Goddin/Imagn Images)

It's crazy that I made it halfway through the list without mentioning the defending national champions, but I think coach Curt Cignetti and crew almost like it that way.

Last year, no one outside of the locker room at Memorial Stadium thought this team had a chance to win the whole thing, but the Hoosiers won't be sneaking up on anyone this year.

Cignetti doesn't have a star-studded roster like Miami, Texas, or Ohio State, but that's never stopped him before (obviously) and the talent in Bloomington is only getting better.

The Hoosiers signed a top-ten portal class, and although it was a relatively small class (17 total players) there were some gems to be found.

Quarterback Josh Hoover comes to Indiana by way of TCU, and will look to be the next big thing in Cignetti and offensive coordinator Mike Shanahan's system.

The last transfer quarterback they took ended up becoming a Heisman winner and number 1 overall NFL Draft pick, so Hoover will hope to continue the tradition.

Former Michigan State wide receiver Nick Marsh will give Hoover an elite target to throw to and will pair nicely with returning wideout Charlie Becker, who had a brilliant 2025 campaign averaging nearly 20 yards per catch.

Indiana likely won't be tested until the midway point of the season in a home game against Ohio State, and by then the team should be firing on all cylinders for the second half of the year.

LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin speaks at SEC Football Kickoff Media Day at Tampa Marriott Water Street in Tampa, Fla., on July 23, 2026. (Getty Images)

Of all the teams on this list, the LSU Tigers are the wild card and have the widest range of potential outcomes to consider.

It's no secret the Bayou Bengals went out and got Lane Kiffin to be their head coach, who can be a bit of a wildcard in his own right.

But, when Kiffin is on, he's one of the best in the business at scoring points and talking smack in the process.

Paired with Kiffin is a pair of elite coordinators in Charlie Weis Jr. (OC) and Blake Baker (DC) as well as a rumored $40 million roster.

LANE KIFFIN MAKES RIDICULOUS EXCUSES FOR SEC'S POOR RECENT PERFORMANCE IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

LSU also landed the number one transfer portal class and has studs at plenty of key positions, so conventional wisdom says they will be contenders right out of the gate.

The truth of the matter is, it doesn't always work out that way, and if you told me the Tigers won a national championship or went 7-5, I'd find both outcomes equally believable.

They have the firepower and an elite coaching staff, but they also play a pretty loaded schedule, starting with Clemson Week 1 and getting two more Playoff teams from last season (Ole Miss and Texas A&M) before the calendar even flips to October.

I could easily see them stumbling out of the gate and imploding, but I could also see them catching fire early and riding that wave to the promised land.

LSU can win a national championship in 2026. The question is will they?

Oregon Ducks quarterback Dante Moore (5) looks to pass against the Indiana Hoosiers in the first half of the Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl, a College Football Playoff semifinal, at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia, on Jan. 9, 2026. (Brett Davis/Imagn Images)

Things have gone about as well as one would want when it comes to coach Dan Lanning's time in Eugene.

The 40-year-old head coach is entering his fifth season with the Ducks, and his resume looks pretty stacked by any metric.

He's 48-8, captured the Big Ten title in Oregon's first year in the league, and has won 10 games or more every year he's been the coach there.

But he's missing that one thing to make his list of accomplishments feel more complete: a national championship.

While 2026 isn't championship or bust in the Pacific Northwest, some fans are starting to question if Lanning will ever get it done as a head coach, especially after last season's beatdown at the hands of Indiana in the CFP Semifinals.

This would be the year for him to slay that dragon, though, as Oregon will once again have one of the most talented teams in the country.

The Ducks and Lanning have been an absolute Death Star on the recruiting trail, and this season could be the culmination in all that hard work on the talent acquisition front.

Veteran signal caller Dante Moore eschewed the NFL Draft to come back and lead his team to a natty, and he will have two absolute weapons to throw the football to this coming year.

Sophomore Dakorien Moore, a former five-star recruit in his own right, had a very good freshman year but will be looking to take the next step in 2026, while senior Evan Stewart is back and 100% healthy and ready to show anyone who forgot about him why he was one of the most coveted players in the country when he transferred from Texas A&M two years ago.

On defense, the Ducks boast a trio of preseason All-Americans in defensive back Brandon Finney Jr., linebacker Teitum Tuioti, and defensive lineman A'Mauri Washington who will look to continue the trend of elite defensive play in Eugene.

The talent will have to rise to the top, because Lanning will be replacing both coordinators, as DC Tosh Lupoi and OC Will Stein departed for head coaching jobs at Cal and Kentucky, respectively.

Notre Dame Fighting Irish head coach Marcus Freeman sings the Alma Mater after beating the Boise State Broncos at Notre Dame Stadium on Oct. 4, 2025. (Michael Caterina/Imagn Images)

When Brian Kelly departed South Bend for Baton Rouge nearly five years ago, I thought Notre Dame had seen their peak as a football program in the modern era.

Always the bridesmaid but never the bride, I figured new head coach Marcus Freeman would, at best, keep them in that 10-win/CFP first round exit realm.

Little did I know the former defensive coordinator turned full time head coach would prove me so wrong.

Two years ago, Freeman had the Irish on the doorstep of a national championship, and after a minor setback in 2025, the Golden Domers look to be right back in the thick of things.

This might be Freeman's most talented group of players yet, and it all starts with quarterback CJ Carr.

The offseason buzz around this young man has been Manningesque, and his growth over the second half of last season should be enough proof that those words aren't just hot air.

The Irish have also started recruiting at a championship level, and that should start to bear fruit as early as this season, as Freeman's efforts on the trail have considerably raised both the floor and ceiling of talent on this roster.

Having to replace two first-round draft picks at running back in Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price will be a tall ask, but I think the sum will be greater than the parts for Notre Dame in 2026 and, aside from their opener against Wisconsin, the team will be able to ease into their schedule before their ultimate test on Nov. 7 against Miami.

Georgia quarterback Gunner Stockton (14) carries the ball for a touchdown against Auburn during the second half of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Oct. 11, 2025, in Auburn, Alabama. (AP Photo/Butch Dill)

No list of national championship contenders is complete without Kirby Smart and the Georgia Bulldogs, but they aren't making this roster of teams on the merits of their logo alone.

Georgia recruits better than almost anyone in the country, and the 2026 edition of this roster will feature a ton of former big-time prospects who waited their turn and were developed the old-fashioned way.

That includes quarterback Gunner Stockton, who has a ton of experience and a very solid 2025 campaign to build off of.

The third-team All-SEC selection will have a familiar face in offensive coordinator Mike Bobo coaching him up and will be able to lean on a fantastic running back in Nate Frazier as well as a trio of all-conference offensive linemen.

The defense will look to return to form as a vintage Kirby Smart unit, led by defensive backs KJ Bolden and Ellis Robinson, both of whom were tabbed as preseason first-team All-SEC selections by the media.

The Dawgs have a tricky six-game stretch in the middle of the season, starting at home against Oklahoma and featuring road games against Alabama and Ole Miss along the way.

It remains to be seen just how high the ceiling will be for this Georgia team in 2026, but they have the requisite talent and a coach who has been to the mountaintop twice in recent history, so count the Bulldogs out at your own risk.

title: Heart-shaped Las Vegas resort gets green light as critics roast wild design online
excerpt:
Rick Harrison of "Pawn Stars" tells Fox News Digital that Las Vegas casinos need to lower prices as tourism drops 7.5%. He credits his own record-breaking months to customer experience.

Nevada offici...
body_text:
Rick Harrison of "Pawn Stars" tells Fox News Digital that Las Vegas casinos need to lower prices as tourism drops 7.5%. He credits his own record-breaking months to customer experience.

Nevada officials unanimously approved plans for a heart-shaped resort hotel and recreational venue on the far south end of the Las Vegas Strip — and the unusual design is already attracting plenty of attention online.

The Clark County Zoning Commission unanimously approved plans for the proposed heart-shaped resort last week, Fox 5 Las Vegas reported.

The development is proposed on about 12 acres east of Las Vegas Boulevard South, between Mandalay Bay Road and Four Seasons Drive near Haven Street.

BARGAIN BUFFET REFUSES TO DIE WHILE LUXURY DINING TAKES OVER VEGAS

Planners trimmed the project's scope to a height of 317 feet and 752 hotel rooms, down from the original proposal of 406 feet and 874 rooms, according to industry publication NVBEX.

Renderings show the project — which doesn't have an official public name yet — centered around a massive, illuminated heart-shaped hotel tower, with a casino, restaurants and retail space spread across the base of the development.

Fox News Digital reached out to Steelman Partners, the project's architectural firm, for comment.

Nevada officials unanimously approved plans for a proposed heart-shaped resort hotel and entertainment destination on the south end of the Las Vegas Strip, seen above. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

The concept is planned as a "pedestrian entertainment corridor," Fox 5 Las Vegas reported.

During the meeting, officials said the site has changed little since the early 2000s, after a previous proposal to build a Ferris wheel stalled.

LAS VEGAS OFFICIALS WEIGH BANNING CRIMINAL OFFENDERS FROM STRIP TO REVIVE TOURISM

On a Reddit forum dedicated to Las Vegas, reactions to the proposal were mixed, with many users criticizing or mocking the design.

"It honestly looks so ugly," one person wrote.

The proposed resort would occupy about 12 acres east of Las Vegas Boulevard South, adding another large-scale hospitality project to the rapidly evolving southern Strip. (iStock)

"We just need a diamond, spade and club hotel," another joked.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

A third user wrote, "This design would make a great 3-story wedding chapel, but not a 29-story hotel."

Officials said the site has seen little development in recent decades, creating an opportunity for a major new hospitality project on the south end of the Las Vegas Strip. (iStock)

Others embraced the over-the-top concept.

"I like this better than the guitar," one commenter wrote, an apparent reference to the guitar-shaped Hard Rock Hotel currently under construction on the Strip and set to replace the Mirage.

"It better bring back heart-shaped tubs and those heart-shaped love beds," another person quipped.

The proposal comes as Vegas continues its shift toward a more upscale tourism market. (Getty Images)

"You guys wanted more theme[d] hotels," another person said. "Here you go."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The proposal comes as Las Vegas continues its shift toward a more upscale tourism market, with luxury hotels, premium dining and major events playing a larger role in the city’s economy.

That transformation has also brought higher costs for visitors, with travelers increasingly voicing frustration over resort fees, expensive meals and rising hotel prices, Fox News Digital previously reported.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: ‘A control freak with a terrible temper’: James Desborough convicted of triple murder
excerpt:
Man already serving life for killing his cellmate while awaiting trial also murdered and dismembered his friends Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman

On a spring day last year, James Desborough marche...
body_text:
Man already serving life for killing his cellmate while awaiting trial also murdered and dismembered his friends Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman

On a spring day last year, James Desborough marched up to Cornwall’s county hall in Truro and began bombarding the offices with dozens of eggs stolen from a supermarket.

It was a drug and drink-addled protest at his plight – homeless, jobless and generally angry at the world. He expected to be arrested and messaged a friend: “If I’m going to get nicked, might as well round the charges up.”

He certainly did that. In the weeks and months after the egg incident, Desborough committed three murders.

He killed two vulnerable friends, Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, whose dismembered and burnt bodies were found in woodland close to a shack where he sometimes lived off-grid in south Cornwall.

Then while awaiting trial, he murdered Steven Kempster, his cellmate in Exeter prison, strangling him to death because he was annoyed with some of his habits.

Desborough, 40, is already serving a life sentence for the prison killing. After a jury at Winchester crown court convicted him of murdering his two friends, he may never be released, putting him on a par with serial killers such as Rose West who are expected to spend the rest of their lives behind bars.

Acquaintances have said Desborough was a control freak with a terrible temper – he has an old conviction for GBH – and was furious at what he saw as his bad luck in life. A civil engineer by profession and a father, he had fallen on hard times.

Quite what tipped him over into an explosion of violence is unclear. He used Aquilino’s and Coleman’s bank cards after he killed them, but police do not believe it was a simple matter of theft.

The prosecutor in his trial, Ahmed Hossain KC, put it to Desborough that he might have killed them because he considered them worthless, deserving to die because of their troubled lifestyle and because they were “dinlos” – a local slang term for fools. Had he simply got annoyed with them and snapped? “I thought they were OK,” he replied in court. “They were good friends.”

The trial has certainly put the focus on a different Cornwall to the one most holidaymakers to the county love.

It highlighted not surfing beaches and historic landscapes, but the deep-rooted social issues that make life for many in the far south-west of England difficult. There are pockets of serious deprivation in Cornwall where people experience homelessness and addiction problems.

Desborough, Aquilino and Coleman were among those who – in the words of the defence barrister, Sean Brunton KC – had slipped through the cracks in society.

The three got to know each other when they lived in a hostel for homeless people in the seaside resort of Newquay.

In the months before he died, Aquilino, 57, was taking hard drugs, suffering from depression and subjected to “cuckooing”, in which dealers take over the home of a vulnerable person.

Coleman, 43, abused alcohol and had cirrhosis. He had been kidnapped and stabbed at the age of 13, leaving him with post traumatic stress disorder.

The police were first called in after Coleman was reported missing. He had last been seen on 3 June 2025, drinking with Desborough.

Police thought they had solved the case quickly when they found a body in woodland between Truro and the village of Probus.

It turned out not be Coleman though, or Aquilino, but a third man, Lee Hockey, who had vanished from Truro. Police believe he too may have been murdered, but have not linked his death to Desborough.

Attention began to focus on Paramoor Woods, near Sticker, once a mining settlement now popular with people who work in the town of St Austell.

Desborough had inherited land there from his grandfather and built a shack, though, to his frustration, he did not have the correct planning permission and had been told by the council that he was not allowed to live there permanently.

He would let homeless friends camp there, grew cannabis and had a “stash tree” where he hid class A drugs in a hollow. Machetes, knives and saws were also scattered around the property.

Police searched the woods for five months, eventually finding the remains of Coleman and Aquilino. The latter had last been seen alive on 18 April 2025, also drinking with Desborough.

Codenamed Operation Honeyfall, the search was extraordinary. More than 700 officers and scientists were involved, with Devon and Cornwall police drawing on resources from five other forces. Dog teams, soil experts and anthropologists were brought in.

The weather was very hot and the nature of the terrain jungle-like and boggy. Officers sometimes had to wade through water up to their chests as they searched.

In excess of 1,900 burnt bone fragments – Aquilino’s remains – were discovered in a stream, while Coleman’s charred body parts were found in a shallow grave. A hatchet hung on a nearby tree.

Another unusual feature was that Desborough kept a beady eye on the search. Before there was enough evidence to remand him in custody, he hung around, at one point telling a forensic biologist that he liked the dismemberment scenes in the serial killer show Dexter.

Sometimes officers smelled burning and at other times heard digging, perhaps as Desborough tried to destroy evidence.

As well as discovering the victims’ remains, police came upon notes and plans Desborough had made that suggested he may have been planning to change his appearance through plastic surgery after the murders and flee the UK, perhaps to south-east Asia.

Detectives also discovered he had used his victims’ bank cards to buy goods and services, including a roast beef dinner soon after cutting up Coleman’s body.

He was eventually charged with the two murders and held in Exeter prison sharing a cell with Kempster, who had been jailed for drunkenly suffocating his 91-year-old father in north Devon.

Desborough’s appearance in the witness box was remarkable. He was considered so dangerous that he was handcuffed to an officer when he was moved from the dock to the main area of the court.

He was articulate when speaking about his time as a civil engineer and building regulations concerning his cabin, but he was less certain when he told the story of finding the bodies of Aquilino and Coleman.

He claimed he had come upon one hanging in a tree, the other naked in a stream. It was, in his words, a “series of unfortunate circumstances”.

Desborough repeatedly denying killing the pair, but accepted burning and hiding their bodies while high on ketamine and drinking tequila.

During the trial there was a suggestion that Desborough might have carried on killing, murdering members of his circle who could have implicated him in the deaths of his friends or who simply annoyed him.

In one note, he had written: “I’m a killer and ready to execute any predators.” In another, headed “bug out” – military slang for a retreat – he set out what appeared to be escape plans but added: “Take out the remaining muppets.”

title: NFL legend praises Sophie Cunningham for saying 'what's true' about transgender athletes in girls sports
excerpt:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher praises Sophie Cunningham for her stance against transgender athletes participating in girls' and women's sports.

Brian Urlacher is hardly a WNBA fan, but th...
body_text:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher praises Sophie Cunningham for her stance against transgender athletes participating in girls' and women's sports.

Brian Urlacher is hardly a WNBA fan, but the NFL legend cannot help but watch Sophie Cunningham.

"She’s great. Bro, she’s so fun to watch... It’s unbelievable. She’s so aggressive. She’s fun to watch. I follow her on Instagram. She’s got great stuff out there," the former Chicago Bears linebacker told Fox News Digital in a recent interview.

But now, Urlacher is an even bigger fan of the Indiana Fever guard.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham brings the ball up court against the Connecticut Sun on July 22, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Urlacher told Fox News Digital last month that he follows the transgender-athlete issue "closely," so when Cunningham said "young girls...shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sports, Urlacher was ecstatic.

"She just says what’s true. She says common-sense things, and she gets so much backlash. She’s like, 'Men should not be playing in women’s sports.' Why is that so controversial? I don’t get it. I don’t understand it," Urlacher said.

The Hall of Famer also praised Cunningham for continuing to stand by her sentiments.

"It’s a simple statement. She stood by it. That’s what I love about when people say things: Don’t back down. If you say something, stand by it. And she said it. She backed it up. She’s not backing down, no matter how much heat she gets from certain people," Urlacher said.

"It’s an 80-20 issue. Eighty percent of the country thinks it’s true. The 20% is crushing her. Let them. Who cares? But I love that she didn’t back down. I love everything she stands for. She plays hard. She’s good. Like I said, I don’t watch the WNBA, but I like those two girls (Cunningham and Caitlin Clark) right there."

Indiana Fever superstars Sophie Cunningham and Caitlin Clark are arguably the two most popular players in the WNBA. (NBAE via Getty Images)

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS' SPORTS

Urlacher also noted that Cunningham probably took a risk in expressing her opinion, given that her peers are largely liberal or part of the gay community.

"It’s a liberal and mostly gay league, which is fine. I have no problem. My daughter is gay. No problem. I’ve got no problem with that... But man, what do you do, right? She said what she said. I cannot disagree with her," he said.

Since her comments surfaced, Cunningham has received support online from various Republican lawmakers and advocates for women's sports, including Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Eric Schmitt, R-Mo.

"I'll always believe in that. It's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category," Cunningham said last week.

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham reacts after scoring during the second half of a WNBA game against the Seattle Storm on Sunday, May 17, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"I'm not a very political person, but I do have beliefs. I have morals, and I'll always stand on those."

OutKick's Alejandro Avila contributed to this report.

title: Black people’s risk factors for stroke ‘rising faster than for white people’
excerpt:
Exclusive: King’s College London analysis finds diabetes and hypertension are more common in Black African and Caribbean people

Stroke risk factors including high blood pressure and diabetes are risi...
body_text:
Exclusive: King’s College London analysis finds diabetes and hypertension are more common in Black African and Caribbean people

Stroke risk factors including high blood pressure and diabetes are rising faster among people from Black African and Caribbean backgrounds compared with their white counterparts, according to analysis.

Researchers at King’s College London analysed data from more than 8,500 adults over a 30-year period from the South London Stroke Register, one of the longest-running population-based stroke registers in the world.

The study found that while the prevalence of stroke risk factors, including diabetes and hypertension, were increasing faster among Black people, people from Black African backgrounds were also twice as likely to experience stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis than white people, at a rate of 12% compared with 6%. About one in six people across the UK will have a stroke in their lifetime.

Diabetes was about twice as common in Black Caribbean and Black Africans on the stroke register compared with white participants, and high blood pressure was 29% more prevalent in Black Caribbean and 47% more prevalent in Black African people. Although diabetes rates increased for all ethnic groups over the 30-year study period, they increased most rapidly among Black African participants, rising from 21% between 1995 and 2004 to 41% between 2015 and 2024.

Dr Eva Emmett, a research fellow at King’s College London and the lead author of the study, said: “Our study shows that the prevalence of pre-stroke hypertension and diabetes is higher and increasing faster in ethnic minority and lower socioeconomic groups. Together with Black people’s younger age at stroke and higher likelihood of having a stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis, these findings call for targeted and earlier primary prevention efforts.

“NHS health checks, which screen for hypertension and diabetes, begin at the age of 40. However, this may be too late for higher-risk groups who often experience stroke at a younger age.”

She called for “universal improvements in cardiovascular risk detection” as well as more targeted prevention strategies, such as younger screening age for those most at risk.

The data also revealed socioeconomic disparities among the study’s participants. The prevalence of diabetes was 23% higher in participants with manual occupations, such as bus drivers, security guards and plumbers, compared with those in non-manual employment such as teachers and nurses. Diabetes prevalence was also 21% higher in those with lower education levels.

While diabetes diagnoses increased in all socioeconomic groups over time, the greatest increases were seen in those with routine and manual jobs and with lower education levels. Similarly, high blood pressure rates increased the most in those with lower socioeconomic status.

Dr Maëva May, the director of policy at the Stroke Association, said the findings were a stark reminder that “the benefits of prevention are not being felt equally”.

“Too many people from Black African and Black Caribbean communities, and those living in more deprived circumstances, are developing stroke risk factors earlier and are experiencing stroke before those risks have even been identified,” May said.

“Stroke is not inevitable. Many strokes can be prevented by finding and treating conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes early, but that only works if people can access the right care at the right time. Preventing stroke means preventing inequalities in who gets the opportunity to stay well.”

title: Young people ‘expected’ to engage with new work support, says McFadden
excerpt:
Exclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he unveils funds to stop families in England losing benefits

Young people will be expected to engage with new support to seek work, Pat M...
body_text:
Exclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he unveils funds to stop families in England losing benefits

Young people will be expected to engage with new support to seek work, Pat McFadden has said, as he unveiled funds to stop families losing benefits when teenagers take up apprenticeships.

Speaking to the Guardian, the work and pensions secretary echoed the comments of Andy Burnham when he suggested that access to support would be conditional on young people properly participating in the support that would be provided.

“We have an obligation to put good support in place,” he said. “And then there is an expectation that people engage with the support.”

McFadden – one of the few ministers to keep his job in the reshuffle when Burnham became prime minister – said the new bursary would compensate for a quirk in the system that could mean families lose some benefits if a teenager took up an apprenticeship.

The penalty – where the family loses the child component of universal credit – is most likely to affect single parents or disabled teenagers under 18.

The policy is the second key announcement from Burnham as he seeks to address the crisis of mounting unemployment among young people – after stating on Tuesday morning he would seek fundamental changes in the education system to emphasise technical and vocational skills, especially those relevant to local businesses.

Both Burnham and McFadden have said they are also determined to reform the welfare system, especially by providing more opportunities for young people on long-term sickness benefits to return to the workforce.

The prime minister also said on Monday he wanted to change the nature of the support and make some of it “conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them … So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits”.

McFadden said the bursary was part of removing those unintended barriers on young people taking up work – £30m funded through the current departmental budget – but added it was crucial that young people responded to the support on offer.

“The key to it is to remove this barrier to opportunity really,” he said. “And to stop people being trapped in the benefit system when they would otherwise take up an opportunity which is in their interest, which would put them on to the next step of a career path.

“These cliff edges are never created by design, they’re just in a big complex system, they are just there and I’m very grateful to the charities and campaigners who drew this to our attention.”

Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts to benefits to get the welfare bill down … Often that just pushes people into even more crisis and then even more public spending in another part of the system.”

McFadden said there would be a significant system redesign when the second stage report from social security minister, Stephen Timms, and disability campaigners reports back in the autumn. An interim has already found that the criteria for personal independence payments was not fit for purpose.

“We’ll need a whole government response, not just a [Department for Work and Pensions] response, because the issues affecting young people go way beyond the boundaries of the DWP, if you take mental health issues among young people, that’s obviously going way beyond the DWP,” he said.

The government is also expected to receive the second part of Alan Milburn’s review this autumn – looking at growing youth unemployment and lack of engagement with education and training.

McFadden said that welfare reform would mean both “opportunities and expectations”. He said: “We are trying to get the system to ask: ‘How do we help you live your fullest life? How do we maximise your opportunities?’

“One of the things that struck me about the benefits system is how sticky it is, how when people get on to these long-term benefits they tend to stay in them for a long time.”

The new bursaries of about £4,500 will be offered to families – particularly single parents with a disabled child – where they could otherwise lose approximately £80 a week because the apprenticeship salary is lower than the lost benefits.

Charities have welcomed plans for the new bursary but warned that young people needed to be directly made aware of its existence by potential employers.

Enver Solomon, the CEO of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “If more young people are to take up apprenticeships, it is vital their family isn’t worse off so introducing a new bursary is a welcome step towards narrowing the income gap.

“As the new scheme is rolled out, the government must ensure it is as easy as possible for young people to apply, and that nobody loses out because they were not directed towards support.

“We know in families where wages should outweigh benefit payments there can still be real difficulty as payments shift from parents to young people who have to take on the responsibility of contributing to overall household income.”

title: Guardian Essential poll: Angus Taylor’s approval rating crashes and One Nation support plateaus
excerpt:
Survey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost of living crisis

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation’s primary...
body_text:
Survey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost of living crisis

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation’s primary vote has plateaued and Angus Taylor’s approval rating has crashed, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll.

But it is not all smooth sailing for Labor with Australians rubbishing the government’s handling of the inflation and cost of living crisis.

Australians have also shown their reluctance to embrace new AI datacentres, with less than a third saying they’d be happy to have a facility in their local area and sharing concerns about energy demands, water supply, environmental impacts and noise.

The Guardian Essential poll, of 1,060 voters last week, found One Nation’s popularity was continuing to level off, attracting a 25% primary vote, down one point from June’s poll. Meanwhile while Labor’s indicative primary vote ticked up one point to 31% and the Coalition’s vote dropped further, down another point to 22%.

All those movements are within the poll’s margin of error, but it is the second consecutive Essential poll where One Nation’s primary vote has dropped since reaching a high of 28% in May. The populist right-wing party has dipped back to where it was in April. It comes after weeks of scrutiny over Pauline Hanson’s European trip, her interview with Tommy Robinson, and comments about domestic violence and immigration policy.

Struggling for political oxygen and attention amidst One Nation’s rise, the opposition leader has seen his own approval ratings plummet in the last month. In June, 36% of people approved of Taylor’s job performance and 37% disapproved, for a net approval of minus-1; but this month’s poll has seen his approvals drop three points and his disapprovals increase by seven points, for a new net approval of minus-12.

Taylor’s approval rating has crashed 16 points among men and four points among women, as well as by 20 points among people aged 35-54 and 13 points among those aged 18-34.

Anthony Albanese’s approval rating ticked up one point to minus-14, with 38% approving and 52% disapproving of his performance as prime minister. It’s the fourth straight month in which more than half of voters have disapproved of his performance.

Respondents to the poll also rejected Labor’s handling of the inflation and cost of living crisis, with a decisive 64% rating the government’s performance as poor; while just 16% of Australians rated it as good.

Nearly 80% of voters said cost of living and inflation was one of the most important issues to them, far and away the most-cited issue among respondents. Next most-cited was Medicare and health (50%), crime (42%) and immigration (35%).

But only 39% of voters rated the Labor government’s performance on Medicare and health as good, with 30% saying poor; on crime, 22% rated Labor as good and 50% as poor, while 24% rated Labor as good on immigration and another 50% as poor.

“Cost of living remains the stand-out issue for voters and the government’s handling of inflation is being rated down,” the executive director of Essential Media, Peter Lewis, said.

On managing technology and AI, the subject of a major speech by Albanese earlier this month, 29% rated Labor’s performance as good and 30% as poor.

The Essential report found only 28% of voters would support a new datacentre being built in their area, with 37% against. Men (34% support and 34% oppose) were far more supportive of new datacentres than women (22% support and 39% oppose).

Asked about their reservations about datacentre development, 61% raised concerns about impact on energy demand and power prices, and another 44% were worried about water supply.

Environmental impacts and noise were raised by 41% of voters, while 39% had general concerns about the growth of AI generally.

Albanese this month announced plans to more strongly regulate datacentres and AI, particularly setting rules for power and water use, and building social license for the construction of facilities.

title: Royal commission into Victorian construction sector could boost Labor’s chances at state election, expert says
excerpt:
Commission promised by new premier would be an ‘important signal’ for voters that the government was acting on alleged corruption

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victoria...
body_text:
Commission promised by new premier would be an ‘important signal’ for voters that the government was acting on alleged corruption

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victorian voters heading to the polls will probably get a taste of the evidence heard by a royal commission – including how taxpayer funds were used on Big Build projects – but it could actually help Labor’s standing, an integrity expert says.

William Partlett, an associate professor of law and a fellow at the Centre for Public Integrity, said the commission promised by the new premier, Ben Carroll, would be an “important signal” for voters that the government was taking action.

Shortly after being sworn in on Tuesday, Carroll said the creation of a royal commission into the construction sector would be his “first action” as premier. This follows sustained pressure to investigate alleged corruption on the government’s Big Build infrastructure projects.

Carroll said the commission’s terms of reference would be “exhaustive”, and it would be established “as soon as possible”, suggesting it could hold hearings before November’s state election.

“Whether it’s the top-tier companies, whether it’s subcontractors, whether it’s businesses or unions, these terms of reference will be thorough,” the premier said.

Carroll also said a special prosecutor would be appointed to work in parallel to the royal commission, and that the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission will be bolstered with follow-the-money powers.

It comes after his predecessor, Jacinta Allan, had resisted calls for a royal commission into allegations that organised crime figures and bikie gangs infiltrated major infrastructure projects, including the Big Build.

Partlett told Guardian Australia the decision to hold a royal commission was not surprising, given the pressure the former premier was under from the Labor caucus over the issue.

“In some ways it was probably the downfall of [Allan] in her failure to call that because it did seem that many wanted that to be called,” Partlett said.

The Big Build is the state’s infrastructure program that has, since 2015, given about $109bn in public money for more than 180 projects, including the Metro Tunnel, level crossing removals and the Suburban Rail Loop.

Many of the projects had suffered cost blowouts, which Allan had previously said was due to inflation, supply chain disruptions and rising labour costs. Her claims came in response to reporting by the Age that money from the projects was being paid to gangland figures, and alleged union corruption was adding premiums of up to 30% to major project budgets.

Allan later acknowledged there had been criminality in the projects but said it was best for police to investigate any allegations of wrongdoing.

A report by the Centre for Public Integrity’s director, Geoffrey Watson SC, tabled during a Queensland inquiry into the CFMEU, found that “the flood of government money” had made the Big Build “ripe for corruption”.

That included “ad hoc corruption on the part of former organisers and delegates” as well as “a more organised or systemic corruption involving collaboration by some elements in the CFMEU with outlaw motorcycle gangs and other crime outfits,” Watson wrote.

The report stated a labourer’s job on the Big Build was so lucrative that a market was allegedly created where corrupt organisers and delegates bought and sold the jobs, and alleged the government “knew and had a duty to know” about wrongdoing but chose to do “nothing about it”.

Partlett said the terms of reference for the commission need to be “as broad as they can be” to include private organisations, the unions, institutions and government officials. The commission should also use its coercive powers to get to the bottom of the allegations in an open and transparent way, he said.

He said it was important that the commission begin sooner rather than later, and would have some potential impact on the election.

“The fact that the Labor party now is showing that it has interest in tackling these issues is an important signal … they are willing to accept something has gone wrong.”

Partlett said Labor getting in before the election allows them to set the terms of reference, and no one in the integrity sector would like to see it turn into “a demonisation of unions”.

“They can make it an inquiry into the construction sector that is done in a responsible way. It doesn’t demonise the unions, but then at the same time tries to understand what went wrong here.”

title: Anger at Labor as Rex Patrick faces potential six-figure legal fee if he loses Aukus documents battle
excerpt:
Australian government insists legal costs should be paid by former senator as FoI fight escalates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The government will insist Rex Patrick p...
body_text:
Australian government insists legal costs should be paid by former senator as FoI fight escalates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The government will insist Rex Patrick pays up to $150,000 to cover its legal costs if he loses a fight to access documents about the Aukus agreement, escalating a battle in which several crossbench MPs have swung behind the former senator.

The transparency campaigner has used freedom of information laws to seek details on where nuclear waste from the submarine fleet will be stored, and won an administrative appeal on the matter in May.

But the Department of Industry, Science and Resources has appealed the matter to the federal court, seeking the decision be overturned and an order for Patrick to pay the government’s legal costs if he loses.

Politicians including Jacqui Lambie and Pauline Hanson have lashed the decision, warning it is a breach of rules requiring the government to act as a model litigant.

They, along with unions and transparency groups, have made appeals to the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, but have been rebuffed.

According to documents seen by Guardian Australia, Rowland last week said the government could rightly insist on Patrick being required to pay costs if he loses, acting “firmly and properly” to protect its interests.

Rowland wrote to a group of crossbenchers – including independents Helen Haines, David Pocock and the Greens’ David Shoebridge – saying the industry department was responsible for conduct of the case.

The department does not accept the model litigant rules prevent it from seeking costs from Patrick. Previous legal fights have seen fees of much as $150,000.

Lambie has accused Rowland of “behaving like a Labor stooge”.

“The government is sending a very clear message to people: stop when we say you can’t have information under FoI, or we’ll take you to court and you could lose all your savings … and maybe your house,” she said.

“I cannot believe the attorney general has handballed what is a whole-of-government principle issue to the secretary of a single department. The attorney is behaving like a Labor stooge, and either doesn’t have any leadership within her or doesn’t care. So which one is it?

“This issue is not going to just go away.”

Organisations including the Media Entertainment & Arts Alliance, the Grata Fund, the Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom and Australian Democracy Network have all called on the government to stop the legal challenge.

Tosca Lloyd, a Whistleblower Justice Fund campaigner, said the risk of a six-figure legal bill would limit ordinary use of FoI rules.

“This chilling effect is neither hypothetical nor unintentional,” she said.

“Public interest journalism depends on the FoI system. Investigative reporters – especially those at smaller and independent outlets – use it constantly to uncover stories the public has a right to know.

“If the cost of challenging a bad government decision is federal court litigation, most newsrooms simply won’t take that risk. The stories then won’t get told. That’s a loss for all of us.”

Bill Browne, the Australia Institute’s Democracy & Accountability program director, said departments and ministers should not fight FoI applicants.

“The Albanese government already tried to restrict Australians’ right to access government information, and was rebuffed by the Senate. This looks like another attempt to raise the cost of scrutinising the government.”

Patrick said legal precedent dating back to a 1912 high court decision showed a “standard of fair play” should be observed by governments.

“I have some experience in courtrooms and have asked the court to ensure fairness from government and that these laws will be decided with competent barristers arguing different sides of the secrecy/transparency questions before it,” he said.

“I can just hope that the courts will address the misguided sense of fairness and proper process exhibited by the attorney general.”

A spokesperson for Rowland declined to comment, referring questions to the department.

title: The professor facing prison in ‘antifa’ case: ‘They want to scare all who oppose ICE’
excerpt:
Erik Davis is accused by the government of a ‘conspiracy’ to obstruct ICE – experts say it’s part of a pattern to criminalize lawful organizing and ruin activists’ lives

Erik Davis was driving to a m...
body_text:
