title: Why has Iran’s economy not collapsed under US war pressure?
excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Millions of people across Iran are struggling for livelihood and survival, but the country’s embattled economy is still far from a state of collapse despite five months of war with the ...
body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Millions of people across Iran are struggling for livelihood and survival, but the country’s embattled economy is still far from a state of collapse despite five months of war with the United States.

The vast and resource-rich country of more than 92 million people has developed a relatively diversified domestic economy for a major oil exporter, as the authorities over decades leaned on self-sufficiency in the face of harsh economic embargoes and confrontation with the US, Israel and the West.

Water-intensive agriculture, manufacturing and services have reduced total reliance on oil, while shadowy oil transfers, cross-border trade, maritime networks and a large informal labour market have helped keep the economy resilient.

Still, the population has paid a huge price by having to absorb much of the strain. More than a decade of all-encompassing sanctions, as well as two wars since June last year, nationwide protests during which thousands were killed and several state-imposed internet shutdowns in the past year, have only made it more difficult to earn a living wage and have a future outlook.

Welfare economist Hadi Kahalzadeh said he defines collapse as famine and the state losing the ability to pay its employees and deliver basic services. In that sense, the economy has not collapsed.

“And I don’t think the combination of war, blockade and sanctions, as painful as it’s been, gets us there anytime soon,” the non-resident fellow at the Quincy Institute and research fellow at Brandeis University’s Center for Global Development and Sustainability in Massachusetts told Al Jazeera.

That combination has pushed up inflation to about 90 percent, with one of the highest food inflation rates in the world more than tripling prices of many staples such as meat, eggs and cooking oil over the past year while wages quickly fall behind.

Imported goods constantly become more expensive too as the national currency continues to sink to new lows against the US dollar, while the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the launch of the US-Israel war in late February blocks fresh supplies.

Kahalzadeh said the fact that economic shocks are often absorbed through inflation and currency depreciation preserves some incentive to import and produce, which keeps goods on the shelves but makes them increasingly unaffordable.

“That keeps the system functioning, but it dumps the cost directly onto households,” said Kahalzadeh. “Then the state tries to soften that with cash transfers and subsidies. It’s an expensive way to survive, but it does avoid collapse.”

The monthly minimum wage is less than $100 and the government offers a monthly cash subsidy and electronic coupons for essential goods, amounting to a few more dollars.

Government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said during a news conference on Tuesday that the government has belatedly managed to pay designated shops in the coupons scheme. But stores have not received the money because several major banks remain disrupted more than a month after authorities said they faced major cyberattacks.

She also highlighted infrastructure damage inflicted by the US during the latest round of bombing this month, saying 12 bridges and two tunnels were struck and parts of Iran’s natural gas production and electricity generation capacity were lost. Mohajerani said it was a “valuable achievement” showing government resolve that manufacturing industries are set to have two days of blackouts per week, instead of the previously projected three days.

A 2025 report by the Saba Pension Strategies Institute, a think tank affiliated with Iran’s state-run pension fund, said that while a little more than 30 percent of Iranians lived below the poverty line five years ago, that rate was projected to have reached 45 percent this year – and was still rising.

Mohammad Reza Farzanegan, a professor of the Economics of the Middle East at Germany’s Philipps-Universitat Marburg, said “endemic corruption” that reduces productivity, weakens institutions and rewards political connections rather than efficiency is the most serious internal threat to the Iranian economy.

Oil incomes have allowed the government to conceal some of the deficiencies and postpone consequences. But they have also encouraged rent-seeking and overdependence on the state, which has weakened the private sector and reduced incentives for innovation and long-term investment, he told Al Jazeera.

“Households reduce consumption, firms postpone investment and educated workers consider emigration. The economy continues to function, but at the cost of a shrinking middle class, lower capital formation, weaker public services and declining confidence in the future,” said Farzanegan.

Zabihollah Khodaeian, head of the General Inspection Organisation of Iran, told state television on Sunday that some of the “trustees” designated by Iran’s top authorities, including the Supreme National Security Council, to bring back proceeds from selling crude oil and other products under sanctions, “betrayed” the country and took the money for themselves.

He said the so-called trustees currently hold at least $11bn, of which $1.6bn has been “misused”.

He said some are still in Iran under arrest, while others fled, including one person who stole more than $200m. But the official did not name any offenders or say anything about whether there will be legal ramifications for those who appointed the offenders as trustees.

Khodaeian also said there are more than 20,000 exporters who have to repatriate 94 billion euros (nearly $107bn) in export yields to the country by law, but have failed to do so. They include 225 unnamed individuals with more than 50 million euros (nearly $57m) in foreign currency commitments each.

Kahalzadeh, the welfare economist, said prolonged sanctions have completely reshaped Iran’s socioeconomic pyramid.

“In 2011, the middle class made up the majority of the population. Today, it has become a minority. At the same time, people who were once a minority, the poor and those vulnerable to poverty, now account for roughly 70 percent of the population,” he said, adding that this trend will continue.

In the capital, Tehran, and many cities and villages across the country, that means meat and dairy disappearing from household diets, medical treatments postponed, rents paid late and many salaries failing to last days, let alone weeks.

“Even if inflation later comes down or economic growth returns, the damage will not disappear quickly. Once families lose their savings, assets, health, educational opportunities and sense of middle-class security, rebuilding them takes many years,” said Kahalzadeh.

Iran and the US continue to communicate messages through mediators, and have largely suspended military action, but the conflict has now spread to the Red Sea and the Caspian Sea while tensions remain high in the Strait of Hormuz.

Philipps-Universitat Marburg’s Farzanegan said with the sanctions and the threat of conflict remaining in place, domestic economic reforms alone cannot generate a sustained recovery.

“Even if the political system survives, the economy may remain chronically sick,” he said, adding that economic relations with China, Russia and neighbouring countries may provide temporary breathing space but cannot fully replace international ties,” said Farzanegan.

“The most important economic policy is therefore the reduction of geopolitical risk through diplomacy. Without a stable environment, the Iranian economy may continue to survive, but it will have little chance of genuine recovery.”

title: First Thing: Pentagon accused of disrespecting war dead as Trump threatens to resume Iran war
excerpt:
Controversial move to classify Iran war as two separate campaigns criticised as attempt to minimise casualty figures. Plus, the man who started an animal shelter after a dog saved his life

Don’t alre...
body_text:
Controversial move to classify Iran war as two separate campaigns criticised as attempt to minimise casualty figures. Plus, the man who started an animal shelter after a dog saved his life

Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. A controversial move by the Pentagon to reclassify casualties in the Iran war as being killed in “overseas 0perations” is being taken by US military veterans as a sign of disrespect for the dead.

Michael E Smith, a retired US rear admiral who completed combat tours in Iraq, Bosnia and Kosovo, said: “It’s such a huge disrespect for the families. To claim that they weren’t killed as a result of the war – oh, it was just overseas operations – is just ludicrous.”

The change came as Donald Trump once again warned that the US would return to “strong military action” against Iran if diplomatic efforts did not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East. “We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.”

What changes did the Department of Defense make? The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), a military database for displaying casualties, introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7”. That splits the count from the beginning of the US-Israel war on Iran into effectively two different campaigns.

How is the administration justifying the change? The War Powers Act of 1973 requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension, which it has not. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation.

The Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said his comments that progressives need to put the head of an “ogre” on a pike was in reference to the US senator John Fetterman – not his opponent, representative Haley Stevens. The comments drew immediate backlash from several high-profile Democrats and charges of sexism by those who believed the remark was a reference to Stevens.

El-Sayed claimed he had been speaking of supporting a primary challenge to Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat who campaigned as a progressive but has moved to the right since taking office. “I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman, who’s a senator from Pennsylvania who has done terrible things, got elected on a set of values, and is now completely throwing those values in the mud.”

A US airman accused of a “spree” of rapes and sexual assaults in England, drugging some women and breaking into the homes of others, was able to avoid English justice after local police handed over part of the case to the American military.

Two British women went to Suffolk police in August 2019 to allege that James Loubeau and another US airman had drugged and raped them. Less than two weeks later, Suffolk police allowed the US air force to take responsibility for investigating the two alleged rapes. It has since emerged that Loubeau, 38, allegedly attacked a total of six women in East Anglia over a four-month period in 2019, in what US prosecutors described as a “frightening and dangerous” pattern of assaults.

The Trump administration has asked the supreme court to clear the way for an executive order from Donald Trump that could dramatically change mail-in voting. The emergency appeal comes after an appeals court upheld a ruling blocking the president’s order in nearly half the country ahead of November’s midterm elections.

What is the president attempting to do? Trump ordered the government in March to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters and deliver mail ballots only to those people on that list. The legal challenge says the constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. Trump promoted the proposed changes as safeguards to keep non-US citizens from voting, which has been shown to be rare.

Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail until their next extradition hearing as they fight being sent to the UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegations, which they deny.

Betye Saar, a pioneering figure of the Black arts movement, has died at the age of 99. She was best known for reclaiming Jim Crow era memorabilia and recasting them as images of Black liberation.

Cracker Barrel CEO, Julie Masino, is to step down after overseeing the logo redesign backlash last year.

The musician Carly Simon has revealed that she has Parkinson’s disease.

Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, has been called to appear before Congress over his ties to the Trump administration.

Johnson & Johnson said it would pay an estimated $5.5bn to resolve tens of thousands of lawsuits alleging its baby ⁠powder and other talc products caused ⁠ovarian cancer, in a landmark ​deal that could end a contentious, decade-long legal battle.

Dropping this week on Hulu in the US, Lucy Mangan says Furious is possibly the birth of a new post-Epstein files sub-genre of television drama. She says it asks how individuals survive such predators and how society survives the knowledge of the depth and breadth of his network of suppliers, enablers and willing (rich, male) participants.

It might be raking it in at the box office, but Emily Wilson, a classicist whose 2017 translation of Homer’s epic was praised by director Christopher Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with “nothing convincing to say”. Ouch.

Soon after his near-death experience, Houssein Hamze founded the Mashala shelter in the village of Zefta, south Lebanon, to take care of animals in the area. In normal times he takes in strays, and in wartime he is the only lifeline for animals in the area.

Wildfires have forced about 375,000 people to leave their homes in France and Spain. These tourists have been caught up in the unfolding disaster as firefighters struggle to regain control amid a warning the fires could burn until November.

I adore the Tour de France, and this picture essay by Pete Goding, who has been photographing it for 20 years, gives an insight into what it’s been like to document this year’s race.

First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now.

If you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please email newsletters@theguardian.com

title: More rail services in England set to slow as heatwave shrinks soil
excerpt:
South Western Railway expected to join operators in east of England in reducing train speeds and changing timetables

Persistent drought conditions caused by the climate crisis are expected to cause f...
body_text:
South Western Railway expected to join operators in east of England in reducing train speeds and changing timetables

Persistent drought conditions caused by the climate crisis are expected to cause further disruption to trains across southern England, as the lack of rainfall affects the ground supporting railway embankments.

South Western Railway is expected to become the latest large rail company to announce timetable changes and reduced speeds to cope with the effects of hot and dry weather, after operators in the east of England said they were going to take similar steps.

Network Rail said last week that late-night speed restrictions and altered timetables would need to come into effect from 3 August “until the ground conditions have recovered”. Routes affected include those run by Great Northern in Cambridgeshire and Norfolk, by Greater Anglia and c2c in Essex, and the eastern end of the Elizabeth line from London.

The moves are in response to “soil moisture deficit” (SMD) caused by spring’s unusually low rainfall followed by hot, dry summer weather as the UK enters its fourth heatwave of the year.

Many sections of Britain’s railway network are built on embankments containing clay soil, which normally contains a lot of water. Long periods of drought reduce the volume of moisture in the soil, causing it to shrink, which in turn disturbs the ground that tracks are built on, causing sleepers to drop or move out of position.

Even relatively small changes in track geometry – the positioning, alignment and measurements of the line – mean trains must reduce their speed to run safely.

SWR is expected to announce its own speed and timetable changes soon, the Telegraph and BBC reported, almost a year after the rail operator took similar steps in response to another dry spring and summer.

Its West of England line, which connects London to destinations including Exeter St David’s in Devon, Salisbury in Wiltshire and Yeovil in Somerset, is particularly vulnerable to the problem.

And because the line between Salisbury and Exeter is a predominantly single-track railway, speed restrictions can cause cumulative delays, with a knock-on impact on other services across the network.

Last week, Great Northern announced timetable changes from 3 August on the Great Northern line to and from King’s Lynn in Norfolk. Greater Anglia will alter some evening Essex services including rail replacement buses, some late c2c services to Shoeburyness will change, and the Elizabeth line will operate a reduced 11pm to midnight service between Gidea Park and Shenfield on certain dates.

Network Rail said its engineers reduce the effects of dried-out soil by using machines called tampers to lift the track, push stone ballast underneath and create a solid foundation so that trains can run smoothly. New ballast is also put down to help raise the level of the track.

Last year, engineers treated about 62 miles (100km) of track on Anglia routes using tampers to help tackle the effects of dried-out soil. In the run-up to summer, teams have already dropped thousands of tonnes of ballast to help keep the track as smooth as possible, with 49,000 expected to be used over the course of 2026.

title: 'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with devastating wildfires
excerpt: For the past week, firefighters have been tackling a series of wildfires ravaging the Spanish countryside, threatening dozens of communities and forcing more than 70,000 people to evacuate their homes...
body_text:
For the past week, firefighters have been tackling a series of wildfires ravaging the Spanish countryside, threatening dozens of communities and forcing more than 70,000 people to evacuate their homes.

Three fires in the Madrid region have caused special concerns, with a new heatwave expected to hit Spain from Wednesday, fuelling fears that firefighting efforts could be hindered.

"It's a hell of a situation," said Madrid regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso, as she visited affected areas on Monday alongside Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Sánchez spoke on Tuesday of highly challenging hours and days ahead but of light beginning to appear "at the end of the tunnel".

Temperatures are expected to approach 40C in some regions in the coming days, with the heatwave forecast to last at least until Sunday.

Spain's state meteorological agency Aemet has warned the "fire danger level will continue to rise to extreme levels, hindering firefighting efforts".

Ayuso confirmed that four municipalities remained under lockdown orders while another 12 were evacuated. She had earlier described the wildfires as "the biggest natural catastrophe in the history of Spain" and of flames turning the area into a "war zone".

In the Madrid region alone, more than 56,500 people have been evacuated since the fires broke out last week. A further 27,797 people have been ordered to stay at home.

Further evacuations have taken place in Ávila, Toledo and Valencia.

Ayuso wrote on X that the situation was now "improving little by little" and some residents may soon be allowed to return home.

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told Spain's La 1 TV channel that firefighting efforts on Monday night had resulted in "relatively positive progress".

"This morning, we are very satisfied with the work done. We are going to consolidate the work that has been done," he said.

He maintained that "we must be positive; we have the emergency under control" but conceded that "weather conditions are not helping us at all".

Wildfire fight is 'David against Goliath' says French fire service, as new heatwave hits

Spain and France brace for new heatwaves as wildfire closes in on Bordeaux

Pedro Sánchez announced on Tuesday that areas affected by the wildfires have been declared "disaster zones".

"The climate emergency is worsening year after year, and we are required to be united to fight against fire, as well as in prevention and reconstruction," he told reporters during a briefing in Madrid.

"Therefore, I make an explicit request, a single appeal to all regional governments: Climate denial is the worst fuel for the fight against the climate emergency."

More than 90,000 people have been evacuated as firefighters continue tackling the wildfires

Spanish journalist Juan Navarro, who is in Cebreros - a town around 40 miles west of Madrid – told the BBC that people were looking on with fear before the next heatwave.

When you drive through villages in the area around Cebreros, "everything is black", he said.

Ahead of the latest meeting of the Integrated Operational Coordination Centre (Cecopi), the mayors of two of the evacuated towns in the Madrid region described the fire as "a kitten by night and a lion by day".

Robledo de Chavela mayor Fernando Casado said his community would continue fighting "with their knives out".

Echoing his sentiments, Valdemaqueda mayor Ricardo Meneses added that "we can't let our guard down and we're on high alert because now is the time to stop the fire".

Some residents have been allowed to return to their homes as firefighters continue to fight the wildfires

The Madrid region is currently under a red weather warning, with temperatures expected to reach 35C in mountainous areas and 38C in other parts of the community.

In its latest update, the national government's delegation in Madrid said the fire "remains active and uncontrolled".

"Today's efforts will focus on surveillance and cooling the affected areas in anticipation of the forecast worsening of weather conditions," it added.

Around 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres) have been affected by the fires in Spain, according to the minister for ecological transition, Sara Aagesen.

The wildfire burning in the Ávila area was the largest in the country's recent history, she added.

In Ávila, where more than 50,000 hectares have burned down since the start of the wildfires, the government's representative said the fire had a "quite favourable" evolution overnight.

Nicanor Sen, however, said there had been "small flare-ups" that were now being monitored by emergency services.

Meanwhile, the government of Valencia lifted a lockdown order for the town of Vall D'Uixo after a fire broke out of 25 July, forcing some 16,000 from 20 municipalities to evacuate.

In neighbouring Portugal, firefighters are tackling a large fire on three active fronts in the eastern Guarda area.

title: Sen Ron Johnson talks Fauci emails, new Senate filibuster strategy on 'Ruthless'
excerpt:
Republican Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson detailed his plan for the Senate filibuster during an interview on the "Ruthless" podcast.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., gave the latest update on what he described ...
body_text:
Republican Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson detailed his plan for the Senate filibuster during an interview on the "Ruthless" podcast.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., gave the latest update on what he described as an effort to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci "accountable" for his controversial handling of the COVID-19 pandemic and detailed his new filibuster strategy for the Senate in a new interview with the "Ruthless" podcast.

"I think our response to COVID was a miserably failed response, freedom robbing," Johnson said in an exclusive interview released Tuesday morning. "It didn't work. I mean, it simply didn't work. And the fact that Fauci has skated now for six years without accountability, this begins that accountability."

In his role as chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Johnson authored a report alleging the Biden administration misled the American public during the pandemic.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., appeared on the "Ruthless" podcast. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

IOWA GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL ZACH LAHN TELLS 'RUTHLESS' DEMOCRATS ARE HIDING THEIR BAD POLICIES

The interview took place just days after the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, led by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., released Fauci’s daily journal entries. In the journal, Fauci chronicles his rapid rise to celebrity status, interactions with the Trump and Biden teams as they grappled with the pandemic, and his thoughts on the virus' origins, which remains a point of dispute.

Fauci will testify in a Senate Homeland Security hearing on Wednesday. Fauci's handling of the pandemic, his guidance on public health measures and lockdowns, his views on what started the virus, and the U.S.' alleged ties to the Chinese lab thought by some to be the cause of the crisis, have been major points of contention for Republicans.

As director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), Fauci served on the COVID task forces under Presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden, and he was the latter's chief medical advisor until stepping down in 2022.

"I appreciate Chairman Paul calling this hearing, doggedly getting the documents," Johnson told the podcast. "Again, it's like pulling teeth getting these documents. Yeah, we finally got some hard drives, whatever those little thumb drives are called, with some of the information from some of his devices… I think there's still a lot more documents to uncover."

Dr. Anthony Fauci is sworn in before testifying at the House Oversight and Accountability Committee Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic at the Rayburn House Office Building on June 3, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

‘FINISH THE DAMN JOB’: HAGERTY TELLS 'RUTHLESS PODCAST' THAT TRUMP WILL COMPLETE IRAN MISSION

Johnson, who recently took the gavel atop the Senate Budget Committee following the death of South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, also outlined a new strategy for putting Democrats on record over the upper chamber’s filibuster process.

In the interview, he said that if Democrats gain back full control of Congress, they could eliminate the filibuster mechanism and pass a slate of left-wing priorities on a simple party-line basis. He then suggested a plan to put the opposition on record.

"The only way I can see Democrats not ending the filibuster is if you have to get them on the record voting not to end it," Johnson said. "Make sure that it is hard-and-fast Senate rule that you can only end the filibuster with 67 votes. You can't do it using the nuclear option."

title: WATCH: E-bike teen takeover swarms downtown city streets blocking traffic, leading to charges

body_text:
Newly released police video shows a massive group of teens on e-bikes and motorized bikes flooding downtown Orlando, allegedly running red lights, blocking intersections and delaying emergency vehicles.

Hundreds of teens on e-bikes caused chaos in a busy downtown stretch of Orlando, Florida, which led to several charges, police say.

The road ruckus happened earlier this month, and police said the large group posed a significant safety risk and traffic delay to nearby residents.

The Orlando Police Department posted a video on social media of the riders swarming cars at intersections and blocking an ambulance with flashing lights.

Teens on e-bikes allegedly took over downtown Orlando, Florida, earlier this month and police say charges are coming. (Orlando Police Department)

VIDEO SHOWS BRIDGE TURN INTO BURNOUT BONANZA IN STUNT-HAPPY TAKEOVER – POLICE SWOOP IN TO CUFF ROAD REBELS

In the same video, officers appear to apprehend a few of the riders, as seen both on bodycam footage and surveillance video.

In the post, the police department said in part, "Reckless riding, running red lights, blocking traffic, and blocking an ambulance and other emergency vehicles from responding puts everyone at risk, including the riders themselves."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Orlando Police detained a teen accused of participating in an e-bike takeover in the city's downtown area. (Orlando Police Department)

The post went on to say, "This type of dangerous behavior will not be tolerated. Orlando Police officers will continue enforcing the law to help keep Downtown safe for everyone."

Orlando police said to FOX 35 Orlando in a statement: "Because of the size and mobility of the group, not every rider was immediately apprehended. However, officers took enforcement action when it could be done safely.

During the alleged teen takeover, one e-biker appears to do a stunt in the middle of an intersection in front of an ambulance. (Orlando Police Department)

It was not immediately clear how many teens were charged during the incident.

title: DNA cracks centuries-old murder mystery involving one of history's most famous families
excerpt:
A rare 15th-century royal document from Louis XI's court was identified using advanced imaging after it went unnoticed for years in a University of Toronto collection.

Researchers at Yale University ...
body_text:
A rare 15th-century royal document from Louis XI's court was identified using advanced imaging after it went unnoticed for years in a University of Toronto collection.

Researchers at Yale University believe they've solved a centuries-old mystery over how a member of one of Italy's most famous families died.

In a study published in the journal iScience, researchers analyzed ancient DNA from Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici, the Renaissance ruler of Tuscany, who died suddenly in 1587.

Francesco I de' Medici and his wife, Bianca Cappello, died a day apart after falling ill with intermittent fevers following a stay at a mosquito-filled villa — fueling centuries of rumors that they had been poisoned.

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

Working with paleopathologists from the University of Pisa in Italy, the team analyzed DNA extracted from the ribs of Francesco I de' Medici, as well as Giovanni de' Medici, his younger brother who died of malaria 25 years earlier.

The research was led by Serena Tucci, assistant professor of anthropology at Yale University, whose work was publicized in a university press release on June 30.

Yale researchers used ancient DNA to identify malaria parasites in the remains of Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici — offering new evidence about his 1587 death. (Valentina Giuffra; Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images)

Researchers found genetic traces of Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite responsible for the deadliest form of malaria — effectively debunking the longstanding poisoning theory.

The team "found a novel strain of Plasmodium falciparum, the species that causes the deadliest form of human malaria, in the bones of Giovanni de Medici," the release said.

ANCIENT ROMAN VILLA BENEATH HIGH SCHOOL GYM REVEALS STUNNING SECRET FROM THE PAST

"The researchers also discovered molecular traces of P. falciparum and a second species, P. malariae, in the remains of Francesco de Medici," the statement added.

While malaria was endemic to central Italy during the Renaissance, the lack of definitive scientific evidence allowed theories to persist.

"Using historical specimens can not only help us understand our past better, but also it can help build a better future."

"Their quick deaths spawned rumors that Francesco’s brother and rival, Cardinal Ferdinando de Medici, had them poisoned with arsenic," said the statement.

It marks the first time researchers have genetically analyzed the brothers' skeletal remains, confirming earlier evidence they had malaria.

SHAKESPEARE'S MISSING LONDON HOME PINPOINTED AFTER CENTURIES-LONG MYSTERY, RESEARCHER SAYS

The results are "scientific proof to dispel persistent speculation that Francesco de Medici was poisoned to death," Yale officials said.

Archival sources, including contemporary reports from court physicians, describe the symptoms the brothers suffered that are consistent with malaria, which was called "febbre terzana" by residents of Central Italy at the time.

A newly published study concludes malaria was the most likely cause of Francesco I de' Medici's death, challenging centuries of speculation that he was poisoned. (Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images)

"The reports also describe the treatments to which the stricken were subjected, including bloodletting, a common practice that likely did patients more harm than good," the release said.

Although historical records described symptoms consistent with malaria, rumors that Francesco had been poisoned persisted for centuries, Tucci told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Asked why the rumors persisted, Tucci said, "We do not know."

The professor added, "Probably because it was still plausible, given that up to now, there were no conclusive reports that indeed they had malaria. Our study is the first one to genetically confirm it."

Historical accounts described symptoms consistent with malaria, and new DNA evidence now strengthens the case that disease, not poisoning, caused Francesco I de' Medici's death. (Valentina Giuffra)

Tucci added that while the researchers cannot completely rule out poisoning, "malaria remains the most likely explanation for his cause of death."

She also noted that "the hypothesis of poisoning doesn't seem to be well-supported from a scientific perspective — it's very speculative."

"We can only say that we found the pathogen that causes malaria in this specimen, confirming that he had malaria," Tucci said.

The same genetic approach could "certainly" help solve other historical mysteries, said Gisella Caccone, a senior research scientist in Yale's Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology and a co-author of the study.

The findings challenge longstanding rumors that Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici, pictured above, orchestrated the poisoning of his brother and sister-in-law in 1587. (Fine Art Images/Heritage Images via Getty Images)

"[It's possible if] there is a clear hypothesis to address and one can address it using genomic-based approaches," added Caccone. "It depends on the questions and the tools we have."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The DNA recovered from centuries-old remains can do more than solve historical mysteries, Caccone pointed out: The newly identified malaria strain could help researchers better understand how the parasite has evolved over time.

"The more we know about how fast it can change, the better our methods and models to control will be," she noted.

"Using historical specimens can not only help us understand our past better, but also it can help build a better future."

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: Savannah Guthrie's emotional plea to mom's kidnapper may signal 'new line of communication': report
excerpt:
Savannah Guthrie issued a new plea on Instagram to those who kidnapped her mother, Nancy Guthrie, in a video posted July 27, 2026. (Credit: @savannahguthrie/Instagram)

Savannah Guthrie's plea Monday ...
body_text:
Savannah Guthrie issued a new plea on Instagram to those who kidnapped her mother, Nancy Guthrie, in a video posted July 27, 2026. (Credit: @savannahguthrie/Instagram)

Savannah Guthrie's plea Monday may signal a "new line of communication," coming as she appealed directly to her mother's kidnapper, more than 25 weeks after the 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie vanished from her Arizona home.

She made the emotional plea on Monday to her Instagram account, saying her family is "in agony" and "will never stop looking for her." On Tuesday, NBC's Erin McLaughlin reported that the new message may have been in response to a new line of communication.

NANCY GUTHRIE'S SUSPECTED ABDUCTION: TIMELINE OF EVENTS IN DISAPPEARANCE OF 'TODAY' HOST'S MOM

Savannah Guthrie, right, has made a new public plea to the person who kidnapped her mother, Nancy Guthrie, center, from her home outside Tucson, Ariz., left, on Feb. 1. (Getty Images/Fox News Digital)

"It's not clear why Savannah decided to release this message now, but it could be a response to a potential new line of communication. Experts say the language appears to be pointed at whoever committed the crime though law enforcement have not provided any public updates in the investigation recently," McLaughlin said.

In Monday's video to followers, Savannah Guthrie urged her mother's kidnappers to "Do the right thing now."

"Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her," she said. "I'm coming on today with a very specific message. It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part, and we will never stop looking for her. We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts. The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place," Savannah Guthrie said. "I truly believe it is never too late to do the right thing. Help us bring this situation to an end. For all of us. No matter where we've been and what we've done, I believe there is always a way home. Please make the right choice."

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

title: 'A lover of life' - Seattle pays tribute to food festival shooting victims
excerpt:
Ashley Whitehead (left) and Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba (right)

Much of the city of Seattle was in mourning on Monday as residents paid tribute to the three lives that were lost during a deadly st...
body_text:
Ashley Whitehead (left) and Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba (right)

Much of the city of Seattle was in mourning on Monday as residents paid tribute to the three lives that were lost during a deadly street gunfight that had erupted the day before.

The city's mayor and police chief were among dozens gathered at a local fountain for a candlelight vigil, while online fundraisers for two of the victims received tens-of-thousands of dollars in donations.

The three people who died on Sunday at the annual Bite of Seattle food festival were Junior Cee Niko Semo, 19, Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56.

A GoFundMe for Villalba described him as "a devoted husband, loving father of three, and a loyal friend who would do anything for anyone".

"His kindness and generosity touched countless lives, and everyone who knew him remembers his gentle spirit and willingness to help others," the write-up said.

"His sudden passing has left his family heartbroken and facing an uncertain future."

The family has said the funds will go towards funeral expenses and help fill the void in his absence. He leaves behind a wife and three children.

Family members of Ashley Whitehead said she was standing in line with her daughter, waiting for cotton candy, as gunshots rang out and ended her life.

She died in hospital during surgery, after exchanging "heartfelt 'I love you's with her eldest daughter", her family said in the GoFundMe page launched after her death.

Whitehead was described as "a lover of life, art and family".

"Family was everything to Ashley - she had recently moved to the west coast from Alabama to be closer to Zoie," the writeup said, referring to her eldest daughter.

At the vigil on Monday evening, people laid flowers and lit candles as they gathered in grief. There was a call for a moment of a silence.

"This is not acceptable," Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said, condemning gun violence in the community. "No father, no parent should have to bury their child."

Police suspect the third deceased victim, Junior Cee Niko Semo, was involved in the gunfight. Another suspect is in custody. A third suspect is still on the loose.

The shots fired on Sunday at the annual food festival near Seattle's Space Needle left three dead and four others injured, during a suspected "gunfight", police said.

Sunday was the final day of the annual three-day free food festival, which draws some 350,000 people each year.

Washington state Governor Bob Ferguson said in a social media post on Monday that the community was shocked and "struggling to make sense of how an iconic community celebration could end in gunfire".

Number of suspects in fatal Seattle food festival shooting rises to three

title: Trump administration forced treatment on hunger striker in ICE detention, document reveals
excerpt:
ICE report reviewed by the Guardian discloses a patient was ‘subject to force feeding, hydration or urinary catheterization’, which experts have described as torture

The Trump administration subjecte...
body_text:
ICE report reviewed by the Guardian discloses a patient was ‘subject to force feeding, hydration or urinary catheterization’, which experts have described as torture

The Trump administration subjected at least one person undertaking a hunger strike in immigrant detention to forcible medical treatment – engaging in medical practice that healthcare associations and international human rights groups have described as torture.

A document from the Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) health service agency, reviewed by the Guardian, confirms for the first time that the administration has used forced treatment on a hunger striker since Donald Trump began his second term. The document, published online in February by the ICE Health Service Corps (IHSC), discloses that an unnamed patient who began hunger strikes between October and December of last year and “was subject to force feeding, hydration, or forced urinary catheterization, or involuntary blood draws”.

It also notes that at least seven detained people were on hunger strike this February, and that IHSC has forecasted a total budget of $4,504.75 for “external medical care” of hunger strike patients and a total budget of $168,928.01 for the fiscal year of 2026 based on costs from last year.

“This revelation is shocking,” said Eunice Cho, an immigrant rights attorney who co-authored a 2021 report documenting the many medical complications that resulted from forced treatment for hunger strikers in ICE detention.

It remains unclear how many hunger strikers and forced treatments ICE has accounted for since February. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about what sort of forced treatment was administered to the detainee in the IHSC report.

This summer, hundreds of people staged hunger strikes at detention centers across the US. Trump officials have repeatedly denied that detainees are rejecting food to protest unsanitary conditions, medical neglect and what strikers have described as physical and psychological “torture” in detention facilities.

At least 300 detainees began a hunger and labor strike at the Delaney Hall detention center in New Jersey from May to June, and their actions became a national flashpoint, and sustained crowds of protesters gathered outside the facility in solidarity. Advocates said the detainees ended their strike after facing retaliation. Meanwhile, attorneys with the Immigrant Defenders Law Center (ImmDef) have said that hunger strikers at the Adelanto detention center in California have been zip-tied, threatened with teargas and were put in solitary confinement or transferred to other ICE facilities.

Sarah Houston, a managing attorney at ImmDef, said that ICE officials denied that her clients at Adelanto who staged hunger strikes were forgoing food. Officials also denied that detainees were facing retaliation for hunger striking, insisting that one of Houston’s clients who led a hunger strike at Adelanto faced disciplinary actions for vague facility violations.

The IHSC document is a “blatant admission” that the government is well aware of hunger strikes, Houston said. “But if they admit openly that there are hunger strikes, they admit that the conditions in detention are so bad that people are willing to forgo food in order to raise awareness about the situation.” she said. “Because no one goes on hunger strike unless they are really desperate.”

The IHSC document disclosing the number of hunger strikers and forced treatments covers the first quarter of the 2026 fiscal year, and was produced in response to the Senate appropriations committee – which in 2024 directed ICE to provide regular updates on the matter.

In a statement, the DHS said that “all detainees are provided with three meals a day” and did not engage with questions about whether ICE had forcibly treated any more hunger strikers since February.

To forcibly treat a detained person on hunger strike, ICE must first seek an order from a federal judge. Often, said Cho, these orders amount to a “rubber stamp” because many detained immigrants lack attorneys to represent their interest in court. Once the order is obtained, the forced treatment can begin immediately. “There’s very little due process in these proceedings,” she said.

The forced treatment can cause a number of medical complications. Force-feeding, for instance, involves the insertion of a nasogastric tube through the nostril – a painful procedure that causes gagging or, in rare cases, the perforation of vital organs, according to the 2021 report. If the tube is misdirected because a patient is struggling or being treated under forced restraint, the procedure can cause serious infections.

Hunger strikes and subsequent force-feedings gained notoriety during the first Trump administration. A series of force-feedings took place at an ICE detention center in El Paso in 2019, overseen by a medical team contracted by ICE.

In 2022, the Intercept published the first-ever video of an ICE detainee being force-fed. It shows private security guards dressed in riot gear approaching an Indian asylum seeker named Ajay Kumar, and holding him down while medical staff inserted a feeding tube through the man’s nose and down his esophagus. After widespread criticism of ICE and its contractor’s tactics, ICE released Kumar and the three other hunger strikers from custody.

Force-feedings were internationally denounced in the early 2000s for their brutality, after detainees inside the Guantánamo military base were force-fed by guards after a hunger strike.

title: Badenoch urges Burnham to cancel prisoners’ early release scheme – UK politics live
excerpt:
The Conservative party leader said that Labour’s plan allows for too many serious offenders to be freed early

Good morning. In his last speech to Labour’s annual conference as party leader, Keir Star...
body_text:
The Conservative party leader said that Labour’s plan allows for too many serious offenders to be freed early

Good morning. In his last speech to Labour’s annual conference as party leader, Keir Starmer called for a fundamental shift in the way education in England operates. While saying he would never “denigrate the aspiration to go to university”, he said that aiming to get 50% of pupils into university was wrong and that it was finally time to show equivalent respect to apprenticeships and technical education. “So, today I can announce we will scrap that [50%] target and replace it with a new ambition, that two-thirds of our children should go either to university or take a gold standard apprenticeship,” Starmer said, to loud applause.

So heaven knows what Starmer is thinking this morning as he hears his successor, Andy Burnham, announce his own plan for “a fundamental change to the education system” that sounds – well, very similar.

Here is our overnight story by Peter Walker and Josh Halliday.

Here is an extract from an article Burnham has written for the Times explaining his thinking. He says:

double quotation markFor too long, we’ve built an education system around the idea that there’s only one route to success: university, a degree, a desk. That opened doors for millions of people, and rightly so. But somewhere along the way, we sent another message too: that if your ambition was to do something that required more technical skills, somehow you were aiming lower.

I think that was one of the biggest mistakes this country has made. In the age of AI, practical and technical skills haven’t become less valuable — they’ve become more valuable than ever. Britain will need brilliant engineers, electricians and cybersecurity experts more than ever before.

Our job — our national task — is to rebuild those ladders of opportunity, rung by rung, step by step, together.

That’s why today we’re putting technical education back where it belongs — not as a second thought, but as a first choice. From the age of 14, we will be giving kids a new option in school: keeping core maths, English and science, but combining them with a real, hands-on technical education. This will include gaining work experience and creating connections with local employers.

And here is the No 10 news release, running to almost 4,000 words.

Life is not fair, and Starmerites will be wondering why Burnham deserves credit for a “change” story that overlaps quite a lot with a headline announcement from his predecessor. Partly it is because, by last autumn, the public had turned against Starmer; Burnham, by contrast, is getting a hearing. But there is also a key difference in what is being proposed. Burnham is linking the need for better vocational education in schools with his belief in localism, his core political philosophy. In his Times article he says:

double quotation markThese new [technical education] routes won’t be designed by Westminster. They’ll be shaped by the people and places they serve. Working with mayors, local leaders, employers and schools, we’ll identify the industries driving growth in local areas and make sure that local kids have a clear route into them.

It is a devolution policy as much as an education policy.

The government news release on this is so long in part because it contains almost 20 endorsements for the policy, from mayors, business groups, union leaders and others. But one organisation not backing it is the Conservative party. It is saying that Burnham’s plans contradict Labour’s Schools Act, which only became law in April.

Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, said:

double quotation markWe all want to see better opportunities for young people and a boost to technical education, but this announcement is all over the place. Labour have literally just legislated to strip schools of their freedom to choose what’s best for the pupils they’re teaching, yet now they imply it should be locally tailored. It’s not clear whether or not Labour intends to replace GCSEs, which would be a disaster. The focus should be on the knowledge rich curriculum that has helped the most deprived children.

9.30am: Kemi Badenoch holds a press conference, where she will challenge Burnham to introduce emergency legislation to stop serious offenders being included in the prisoner early release scheme due to start in the autumn.

Morning: Burnham is on a visit in Derbyshire, where he is due to speak to the media.

Noon: Labour’s national executive committee meets, with Bridget Phillipson, appointed last night as the new party chair, attending.

2pm: Lucy Powell, the education secretary, is interviewed by Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live.

As I explained earlier this month, we are no longer going to have comments open below the line on this blog. From today, if you want to contact me, or anyone else writing the blog when I am not here, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints. There is a longer post here about how we hope this will work.

Aletha Adu is a Guardian political correspondent.

Back to the Kemi Badenoch press conference, and the Conservative leader made an uncharacteristic statement when speaking to journalists this morning; she apologised for the record of the last government.

It was quite fleeting, but it was definitely an apology. She said:

double quotation markOn the crisis in prison places, this has been a long time coming. We did some things, as I said [see 10.11am], it wasn’t enough, and I’m sorry about that.

But I can’t fix the past, but what I can do is come up with solutions for now, and for tomorrow.

The government says it needs to release prisoners early because otherwise it will run out of space in jails in England and Wales before the end of the year. Asked how she would address this problem, Badenoch mentioned three ideas.

First, she proposed renting prison places overseas.

double quotation markThis was something which we were doing in government. We had plans to rent prison places, just like Sweden has done with Estonia, so that we didn’t have to just release these sorts of violent criminals early. We could have put them in other countries.

She also called for more foreign prisoners to be deported, as well as saying the government needed “to build new prison places more quickly and cheaply”.

Badenoch also urged the public to support the building of new prisons.

double quotation markIf everybody says ‘no prison near me’, we won’t get these [prison places] built, so this is something the public can help with … We cannot say ‘no’ to every potential site for a prison.

In September around 6,000 offenders were set to be released from prison after serving a third of their sentence, rather than half, to ease overcrowding in prisons.

The changes were due to be phased in starting with prisoners serving sentences of less tan 575 days before slowly going up to prisoners who had been jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release next June.

Andy Burnham has paused this process (see 9.51am) but not yet said how he will change the plans.

Reform UK has issued its response to Andy Burnham’s proposal for more localised, vocational education. It is in the form of a statement from Suella Braverman, the former Tory home secretary who is now Reform’s education spokesperson. She is a bit more positive about it than her old party. (See 9.16am.) She says:

double quotation markReform UK has long argued that Britain needs a technical and vocational renaissance alongside a genuine skills revolution.

For too long, the philosopher has been valued more than the plumber. We welcome any effort to rebalance the scales, but we’ve been here before. Successive prime ministers have promised parity of esteem and failed to deliver.

It’s time to end the great university scam and ensure every child, regardless of their background, has the opportunity to thrive.

For his warm words, we do not expect the prime minister to deliver.

Braverman is right to say successive governments have promised to ensure that technical education gets parity of esteem with university education. Andrew McDonald and Megan McElroy have a good summary in their London Playbook briefing for Politico. They say:

double quotation markSpot the difference: “A new ‘T-level’ system, which overhauls how technical education is taught and administered, aims to put the courses on an equal footing with academic work,” announced in Philip Hammond’s 2017 budget … “We need finally to do what we always promise we will — to elevate practical and technical qualifications, so that we recognize their immense value to society and to the individual,” Boris Johnson, 2019 … “Technical education is not given the respect it deserves but today, I am changing all of that, pulling one of the biggest levers we have to change the direction of our country,” Rishi Sunak in 2023 as he announced plans for a British baccalaureate … “While you will never hear me denigrate the aspiration to go to university, I don’t think the way we currently measure success in education — that ambition to get 50 per cent of kids to uni — I don’t think that’s right for our times,” Keir Starmer, 2025 … “That’s why today we’re putting technical education back where it belongs — not as a second thought, but as a first choice,” Andy Burnham, 2026.

In fact, this trend goes back way, way further. The first political speech I covered as a reporter, in 1990 (when I was on the South Wales Echo), was by Peter Walker, the then Welsh secretary. He was talking about the need for better technical education and he quoted from a select committee report saying Britain should copy what the Germans were doing in this area; it was a report written in the 19th century.

Andy Burnham has been criticised by Reform UK, and some figures at GB News, for not mentioning small boats during his first week in power. In his pooled TV clip this morning the interviewer, who has to ask questions on behalf of all UK broadcasters, posed the GB News question, asking Burnham about the almost 900 people who arrived on small boats in the past week.

double quotation markThe home secretary [Shabana Mahmood] has brought forward a very rigorous plan in relation to this, and let’s remember, the numbers can fluctuate but overall boat crossings are down, down quite significantly year on year. So that does suggest that the plan is working.

Burnham also said he discussed small boats “repeatedly” during the Makerfield byelection campaign.

double quotation markThe public wants to see control being exerted, and while we’ve made progress, there is more to do, and I recognise that completely.

But the trend is down, and the number of people being removed is up, so the figures are pointing in a better direction. But there is much more to do.

According to recent Home Office figures, 13,007 arrivals have been recorded this year, the Press Association reports. This is 45% lower than the number recorded by this time last year and down 18% on the same period in 2024.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister, is carrying out a government review intended to address the crisis of the growing number of Neets – young people not in education, employment or training. His first report, analysing the causes of the problem, was published in May to wide acclaim. He is due to publish a final report with recommendations in the autumn.

The plan announced by Andy Burnham today for more localised, technical education is not just a response to the Neets problem. But it overlaps with what Milburn is recommending, and in a statement Milburn said:

double quotation markThe changes the PM is announcing today are very welcome. They are a big step in the right direction and consistent with the findings of my review. A whole system reset is needed across health, welfare and labour market policy as well as in education and skills. I know the PM recognises this and my final report will outline the further changes that are needed.

Milburn was with Burnham on a visit to promote the plan in Derby this morning.

Speaking to the media this morning, Burnham said he was committed to getting Neet numbers down. He said:

double quotation markObviously, the trend is rising at the moment, so first thing I’ve got to do is to stop that rise.

It’s hard to say and put a firm date on it at the moment when you can say there are fewer than now, but certainly I am completely on a mission with relation to this. I cannot accept the situation where we have so many young people in their 20s on benefits. It’s just not right for them.

Burnham also said young people were not to blame for the fact they could not find work.

double quotation markIt would be wrong to blame the young people when we have an education system that doesn’t set them up properly, where some struggle to find opportunities at 16, where work experience and work placements aren’t there for them. We’ve got to put those building blocks in place, and then, in time, that number will come down.

And I will commit, in my time in office, to get the number of young people who are not in education, employment, and training down. I will commit to that. When precisely I can get there is a hard thing to say right now.

At her press conference, Kemi Badenoch blamed Covid for the fact that the last Conservative government left the country short of prison places.

double quotation markWe know that the situation with prisons is challenging. When we were in government, we saw the challenge. We created 14,000 new prison places – it was nowhere near enough.

We had a prison-building target in our manifesto. Covid derailed that programme.

We’d sold some prisons to get the money to build new ones but the programme, as I said, was derailed.

Badenoch conceded that the Tories also had an early release scheme. But she said theirs was not like Labour’s.

double quotation markWe also had early release but not like this. We never had this category of prisoners being released. We never had killers, rapists, paedophiles on early release. That is what I want to stop.

She also said that Burnham could act “today” to stop the releases. She explained:

double quotation markIf Andy Burnham wants to prove that he is serious about this, he needs to revoke the commencement order [the regulation saying the Sentencing Act measures will come into force on 2 September]. That is a simple action that I’m asking for today.

It’s quite clear that the prime minister sees that this is a problem, but I don’t think he knows what to do about it.

We have done the work. We know that we need to revoke the commencement order immediately – he could do that today. That would show that he is really pausing it.

And then he needs to bring in emergency legislation by 2 September.

This can be done – we heard the government talk about bringing in emergency legislation for a bank holiday if we won the World Cup. They can do this and we will be here to help them facilitate that.

Kemi Badenoch is holding her press conference now. She is speaking alongside women who are victims of rape and sexual assault and who are speaking about the trauma they are experiencing knowing that their attackers will be released early in the autumn.

Badenoch said that Andy Burnham’s announcement of a “pause” in the process was pointless, given that offenders were not due to be released until Septembe anyway.

She said the government should already have a plan to address the problem. This should not be a party political issue, she said.

Andy Burnham has recorded a pooled TV interview this morning.

Asked about the Sentencing Act, and whether he was considering amending the legislation before it came into effect, Burnham just insisted that the pause in the process he announced last week was “real” and that further statements would be made in due course.

double quotation markThe pause is real, and it was one of the first things I did coming into office last week. So the September releases [are] on hold.

And … the review that I have instigated is also a real process. We are taking a very serious look at the situation.

Of course, this goes back a number of years when the previous government failed to put in place the prison places needed, so it is a challenging situation, and we shouldn’t actually be in this position as a country.

But we have to deal with the reality of where we are. But I will do anything I can to minimise risk to the public. And that is why I am looking again …

We’ll make further statements on this in due course.

Kemi Badenoch is about to hold a press conference where she will be urging Andy Burnham to pass emergency legislation to stop serious offenders being included in the prisoner early release scheme due to start in the autumn. This is what the party said about the announcement in a news release overnight.

double quotation markThe Conservatives have been campaigning against the early release of violent and sexual offenders since Labour decided to do this in 2024 and we welcome the prime minister’s U-turn. But the prime minister’s review, or as he is now calling it a “brief pause”, has changed nothing in law – without legislation violent and sexual offenders will be released on 2 September. Given parliament is only scheduled to return on 1 September, Conservatives will back fast-tracked emergency legislation.

Sex offenders, including rapists and the evil rape gang perpetrators, should remain behind bars where they belong, but Labour want to let them back on the street. To make matters worse, many victims have not been properly informed about the release of their abusers.

The Conservatives warned this would happen when we opposed Labour’s Sentencing Act … We tabled amendments to the original Sentencing bill when it was in Parliament to exempt rapists, paedophiles, and other serious offenders from automatic early release. These Conservative amendments were blocked by Labour and the Liberal Democrats.

Of course, Labour says it had to pass the Sentencing Act because, during the 14 years when the Tories were in power, they regularly passed laws imposing longer while at the same time refusing to build the extra prisons needed to house a growing jail population. As a result, when Rishi Sunak called the general election in 2024, the overcrowding crisis was so serious that the system was days away from collapse.

title: People trapped inside Japan shopping centre after earthquake
excerpt:
The fire department said the second floor of the mall collapsed, "leaving many people trapped inside"

Several people are trapped inside a shopping centre after a strong earthquake hit south-west Japa...
body_text:
The fire department said the second floor of the mall collapsed, "leaving many people trapped inside"

Several people are trapped inside a shopping centre after a strong earthquake hit south-west Japan, officials say.

Some local media reports that there was an explosion at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, following the magnitude 7.1 earthquake.

The quake hit inland on Kyushu island at 16:27 local time (07:27 GMT), with more than 150,000 people being told to move to evacuation shelters. There was a brief tsunami warning that was lifted within the hour.

Emergency services said "many people" were trapped inside the Aeon Mall in the Kumamoto region.

In the town of Kashima, "a shopping complex's second floor collapsed, leaving many people trapped inside," the fire department said in a statement.

Japan is one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries, experiencing about 1,500 quakes a year.

The meteorological agency has warned of strong aftershocks given the shallow epicentre - 10km (six miles). Footage aired by national broadcaster NHK shows cracked roads and bridges and several buildings on fire.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Tuesday.

About 10 of the injured were in an elderly care home and at least 50 people are being treated in hospital, NHK reported.

Train services have been suspended and electricity has been cut off for thousands of homes.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said first responders had been deployed, including Japan's self-defence force, fire services and coast guard.

"We urge residents in areas where the shaking was particularly severe to pay close attention to evacuation information issued by local authorities via radio, television and the internet, and to act calmly," he said.

title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years for Radio 5 Live
excerpt:
Move comes after the presenter has faced allegations of bullying, but there is no suggestion it is related

Naga Munchetty is to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years on the television show to become co-...
body_text:
Move comes after the presenter has faced allegations of bullying, but there is no suggestion it is related

Naga Munchetty is to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years on the television show to become co-presenter of Radio 5 Live’s breakfast show.

The current 5 Live Breakfast hosts, Rachel Burden and Rick Edwards, announced on Tuesday’s programme that they would step down in December.

Munchetty, who has presented the station’s weekday mid-morning programme since 2021, and will move to 5 Live Breakfast alongside a new co-host to be recruited in due course, the BBC said.

The move comes after reports that Munchetty had faced allegations of bullying on the breakfast TV show. There has been no suggestion her move and the allegations are connected.

The BBC has been contacted for comment, but at the time that the bullying allegations were reported it said: “We do not comment on individual HR matters.”

Munchetty said of her move: “I’m thrilled to be joining 5 Live Breakfast in January. Live news, great conversations and connecting with audiences are what I love most about broadcasting, and 5 Live does all of that brilliantly.

“It has been a privilege to be part of the BBC Breakfast TV team for the past 17 years, working alongside an incredibly talented and hard-working group of journalists who are not only outstanding colleagues but also great friends.

“Presenting a flagship programme on 5 Live is an opportunity that was simply too good to pass up. It will take a huge amount of work and require 100% of my focus and energy, and I’m really looking forward to throwing myself into the role.

“Over the last five years, I’ve been privileged to build a relationship with 5 Live listeners on the mid-morning programme and help shine a light on the issues that matter most to them. I’m excited to build on that in the Breakfast slot and to start each day with our listeners every morning.

“Between now and January, I’ll continue presenting the two programmes I love. I’m sure there will be plenty of news to cover, and it will very much be business as usual.”

Burden will move to present the weekday mid-morning programme, Monday to Wednesday from 11am to 2pm, after 15 years on the station’s breakfast show, while Edwards will continue to front Fighting Talk on Saturday mornings.

It was revealed earlier this month that Munchetty earned between £360,000 and £364,999 in the 2025-26 financial year.

title: Marmite and Dove owner Unilever warns of price rises due to growing costs
excerpt:
Consumer goods group reports strong sales growth, owing in part to World Cup marketing campaigns

Unilever has warned it will push through further price rises over the coming months, as the Marmite, D...
body_text:
Consumer goods group reports strong sales growth, owing in part to World Cup marketing campaigns

Unilever has warned it will push through further price rises over the coming months, as the Marmite, Dove and Hellmann’s owner tries to recoup its own growing costs.

The Anglo-Dutch company said that while the pace of price rises slowed in the second quarter, owing in part to World Cup-related discounts and efforts to stay competitive in Brazil, it said these were “temporary factors” and would not shield consumers for long.

“We expect underlying price growth to accelerate in the second half as commodity-driven pricing continues to land in market,” the company told shareholders on Tuesday.

That could end up translating to higher profits for Unilever, depending on whether consumers keep buying its products, despite the price rises. Unilever said in its release that its underlying sales were up 5.8% in the second quarter, pushing turnover up 3.8% to €13bn (£11.1bn).

“Consumers continued to demand Unilever’s branded products, rather than switching to unbranded cheaper alternatives, despite cost-of-living pressures, proving the strength of Unilever products’ brand loyalty,” Victoria Scholar, the head of investment at Interactive Investor, said.

Companies such as Unilever have been grappling with a rise in costs for ingredients and services, owing to higher oil prices since March, when the US-Israeli war on Iran effectively stopped tanker traffic through the strait of Hormuz.

Although oil prices have been oscillating amid temporary ceasefires, that has yet to lead to a sustained drop in prices for manufacturers, which are hoping to pass higher costs on to customers.

UK inflation dropped by more than expected in June to 2.6%, but City economists are warning that Bank of England could be forced to tear up its economic forecasts and raise interest rates later this year if oil prices return to above $100 a barrel.

Mohamed El-Erian, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania and a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, suggested a sustained increase in oil prices to $90 a barrel could be enough to rewrite UK policymakers’ forecasts.

“Should oil prices remain above $90 a barrel, an important ‘if’, then headline inflation would face significant upward pressure. This, in turn, would heighten concerns over immediate indirect effects, including rising food prices driven by diesel transportation costs, and broader second-round effects over time,” he said.

That could put further pressure on customers of London-listed Unilever, which has factories across the country making Pot Noodle in Crumlin, Wales, and Hellmann’s, Marmite and Colman’s in Burton-on-Trent.

title: Zelensky to press Trump on air defences while in Washington
excerpt:
Volodymyr Zelensky has said peace must be brought closer, ahead of talks at the White House

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky is due to hold important talks with US President Donald Trump at the White Hou...
body_text:
Volodymyr Zelensky has said peace must be brought closer, ahead of talks at the White House

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky is due to hold important talks with US President Donald Trump at the White House, where he is hoping to firm up commitments to bolstering Kyiv's anti-ballistic missile defences.

Zelensky has arrived in the US at a significant stage in Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, with Moscow's mayor saying the capital was targeted by 390 drones in a matter of hours overnight.

The Ukrainian leader is expected to press Trump over support he gave earlier this month for Kyiv to be given a licence to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

Russia has escalated deadly ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine's capital recently, and Zelensky has said interceptors are urgently needed.

Patriot missiles have been at the top of Zelensky's wish-list for some time, but after the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, these US air defence interceptors are in very short supply.

Promising a licence is one thing, but co-producing the highly sophisticated PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors on Ukrainian soil is another, because it involves a lengthy political, legal and technical process.

A delegation from US manufacturer Raytheon visited Kyiv last week and Zelensky said the defence firm had expressed "readiness to take our partnership to an even higher level".

Watch: What to expect from Zelensky and Netanyahu's visit to Washington

After he speaks with Zelensky, Trump will have another important meeting - with Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu. It is the first time the two have met in person since the war on Iran started in late February.

Zelensky and Netanyahu are in Washington to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, who died this month aged 71.

The Ukraine war appeared to coincide with the US-Israel war with Iran at the weekend, when Ukrainian forces targeted an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea.

Kyiv has described Iran as a "direct accomplice to Russian aggression against Ukraine" and Zelensky has said Ukrainian intelligence has evidence that Russia has shared satellite imagery with Tehran, enabling Iran to attack US military facilities and Gulf states.

Trump has said he will "find out if that's true. I'll ask Putin about it", while saying if true, it had no impact at all.

Meanwhile, in Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said more than 390 Ukrainian drones had targeted the region between 20:30 on Monday and 06:30 on Tuesday local time, and that most had been intercepted by air defences.

Footage confirmed by BBC Verify showed damage to a high-rise building in Chekhov, south of the capital and a fire at a warehouse in Berezhki to the west. Local officials in Chekhov said there had been no casualties.

Since Zelensky last spoke to Trump in early July, Ukraine has repeatedly targeted logistics hubs, many belonging to Russian e-commerce company Wildberries, exacerbating issues faced by small and medium-sized business in parts of Russia.

Four Wildberries warehouses have been targeted, including this one in Nevinnomyssk

Speaking at the Kremlin on Monday, President Vladimir Putin told members of Russia's parliament, the Duma, that their country's enemies were resorting to "terrorist methods" against civilians but would "never break" the Russian people.

"We will achieve our objectives and will together do everything for victory, for Russia," Putin said.

At the weekend, he was confronted over the war's objectives by an ally, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who said the roots of the war were "not understandable".

Tokayev said a peace deal with Ukraine could be reached if the war was halted for negotiations to take place.

"Perhaps it is time to freeze this conflict and return to the Istanbul formula 2.0," Toyakev suggested, referring to talks that began shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that freezing the war now was impossible "given Kyiv's position

Zelensky tries to fix crisis over removal of defence minister and counts the cost
