title: Fauci privately took credit for COVID-19 lockdowns despite public denial, newly exposed diary entries reveal
excerpt: Dr. Anthony Fauci's private diary entries reveal his fixation on personal fame during the COVID-19 pandemic. Critics point to his diary's lack of focus on public health terms versus personal accolades...
body_text:
Dr. Anthony Fauci's private diary entries reveal his fixation on personal fame during the COVID-19 pandemic. Critics point to his diary's lack of focus on public health terms versus personal accolades, raising questions about his priorities and the pandemic's origins.

Despite denying on multiple occasions during and after the COVID-19 pandemic that he personally recommended lockdowns, excerpts revealed from Dr. Anthony Fauci's private diary prove a clear contradiction.

In a March 15, 2020, entry in the diary, which begins with "BIG DAY!" written in red letters, Fauci, then the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID) recalled a striking conversation he had with then-New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio.

"I spoke with Bill de Blasio (Mayor – NYC) and convinced him based on what I was saying publicly and my conversation tonight to close the NYC schools (he had already decided based on what I was saying on TV)," Fauci revealed in his private notes.

National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Director Anthony Fauci testifies before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee about the COVID-19 response in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4, 2021. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"I had a similar call with Ann O’Leary, the [Chief of Staff] of Gov. Gavin Newsom of California," this particular entry went on. "Ann said that based on my TV appearances today and yesterday, the Governor has decided to close the schools in California as well as the bars and restaurants."

But seven months later, on an Oct. 16, 2022 interview with ABC News' Jonathan Karl, Fauci denied any involvement in inspiring lockdowns.

"Let's go back and look at the transcript. We said we should try as best as we possibly can to keep the children in school," Fauci said. "Nobody plays that clip."

"They always come back and say, 'Fauci was responsible for shutting schools down.' I had nothing to do [with it]!" he insisted at the time.

EXPOSED FAUCI DIARY SHOWS HE ESTIMATED COVID-19 DEATH RATE TO BE MUCH LOWER THAN WHAT HE TOLD CONGRESS

In 2022 he told The Hill that he "didn't recommend locking anything down," clearly going against his own privately recorded entries.

In January 9, 2024, years after the end of lockdowns ended, Fauci testified the same thing before the House Oversight Committee.

"I did not close the schools," he said, according to the hearing transcript. And it became the widespread situation where I became a political target."

Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, throws out the ceremonial first pitch prior to the game between the New York Yankees and the Washington Nationals at Nationals Park on July 23, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

Fauci recommended to government leaders lockdown measures besides just closing schools, which he would also later deny.

INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

In the March 15, 2020, diary entry, Fauci, once the nation's leading infectious disease expert, said he directed de Blasio to close the city's bars.

"I went on to tell him he should close the bars and restaurants in NYC. He said that he would base this on my recommendation," Fauci wrote.

Five days later, he said he told the mayor to close all of New York City.

"Also, had phone call with Major de Blasio who wants to go to 'shelter in place for the entire city.['] He is asking my advice since Gov. Cuomo is pushing back. I advised DeBlasio [sic] to go ahead and do it. I will try to speak with Cuomo," the entry said.

2020 Democratic presidential candidate and New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio visits FOX Business Network’s "Bulls & Bears" in New York City on Aug. 13, 2019. (Steven Ferdman/Getty Images)

On March 29, 2020, Fauci recounted a tense meeting with President Donald Trump, who he described as "incorrigible."

The goal of the meeting was to get the president to extend lockdowns after the initial "15 days to stop the spread" period, which began on March 16 of 2020 — about a month after the first case of COVID-19 was recorded in the U.S.

"At the end of the day it was a good outcome since we convinced him to go with 30 day (sic) instead of ending the mitigation prematurely, which I feel would be a disaster," Fauci said.

In a November 28, 2020, diary entry, he recalled lending support to a Los Angeles County health official who wanted to lock the county down.

"Got call last night from Mark Ghaly (Deputy Director for Community Health for the LA County Dept of Health Services). He has called me several times for advice," the diary says. "Frantic call saying that they are surging in LA County and very soon hospital beds will be overrun. He wants to do a 3 weeks shutdown of the city to 'stop the surge' and wants my support since there is a large pushback to locking down. I agreed to support him."

A signboard reminds people of the face covering requirement as pedestrians wear facemasks due to the coronavirus in Los Angeles, California on November 12, 2020. - European and world leaders on November 12, 2020 insisted that when Covid-19 vaccines are launched they should be made a available to everyone, under an international project which still needs $28 billion of funding. (Photo by Frederic J. BROWN / AFP) ((Photo by FREDERIC J. BROWN/AFP via Getty Images))

But again in 2022, when he joined The Hill's "Rising" podcast, Fauci denied responsibility for lockdowns.

"Well, you know, again, first of all, I didn't recommend locking anything down," he claimed. "You're asking me questions. You're talking about the CDC is the public health agency that uses their epidemiologists and their science-based approach to make recommendations..."

Despite his own denials, Fauci himself told CBS news in the midst of the 2020 chaos that he was behind the lockdowns.

"When it became clear that we had community spread in the country, with a few cases of community spread — this was way before there was a major explosion like we saw in the northeastern corridor driven by New York City metropolitan area — I recommended to the president that we shut the country down," he said on Oct. 7, 2020.

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Washington mother says she found adult male showering in women's locker room during children's swim meet
excerpt: West Virginia teen Adaleia Cross shares her shocking claims of alleged sexual harassment by a trans athlete in a locker room, leading to severe backlash from her teacher and friends. The incident come...
body_text:
West Virginia teen Adaleia Cross shares her shocking claims of alleged sexual harassment by a trans athlete in a locker room, leading to severe backlash from her teacher and friends. The incident comes amid a recent Supreme Court ruling upholding state laws that require student athletes to compete based on biological sex. Rachel Campos-Duffy, a 'Fox & Friends Weekend' co-host, discusses the profound impact on female athletes and societal implications.

A Washington mother says she encountered an adult male showering in a women's locker room while children were attending a swim meet at a local recreation center, prompting renewed debate over policies governing access to sex-segregated facilities.

"Right before my daughter's first race, I went into the women's locker room to use the restroom," Maria Varchetto, whose daughter was participating in a swim meet at Seattle-area Lynnwood Recreation Center, told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"The locker room is set up like most public locker rooms, with an open shower area and two private shower stalls that have curtains. I know these showers well because my daughter uses them regularly," she said. "The curtains are too narrow for the width of the shower opening, and even when they are pulled closed, they often slide back open on both sides with movement or from the water hitting them."

"As I walked toward the back of the locker room where the restrooms are located, I saw what appeared to be an adult male's exposed, erect penis through the gap in one of the shower curtains," Varchetto continued. "The exposure was not something I was looking for — it was simply visible as I walked by, and it immediately caught my attention. I was shocked and unsure how to respond, so I continued to the restroom."

MAN FIRED BY FIRM AFTER VIRAL VIDEO SHOWS HIM SCOLDING DAD FOR TAKING YOUNG DAUGHTERS INTO WOMEN'S RESTROOM

FILE - In this May 17, 2016, file photo, a new sticker is placed on the door at the ceremonial opening of a gender-neutral bathroom at Nathan Hale High School in Seattle. (AP Photo/Elaine Thompson, File)

The incident occurred at the Lynnwood Recreation Center on July 12 in suburban Seattle during Varchetto's daughter's swim meet.

"When I came out, I saw a mother and her young daughter washing their hands at the sink," Varchetto said. "As I walked toward the exit, the person's genitals were again plainly visible from the walkway. At that point, I decided I needed to say something. I said, 'Excuse me, this is the women's locker room.'"

SIX TRANSGENDER IDAHO RESIDENTS FILE LAWSUIT TO BLOCK NEW BATHROOM LAW

Empty school hallway with royal blue metal lockers. (Getty Images)

Varchetto said she took up the issue with the front desk to inform them that there was a male showering in the female locker room.

Management then went into the women’s locker room and addressed the man.

"The manager addressed the individual and said, 'Excuse me, are you confused? This is the women's locker room.' The individual responded only, "I'm trans.'"

LOUDOUN COUNTY PARENTS NOT 'SATISFIED' AFTER SCHOOL OFFICIALS TESTIFY ON TRANSGENDER POLICIES

Varchetto said the man in the women's locker room was taking a shower behind a curtain that was partly open. (Boroux)

Varchetto said the manager left after the exchange.

"My family loves the Lynnwood Recreation Center, but after this experience, I no longer feel comfortable allowing my daughter to use the women's locker room by herself," Varchetto said.

"If I'm not with her, I ask her to use one of the family locker rooms instead," she added. "She has told me she feels guilty doing that because there are only a handful of family locker rooms, and families with small children are often waiting to use them."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

A teenage girl swimming butterfly in an outdoor swim meet. (Getty Images)

Nathan MacDonald, manager of communications and public affairs for the City of Lynnwood, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "On Sunday, July 12th, our Lynnwood Recreation Center staff received a complaint that a self-identifying trans woman was using a shower stall inside the women’s locker room. We can confirm that the complaint was filed and that our staff conferred with both parties."

"Our Recreation Center facilities comply with Washington Administrative Code 162-32-060, which requires all entities to allow individuals to use gender-segregated facilities, including locker rooms and dressing rooms, that correspond with their gender expression or gender identity," MacDonald continued.

"Since the incident, our facilities team has installed new full-sized shower curtains in the locker rooms and is exploring other modifications to our shower facilities to ensure the privacy of all our Recreation Center patrons," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Lynnwood Recreation Center for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

title: Prisoners at Iran’s largest jail sew lips shut in hunger strike as executions soar
excerpt:
At least 1,500 protest after six men on drug-related charges put in solitary confinement before possible execution

Prisoners at Iran’s largest jail have sewn their lips shut as hundreds of them joine...
body_text:
At least 1,500 protest after six men on drug-related charges put in solitary confinement before possible execution

Prisoners at Iran’s largest jail have sewn their lips shut as hundreds of them joined a mass hunger strike amid a surge in executions over drug offences and charges linked to anti-government protests.

The hunger strike, involving at least 1,500 death row prisoners at Ghezel Hesar prison near Tehran, began two weeks ago after six men convicted on drug-related charges were transferred to solitary confinement before their possible execution, according to Iranian rights groups.

In a series of videos shared by rights groups in exile, prisoners are seen sitting in a prison hallway, holding placards reading “No to Executions” and chanting “Be our voice”.

In one graphic video, a prisoner addresses the camera to say he is sewing his lips shut because, six days into the hunger strike, no prison official has responded to the protest.

The footage then shows another prisoner off camera using a needle and thread to stitch the man’s lips together. In another video, a prisoner calls for urgent medical help for those whose conditions he says are deteriorating. “The guards will not open the door so we can take them to the prison infirmary,” he says.

The protest is the latest act of defiance in the prisoner-led campaign against executions, which began in January 2024 and has spread across prisons in Iran amid a sharp rise in the use of the death penalty.

According to the Oslo-based non-profit Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), at least 424 executions have been carried out this year, with hundreds more on death row. Most executions were handed down in drug-related cases, IHRNGO said.

On Tuesday, officials hanged two men who were convicted of “waging war on God” over the deaths of two police officers during the anti-government protests. Twenty-six people linked to the January protests have been hanged this year.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, the director of IHRNGO, said people sentenced to death for drug offences were among the most marginalised and voiceless prisoners on death row.

“They have become the lowest-cost victims of the Islamic Republic’s execution machine. Last year alone, at least 795 people were hanged on drug-related charges, with almost no international reaction and hardly any domestic or social media campaigns to save them. By staging this protest, the prisoners in Ghezel Hesar are taking an extraordinary risk. They know that the authorities can execute them at any moment, yet they have chosen to raise their voices in the hope that the international community will finally hear them and increase the political cost of these executions,” he said.

According to Amnesty International, revolutionary courts, which have jurisdiction over national security and drug-related offences, lack independence and routinely impose harsh sentences, including death sentences, after grossly unfair trials.

In a message relayed to the Guardian, one death-row protester said: “We are prisoners who turned to such mistakes simply to afford the basic necessities of life, and deeply regret our actions. Where else in the world is a human life taken for a first mistake?”

A similar protest was held at the prison in October 2025, when more than 1,500 prisoners went on a six-day hunger strike, leading to a rare visit by authorities. But activists say conditions have not improved since. Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said executions continue following unfair trials over drug-related offences.

“In many cases, defendants do not have access to lawyers or a meaningful right to defend themselves. There are also cases in which charges are fabricated against people from ethnic minority or poor backgrounds,” Khazaeli said. “Death sentences issued by the revolutionary courts are a violation of human rights and even Iran’s own laws.”

There has been a huge spike in executions this year amid the war with the US, and families of those on death row and rights groups have raised the alarm over the worsening human rights crisis in the country.

Executions have also surged among political prisoners and protesters arrested after the nationwide protests in January. Many of the death sentences were issued on the basis of confessions extracted under torture, Amiry-Moghaddam said.

“The Islamic Republic has no legitimate justification for using the death penalty for drug offences. It is not required by Islam, and the authorities themselves have repeatedly acknowledged that executions have failed to deter drug trafficking or drug use. On the contrary, both drug trafficking and addiction have continued to rise over the years. Those sentenced to death are rarely major traffickers; they are typically the lowest-ranking couriers, recruited because of poverty for a small payment. Many are convicted solely on the basis of confessions extracted under torture,” he added.

Families of those on death row in Ghezel Hesar have staged protests outside the prison in support of those inside, but sources said authorities violently cracked down on their gathering.

title: Javier Milei accuses US Democrats of financing ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ at World Cup
excerpt:
President also blames Brazil and Mexico and says online critics ‘do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed’

More than a week has passed since Ferran Torres scored the extra-time goal that gave Spai...
body_text:
President also blames Brazil and Mexico and says online critics ‘do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed’

More than a week has passed since Ferran Torres scored the extra-time goal that gave Spain its second World Cup, but – at least for Argentina’s president – the tournament is not over.

Javier Milei has claimed that a coordinated “anti-Argentina campaign” was behind criticism of the country’s team, accusations of racism among its fans and conspiracy theories alleging that Lionel Messi’s side was secretly being favoured by Fifa.

Now, the far-right president has taken the narrative a step further, alleging that the supposed campaign was financed by the US Democratic party and the governments of Brazil and Mexico.

“It was the work of progressive minds who do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed,” claimed the self-styled libertarian in an interview with a local radio station on Sunday.

He went on to claim that the “government of Brazil”, led by the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had allegedly provided the largest share of the funding.

Analysts in Argentina said Milei had embraced the narrative as a distraction from his plummeting popularity, while others argued that the “real anti-Argentina campaign” was the one the president was waging “with his chainsaw” austerity plan.

Yet the narrative has gained traction, even reaching people who do not support Milei. Pablo Torres, a 52-year-old bookseller from Buenos Aires who “never voted for him and never would”, said there had been a social media “bombardment” against the country that left him feeling “outrage” and “disgust”.

He said some of the accusations of racism had come from “great colonial powers that enslaved people, trafficked enslaved people and decimated populations”, adding: “They denied the existence of the black population in Argentina, and ignored our idiosyncrasies and our history … We are a welcoming home for all nations.”

During the tournament, incidents involving racist behaviour by some Argentine supporters drew widespread attention. Hours before the final, the US actor Samuel L Jackson posted an Instagram story that said: “Dear black people, please do not cheer or root for Argentina to win the Fifa World Cup. Argentina has historically been one of, if not the most, racist countries in the world.”

The post prompted reactions even from human rights organisations such as Amnesty International Argentina, which acknowledged racism in the country but criticised “reducing the country to a stereotype”.

Milei, meanwhile, posted that the criticism could be attributed to Argentina’s opposition, which had “validated the woke movement that is now accusing us of being racist”. Over the weekend, he also decided to blame Brazil – while on Brazilian soil.

On Saturday, the Argentinian president attended the launch of the presidential campaign of the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro and Lula’s main challenger in October’s presidential election.

In his speech, as well as calling Lula a “thief” and a “prisoner” – prompting a strong reaction from the Brazilian government – Milei said: “If you examine the data from the recent anti-Argentina campaign, the place from which the most attacks came was Brazil.” He reinforced the claim on Sunday, this time adding Mexico and the US Democratic party.

The digital anthropologist Mercedes Máspero analysed more than 2m posts on social media and wrote that she had found “some undeniable patterns” of orchestration such as the repeated use of variations of “disgusting human beings” in different languages. Even so, it was “a tough call” to describe it as a coordinated campaign “because the narrative is incredibly widespread”, she wrote.

Natalia Aruguete, a researcher at Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council who specialises in social media and political agendas, said she had seen “no evidence of a large-scale coordinated operation”, despite the existence of “a hostile, widespread and transnational conversation centred on Argentina”.

“Brazil had a significant presence [in those messages],” she added, “particularly in the conversation about racism, but … Milei’s accusation of alleged Brazilian involvement was not backed up by any public evidence.”

Some critics said that the last time the idea of such a campaign was propagated by the state was during the brutal 1976–83 dictatorship, whose crimes Milei has repeatedly downplayed. During the 1978 World Cup, hosted by Argentina, the military junta claimed that criticism of the regime’s human rights violations was part of an “anti-Argentina campaign”.

Aruguete said Milei had turned a “diverse online conversation” into a political conflict that fits his narrative of a “culture war” against the left, at a time when his administration is facing “internal deterioration”: inflation appears to be under control, but rising unemployment and corruption scandals have driven the president’s popularity to its lowest point since taking office.

The narrative that suggests Argentinians are all victims of a supposedly orchestrated campaign by leftwing foreign governments “allows Milei to shift the focus of the debate away from his own governance issues and on to an external adversary”, said Aruguete.

title: Soros network rebuilds progressive prosecutor push after string of election losses
excerpt: Congressman Wesley Hunt, a Republican from Texas, strongly condemns the Democratic Party's anti-police rhetoric and 'defund the police' movement. Hunt argues that leftists believe criminals are victim...
body_text:
Congressman Wesley Hunt, a Republican from Texas, strongly condemns the Democratic Party's anti-police rhetoric and 'defund the police' movement. Hunt argues that leftists believe criminals are victims, leading to increased crime rates and unsafe communities for the most vulnerable. He emphasizes the need for strong law enforcement, contrasting it with the left's demonization of police.

The Soros family has pumped more than $1 million into political action committees (PACs) dedicated to electing progressive prosecutors this election cycle, campaign finance documents show.

While some predicted that Soros-backed district attorneys would become a thing of the past after sustaining a string of defeats between 2022 and 2024, records suggest that the liberal family is giving their criminal justice reform crusade another go. Democracy PAC, now run by George Soros’s son Alex pumped roughly $1.7 million into the federal and non-federal arms of the Justice & Public Safety PAC between March 2025 and April 2026, according to public records.

The renewed spending signals that the Soros network is rebuilding its effort to shape local criminal justice policy ahead of the 2026 elections, despite a voter backlash that removed or replaced dozens of prosecutors linked to its funding.

By directing significant resources to Justice & Public Safety PAC, the family is positioning the group to again influence races where decisions on bail, charging and sentencing can drastically reshape public safety.

REPEAT OFFENDER WITH DOZENS OF PRIOR CHARGES ARRESTED FOR BURGLARIZING CHURCH IN SOROS-BACKED DA'S COUNTY

Alex Soros, son of billionaire George Soros, revealed he voted for Zohran Mamdani for New York City mayor. (Chris Kleponis / AFP/Getty Images)

The Soros family, led for decades by billionaire investor and philanthropist George Soros, has spent heavily on charitable foundations and political committees to advance liberal candidates and human rights worldwide, including efforts to make society more equitable through criminal justice reform and other initiatives. The elder Soros transferred control of the family’s roughly $25 billion philanthropic and political network to his son Alex in 2023.

Justice & Public Safety PAC is the organization responsible for providing financial backing to a number of prosecutors who have since become infamous in conservative circles, according to Influence Watch. Among these are former Alameda County, California, District Attorney Pamela Price, former Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascon, Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner, former St. Louis Circuit Attorney Kim Gardner and former Cook County, Illinois, State Attorney Kim Foxx.

Critics charge that these prosecutors fail to incarcerate dangerous members of society, leading to increased crime. Supporters, meanwhile, maintain that addressing the root causes of crime, such as poverty and inequality, will stop offenses before they occur and that harsh punishments for criminals incentivizes recidivism.

Gascon, for one, attracted criticism for ordering his prosecutors not to pursue many sentencing enhancements, which can result in criminals being put away for longer, and for drastically reducing the number of misdemeanors tried by his office, according to the Los Angeles Times. He faced significant internal dissent as crime rates climbed, with rank-and-file prosecutors voting nearly unanimously to support a recall effort against him, Politico reported.

Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascon speaks during a press conference about the facts surrounding the fatal shootings of two El Monte police officers at the Hall of Justice in Los Angeles on Tuesday, June 21, 2022. (Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images)

AS SOCIALIST MAYOR BATTLES ICE, SEATTLE POLICE AND CRIME VICTIMS SAY REPEAT OFFENDERS ARE TERRORIZING THE CITY

Krasner, meanwhile, has been denounced for presiding over a historic homicide spike in his city while he reduced prosecutions.

These controversies were not without consequences for Soros-backed prosecutors.

Of the 25 district attorneys with links to Soros that appeared on the ballot in 2024, 12 were either defeated or recalled, including Gascon. Sean Kennedy, the Law Enforcement Legal Defense Fund’s policy director, told Fox News Digital at the time that, of the 75 Soros-linked prosecutors his organization had identified since 2022, 50 had either left office or been replaced with more moderate officials.

DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY'

Hungarian-born US investor and philanthropist George Soros addresses the assembly on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum (WEF) annual meeting in Davos on May 24, 2022.  (Fabrice COFFRINI / AFP via Getty Images)

Justice & Public Safety backed a progressive prosecutor in Virginia’s 2025 election, providing some potential insight into the kinds of candidates it will bankroll as Election Day 2026 approaches.

The committee spent six figures backing the candidacy of Norfolk Commonwealth Attorney Ramin Fatehi, campaign finance records show. Conservatives criticized Fatehi over his opposition to cash bail, his resistance to prosecuting crimes like shoplifting and his participation in a coalition of prosecutors aiming to prosecute federal immigration agents.

"The old-fashioned view about public safety was not taking into account externalities. It was focused on the idea of crime as an evil unto itself," Fatehi said in a 2021 interview. "Where I part ways is in recognizing that crime is a symptom. It’s a symptom of structural racism, of systematic community disinvestment, of redlining, unequal school policy, the lack of jobs, lack of transportation, a lack of opportunities, intergenerational barriers to wealth building, the disinvestment in the treatment of the mentally ill."

Soros himself similarly argued in a 2022 essay that progressive prosecutors can improve public safety by using resources to address the root causes of crime rather than resorting to jailing criminals for long periods of time. Supporting his claim, he wrote that "black people in the U.S. are five times as likely to be sent to jail as white people," which is "an injustice that undermines our democracy."

The Soros family has other sources of cash available to fund its political goals ahead of 2026, including the Open Society Policy, a 501(c)(4) advocacy group that brought in nearly $160 million in 2024, according to tax documents.

The Open Society Foundation, the Soros family’s philanthropy, did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital Monday.

title: Far-left Senate hopeful explains ‘ogre on a pike’ remark after getting torched by his own party
excerpt: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., was the target of his controversial "ogre on a pike" remark during the candidates’ final primary debate but did n...
body_text:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., was the target of his controversial "ogre on a pike" remark during the candidates’ final primary debate but did not take it back. (Credit: WJBK)

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, declined to apologize Monday night for his "ogre on a pike" metaphor after critics from both parties condemned the leaked remark as violent and, in some cases, sexist.

Pressed during the final primary debate before next week's election, over whether he regretted the rhetoric, El-Sayed defended the substance of his comments before revealing whom he had been referring to — and it was not primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

"I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman," El-Sayed said, accusing the Pennsylvania Democratic senator of getting elected on one set of values before "completely throwing those values in the mud."

GRETCHEN WHITMER ENDORSES MODERATE HALEY STEVENS IN TIGHT UPCOMING SENATE PRIMARY

The controversy stemmed from comments El-Sayed made during a recent Zoom meeting with donors, Politico reported, adding that El-Sayed was discussing how to use his victory in Michigan’s upcoming Aug. 4 primary and the November election to build a national platform to move the Democratic Party further left and support future primary challenges, such as against Fetterman.

U.S. Sen. John Fetterman (D-PA) walks through the Senate Subway during the Senate War Powers vote on April 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

"Ideally, you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message," El-Sayed said, according to audio obtained by Politico. While El-Sayed did not name Stevens in the recording, some Democrats interpreted the remark as referring to her. Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., who has endorsed Stevens, called the remark a "violent, vulgar" threat and said candidates should be working to lower the political temperature.

Neera Tanden, a former Biden administration official who returned to leading the left-wing think tank the Center for American Progress, connected the remark to broader accusations of sexism that have roiled the primary. "Calling your female opponent an ogre you want to put on a pike is not beating the rap that this race has some serious sexism," Tanden wrote on X.

SWING-STATE POLL SPELLS TROUBLE FOR FAR LEFT AS SCHUMER-BACKED CANDIDATE DOMINATES WITH CRITICAL VOTING BLOCS

El-Sayed did not apologize for or retract the metaphor. He instead argued that senators should be willing to challenge colleagues who fail to act according to the values on which they campaigned. The progressive candidate then pivoted to accuse the United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC, of running repeated attacks against his character on Stevens’ behalf. He invoked his wife, mother and two daughters while rejecting accusations that his rhetoric toward women had been disrespectful.

Michigan Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at The People V. The Powerful rally at the Detroit Opera House on July 18, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

"I was raised by strong women," El-Sayed said, arguing that claims he was sexist because he had criticized former first lady Michelle Obama in a years-old opinion piece and challenged Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in the 2018 gubernatorial primary were "inconsistent with the truth."

Stevens responded by highlighting other comments attributed to El-Sayed during the leaked donor call, including attacks involving Whitmer, former Sen. Debbie Stabenow and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who was in the race with El-Sayed and Stevens before dropping out earlier this month.

"Only he can account for saying that Whitmer is bought and paid for, or that no one cares about Debbie Stabenow, or that Mallory McMorrow isn’t smart enough," Stevens said.

She later delivered a pointed response to El-Sayed’s clarification.

"Thank you for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre," Stevens said.

Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, right, and former Wayne County Health Department Director Abdul El-Sayed are facing off in the August 4, 2026 Democratic Senate primary in the Great Lakes battleground state. (Getty Images)

MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT MALLORY MCMORROW DROPS OUT OF SENATE RACE WEEKS BEFORE PRIMARY

Meanwhile, Stevens campaign spokesperson, Arik Wolk, accused El-Sayed of resorting to personal insults and focusing on his national political ambitions rather than Michigan.

"Abdul continues with personal insults and making this race about his personal political ambitions and the other 49 states," Wolk said. "Haley is focused on getting things done for Michigan, and only Michigan."

Republicans also took advantage of the remarks. RNC Research characterized El-Sayed’s debate response as a "double down" on calling Fetterman an "ogre," while Michigan Republican strategist Dennis Lennox argued that El-Sayed’s candidacy was "about propelling the hard Left’s ascent nationally."

The "pike" imagery has triggered political controversy before. In 2020, former Trump White House strategist Steve Bannon said he would place the heads of Dr. Anthony Fauci and then-FBI Director Christopher Wray "on pikes" outside the White House as a warning to federal officials.

X, then-Twitter, suspended Bannon’s podcast account following backlash over the remarks, while Facebook and YouTube removed the video they were included in, citing policies addressing violent or incendiary content. Bannon later maintained that he had been speaking metaphorically — similar to El-Sayed.

Steve Bannon speaks at the National Conservatism Conference in Washington D.C., Sept. 3, 2025.  (DOMINIC GWINN/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

Earlier that year, a separate "head on a pike" controversy erupted during President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial after CBS News reported that an unnamed Trump confidant said Republican senators had been warned, "Vote against the president and your head will be on a pike."

Then-House impeachment manager, now Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., repeated the report on the Senate floor while stressing, "I don’t know if that is true" and "I hope it is not true." Republican senators immediately disputed the account, with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, saying she knew of no senator who had been threatened by the administration and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, said of Schiff’s remark about the alleged comments: "That’s when he lost me."

"Not only have I never heard the ‘head on the pike’ line but also I know of no Republican senator who has been threatened in any way by anyone in the administration," Collins told reporters at the time.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Prominent Holocaust museum challenges Mamdani with offer in response to claims about 'genocide' in Gaza
excerpt:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani delivered remarks from Gracie Mansion on St. Patrick’s Day. (Credit: NYC Mayor's Office)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is yet to publicly respond to an invitation from a...
body_text:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani delivered remarks from Gracie Mansion on St. Patrick’s Day. (Credit: NYC Mayor's Office)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is yet to publicly respond to an invitation from a prominent Holocaust museum to visit in order to "truly understand" what "genocide looks like" as he faces criticism from the Jewish community for repeatedly using that label to describe the situation in Gaza.

"You keep using the word ‘genocide’ when talking about Israel," Jeff Miller, chair of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, posted on X on Friday, inviting Mamdani to visit the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C.

"If you truly want to understand what genocide looks like, as Chairman of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, I would be happy to personally arrange a tour of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum for you."

Miller was responding to a post from the UJA-Federation of New York expressing grief over a pair of recent stabbings in New York City carried out by an attacker who allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" during the attacks. Authorities say one of the victims is Jewish, and the attack is being investigated as a hate crime.

JEWISH LEADERS FAULT MAMDANI RHETORIC AS UPPER WEST SIDE STABBING, HATE CRIME PROBE CONTINUES

Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks at a rally in New York alongside 1199SEIU members and immigration advocates after the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can revoke protections for Haitians and Syrians. (Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Miller’s post went on to say that "words matter especially from elected leaders" and that "rhetoric that demonizes Israel and the Jewish state has consequences."

"I hope you are simply ignoring the impact of your words and not purposely trying to normalize antisemitism," Miller wrote. "My invitation is sincere. Come to the Museum. Learn what genocide actually means. "

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office multiple times inquiring whether the mayor intends to take Miller up on his offer but did not receive a response.

SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY YELLING ‘ALLAHU AKBAR,' STABBING 2 MEN IN NYC ATTACK

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said his administration is exploring whether the city has legal authority to arrest Netanyahu if he visits for the U.N. General Assembly. (Ronen Zvulun/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Miller told Fox News Digital that he felt an "obligation" to speak up and that he would be "happy" to personally walk Mamdani through the museum.

"If the Mayor wants to repeatedly invoke that word, I invite him to come with me to the Holocaust Museum and confront what genocide actually looked like: the systematic attempt to annihilate an entire people," Miller said. "If he does not want to come to our Museum, he should visit Rwanda or another place whose people have endured genocide and listen to survivors."

Miller added that Mamdani is free to "criticize the Israeli government" and disagree with policies, "but there is a profound difference between legitimate criticism of a government and rhetoric that demonizes the world’s only Jewish state and helps normalize hostility toward Jews."

Miller’s invitation was celebrated by many on social media, including Republican Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who posted on X that he hopes Mamdani takes the offer.

MAMDANI'S LATEST NETANYAHU REMARKS DEEPEN CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH LEADERS

People participate in a "Climate Justice Means Free Palestine" rally outside Citibank headquarters in New York City on June 18, 2024. Protesters carried pro-Palestinian signs and climate justice messaging during the demonstration. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"The US Holocaust Memorial Museum — where I proudly serve on the Council — is an important institution that shows the truth about what happened," Scott wrote. "I urge anyone visiting Washington, DC to stop by. "

"The @NYCMayor Mamdani should take up the Chairman’s offer for a tour of the Holocaust Museum so he understands what is genocide," billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman posted on X.

Mamdani has faced intense criticism for his position on Israel since jumping into the mayoral race last year and since taking office, he has often angered the Jewish community with comments calling for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and repeatedly accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza after the October 7th Hamas terrorist attack.

"Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people," Mamdani said last week in a video announcement that he did not have the authority to arrest Netanyahu in accordance with an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant, a warrant the United States does not recognize.

"He is responsible for the killing of more than 73,000 people, for the maiming of tens of thousands of children as those who survive undergo amputation without anesthesia. For the targeting of neonatal hospitals and maternity care centers, denying newborns even the chance to live. For the countless people he starved as he blocked food and humanitarian aid from reaching them. For the gunning down of hundreds of aid workers and journalists."

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Freed American reveals brutal Iran prison ordeal, warns hostages face greater danger
excerpt: Morad Tahbaz, who spent nearly six years in Evin Prison, says Western governments have failed to deter Iran’s hostage-taking and warns renewed conflict could worsen conditions for Americans still held...
body_text:
Morad Tahbaz, who spent nearly six years in Evin Prison, says Western governments have failed to deter Iran’s hostage-taking and warns renewed conflict could worsen conditions for Americans still held.

For nearly six years, American conservationist Morad Tahbaz lived in what he described as hell inside Iran’s prison system. The worst four months were spent completely alone in a small cell, beneath a bright light that never went dark.

Tahbaz was held in Ward 2A of Iran’s Evin Prison, which he described as a high-security detention facility controlled by the intelligence branch of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

He was allowed out only twice a day for about 10 minutes and was forced to wear a blindfold whenever he left, Tahbaz told Fox News Digital. His weekly call with his wife lasted only a few minutes and was monitored so closely that an official interrupted whenever he spoke in English.

"This is probably the harshest and toughest imprisonment that any prisoner will go through," Tahbaz, who was finally released in September 2023, told Fox News Digital of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence detention facility inside Iran's Evin Prison.

WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

Morad Tahbaz, an Iranian American conservationist, in Golestan National Park, Iran. Tahbaz spent nearly six years in Iran’s Evin Prison before being released with four other Americans in September 2023. (Morad Tahbaz)

Tahbaz was living and working in Iran as a conservationist when authorities arrested him alongside several colleagues in January 2018. He had co-founded the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, which worked to protect endangered species including the Asiatic cheetah and Persian leopard.

One of the accusations leveled against him, Tahbaz said, was that he had trained lizards to spy on Iranian military installations for Israel.

"You can’t make this stuff up," Tahbaz said in the Zoom interview with Fox News Digital. "It just gives you an idea of the kind of narrative that this regime comes up with. They’ll come up with anything."

What began with interrogations in January 2018 turned into nearly six years of imprisonment for the Iranian American conservationist.

Now free and back in his home in the U.S., Tahbaz fears the war between the United States and Iran could make the Americans still held by Iran both more vulnerable and more valuable as negotiating assets.

"I do think the strikes in Iran will have an impact on the hostages’ situation and their circumstances," he said.

TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR

Morad Tahbaz reunites with his family following his release from Iran in September 2023. (Morad Tahnaz)

Tahbaz said he spent his first two years inside the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence facility at Evin.

After his conviction, Tahbaz was transferred into the general prison population. He said his cellmates ranged from suspected ISIS members to former Iranian government ministers.

The isolation and physical conditions were accompanied by constant uncertainty.

"The uncertainty when you are a hostage is not like you think at the end of your sentence they’ll necessarily let you go," Tahbaz said. "They’ll just come up with another charge to keep you there for as long as you’re of value to them."

Tahbaz was released Sept. 18, 2023, with four other Americans in a Qatar-mediated agreement between Washington and Iran. The exchange also involved five Iranians held by the United States and the transfer of $6 billion in previously frozen Iranian funds into a restricted account for humanitarian transactions.

The negotiation brought Tahbaz home, but he believes Western governments have failed to establish consequences strong enough to stop Iran from detaining more foreign and dual nationals.

"This business of hostage-taking has been going on essentially since the beginning of the revolution," he said.

LAWYER FOR AMERICAN DETAINED IN IRAN SAYS HOSTAGE DEAL IS 'EASIEST PROBLEM ON THE TABLE' FOR BOTH SIDES

Freed hostage Morad Tahbaz surrounded by his family just after landing in the U.S., September 2023. (Morad Tahbaz)

"It will continue, in my opinion, as long as there is no deterrence," Tahbaz added. "None of the Western governments, in reality, have done anything significant about stopping this practice."

The issue returned to the forefront in July with the release of Dena Karari, a 53-year-old Iranian American from California.

Karari had been unable to leave Iran since December 2024 after authorities confiscated her passports. Her attorney said she faced allegations of espionage and collaboration with a hostile state. President Donald Trump announced in July that she had been allowed to leave and called the decision a "gesture of goodwill."

Karari was not continuously imprisoned, according to reporting about her case, but she remained under an exit ban and was repeatedly interrogated.

Her release offered relief during a widening conflict, but Tahbaz said dual nationals remain particularly vulnerable because Iran does not recognize their foreign citizenship.

"Iran doesn’t recognize any other nationality other than the Iranian," he said.

Authorities can develop a national-security case, secure a sentence and then preserve the prisoner for use in future negotiations, Tahbaz said.

"You’re condemned and they pass sentence and you’re in the system, and now you are a bargaining chip," he said.

The precise number of Americans currently imprisoned or prevented from leaving Iran remains unclear.

Reuters reported in March that at least six U.S. citizens or permanent residents were detained in Iran, including journalist Reza Valizadeh, businessman Kamran Hekmati and U.S. permanent resident Shahab Dalili.

Valizadeh, a former Radio Farda journalist, was sentenced to 10 years for allegedly collaborating with a hostile government. Hekmati was sentenced to two years for having visited Israel more than a decade earlier, according to his family. Dalili, who was arrested after traveling to Iran for his father’s funeral, was sentenced to 10 years for allegedly cooperating with a hostile government.

Advocates warned that escalating strikes could increase the risk that detainees would be harmed or used as leverage.

The State Department formally designated Hekmati, who has bladder cancer, as wrongfully detained in March.

Tahbaz said he believes three Americans remain in custody, although that number could not be independently confirmed. Some cases are deliberately kept private because families fear publicity could increase the danger to detainees.

His concerns about the current war are rooted in how Iranian interrogators responded to tensions with Washington during his own imprisonment.

"When I was taken in in January of 2018, and it was right at the beginning of the first Trump administration, the amount of frustration and anger at the rollback of the JCPOA at that time, I mean, it was thrown into my face just about every day of my interrogation in some way, shape or form," Tahbaz said, referring to a 2015 nuclear deal, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action.

The United States formally withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement, known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, in May 2018, several months after Tahbaz’s arrest.

Tahbaz believes the current conflict could similarly be transferred onto prisoners who have no control over decisions made in Washington.

"It definitely will worsen the case of prisoners in custody and those who may be just under surveillance or potential hostages," he said.

US ‘LOCKED AND LOADED’ FOR ‘MUCH HIGHER’ STRIKES IF IRAN TALKS FAIL AS TRUMP PAUSES HORMUZ OPS

Morad Tahbaz with Eskandar Firouz, the founding head of Iran’s Department of the Environment, at Lar National Park in Iran. Firouz, who was imprisoned for six years following the 1979 revolution, died several years after the photo was taken. (Morad Tahbaz)

He described prisoners as one more source of leverage in Iran’s broader confrontation with the United States.

"You’re seeing that playing out even with the war, this tit for tat, you do this, we’ll do that," he said.

"The hostages are, you know, just a commodity from Iran’s perspective, to be used at the right time."

Tahbaz’s experience with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps also shapes his analysis of the struggle unfolding inside Iran.

He stressed that he is not a political analyst and described his conclusions as personal assessments based on his experience and conversations with contacts familiar with the country.

Tahbaz said he believes competing interests within the Revolutionary Guard are fighting to preserve their political and economic power.

He pointed specifically to Khatam al-Anbiya, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' engineering and construction conglomerate. Tahbaz argued that sanctions have benefited powerful IRGC-linked entities by forcing oil sales, imports and money transfers into opaque black and gray markets.

"They have created a huge franchise for themselves because of these sanctions," he said.

"They don’t want to see the sanctions go away, because they will lose their franchise, if you will. They will lose their power, their control over the money and everything that goes along with it."

He said ordinary Iranians have suffered most from the resulting economic isolation and wartime conditions.

"The people who are hurt most by all of this are the people of Iran," Tahbaz said. "They’re unfortunately taking the brunt of all of these in their daily lives."

Tahbaz predicted Iranians would eventually return to the streets, but said many had lost confidence that Western governments would intervene to help remove the regime.

"I’m sure they’ll be back on the streets," he said. "But I think this notion that the Western states are going to step in and help them overthrow this regime, that went out the window."

Tahbaz said many Iranians had previously been strongly sympathetic toward the United States and initially hoped the conflict might end the Islamic Republic. That characterization reflects his assessment and conversations and could not be independently quantified.

He believes any future political movement will have to develop primarily inside Iran rather than being directed by opposition groups abroad.

"There’s a lot of hatred and anger just boiling there," Tahbaz said. "So it will boil up and over again without a doubt. The question is when, how, but it will happen again."

Tahbaz is recounting his imprisonment in his new book, "Green Parrots: A Memoir of Survival in Iran’s Evin Prison," scheduled for publication Sept. 29. The publisher says the book describes how he relied on skills developed while tracking endangered wildlife to survive nearly six years in Evin, including solitary confinement.

His release illustrates the contradiction confronting governments trying to recover their citizens: negotiations can bring individual prisoners home, but Tahbaz believes the broader practice will continue unless Iran faces meaningful deterrence for taking them.

Military members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in western Tehran, Iran (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

He survived because governments ultimately negotiated for his freedom.

His warning is that as the war intensifies, the Americans still held in Iran could become more valuable to Tehran at precisely the moment their circumstances become more dangerous.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is an investigative journalist, filmmaker and war correspondent. She has directed and produced over 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries. Recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award, Lachter is also a 2023-24 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Chili's revives iconic red booths and classic design in nationwide restaurant overhaul
excerpt:
Daland Corporation president Tim Sparks talks the return of retro Pizza Hut restaurants as franchise owners renovate locations to bring back the classic dining experience on ‘America Reports.’

Chili'...
body_text:
Daland Corporation president Tim Sparks talks the return of retro Pizza Hut restaurants as franchise owners renovate locations to bring back the classic dining experience on ‘America Reports.’

Chili's is betting that what's old is new again.

The casual dining chain is rolling out a nostalgic restaurant redesign across the country, bringing back signature red booths, quirky artwork and other throwback touches that helped define the brand for decades.

The makeover is expected to reach every U.S. Chili's restaurant over time. The company plans to remodel about 10% of its roughly 1,200 domestic locations each year until all restaurants have been refreshed, a Chili's representative told Fox News Digital.

CHILI'S GOES VIRAL AFTER ROASTING FAST-FOOD PRICES: 'WHY LET THEM PLAY YOU LIKE THIS?'

The redesign comes after the chain spent the past several years investing in food quality and service. Now, the focus has shifted to the dining experience itself.

"The guiding idea behind the project was simple: 'Make Chili's More Chili's,'" according to a company fact sheet.

Chili's is getting a nostalgic makeover. (Chili's)

The updated design draws inspiration from the brand's original Greenville Avenue restaurant in Dallas, as well as the colorful look that became synonymous with Chili's during the 1990s.

Before launching the redesign nationwide, Chili's tested several versions at four Dallas-area restaurants.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Those locations were selected because of their proximity to Chili's restaurant support center, allowing team members to visit frequently and gather real-time customer feedback. Lessons from those prototype restaurants helped shape the final design package now being introduced across the country, a company representative said.

Chili's has tested out remodeled restaurants in the Dallas area and will eventually roll out the retro look throughout the country. (Callaghan O'Hare/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The first remodeled restaurants outside the test market reopened July 1 in Fayetteville, Arkansas; Monrovia, California; Kennesaw, Georgia; Lake Charles, Louisiana; Baton Rouge, Louisiana; Greensboro, North Carolina; Cookeville, Tennessee; and El Paso, Texas, according to Chili's.

Among the most noticeable changes are the return of the chain's iconic red booths, tile-inspired tabletops influenced by Southwestern ceramics and refreshed bars accented with neon signage.

The new-look Chili's concept includes its iconic red booths and tile-inspired tabletops influenced by Southwestern ceramics. (Chili's)

Guests will also discover playful references to Chili's history throughout the restaurants, including framed sheet music from the brand's famous baby back ribs jingle, the original 1975 menu and custom wallpaper featuring whimsical scenes such as chili peppers being abducted by a tortilla chip UFO and a margarita swimming pool.

As Chili's begins refreshing restaurants nationwide, it joins another chain looking backward to move forward.

The updated bar areas include larger horseshoe-shaped layouts, additional televisions and oversized "Margarita Bar" signs celebrating one of the chain's signature drinks.

Chili's retro "Margarita Bar" celebrates one of the chain's signature drinks. (Chili's)

Chili's said it sold nearly 30 million margaritas in 2025, more than any other restaurant brand in the country.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As Chili's begins refreshing restaurants nationwide, it joins another chain looking backward to move forward.

Pizza Hut franchisees have found success by bringing back iconic design elements like red roofs, vinyl booths, red cups and Tiffany-style lighting, suggesting that nostalgia has become part of the menu for many diners.

Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

title: Firefighters hasten efforts to contain massive wildfires in France and Spain ahead of heatwave – Europe live
excerpt:
Emmanuel Macron warns that ‘we have to hold out’ as fires burn near city; Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sanchez warns of ‘difficult hours’ ahead

France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before ...
body_text:
Emmanuel Macron warns that ‘we have to hold out’ as fires burn near city; Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sanchez warns of ‘difficult hours’ ahead

France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins

The return of searing temperatures, from today in France and tomorrow in Spain, will complicate efforts to fight massive wildfires raging in the Bordeaux region and a number of sites in Spain.

On a visit to a crisis centre in Bordeaux, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, warned:

“The coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out.”

Over the past week, the gigantic blaze in the region has ravaged 42,000 hectares (103,000 acres), forced 220,000 people to flee and destroyed 240 houses. Such is its size and intensity, it has created a rare pyrocumulonimbus cloud, packing lightning.

But as of Tuesday morning, it remained stable for the second night in a row, which offers hope that firefighters will be able to make further progress before the new heatwave complicates their efforts.

Macron confirmed that a forest fire in nearby Landes – which had forced the evacuation of more than 30,000 people – was now under control. But he warned it “remains virulent and we must be extremely cautious over the next few hours and the coming days”.

Spain has one crucial day to tackle the wildfires before weather conditions worsen again.

Ahead of the new heatwave, Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez told his fellow citizens: “We face difficult hours, complex hours.”

About 60,000 people have been forced to flee in Spain and 220,000 in France, often with just minutes’ notice. Hundreds were also evacuated from Italy.

The fires in Spain have affected an area of 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres) – nearly the size of New York City – according to authorities.

Spain’s state meteorological agency, Aemet, officially declared that a heatwave, the fourth of the summer, would begin on Wednesday, lasting until “at least” Sunday.

It’s Tuesday, 28 July 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Madrid’s regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso said this morning that the wildfires situation is “gradually improving” and allows authorities to be a bit “more optimistic,” as she thanked the emergency services for their work.

Firefighters in France and Spain are facing another day battling wildfires that have resulted in hundreds of thousands of people being evacuated, with another heatwave expected to hit this week.

French authorities have said this year’s wildfires, particularly the Gironde fire near the south-western city of Bordeaux, are ‘completely exceptional’, with more than 116,000 hectares of forest and vegetation burned since the beginning of the year, compared with 70,000 in total last year.

For our “The Latest” podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan about what it means for the continent.

France was also in “a race against time” to control wildfires before another heatwave this week, said Eric Brocardi, a fire service spokesperson.

Weather forecasters have said temperatures could reach 40C (104F) is some parts of the country from Tuesday.

This would complicate efforts to control the wildfire in Gironde in south-west France, which the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as “extremely intense and unpredictable … generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area”.

As firefighters continue to battle the blazes, there is also some concern about the air quality in the affected region.

France’s health agencies warned that the air quality in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region covering Gironde is “degraded” with fine particulate matter way above the limits.

Residents were told to keep doors and windows closed, cover vents with damp clothes, and turn off ventilation systems.

3.5 million filtering FFP2 masks will be delivered to the region by Wednesday.
