title: US diplomats walk out as France addresses UN Security Council
excerpt:
United States diplomats walked out of a United Nations Security Council meeting on Russia’s war against Ukraine as France’s delegation took the floor.

The walkout on Monday came two days after an onl...
body_text:
United States diplomats walked out of a United Nations Security Council meeting on Russia’s war against Ukraine as France’s delegation took the floor.

The walkout on Monday came two days after an online exchange between US and French officials over Washington voting against renewing the four-year term of UN human rights chief Volker Turk.

France’s UN Mission in Geneva wrote on Saturday that the US was no longer a “beacon of human rights” and stood isolated alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali and Russia.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz replied on X that France had voted for a rights chief who “has been lecturing free, sovereign democracies like the United States, the UK, and Israel, while cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors”.

After the walkout, Dan Negrea, an alternate US representative, told the council that his delegation would keep walking out until France renounced its “condescending and disrespectful rhetoric”.

France’s ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, did not mention the walkout when he spoke, saying France was working to preserve the UN’s independence and its capacity to act.

Turk, who has criticised violations of international law by Israel and the US in Palestine and Iran, was reappointed by a UN General Assembly vote of 144 in favour, 10 against and 13 abstentions.

The administration of US President Donald Trump has cut funding to UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of UN entities since 2025. It had also threatened to reassess its engagement over Turk’s mandate.

Washington and Paris have also clashed over NATO spending, trade policy and Trump’s threats to occupy Greenland, a territory of NATO member Denmark.

France, along with other European states, has also drawn Trump’s ire for refusing direct participation in the US-Israel war on Iran.

title: Netflix exec claims ketamine confession in ‘trust exercise’ cost him $1.1M job: lawsuit
excerpt: President Donald Trump signed a groundbreaking executive order allowing research into psychedelic drugs to treat PTSD and other mental health conditions. Many Americans, especially military veterans, ...
body_text:
President Donald Trump signed a groundbreaking executive order allowing research into psychedelic drugs to treat PTSD and other mental health conditions. Many Americans, especially military veterans, are cheering the move, with former Energy Secretary Rick Perry and retired Navy SEAL Marcus Luttrell advocating for the treatments. FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary discusses the potential for breakthrough therapies.

Former Netflix executive Kevin Baillie has sued the streaming giant, according to court papers reported by The New York Post Sunday, after he said he was fired in April from its Eyeline Studios division because he disclosed medically supervised ketamine treatment for depression during a workplace retreat.

"The ketamine therapy issue has factored into the termination," the attorney said, according to the lawsuit.

Baillie, who served as vice president and head of creative at the visual effects division, earned about $1.1 million annually. The complaint said Netflix also denied him as much as one year of severance pay following his dismissal stemming from his comments in January at Netlix-owned Sendero Ranch in Northern California, according to the suit.

He said he underwent ketamine therapy at a Santa Barbara clinic in 2022 while experiencing clinical depression following his mother's death. He said the drug was prescribed and administered under medical supervision, according to the report.

Former Netflix executive Kevin Baillie alleged he was fired in part for disclosing medically supervised ketamine treatment during a workplace trust exercise. (Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDER DIRECTING FDA TO REVIEW PSYCHEDELICS DESIGNATED AS BREAKTHROUGH THERAPY DRUGS

The executive disclosed the treatment during a vulnerability-trust exercise that encouraged employees to share personal experiences. When a Netflix investigator questioned him March 18, the complaint said the therapy was presented as potential recreational drug use.

The investigator raised the treatment "in a manner suggesting suspicion of recreational drug use," the complaint said, according to the Post.

Baillie said the company’s investigation also examined allegations that he used profanity and consumed alcohol. His previous performance review had addressed his language but did not direct him to stop swearing entirely.

"Drop one or two less f-bombs but don’t stop entirely," the performance review said, according to the complaint.

Baillie sued Netflix after his April termination from Eyeline Studios, where he served as vice president and head of creative. (Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images)

VALERIE BERTINELLI APOLOGIZES AFTER DROPPING F-BOMB ON LIVE TV

The lawsuit said Baillie also told colleagues during the retreat that his former father-in-law had taught him to drink a Guinness while standing on his head. A colleague then asked Baillie to demonstrate the trick.

"His colleague immediately asked for a demonstration," the complaint said. "Rather than withhold the openness that the session had encouraged, he performed the trick."

Netflix’s public culture memo promotes vulnerability and candor while describing the company as a professional sports team rather than a family. Managers apply a "keeper test" when deciding whether to retain employees, although the memo also said workers should receive regular feedback and be evaluated on their entire record.

"If the answer is no, we believe it’s fairer to everyone to part ways quickly," Netflix said of the "keeper test," which entails candidly assessing if one would fight to keep a worker if they wanted to leave, or if they would hire the person again if they knew everything they do now.

"You willingly receive and give feedback; you are open about what’s working and what needs to improve; you admit mistakes openly and share learnings widely," the site states.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Baillie said he disclosed the treatment for depression during a January employee retreat at Netflix-owned Sendero Ranch in Northern California. (Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua via Getty Images)

Ketamine is a Schedule III controlled substance that is federally approved as an anesthetic and is also prescribed off-label for depression. The FDA has separately approved the ketamine-derived nasal spray Spravato for treatment-resistant depression under medical supervision.

Baillie is seeking a jury trial, lost wages, compensatory and punitive damages and damages for emotional distress. He previously worked on visual effects for the "Pirates of the Caribbean" and "Harry Potter" franchises.

Netflix had not publicly responded to his allegations as of Monday. Fox News Digital reached out to Baillie and Netflix for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

title: Biden's classified docs narrative crumbles amid release of ghostwriter tapes: 'Be careful'
excerpt:
Fox News senior political analyst Juan Williams discusses why former President Joe Biden is suing the Justice Department to block the release of audio recordings on 'Special Report.'

Former President...
body_text:
Fox News senior political analyst Juan Williams discusses why former President Joe Biden is suing the Justice Department to block the release of audio recordings on 'Special Report.'

Former President Joe Biden's recordings from interviews with his memoir ghostwriter — obtained during special counsel Robert Hur's classified documents investigation — have been released to the public.

After a months-long fight from Biden’s attorneys to block the release of the tape, they abandoned their lawsuit calling for dismal Friday in which a judge accepted Monday.

The plaintiff, Mike Howell formerly with conservative think tank Heritage Foundation and now at Oversight Project, has fought for more than two years to obtain the materials through FOIA requests, arguing that the public has an interest in reviewing the recordings and transcripts on which Hur based his decision.

BIDEN'S HUR INTERVIEW TAPES COULD NOW GO PUBLIC AFTER HIS ATTORNEYS WAVE WHITE FLAG

Former President Biden was dogged throughout his term by rumors of his purported cognitive decline. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

The Oversight Project published more than 70 hours of recordings from Biden's 2016 and 2017 conversations with his "Promise Me, Dad" ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, in which the then-former vice president frequently pauses, speaks haltingly and struggles to recall events — reinforcing Special Counsel Robert Hur's characterization in his report.

"Joe Biden didn’t want these tapes to come out. But now they have — after two years of painful delay. There is no joy in Bidenville today. Robert Hur’s and Merrick Garland’s decision to give Biden a free pass for keeping and disclosing classified information must now be reexamined from top to bottom," Oversight Project Vice President of Litigation Jeff Clark exclusively told Fox News Digital.

Hur investigated Biden’s handling of classified documents dating from his time as vice president in the Obama administration and as a U.S. senator from Delaware. He declined to pursue criminal charges because he concluded prosecutors could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Biden willfully retained or disclosed the material.

HUNTER BIDEN RESURFACES IN LA, REACTS TO QUESTIONS ABOUT BIDEN TAPES, UFO FILES

US President Joe Biden speaks during a State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Feb. 7, 2023. (Nathan Howard/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

In his report, Hur wrote that Biden’s conversations were "painfully slow" and said Biden was "struggling to remember events and straining at times to read and relay his own notebook entries."

"Mr. Biden's memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017 and in his interview with our office in 2023," wrote Hur.

Then-Sen. Joe Biden delivered a fiery speech in 1989 calling on the H.W. Bush administration to launch an "international strike force" on narco-terrorists. (Cynthia Johnson/Getty Images)

He also said, in shocking reasoning for the lack of prosecution, that Biden could appear to a jury as a "sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory" rather than an intentional violator of classified document laws.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of 14-year-old
excerpt:
A judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of a teenage girl.

The decision came after a five-day preliminary hearing, in which Los Angeles prosecutors question...
body_text:
A judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of a teenage girl.

The decision came after a five-day preliminary hearing, in which Los Angeles prosecutors questioned a dozen witnesses and displayed photographic evidence as 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez's family watched on.

The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, is accused of killing the girl, whose remains were found last September in a Tesla registered to his address.

Burke, 21, has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing her.

Texts reveal 14-year-old allegedly murdered by singer D4vd had pregnancy and abortion

Burke's arraignment is scheduled for 31 August. The trial is to start within 90 days of that date.

Prosecutors have alleged Burke stabbed the teen before dismembering her body after years of alleged sexual abuse.

They allege he killed her because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.

Evidence read in court on Monday showed threats Hernandez made to Burke on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl.

"I swear to GOD I will kill u", one expletive-laden text said, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," one text said.

The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.

During questioning at the hearing on Monday, Detective Corey Farrell of the Los Angeles Police Department said text messages indicated that the defendant and the girl had attended church with her family.

The detective also told the court that the teen had misrepresented her age to the defendant, telling him she was 16 and 18 at different times.

Burke's defence lawyers argued there was not sufficient evidence that he had committed the crime.

They said her parents were aware of what was going on between them and had even given written consent for her to travel to London with Burke for a week.

The defence highlighted texts that suggested Celeste had insisted on going to Burke's Hollywood Hills home the night of 23 April 2025 and that he had argued against her coming that night.

He "repeatedly expressed love and care for Ms Hernandez after they broke up", defence attorney Marilyn Bednarski said in court.

The medical examiner's inability to prove how the two penetrating wounds found in the girl occurred and the lack of surveillance video capturing Burke being home on the night of 23 April showed a lack of evidence, the defence argued.

Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Charlaine Olmedo ultimately said the prosecution met the threshold for proving that Burke had probable cause to commit the crime, a lower standard than beyond a reasonable doubt, which the prosecution will have to prove in trial.

"The people have met their burden on all counts," Judge Olmedo said.

She found that prosecutors met the threshold for the charge of murder with special circumstances, including lying in wait, motive for financial gain and eliminating a witness.

Following the hearing, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said his office only presented a fraction of the evidence it had against Burke, and that it would present everything in the coming trial.

Hochman also said his office had not yet determined if it would pursue the death penalty against Burke.

The BBC's Fame Under Fire podcast brings you the latest from inside the Los Angeles courtroom at the D4vd preliminary hearing.

title: DNC chair faces growing scrutiny amid financial pressure and internal turmoil
excerpt:
Fraught time for Ken Martin as new reporting details cash-flow problem and divisions over party’s direction

Mounting financial pressures and growing internal turmoil at the Democratic National Commit...
body_text:
Fraught time for Ken Martin as new reporting details cash-flow problem and divisions over party’s direction

Mounting financial pressures and growing internal turmoil at the Democratic National Committee (DNC) have intensified scrutiny of chair Ken Martin, as new reporting detailed a deepening cash-flow problem, management concerns and widening divisions over the party’s direction less than 100 days before the November midterm elections.

The latest reporting has underscored both the committee’s financial distress and the toll it has taken on Martin personally. The New York Times reported that the embattled DNC chair, who took the helm last year, became the subject of an internal HR inquiry after throwing his phone in the direction of a junior aide’s desk during a heated exchange in early July, prompting a formal complaint. The Times, citing people familiar with the matter, also reported that the incident nearly cost him his job and has contributed to growing isolation with the party as the committee grapples with mounting financial strain.

The latest revelations include that the DNC put its physical Washington DC headquarters up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15m line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, Notus reported, citing Washington DC deed records. The New York Times separately reported that the DNC is about $2m in debt, compared with roughly $130m cash on hand held by the Republican National Committee.

The committee argued that the arrangement was “not new” and that it had done so to secure loans previously. However, one DNC member told the outlet: “Ken is gaslighting us about the DNC’s finances and not being transparent about the financial situation makes us doubt if he can oversee the DNC during the most important primary of our lifetime.”

Another Democrat close to Martin told Notus he had struggled to convince donors to maximize their contributions, which had contributed to the small cash-on-hand total.

Adding to the party’s financial woes, the Times reported that the DNC had asked vendors not to send invoices until after the midterm elections in November.

Roger Lau, the executive director of the DNC, told the Times in a statement that the bill-deferral discussions were “nothing more than standard negotiations with vendors over contracts and payment processes”.

It’s an increasingly fraught time for Martin, whose tenure has been marked by turbulence almost since the start, when he became embroiled in a public spat with then vice-chair David Hogg. Their philosophical disagreement proved irreconcilable and Hogg eventually quit.

Faith in Martin’s leadership had eroded further following his botched handling of a long-promised autopsy of the 2024 election that ultimately failed to address what actually went wrong for the party – from Gaza to the Biden-Harris transition. The release in May prompted a round of calls for Martin’s resignation.

Last week, Martin defended the state of the DNC’s finances in an op-ed on Substack, writing that the committee had made the “conscious decision” to spend the cash it raises on “electoral assets” rather than stockpiling resources.

He said the DNC had “done exceptionally better with high-net worth donors”, citing an increase of donations from major donors relative to comparable years. “We must measure success by power built, not simply dollars retained,” he added.

But some veteran Democratic fundraisers remain unconvinced. In a Substack essay published on Monday, former Democratic finance chair and former US ambassador Rufus Gifford argued the party’s financial problems stem from a broader collapse in donor confidence.

“I think there is no saving Martin’s chairmanship,” Gifford wrote, arguing that the “two main jobs” of the DNC chair were to “raise money and message relentlessly on every form of media”. The committee, he warned, was at risk of becoming “irrelevant” unless it found a way to restore donor trust and rebuild its national fundraising operation before the 2028 presidential campaign.

The reports renewed calls for Martin to step aside, which he has firmly resisted.

“Ken Martin must resign,” Congressman Sam Liccardo, a California Democrat, wrote on X. “As Democrats, we have become too captured by failing strategies. We must fail forward, and pivot. The urgency of this moment will not reward – and our children will not forgive – torpidity.”

But at a campaign event in Pennsylvania on Sunday, Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, expressed confidence in Martin, telling reporters covering the rally that the DNC chair had his “full support”.

title: Fishing content creator who filmed himself being bitten by a shark while spearfishing lucky he still has leg
excerpt: Jesse Watters hosts Chris Fischer, founder of OCEARCH, to discuss the early surge in shark attacks this summer. Recent incidents include a New York beach closure due to bull sharks, a swimmer bitten i...
body_text:
Jesse Watters hosts Chris Fischer, founder of OCEARCH, to discuss the early surge in shark attacks this summer. Recent incidents include a New York beach closure due to bull sharks, a swimmer bitten in Queens, and a child attacked in knee-deep water in Florida. Fischer notes a rebound in shark populations to 1960s levels, advising beachgoers to avoid swimming when bait fish are active to stay safe.

A fishing content creator from New Zealand is lucky to still have his leg after going for a dive in Fiji. Henry Gibbs was spearfishing earlier this month in the water near the South Pacific island when he was bitten by a grey reef shark.

The damage from the bite to his right leg required four surgeries and a skin graft, but didn’t cause him to lose any ability to use his foot.

"No hard feelings towards the shark. I was in its environment hunting its food," Gibbs wrote in an Instagram post a few days ago that included pictures of him in a hospital bed.

Fishing content creator Henry Gibbs was bitten by a grey reef shark while spearfishing in Fiji. (Getty Images)

"Wrong place, wrong time, and there are definitely a few lessons I'll share when I post the footage in the hope it helps someone avoid ending up in the same situation and a bit on how to respond to it."

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

On Sunday, the fishing influencer followed through on that and shared the footage of the shark circling below before racing toward him and taking a bite out of his lower leg.

Gibbs explained that they had been diving in the reef for an hour or two before making their way to clearer blue water. They were trying to do some spearfishing and had a "handful of grey reef sharks" hanging out near them.

Palm Beach closed as beaches in Sydney's north have been closed since Tuesday due to shark attacks and dangerous currents during summer in Sydney on January 22, 2026 in Sydney, Australia. (Corbis via Getty Images)

One of the sharks in particular hung around longer than the others. He doesn’t know if it was the commotion coming from the boat, the speargun sounds or the general activity in the water that made the shark excited.

'SHARK WEEK' HOST FORREST GALANTE EXPLAINS WHY CRUSHING BEERS IN THE OCEAN IS A BAD IDEA

"I'll never know exactly what caused the change, but eventually it started making tight semicircles beneath us, became increasingly agitated and even sprinted at the boat," Gibbs wrote in the caption of the shark attack footage.

"Looking back, that should've been enough of a sign to call the dive. I never thought a shark of that size posed much of a threat, and that was a mistake."

He added that most of his encounters with sharks have come in New Zealand, where he says the sharks are less aggressive. A big mistake on his part was expecting this shark to act in the same manner.

Having been bitten by a shark, Gibbs has some takeaways he'd like to pass along. The first is to end the dive and move on if a shark's behavior changes. He also suggests sticking to plain black wetsuits in the tropics.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

He's heard of several incidents now that he's been attacked of grey reef sharks going after divers in camouflage wetsuits. His last two takeaways are to not ignore an agitated shark and to not judge the risk by the shark's size.

A grey reef shark attacked fishing influencer Henry Gibbs in Fiji and he released footage of the bite on social media. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Gibbs teased that there's more footage that's more graphic than what he already shared. He also thanked those who reached out and who have cared for him since the bite.

"I'm still deciding whether to share the rest of the footage as it becomes very graphic, but I do want to share more about carrying proper trauma gear, knowing how to use it, and diving with people you trust," he wrote.

"A huge thank you to everyone who's reached out, and to all the doctors, nurses and hospital staff, family and friends who've looked after me."

You can add spearfishing in Fiji near grey reef sharks to the list of activities you're not going to find me attempting.

title: Shot fired outside US consulate in Canada for second time this year
excerpt:
At least one shot has been fired outside the US Consulate General in Toronto, in the second such incident in just four months.

Nobody was injured in the attack, police said on Monday, adding that a s...
body_text:
At least one shot has been fired outside the US Consulate General in Toronto, in the second such incident in just four months.

Nobody was injured in the attack, police said on Monday, adding that a shell casing was found and the building’s facade had been damaged.

A white sedan was seen fleeing the scene at about 5am local time (09:00 GMT), which police said they briefly pursued before giving up the chase over safety concerns due to its ultra-high speed.

No suspects have been arrested, and the investigation is ongoing.

A US Department of State spokesperson said Washington was working closely with Canadian authorities following the incident.

Toronto police declined to speculate on a possible motive for this weekend’s shooting and whether it was linked to previous incidents.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he expected “all those responsible to be found, prosecuted and punished to the fullest extent of the law”.

This is the second time in four months that shots have been fired at the US Consulate in Toronto.

On March 10, several shots were fired at the same building, and one police officer was later killed in an operation to arrest those responsible.

Toronto police claimed in June that young people in the Toronto area were being recruited via encrypted messaging apps to shoot at various targets and record the shootings for payment.

The targets the police mentioned included synagogues, Jewish schools, a waste management company, and the US Consulate.

The police did not provide evidence, only mentioning that investigations were ongoing in cooperation with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the US FBI.

title: Store clerk foiled ex-Navy SEAL's explosives plot targeting police at No Kings protest, feds say
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A former U.S. Navy SEAL was convicted in a foiled plot to attack law enforcement officers with explosives during a "No...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A former U.S. Navy SEAL was convicted in a foiled plot to attack law enforcement officers with explosives during a "No Kings" protest in California after a store clerk's tip led federal investigators to him.

Gregory Vandenberg, 49, was found guilty after a five-day federal trial of transportation of explosives with intent to kill, injure or intimidate and attempted transportation of prohibited fireworks into California, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico.

Jurors deliberated for about three hours before returning the guilty verdict.

Prosecutors said Vandenberg was driving from El Paso, Texas, to San Diego ahead of the June 14, 2025, demonstrations when he stopped at a travel center near Lordsburg, New Mexico, and purchased six mortar-style fireworks and 72 M-150 firecrackers.

FORMER MARINE GETS 100 YEARS IN PRISON AS JUDGE CALLS ICE DETENTION CENTER AMBUSH 'AN ASSAULT ON DEMOCRACY'

Surveillance video shows Gregory Vandenberg speaking with a store employee while purchasing fireworks in New Mexico. Employees later contacted law enforcement after he discussed attacking officers at California's No Kings protests, federal authorities said. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)

While making the purchase, Vandenberg told a store clerk he intended to throw the explosives at law enforcement officers during the protests, federal authorities said.

He repeatedly asked about the amount of gunpowder in the fireworks, whether taping multiple mortars together would increase their explosive force and said he was interested only in their ability to injure officers, prosecutors said.

'SOMETHING BIG': FEDS REVEAL HOW RELATIVES OF SUSPECTS IN FOILED WHITE HOUSE UFC PLOT SAW WARNING SIGNS

Gregory Vandenberg wears a shirt reading "AMALEK" while purchasing fireworks at a New Mexico travel center on June 12, 2025. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)

Vandenberg also encouraged the clerk to attend the protests and hand out fireworks to others, telling the employee he would not get hurt because of his military experience, according to trial testimony.

The conversation alarmed employees enough that they wrote down Vandenberg's license plate and contacted law enforcement before he reached California.

Federal agents tracked Vandenberg to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Tucson, Arizona, where he was arrested the following morning while sleeping inside his vehicle.

ANTI-ISRAEL DEMONSTRATOR SENTENCED TO YEAR IN JAIL FOR MANSLAUGHTER DURING 2023 PROTESTS

Prosecutors said he falsely claimed he was traveling for work despite being unemployed and later told investigators he was visiting friends in Phoenix.

A search of Vandenberg's vehicle uncovered the fireworks along with clothing displaying antisemitic, anti-Israel and extremist imagery, according to prosecutors.

Among the items recovered were shirts bearing an Al-Qaeda flag, a shirt calling for the destruction of Judea, a hat featuring the Al-Qaeda flag and apparel displaying a variation of the Black Sun, a symbol associated with neo-Nazi ideology.

Federal prosecutors said investigators recovered an Al-Qaeda flag hat from Gregory Vandenberg's vehicle after his arrest en route to California's No Kings protests. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)

Jurors were also shown photographs of Vandenberg wearing a custom-made T-shirt bearing the word "AMALEK" while inside the travel center. Prosecutors said Vandenberg told investigators the word meant "destroyer of Jews."

Investigators also discovered Vandenberg's cellphone home screen displayed a Taliban flag. A forensic review of the phone uncovered what prosecutors described as violent extremist content, including antisemitic, anti-Israel and anti-U.S. material, as well as messages discussing the upcoming protests.

Federal investigators recovered clothing bearing extremist and antisemitic imagery from Gregory Vandenberg's vehicle, according to court records. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)

According to prosecutors, those messages suggested Vandenberg believed the U.S. government, including President Donald Trump, was controlled by Israel and Jewish people, evidence they argued helped establish his motive for targeting law enforcement officers.

"People in this country are free to hold their own beliefs and to express them peacefully," Acting U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison said in a statement. "What they are not free to do is use explosives to threaten or terrorize others."

Ellison added that Vandenberg "intended to turn explosives into a tool of intimidation," and said the verdict "sends the message that attempts to substitute violence for expressing one's opinion has no place in our communities and will be met with federal consequences."

Vandenberg was later sentenced to 16 months in federal prison, where he remains in custody. Upon his release, he will serve one year of supervised release.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Kyle Shanahan 'this close' to losing his right eye in horrible car crash, NFL analyst reveals
excerpt: RB Raheem Mostert joins Colin Cowherd to discuss playing for Mike McDaniel and Kyle Shanahan and how both coaches compare to each other. He also dives into how McDaniel will positively impact the Los ...
body_text:
RB Raheem Mostert joins Colin Cowherd to discuss playing for Mike McDaniel and Kyle Shanahan and how both coaches compare to each other. He also dives into how McDaniel will positively impact the Los Angeles Chargers, then breaks down the difference between playing for teams with good and bad cultures. Mostert also shares the players he enjoyed playing with the most, including Maxx Crosby.

Former NFL quarterback Chris Simms revealed that his close friend, San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan, almost lost an eye during a horrible car crash he was involved in earlier this month.

Simms, who is a current NFL analyst, made an appearance on "PFT Live" where he explained pictures he received from Shanahan’s wife, Mandy, after the July 14 accident occurred.

"When you first see it, and it’s fresh, and some of the cuts are still wide open, I mean, it’s jarring," Simms explained. "It’s jarring.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

NBC Sports Chris Simms before an AFC divisional playoff game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs on January 21, 2023, at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

"He was this close to maybe losing his right eye."

The injuries were quite significant for Shanahan, who is limited to starting training camp with the 49ers, the team announced.

Shanahan suffered a broken nose, three broken ribs and a broken hand. He also needed over 40 stitches in his face and had a severe concussion after colliding with another SUV by his home in Northern California, per ESPN.

ROGER GOODELL DISMISSES 49ERS COACH'S CONCERNS ABOUT PLAYING IN AUSTRALIA, SAYS IT'S PART OF LONG-TERM PLAN

"San Francisco 49ers Head Coach Kyle Shanahan was involved in a car accident last week when he suffered non-life threatening injuries. Coach Shanahan will participate in team activities on a limited basis at the start of training camp while he recovers," the team said in its statement.

"Coach Shanahan and the 49ers organization would like to sincerely thank all first responders involved for their efforts and care."

Simms pointed to his forehead when he said, "The scar is so big right here."

San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan speaks at a news conference after an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams in Santa Clara, Calif., Thursday, Dec. 12, 2024. (AP Photo/Godofredo A. Vásquez)

"So, all that stuff was just crazy to see," he added.

While Shanahan has yet to speak on the crash, Simms did reveal some of what he is feeling at the moment.

"He was emotional about it because he realized how close it was to being just a complete, you know, utter disaster," Simms, who mentioned the other driver was a woman, said. "Like, really, it was a disaster anyways. But, when you’re a part of that accident, like I said, he could have lost his right eye. It could have been a lot worse. You know, he’s very concerned about the woman he got in the accident with and how she is and handling that situation. So there’s just a lot there. And I think it was a lot for him to process."

Shanahan was spotted at 49ers training camp on Sunday, where his face was masked by a baseball hat and sunglasses.

GM John Lynch also noted that, "Kyle basically is going to be like in the protocol," in reference to his concussion. Simms said it is giving him "some issues" he must deal with through the healing process.

San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan watches from the sideline during the second half of an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Tampa, Florida, on Oct. 12, 2025. (AP Photo/Chris O'Meara)

While Shanahan serves his team on a limited basis, Chris Foerster, the 49ers’ assistant head coach, is acting in his place.

The 49ers open the season against the Los Angeles Rams on Sept. 10 in the first-ever game played in Australia.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Swathes of Cairngorms unrecognisable after 12 days of ‘cataclysmic’ wildfires
excerpt:
With large areas still burning, damage from national park’s worst blaze could take decades, if not longer, to put right

It is the jewel in the crown of the Highlands, one of Scotland’s most impressiv...
body_text:
With large areas still burning, damage from national park’s worst blaze could take decades, if not longer, to put right

It is the jewel in the crown of the Highlands, one of Scotland’s most impressive natural landscapes, but 12 days on from the start of an enormous wildfire that is tearing through moorland and forest, the Cairngorms national park is unrecognisable.

Hectares of blackened land were visible as low cloud cleared on Sunday, with smoke billowing into the air from large areas still ablaze. In the evening, the sky glowed an eerie orange.

Authorities have warned the danger is far from over in what has been described as the worst fire the Cairngorms has ever seen. It will be weeks, if not months, before the blaze is fully extinguished but emergency services are hoping they can stop it spreading much further. The damage so far has been significant and it will take decades to put right.

Flames have claimed areas of the Caledonian pinewood forest, which contains Scots pine trees 300 years old, but most of the older forest has been saved by fire breaks urgently bulldozed into the land in the early days of the fire.

“For rare habitat loss, it really is a challenge,” says Ian Allsopp, the Forestry and Land Scotland planning manager for the north region, saying larger animals, such as deer, would have escaped but smaller mammals, lizards, insects and ground-nesting birds would have perished.

Grant Moir, the chief executive of the Cairngorms national park, told the Guardian it was the worst fire the park had seen. “The fact that this is right in the centre of the Cairngorms, in the actual Cairngorm mountains and Abernethy – it is such a precious place,” he says.

A national park bylaw was introduced in April, banning campfires and barbecues over the summer to help reduce ignition points. It is still unknown what caused this fire but the vast majority of UK wildfires have a human origin and can be something as small as a discarded cigarette or abandoned glass bottle.

Police Scotland said on Saturday night it was no longer treating the fire as a major incident. However, anxiety is still high, particularly among local people who were told it was “contained” last week, only for strong winds to fan the flames, leading to the evacuation of Nethy Bridge village on Friday night.

Residents have been told they can return home. Inside Nethy Bridge community centre, which is being used as a makeshift base for the emergency services, a long table against a wall is groaning under the weight of donated food, while the fire service, police and volunteers bustle around, many looking exhausted.

“It’s absolutely heartbreaking,” says Sandy McCook, a retired press photographer from the village. “The flames on Friday were cataclysmic.”

He is angry too. Many locals feel the fire could have been prevented. McCook shows the Guardian a photo he took of the wildfire when it was only the size of a tennis court.

“Had we had a helicopter there on government contract to deal with such incidents, that fire could have been dealt with within two hours of it being reported,” he says. He wants to see a model similar to the Scottish air ambulance, with a specialist firefighting helicopter and crew able to scramble to tackle hard-to-reach fires, and he is not the only one.

Three private helicopters have been contracted to provide assistance in the Cairngorms, depositing approximately 750,000 litres of water a day on wildfire hotspots, something that is essential to getting the blaze under control. Allsopp says it was “so lucky” the helicopter companies were able to assist in water-bombing what he says was an “inferno”.

The Cairngorms area is an “extremely challenging landscape”, including steep mountains and forest, “access is so difficult, you just can’t get people up here”.

On Monday, the Scottish Green party called for publicly available firefighting aircraft during the wildfire season, saying Scotland “cannot continue to rely on a patchwork of private operators and borrowed resources”.

It came after the UK government offered military support on Sunday but said it had no access to specialist firefighting helicopters requested by the Scottish government.

Firefighters said an “intensive operation” was still under way but better weather conditions, including heavy rain and low winds, had slowed the fire and limited its spread. More than 75 firefighters remained at the scene, the Scottish fire and rescue service said on Sunday.

Light rain has brought some relief but everyone on the ground is anxious in the face of more dry weather to come. “Wet weather is not enough to put out the fire on its own,” says Allsopp. It requires helicopter water-bombing “for days and days and days” to contain it.

The operation is a massive coordinated effort between Forestry and Land Scotland, the national park authority, the police, fire service, RSPB, Highland Council and other partners, with assistance being offered from the Scottish and UK governments.

Allsopp says each organisation has worked well together, pooled skills and knowledge, and helped each other out. “Even our accountants are here, running errands and getting water and sun cream for people,” he said. “At times, it has been completely overwhelming and we’ve been struggling to keep up. It feels like a war strategy.”

title: Your home is empty. Do burglars already know?
excerpt:
Retired LAPD lieutenant Jeff Wenninger explains how criminals exploit obituaries, routines and public clues to time home break-ins and what families can do to reduce risk.

In Argentina, authorities r...
body_text:
Retired LAPD lieutenant Jeff Wenninger explains how criminals exploit obituaries, routines and public clues to time home break-ins and what families can do to reduce risk.

In Argentina, authorities recently arrested three Chilean men wanted in the U.S. in connection with a South American theft group accused of burglarizing the homes of professional athletes.

Federal prosecutors linked the group to break-ins involving Kansas City Chiefs stars Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce, Milwaukee Bucks player Bobby Portis and other athletes. Two of the suspects were also arrested in connection with a burglary at the home of tennis legend Juan Martín del Potro in Argentina.

According to prosecutors, the group identified targets through publicly available schedules and location information, then struck while athletes were away or playing games. Separately, the FBI has warned that international theft groups surveil homeowners to learn their routines and advises travelers to avoid announcing vacations on social media.

Online criminals can research your address, family, travel plans and estimated property value without ever driving down your street. Here's how criminals piece together those digital clues and what you can do to make your home harder to target

ALLEGED BURGLARY CREW THAT TARGETED PATRICK MAHOMES AND TRAVIS KELCE HOMES ARRESTED IN ARGENTINA: REPORT

Alleged members of a South American theft ring pose with stolen valuables. Federal investigators say the group targeted professional athletes while they were away competing in games. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida/Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images)

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

It may be tempting to assume these crimes only affect people with mansions, expensive cars and celebrity lifestyles. Those cases make the news, but professional athletes and entertainers are far from the only targets. Security researchers and law enforcement agencies have tracked burglary crews using the same methods against everyday homeowners.

One recent case involved a Los Angeles content creator whose Silver Lake home was burglarized while she was traveling. Thieves reportedly took tens of thousands of dollars in designer goods. She had shared that she was away, which gave anyone watching her public account a useful clue.

For retirees, the risk can grow as travel becomes more frequent. You may finally take the cruise you have planned for years, spend a month in Florida each winter or take a road trip to visit your grandchildren. Those trips also create more opportunities to post "we made it" from an airport, beach or campground while your home sits empty.

Maybe you wait until you return home before posting vacation photos. However, someone in your life may share the information for you. A spouse might tag the airport. An adult child could post a picture of the grandchildren in front of your house. A neighbor might mention that you are away on your annual trip.

You have limited control over what other people share, so talk with your family before traveling. Ask everyone to wait until you return before posting locations, travel photos or details about how long you will be gone. Watching what your family posts helps, but social media provides only part of the information criminals can collect.

Investigators in Riverside, California, say they routinely find Zillow and Redfin searches on the phones of arrested burglary suspects. These sites may reveal an estimated property value, past sale prices and photos from an old listing. In some cases, criminals can view interior layouts, doors, windows and rooms before they approach the property.

Public property records can also reveal the owner's name, mailing address and purchase history. Meanwhile, data broker and people-search sites may connect that address with phone numbers, relatives, previous homes and other personal details. Combine "this person is traveling" with "this home has significant value," and criminals have the beginnings of a target list.

AI VOICE SCAMS CAN CLONE YOUR FAMILY’S VOICE

Burglars can use social media posts, public records and real estate listings to determine when a home may be empty. (PC Photography / Getty Images)

Search your name, phone number and home address to see what appears. You may find people-search profiles that list your age, relatives, address history and possible phone numbers. Real estate websites may still display old interior photos, even when you purchased the home years ago. Someone could use those details to connect your social media account with a specific property.

Want to see what information data brokers may have about you? Run a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: Cyberguy.com. You should receive the results within an hour.

These steps can reduce the amount of useful information available to someone researching your home. They work best alongside basic home security measures, such as an alarm system, a doorbell camera, light timers and secure storage for valuables.

Save airport, hotel and sightseeing photos until you are back home. Real-time posts can tell strangers where you are and confirm that your house may be empty.

Tell your spouse, children, grandchildren and travel companions to wait before sharing your location or mentioning your travel dates.

Limit posts to people you know. Remove followers you do not recognize and check whether old public posts reveal your routines, vehicles or home address.

Ask a trusted neighbor to collect mail, newspapers and deliveries. You can also place a temporary hold on your mail before an extended trip.

Use timers or smart plugs to turn lights on and off at different times. Leaving every light off for two weeks can make an empty home easier to spot.

WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

Surveillance footage shows a 2024 looting carried out by a Chilean crime ring at a Michigan home, shared with Fox 2 Detroit by a homeowner. (WJBK)

Search your address on Zillow, Redfin and other real estate sites to see whether old listings reveal interior rooms, entrances or the layout of your home.

On Redfin, use a desktop browser and sign in. Select your name in the upper-right corner, choose My homes, select your claimed property and click Edit Photos. Check Hide listing photos, then select Yes, Hide Photos. This feature applies to off-market homes and currently does not appear in the Redfin mobile app.

On Zillow, sign in and select your profile icon, followed by Your Home. Choose your property and claim ownership if you have not already done so. From the Owner View, select Edit Facts. You can remove individual photos, delete all photos or check the option to hide photos from public view. Select Save Changes when finished.

Some off-market homes may not offer the editing option. In that case, submit a request to Zillow Customer Support. Other real estate sites may require you to claim the property, contact customer support or ask the original listing agent for help.

Data broker and people-search sites can connect your name, phone number, relatives and home address. Search for your information and request removal from sites that display it.

A data removal service can automate requests across hundreds of covered brokers and continue checking whether your information returns. It cannot erase government property records or every old real estate listing, so use it alongside the other home protection steps above.

You can also submit removal requests yourself, though the process may take more time and require repeat checks.

Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

Search your name, address and phone number every few months. Look for new people-search profiles, outdated listings and social media posts that reveal more than you intended.

Burglary crews no longer need to spend days watching your street. Social media can reveal when you are away, while property records, real estate listings and people-search sites can reveal where you live and what your home may be worth. Retirement often brings more time for travel, which creates more opportunities for you or a family member to announce that your home is empty. You have limited control over public records and what your relatives post. However, you can delay travel posts, tighten privacy settings, remove old listing photos and reduce your exposure on data broker sites. Removing your personal information will never make you invisible. It can still make your home harder for online criminals to research and target.

Have you ever found personal details about your home online that surprised you? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
