title: MARTHA MAcCALLUM, KELLY McKENNA: America's next 250 years begin on the playground
excerpt:
‘Fox News @ Night’ panelists assess what went wrong in students’ testing scores, despite higher funding for education.

As we enter the "dog days" of summer in this 250th, since our nation boldly asse...
body_text:
‘Fox News @ Night’ panelists assess what went wrong in students’ testing scores, despite higher funding for education.

As we enter the "dog days" of summer in this 250th, since our nation boldly asserted its independence, there is, as there should be, a good deal of reflection about who we are, what we truly value. As we look to the future there is perhaps no more important measure than how we educate our children so that they can be strong protectors of our country and our democracy deep into the decades to come.

It turns out that a basic truth of well-being, getting fresh air and play time, plays a pretty big part in achieving that goal. It’s simple. It’s free. It stimulates and restores learning power, and, as it turns out, many of our children are getting precious little of it.

From the earliest days of the republic, education was never intended to be merely the efficient transfer of information. Reformers like Horace Mann, whose vision helped shape modern American education, argued that schools should prepare children not only for work, but for democratic life. Even the word kindergarten — German for "children’s garden" — reflects an understanding that young minds need room to grow, explore, play, and develop.

NEBRASKA ENDS IN-STATE TUITION BENEFITS FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER DOJ DEAL

Over time, however, our definition of educational success narrowed. Beginning with A Nation at Risk in 1983 and accelerating through the accountability era of No Child Left Behind, schools came under increasing pressure to maximize instructional minutes and standardized test performance. One of the first casualties was often recess, treated as expendable time rather than an essential part of learning.

Today, modern neuroscience has confirmed what America’s earliest education reformers understood intuitively: children learn best when schools develop the whole child — not just the test taker. In many ways, the science has finally caught up with the philosophy. Earlier this summer, the American Academy of Pediatrics released its first updated policy statement on recess since 2013. Rather than simply reaffirming its earlier recommendations, the new statement reflects an explosion of research over the past decade, expanding from roughly 44 references to more than 100 studies documenting how recess supports learning, memory, executive function, social development, mental health, and physical well-being. As they concluded, recess is not a break from learning — it’s part of how children learn.

That’s because recess is not simply exercise. It’s the only part of the school day designed around child-directed play. As two middle school children explained this month in an op-ed in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, it gives students the opportunity to "refresh themselves." It also lets them negotiate disagreements, practice leadership, build friendships, manage stress, solve problems, and return to the classroom better able to focus and learn. These are not "soft skills." They are the very qualities that fuel innovation, civic engagement, resilience, and collaboration, the qualities every generation of Americans needs.

In other words, the Academy’s recommendation remains clear: recess should be protected, never withheld as punishment or exchanged for more academic time seated. That conclusion has not changed since 2013. What has changed is the strength of the evidence behind it. More than a decade of new research has deepened our understanding of why recess matters — not only for children’s physical health, but for their cognitive development, emotional well-being, and long-term success.

The lesson is remarkably consistent with America’s oldest educational ideals. If the purpose of education is to develop thoughtful, resilient citizens — not simply higher test scores — then recess is not a distraction from learning, but key to it.

This summer, as Americans gather to celebrate our nation’s 250th birthday, we’re also celebrating examples of teamwork, perseverance, and excellence across the country — from neighborhood ballfields to championship arenas. Yet those qualities don’t begin under stadium lights, as in the stunning athleticism displayed from countries around the world in the FIFA World Cup, or the college sports teams we’ll start watching in August. They begin on playgrounds. Long before children wear a team uniform — whether as professional athletes, college athletes, or even on little league fields — they learn to cooperate, lead, compromise, recover from failure, resolve conflict, and celebrate success together during recess.

Two hundred fifty years after our nation’s founding, only twelve states currently mandate daily recess for kids in school. But several states, including New York, are considering legislation that would change that. As we prepare for "back-to-school" in August, and as mandatory recess bills are considered in the next legislative season, the nation will be watching to see how states decide to let kids play, or not.

We have all seen the evidence that children have become more isolated, depressed and anxious in a society that has all of us glued to our screens. Protecting children's play time, fresh air, and opportunities for social connection is one of the simplest ways we can improve their health and well-being.

The children on today’s playgrounds will become tomorrow’s architects, engineers, scientists, physicians, diplomats, entrepreneurs, artists, teachers, military leaders, parents, and elected officials. They could even become America’s World Cup soccer stars. They will shape America’s next 250 years.

The skills they’ll need — creativity, collaboration, resilience, curiosity, leadership, empathy, and the confidence to solve problems together — will require commitment to academic rigor in the classroom, balanced with the promise of play time and fresh air to ‘refresh’ young minds and bodies in every single school day

Kelly McKenna is CEO of End Chronic Disease, former captain of Stanford's varsity sailing team, and a three-time All-American.

Martha MacCallum currently serves as the anchor and executive editor of The Story with Martha MacCallum (weekdays, 3 PM/ET) on FOX News Channel (FNC), co-anchor of the network’s election coverage, and hosts the podcast, The Untold Story with Martha MacCallum. She joined FNC in 2004 and is based in New York.

title: German officials call for tighter extremism laws after Berlin Pride attack
excerpt:
Alternative für Deutschland, topping polls ahead of state elections, accuses government of failing to tackle Islamist radicalism

German officials have called for a tightening of laws for known extrem...
body_text:
Alternative für Deutschland, topping polls ahead of state elections, accuses government of failing to tackle Islamist radicalism

German officials have called for a tightening of laws for known extremists after a deadly attack in Berlin on one of Europe’s biggest Pride parades, as the far right seeks to mobilise outraged voters before three key state elections.

The anti-migration, anti-Islam Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the top party in national opinion polls, accused the government of failing to tackle Islamist radicalism on German soil, while the conservative chancellor, Friedrich Merz, pledged to act with “prudence but also determination” to address security gaps.

Abdul Ballout, a 21-year-old German national with Lebanese roots who was well known to police, is believed to have rammed a van into a crowd in the Tiergarten park late on Saturday, next to the finale of annual LGBTQ+ celebrations that drew hundreds of thousands of people.

After the vehicle, which had been rented in Ballout’s name, crashed into a tree, he allegedly attacked people with a large knife. A 65-year-old Polish woman died and 29 others were injured.

Following an hours-long manhunt, police said they shot Ballout dead in a garden allotment in the Spandau district on Sunday after he ran at them with a “bladed weapon” when they attempted to arrest him.

Merz said on Monday the victims had been rallying for “openness, diversity and freedom”, and were assaulted by “an Islamist who sought to attack those values”.

As thousands gathered for a sombre ceremony at the Brandenburg Gate in central Berlin to mourn the victims, it emerged police had been aware of the risk posed by Ballout as an avowed Islamic extremist with previous arrests for bodily harm, extortion and robbery.

Security authorities said Ballout was a supporter of Islamic State and last year attempted to join the group in Syria. He was arrested in Lebanon and repatriated, and in May was convicted in Germany of “preparing a serious act of subversive violence”.

Berlin-born Ballout, who lived with his divorced mother and two sisters in the capital, was sentenced as a juvenile to a year and 10 months in prison. But the Berlin court suspended the sentence and he was allowed to walk free, albeit under sporadic police observation.

Berlin’s top justice official, Felor Badenberg, on Monday acknowledged public anger over the case after a deadly series of car ramming and knife attacks in Germany, and urged an overhaul of juvenile criminal law.

“In the wake of this attack, my conclusion is that, in cases such as this, the perpetrators must indeed be punished more severely,” Badenberg, a member of Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told public broadcaster ARD.

While acknowledging the courts’ independence, she said: “We must fundamentally examine whether the legal criteria we currently have for applying juvenile criminal law are still appropriate for the times.”

Berlin, one of Germany’s federal states, will go to the polls in September along with two other eastern regions. In all three elections, the far-right AfD is expected to perform well, and is poised to take first place in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The AfD, founded 13 years ago as a Eurosceptic movement, has seized on fears around immigration and crime and more recently zeroed in on economic woes linked to German deindustrialisation, allowing it to make inroads beyond its eastern heartland.

Party co-leader Alice Weidel accused Merz on Monday of failing to take the problem of Islamist extremism and “migrant violence” seriously.

“Merz remains silent on Islamism – we are ready to take action!” she posted on X.

The AfD’s main candidate for the Berlin election, Kristin Brinker, blamed the Pride attack on the “catastrophic migration policy of the last few years”.

Experts said the AfD could stand to gain from the tragedy. The party is already polling at between 38 and 40% in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, within striking distance of an absolute majority for the first time at the state level.

Guido Friebel, dean of the economics faculty at Goethe University in Frankfurt, has conducted research with a team of colleagues on how terrorist attacks affect the AfD’s electoral outcomes.

“The AfD has made [the interplay between] migration and internal security one of its key issues,” he told Der Spiegel magazine. “It will capitalise politically on this attack.”

Friebel said the AfD even benefited at the polls from attacks carried out by rightwing extremists, creating a dilemma for mainstream democratic parties such as the CDU, which have sought to establish a law-and-order profile.

“If it [the CDU] ignores the issue, the AfD can claim that it is the only party taking the threat seriously,” he said. “If it adopts their issues and rhetoric, there is a risk that it will contribute to strengthening the AfD’s political agenda.”

Counter-extremism expert Hans-Jakob Schindler, who advises the German government, told local media there were more than 9,000 Islamists living in the country in 2025, including 2,590 in the capital, 1,940 of whom are believed to be violent.

The LSVD+ queer advocacy group said homophobic and anti-trans attacks had increased tenfold in Germany in recent years.

With several LGBTQ+ marches still to come this summer including in Hamburg, Nuremberg and Dortmund, community activists said they had been sounding the alarm about a rising threat from Islamists as well as far-right extremists, but were not being heard.

“Now we see that comes at a price,” said Alva Träbert, an LSVD+ board member.

title: Israel’s approval of limited Gaza force a calculated manoeuvre, experts say
excerpt: Months after the United Nations Security Council backed a comprehensive framework to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Israel’s security cabinet has approved a highly constrained pilot project to al...
body_text:
Months after the United Nations Security Council backed a comprehensive framework to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Israel’s security cabinet has approved a highly constrained pilot project to allow foreign security forces into a narrow pocket of the devastated territory.

Israeli media reported on Sunday that the so-called International Stabilization Force (ISF), part of United States President Donald Trump’s 20-point “peace plan”, will include 200 members from countries such as Morocco and Uganda deploying to a designated “test” zone in the southern city of Rafah.

While international officials have welcomed the move, analysts describe the limited deployment as a calculated diplomatic gesture with little practical effect that comes as the US-backed peace process has largely stalled and as Israel’s deadly attacks continue.

Instead of a genuine transition towards peace, they argue, the move is a political manoeuvre designed to deflect US pressure ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to Washington this week, while simultaneously entrenching the geographic fragmentation of the Gaza Strip.

“Netanyahu is going to Washington to say ‘no’ to the broader demands of withdrawal” from the Strip, says Wissam Afifa, a Gaza-based political analyst. “Instead, he is offering this alternative: ‘Take this small appetiser, take this minor achievement, and play within this highly restricted space.'”

The Israeli daily Haaretz reported that the original plan anticipated the deployment of 500 Moroccan troops to a refugee camp in the city. The drastic reduction to just 200 troops may indicate that Israel’s political-security cabinet has decided to divide the deployment into even smaller, heavily controlled stages.

The force will operate in full coordination with the Israeli military. According to the Israeli news outlet Ynet, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir was the sole cabinet member to vote against the measure, arguing that the Palestinian group Hamas had failed to fulfill its commitment to disarm and insisting that “the solution in Gaza is to encourage migration”.

Israeli media also reported that the government maintains that the Israeli military will retain control of the “Yellow Line” – a unilaterally imposed boundary that effectively places up to 70 percent of the Gaza Strip under tight Israeli control – and that no withdrawal will take place until Hamas has fully disarmed.

The original framework endorsed by UNSC Resolution 2803 called for the deployment of an international force alongside a transitional Palestinian administration.

Earlier this month, Hamas announced it would dissolve its government in Gaza and hand over power to a new, Palestinian technocratic governing authority called the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).

Analysts said Hamas’s move was likely designed to apply pressure on Israel and demonstrate the group’s commitment to handing over governance and allowing the rebuilding of the territory.

The pilot programme also envisions the NCAG’s entry to oversee civil affairs in Gaza. Yet, according to Haaretz, the Palestinian police accompanying them will be stripped of firearms, permitted to carry only “rubber batons and tasers”.

Meanwhile, preparations on the ground appear to be moving forward to accommodate this new security architecture. Israeli Army Radio recently broadcast a video showing a military base under construction in the southern “Gaza envelope” near the Karem Abu Salem (Kerem Shalom) crossing.

The station reported that the sprawling facility is being built specifically to host the incoming multinational forces before their deployment.

Despite the severe Israeli restrictions, Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative for the Board of Peace, welcomed the Israeli cabinet’s decision, praising it as a “critical part of the agreed framework for stabilizing Gaza, supporting demilitarization, and enabling the transition to effective Palestinian transitional administration”.

To understand the timing and motivation behind the decision, experts pointed to the diplomatic deadlock surrounding the US-brokered peace initiative. Trump’s plan envisioned a phased approach, bridged by the handover of Gaza to a technocratic committee. However, this framework has been stalled by Israel’s refusal to link a ceasefire to the broader political situation and its rejection of a phased withdrawal.

Afifa said the “failure” of the US administration’s flagship initiative had left it “embarrassed” as the project that was repeatedly highlighted by Trump “as a great achievement, resulted in zero”.

With Netanyahu heading to Washington, the Israeli prime minister desperately needed a deliverable, said Afifa. The cabinet’s decision, passed hastily via a telephone vote during a Knesset recess to avoid internal coalition fractures, provides exactly that, he added.

Mamoun Abu Amer, an expert on Israeli affairs, echoed this assessment. He viewed the rushed cabinet vote as an attempt to preempt US pressure and present an image of compliance to Trump, while fundamentally altering the agreement’s core terms to suit Israel’s long-term security strategy.

Abu Amer also said that Israel has effectively turned Resolution 2803 upside down through selective and highly conditional implementation.

“This is an inverted process,” said Abu Amer. The original text implied that the NCAG would enter Gaza, the ISF would deploy and the Israeli military would withdraw to new lines to allow for stabilisation. Instead, Israel is demanding unilateral disarmament first, while keeping the technocratic committee besieged within an Israeli security envelope.

Abu Amer also suggested the requirement for the Palestinian police force to only carry rubber batons and tasers reflects a premeditated Israeli strategy to strip the Palestinian administration of genuine law enforcement capabilities, reducing them to subcontractors managing municipal decay in a thoroughly devastated environment under a strict military occupation.

The NCAG itself appeared to reject this Israeli paradigm. In a recent statement, the committee declared it would only assume responsibility for Gaza after UNSC approval of the force’s deployment and, crucially, a full Israeli military withdrawal.

The spatial realities of the Israeli plan reveal a strategy of deep fragmentation and long-term control, experts said, pointing to the cabinet’s decision to explicitly restrict the ISF and the technocrats to operating strictly outside the “Yellow Line”.

Afifa warned that transforming a small pocket of Rafah into an “experimental bubble” subverts the idea of Gaza as a single, contiguous territorial entity.

“This raises a massive question about the fate of two million people,” he said. “If this entire project is reduced to a few thousand individuals selected under Israeli criteria, it means a tacit agreement from the international community to leave two million Gazans hostage to a catastrophic humanitarian crisis while Israel claims to be implementing a peace plan.”

This also carries significant diplomatic risks for the participating nations. Israeli media reported the cabinet’s decision stipulated that ISF contributors must be nations that have peace agreements with Israel and do not pursue legal actions against it in international forums.

“It is not wise for an Arab country like Morocco to be a party to helping Netanyahu implement his political agenda,” said Abu Amer, urging participating nations to reject the altered Israeli formula and insist on a comprehensive withdrawal.

Failing to do so, he cautioned, would reduce foreign troops to mere security buffers, acting as “false witnesses” to the continuation of the occupation and the destruction of the Palestinian society.

title: Three killed in suspected shootout in US city of Seattle, police say
excerpt: Three people have been shot dead at a crowded food festival in Seattle in the United States. Four others were wounded, including a toddler, in what city police believe was a shootout involving two sus...
body_text:
Three people have been shot dead at a crowded food festival in Seattle in the United States. Four others were wounded, including a toddler, in what city police believe was a shootout involving two suspects.

One of them surrendered to police after the shooting on Sunday – the other fled.

Assistant Seattle Police Chief Tyrone Davis told a news conference on Sunday night that there was no ongoing threat to the public, but added that police did not have a description of the suspect who remained on the run.

“We’re still trying to figure this out,” Davis said.

Police said the suspect in custody was a “young person” but declined to provide more details.

The gunshots at the Bite of Seattle food festival beneath the famous Space Needle were heard at around 6pm local time (01:00 GMT Monday).

“What happened here today at the Seattle Center was an unbelievable tragedy and a horrific act of violence,” Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said at the news conference.

“We have far too much gun violence in this city and in this country, and we’re coming off of a week in Seattle where we’ve had three major incidents of gun violence in just a few days.”

Police said the dead were two men, aged 19 and 44, and a 56-year old woman. The wounded, including a two-year-old boy, were in a stable condition in hospital.

One of the vendors was livestreaming a promotional video when the shooting began, accidentally capturing the moments that followed. Crowds of people can be seen running as gunshots ring out.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump admin fast-tracks asylum cases, bypassing interviews to slash backlog
excerpt: The Supreme Court delivered two significant immigration victories to the Trump administration, affirming DHS's authority to limit asylum processing claims and terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS...
body_text:
The Supreme Court delivered two significant immigration victories to the Trump administration, affirming DHS's authority to limit asylum processing claims and terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for hundreds of thousands of Haitian and Syrian migrants.

FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is changing how some asylum claims move through the immigration system, allowing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to refer certain applications directly to immigration judges without first interviewing applicants in an effort to reduce the nation's asylum backlog.

The interim final rule, which takes effect immediately, gives USCIS the authority to send some asylum applications to immigration court without conducting an affirmative asylum interview, eliminating what the administration called an unnecessary step in the adjudication process.

The change applies to affirmative asylum claims, which are filed by immigrants who are not in removal proceedings. Defensive asylum claims, in contrast, are raised before an immigration judge after the government has initiated removal proceedings.

TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

FILE - USCIS generally interviews affirmative asylum applicants before either granting asylum or conducting a separate review, which DHS said allows immigrants to "get a second chance at asylum." (iStock)

Currently, USCIS generally interviews affirmative asylum applicants before either granting asylum or referring the case to an immigration judge for a separate review. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Fox News Digital the process can result in some applications being reviewed twice — first by USCIS and then again by an immigration judge — adding to the agency's growing backlog.

Under the new rule, USCIS can refer certain asylum applications directly to immigration court without first conducting an interview, a change administration officials said will allow both asylum officers and immigration judges to process cases more efficiently while directing resources toward applicants with legitimate claims of persecution.

The rule is the latest step in the Trump administration's broader effort to tighten the asylum system and speed up immigration enforcement, with officials arguing the current process has been exploited by immigrants seeking to delay removal proceedings and obtain work authorization.

HOUSE REPUBLICANS MOVE TO MAKE TRUMP'S BORDER POLICIES PERMANENT

FILE - People wait inside a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services office. The Trump administration issued a new rule allowing USCIS to refer certain asylum applications directly to immigration judges without first conducting an affirmative asylum interview. (John Moore/Getty Images)

"For far too long, the asylum system has been exploited for purposes of delay and work authorization, not legitimate claims of protection," USCIS Director Joseph Edlow told Fox News Digital. "America's asylum system exists to protect individuals who genuinely fear persecution and this rule will help ensure that resources are directed to the timely adjudication of those claims instead of to those seeking to use the system as a loophole."

DHS general counsel James Percival said delays within the asylum system have hindered immigration enforcement.

FILE - USCIS Director Joseph Edlow said a new rule allowing certain asylum applications to be referred directly to immigration judges without first conducting an affirmative asylum interview will help reduce the asylum backlog. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"One of the greatest barriers to effective immigration enforcement is intentional delay by illegal aliens and the open borders attorneys who represent them," Percival told Fox News Digital. "My office works every day with the immigration components of DHS to improve efficiency and fulfill the president's mandate. The rule would do just that."

The rule takes effect immediately, though USCIS said it will continue accepting public comments before issuing a final version, responding to the feedback it receives.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: NASCAR race looks pathetic with empty seats, driver gives the finger & the most embarrassing command ever?
excerpt:
Watch the post-race interviews from Corey Heim, Kaden Honeycutt and more after the Black's Tire 200 at Rockingham Speedway.

Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com ...
body_text:
Watch the post-race interviews from Corey Heim, Kaden Honeycutt and more after the Black's Tire 200 at Rockingham Speedway.

Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists.

Well ... Once a crown jewel, always a crown jewel, I reckon.

That wasn't your daddy's Brickyard 400. Sure, we got a decent finish and solid final 10 laps, but goodness gracious, does NASCAR have a problem on it's hands with this car.

There's no real point in relitigating it this morning. We all know it's garbage. Frankly, NASCAR knows its garbage. And if they didn't before Sunday's race, they certainly do now after seemingly every driver complained about it after the race.

NASCAR STAR SAYS QUIET PART OUT LOUD ABOUT EUROPE, PUNCHES NEARLY THROWN & GET THESE 'S---BOXES' OFF THE TRACK

Every driver except Corey Heim, of course! Who? That's right. Corey Heim. He's now a two-time NASCAR Cup Series winner, folks, and he isn't even a full-time driver! Better get used to the name, because he appears to be the real deal.

What else should we break down after Sunday's semi-snoozer in Indy? How about that crowd? Wasn't the best optics for NASCAR, although there is a catch.

HAS NASCAR LOST THE SOUTH? EX-DRIVER UNLOADS AFTER SEEING "100,000 EMPTY SEATS"

I've also got Carson Hocevar flipping off our winner while merging into traffic, Taylor Reimer kissing the bricks, the worst starting command in the history of commands, and are NASCAR races too long?

Kyle Larson thinks so, and boy, did it create a firestorm this weekend. He's right, by the way, but only sort of.

Four tires, a splash of Sunoco racin' fuel, and maybe a Red Bull for Kyle so he doesn't fall asleep at the wheel ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'Everybody Hates This Stupid Car' edition — is LIVE!

Which negative thing should we start with today? Look, I don't love coming out of the gates with this kind of attitude on the final Monday of July, but I don't dictate the content.

The racing does, and it wasn't great this weekend.

You know what? Before we get into any of the negative stuff (the car, the racing, the crowds, the length of a race), let's hit the refresh button on this Monday and get our minds right.

And I know the PERFECT person to help us do just that!

Lordy. Is Carson Hocevar a content machine, or what? Imagine what he's gonna do when he gets into a legit car? He is, easily, the best thing going in NASCAR right now.

Frankly, it's not particularly close. Listen to Dale Jr.'s voice in the above clip. It's the most excited he got all day! Also, may have reminded him of this gem of a moment from his daddy's final race:

Dale Earnhardt giving a rookie Kurt Busch the finger at his first Daytona 500? I mean, how good did we have it back in the day? The racing. The broadcast booth. The drivers.

We had it all, and we just pissed it away. Sad.

NASCAR Cup Series driver Carson Hocevar gives a thumbs up to fans on Saturday, July 25, 2026, during qualifying for the Brickyard 400 at Indianapolis Motor Speedway. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Anyway, we've gone from that to just a brutal scene Sunday at Indianapolis. Again, the Brickyard 400 is still considered a "crown jewel," but Lordy, it didn't look — or feel — like one.

Covered grandstands. Empty seats. I know it's an absolutely massive venue — I get it — but it just looked bad:

NASCAR Cup Series driver Corey Heim (67) does a burnout after winning the Brickyard 400 on Sunday, July 26, 2026, at Indianapolis Motor Speedway. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Fans stand in the grandstands as racing resumes following a caution period Sunday, July 26, 2026, during the NASCAR Brickyard 400 at Indianapolis Motor Speedway in Speedway, Ind. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

We do this every time we go to Indy, by the way. The place is huge. It holds 400k. Do you understand how massive that is, especially in terms of other venues?

I think they'd have a hard time selling out an NFL game there, much less a NASCAR race in 2026. The folks who run the ticket stands tell me there were around 70,000 fans at the track yesterday, which looks horrific on TV — as you can see — but is actually a pretty decent number for NASCAR.

The Daytona 500 is easily the biggest race of the year, and that one gets around 101k. No other race, track, or venue comes even close. Any other race weekend, NASCAR would LOVE to see 70k.

NASCAR Cup Series driver Todd Gilliland (34) leads Connor Zilisch (88) on Sunday, July 26, 2026, during the Brickyard 400 at Indianapolis Motor Speedway. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co)

But when you spread them out at the biggest venue in North America (unofficially), it's just a tough look. Also a tough look considering NASCAR used to pack this place to the brim. But it also used to get 20 million TV viewers a week, so, you know, times have changed.

You know what else has changed? The racing itself.

It stinks, especially at a place like Indy where it's quite literally follow-the-leader from start to finish.

The ONLY time you could gain spots yesterday was on a the restart. That's it. If you were in the lead, you stayed there.

Joey Logano ... how do we fix this bad boy?

"What would it take for you guys to pass here?"

Whoooooooooooof. Just a brutal day. Just a brutal look for NASCAR at Indy, where there was NOT ONE green flag pass for the lead. Not one. We had lead changes during the pit cycles and restarts. That was it.

Do you know how embarrassing that is? That's an F1 stat. That's the crap I literally mock all the time. I don't have a leg to stand on today! I'm cooked. All NASCAR fans should be furious at that one stat today. If nothing else, be pissed at THAT.

"Yes I agree a lot of our Cup races are too long. Three hours is too long," Kyle Larson said before crashing out 100 miles into Sunday's race.

That comment took a ton of heat this weekend. A TON. Fans are pissed at Larson. It all stems from IndyCar driver Scott Dixon's comments last weekend saying a NASCAR race is a good time for a nap (objectively true), and it has everyone fired up right now.

Here's the thing ... Larson is halfway right. NASCAR races are too long, but not because of the mileage. They're too long because we can go nearly 30 minutes without any actual racing:

LOOK at those numbers. Truly astonishing.

Yeah, that's too long. I don't think Larson was speaking out of turn. Sleep tight, race fans!

Perhaps the only thing that could keep folks awake yesterday was this ELECTRIC command to get the day going:

Thanks, Mike! Who else is ready to run through a brick wall today? You reckon he gives pep talks on the side?

OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Let's get this thing back on track next week at ...

Wait. Never mind. The fellas are off next week.

body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Acting Director of National Intelligence William Pulte announced Sunday that his office has completed a fourth batch of layoffs.

"Since becoming Acting Director of National Intelligence, our team has been smartly, and carefully, reducing the size of [the Office of the Director of National Intelligence], re-focusing ODNI on national security, the law, and the statute," he wrote in a post on X.

"As of this evening, we just finished a 4th round of thoughtful, measured layoffs. Thank you!" he noted.

TRUMP GREEN LIGHTS NEW DNI PULTE TO 'START THE PROCESS' ON MASS INTELLIGENCE FIRINGS

Acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte attends a kick-off celebration for the "Great American State Fair" on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., June 24, 2026. (Jemal COUNTESS / AFP via Getty Images)

Pulte had previously noted in a July 10 post, "U.S. National Intelligence is operating more efficiently and effectively than ever before, and today, we started a third round of reducing redundant, or non-critical, personnel. DNI’s future is exceptionally bright, and will be focused on following the law and the statute."

President Donald Trump chose Pulte, the director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, to serve as acting DNI as well.

Tulsi Gabbard, who had been serving as DNI, departed the role last month. She had previously announced in May that she planned to exit the role due to her husband's bone cancer diagnosis.

WHY TRUMP PICKED BILL PULTE TO LEAD US INTELLIGENCE AS CRITICS QUESTION HIS QUALIFICATIONS

Tulsi Gabbard, then-director of National Intelligence, during a House Intelligence Committee hearing on worldwide threats in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, March 19, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Prior to when Pulte took the reins at ODNI last month, The Wall Street Journal reported that during an interview, Trump said he had informed Pulte that he thought ODNI was "unnecessary and/or too big."

"I’d like to see it smaller. I think there are a lot of people in there that shouldn’t be there," the president said, pointing to Obama and Biden administration carryovers, according to the Journal. Asked if he was calling for Pulte to engage in firings, the president indicated he wanted Pulte to "start the process," noting that the eventual DNI nominee should carry on with the effort, the outlet reported.

Trump later announced U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Jay Clayton as his nominee for the DNI role.

TRUMP'S DNI PICK CLEARS KEY HURDLE, REVIVING PATH FOR NATION'S TOP ANTI-TERROR SURVEILLANCE PROGRAM

U.S. President Donald Trump motions to reporters after getting off Air Force One on July 22, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"So deeply grateful to POTUS for letting me be acting Director of National Intelligence. He is, truly, the best, and it is a blessing to work for him. While it’s been only a few weeks, so much has already been accomplished —Operationally, AND, Transparency. Thank you, POTUS," Pulte wrote in a Sunday post on his personal X account.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Anger, shock and grief - questions remain in the wake of the Berlin Pride attack
excerpt:
Mourners gather near the Brandenburg Gate on Sunday

In Germany there is grief, shock and, increasingly, anger about the attack at Berlin Pride on Saturday night which left one Polish woman dead and i...
body_text:
Mourners gather near the Brandenburg Gate on Sunday

In Germany there is grief, shock and, increasingly, anger about the attack at Berlin Pride on Saturday night which left one Polish woman dead and injured at least 29 others.

The main suspect, Abdul Ballout, a 21-year-old German citizen with Lebanese heritage, was shot and killed by police on Sunday.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Ballout "had previously drawn attention to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene."

As details emerge about his criminal convictions, many are asking why Ballout was not in prison.

Abdul Ballout was shot and killed in a police operation on Sunday afternoon

Prosecutors say that in 2025, Ballout decided to try to join Islamic State group's armed struggle in Syria, travelling via Turkey to Lebanon. In Lebanon, they say, he met several people he believed were members of IS.

He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict.

Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany, where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention.

In May this year, a Berlin court sentenced Ballout to a juvenile sentence of one year and ten months, for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state".

The sentence was suspended while prosecutors appealed against the verdict, calling for a longer sentence.

Ballout was released and placed under the supervision of a probation officer.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told RTL that the decision to impose a suspended sentence was "certainly incomprehensible... given the level of danger involved in this case".

He said the authorities were investigating how that happened.

Berlin's Governing Mayor, Kai Wegner from the centre-right Christian Democrat party (CDU), said he was dumbstruck at the way the Berlin judiciary had handled Ballout's case.

"He was sentenced... under juvenile criminal law," he told RBB TV. "And then, unfortunately, the court handed down a suspended sentence. I don't want to pass judgement on that – that's the independence of the judiciary – but I'm really at a loss for words."

The opposition far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party described the attack as a total failure of security policy.

"If an Islamist threat known to the police was able to carry out such an act, a thorough investigation must be carried out to establish why he was still able to move about freely in the first place," said Martin Hess, the AfD's home affairs spokesperson.

According to Der Spiegel, Ballout told the Berlin court this spring that he had distanced himself from extremist ideology and violence.

Thomas Mücke, an extremism expert at the Violence Prevention Network VPN, told ARD television that he had met the suspect.

He said Ballout had given social workers "a very composed, very cautious, very controlled and very friendly impression".

"And those are precisely the criteria where we realise we can't really get to know the person," he continued.

Some have called for Germany's laws against terrorism to be made stricter.

Peter Neumann at King's College London told ZDF that Germany's criminal law on terrorism is "too lenient," and sentences too short by European standards.

He also called for a rethink of Germany's juvenile justice system, which he said prioritises education rather than the protection of the public.

The home affairs spokesperson for the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), Sebastian Fiedler, told Deutschlandfunk radio that criminal law was not the problem, but the way it was applied.

"We need to look more closely at why [Ballout] still at large. Another key question is: 'What actually happened after his release from prison? Who was he still in contact with?' Although he was under surveillance, there was clearly a gap in the system."

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was too early to say what political consequences will be drawn from the attack, but promised there would be action: "We will have to respond with prudence, but also with determination."

He said if individuals classified as threats could not be detained, their freedom of movement should be restricted "as much as possible."

"I cannot understand how I can track my mobile phone from anywhere in the world... yet it is supposedly impossible, or technically unfeasible, for security authorities in Germany to determine the whereabouts of individuals classified as security threats to that same extent."

He said he had asked the interior ministry to review the law regarding monitoring jurisdiction.

title: Potential for first Australian oil refinery in 60 years as treasurer braces for inflation from Middle East war
excerpt:
Commonwealth and Western Australia to fund study into construction of large-scale petrol refinery as buffer against fuel vulnerability

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Aus...
body_text:
Commonwealth and Western Australia to fund study into construction of large-scale petrol refinery as buffer against fuel vulnerability

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s first new oil refinery in 60 years could be built in Western Australia under the Albanese government’s long-term strategy to shield the country from future global oil shocks.

The commonwealth and the WA government will fund a $4m early-stage feasibility study into construction of what would be the country’s third large-scale petrol refinery.

A series of refinery closures over the past 25 years means Australia now imports about 90% of its liquid fuels, a vulnerability exposed by the international oil crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

The announcement comes as Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, warned the recent escalation of the Middle East conflict posed “a substantial threat to global inflation”.

Treasury officials in a special weekend government briefing warned the collapse of the ceasefire meant oil prices were likely to remain high in the near future.

“The oil market is now more vulnerable, with weaker buffers against future supply shocks,” the officials said.

With petrol and diesel prices up by 25 cents and 50 cents a litre this month, respectively, the rekindling of the conflict has also boosted expectations that central banks will need to do more to bring inflation back under control – piling more pressure on households.

“The longer this drags out the more serious the consequences for inflation and growth here and around the world,” Chalmers said.

Financial markets were pricing a one-in-three chance of a Reserve Bank rate hike on 11 August. That was down from an even chance on Friday after Brent crude, the oil benchmark, tumbled more than US$10 a barrel on Monday to about US$87 after a pause in fighting over the weekend.

Australia’s oil refining industry has struggled to compete with cheaper overseas providers.

There are just two local refineries in operation: Ampol’s Lytton refinery in Brisbane and Viva Energy’s facility in Geelong.

Building a new refinery would cost billions of dollars, and would probably require ongoing government support to stay competitive.

The proposed WA project, were it to go ahead, would be constructed by Perdaman, the large multinational behind a $4.5bn fertiliser plant in the Pilbara. Perdaman would privately fund the project but could be eligible for taxpayer-funded assistance, such as concessional loans.

BP closed an oil refinery in Fremantle, just south of Perth, in 2021.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and WA premier, Roger Cook, will announce funding for the scoping study after visiting Perdaman’s urea plant in Karratha.

“The longer war in the Middle East goes on the greater the impact on Australia will be, and my government will continue to do everything we can to shield Australia from the worst effects – and set us up for the future,” Albanese said in a statement.

The federal government’s $10.7bn fuel security package, announced in May, included $10m to support feasibility studies into potential projects.

The package also funded a $7.5bn facility to secure extra fuel and fertiliser shipments during the Middle East conflict, and $3.2bn to build an extra 1 billion-litre reserve of diesel and jet fuel.

Chris Bowen, the energy minister, described plans to boost domestic refining capacity as “a sensible and prudent response to secure our energy security”.

But the early-stage support for a new oil refinery will probably face push-back from environmentalists, who have criticised the federal government for doubling down on petrol and diesel rather than using the oil shock to reduce Australia’s reliance on fossil fuels.

title: 'Dr Death', Body Worlds creator Gunther von Hagens, dies at 81
excerpt:
Von Hagens has suffered from Parkinson's Disease for many years

Gunther von Hagens, the creator of the controversial "Body Worlds" exhibitions where dissected human and animal bodies were displayed, ...
body_text:
Von Hagens has suffered from Parkinson's Disease for many years

Gunther von Hagens, the creator of the controversial "Body Worlds" exhibitions where dissected human and animal bodies were displayed, has died at the age of 81, according to his family.

Sometimes known as "Doctor Death", he became famous for developing a technique called plastination, by which fluids and fatty tissue in corpses are replaced by rubber and polymers.

His family said in a statement that he had asked for his body to be made available for plastination and that they intended to carry out his wish.

More than 58 million people worldwide have viewed his exhibitions, the statement said. However, religious groups and others have frequently objected to his display of human remains.

His family's statement said von Hagens died on Friday, a day after being admitted to a clinic in Heidelberg, Germany, with a brain haemorrhage. He had suffered from Parkinson's Disease for nearly two decades.

"It was Gunther von Hagens' own wish to make his body available for plastination after his death," the statement reads. "His family will respect and carry out this wish."

Born in Nazi-occupied Poland in the last months of World War Two, von Hagens grew up in communist East Germany before fleeing to the West in 1970.

In the next few years he developed the plastination process. Specimens came to be used as teaching aids at universities or by research institutes.

But it was not until the late 1990s that he began taking his Body Worlds exhibitions around the world.

Colleagues paid tribute to a "pioneer, a researcher, an inventor" who made "anatomy accessible to the general public", but critics have accused him of voyeurism and profiting commercially from death.

In 2002 he caused further controversy by performing the first public autopsy in London for 170 years on camera. Authorities had warned the event could be illegal but no charges were brought.

'Real bodies' show in Australia controversy

title: Chinese chipmaker shares surge nearly 470% in blockbuster stock market debut
excerpt:
Shares in China's biggest memory chip maker have soared by nearly 470% as they made their debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's tech-heavy Star Market.

The surge has pushed ChangXin Memory Technolog...
body_text:
Shares in China's biggest memory chip maker have soared by nearly 470% as they made their debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's tech-heavy Star Market.

The surge has pushed ChangXin Memory Technologies' (CXMT) stock market valuation to around 3.3 trillion yuan ($487bn; £365bn), making it the most valuable listed company in mainland China.

The spectacular debut comes despite a sharp sell-off in technology stocks around the world this month.

CXMT manufactures dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips that power AI data centres, mobile phones, PCs, tablets and other devices.

The firm, which was founded in 2016 by Chairman Zhu Yiming, is headquartered in Hefei, Anhui Province in eastern China.

The company has said it plans to use most of the proceeds from the initial public offering (IPO) to boost production of memory chips and carry out more research and developments.

The stellar performance of its IPO will offer some comfort to Chinese financial officials, who have been rolling out measures to help curb a stock market slump that wiped out more than $1.5tn in recent weeks.

Analysts said the jump was also being driven by demand for the shares far outstripping supply.

"The reason for the extraordinary bounce this morning is that only 7% of the shares are available for trading," Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at Hargreaves Lansdown told the BBC's Today programme.

It also highlights Chinese investors' strong appetite for a homegrown chipmaker, as the government in Beijing pushes ahead with plans to make its technology industry self-reliant.

South Korean tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix and US-based Micron dominate the Dram market, with the three companies accounting for around 90% of global production.

Earlier this month, SK Hynix raised $26.5bn (£19.8bn) in its New York share offering, marking the largest ever listing by a foreign firm in the US.

The company, a key supplier to AI chip giant Nvidia, said it had sold 177.9 million American depositary shares for $149 each.

The shares surged as much as 17% on Friday in their first day of trading on the Nasdaq but have since given up some of that gain.

SK Hynix saw its market value top $1tn in its home country in May, lifted by the boom in demand for AI chips.

Once an affordable component used to build devices, memory prices have more than doubled in recent months - and are still rising.

Some big tech firms have hiked the price of popular gadgets, such as tablets and video game consoles, to cope with rising component costs.

Ellie Wong, an analyst at technology research firm TrendForce, told Reuters, external such price increases were expected to continue until the end of 2027.

"Amid persistent supply shortages, many customers are seeking to diversify their memory supplier base, which should significantly benefit CXMT and create more business opportunities," she said.

Booming AI chip demand helps create two new $1tn club members

Samsung profits jump 1,800% as AI chip sales soar

World's largest chipmaker does not rule out price rises as costs increase

body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky argued Sunday that the war with Iran has "weakened" the United States.

"The U.S. has been significantly weakened by the war with Iran," the congressman wrote in a Sunday post on X.

"This administration depleted our missile defenses, drained our oil reserves, sacrificed our men & women, inflated the price of consumer goods, increased our debt, and neglected our domestic needs…" he continued, adding, "all for Israel."

Some parts of Massie’s criticism align with publicly reported effects of the conflict. The Energy Department authorized the release of 172 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, while news reports and congressional spending measures have pointed to heavy demand for U.S. missile-defense systems and billions of dollars in additional defense funding. His broader assertion that the United States has been "significantly weakened" is a political judgment.

HOUSE REPUBLICAN THOMAS MASSIE SUGGESTS OBAMACARE COULD NOW BE LABELED 'TRUMPCARE'

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House early on Monday morning to request a comment.

Massie, who has served in the U.S. House of Representatives for more than 13 years, lost the May Republican primary in Kentucky's 4th Congressional District to President Donald Trump-backed challenger, retired Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein.

MASSIE LASHES OUT WHEN PRESSED ON EX-GIRLFRIEND'S ALLEGATIONS OF AFFAIR WITH GOP FIREBRAND

In a Friday post on X, Massie accused Trump of shifting toward a neoconservative foreign policy, writing, "Why did he flip to neocon?"

Former National Counterterrorism Center Director Joe Kent, who quit earlier this year due to his opposition to the Iran war, has been calling for President Trump to withdraw U.S. forces from the region.

EX-COUNTERTERRORISM OFFICIAL JOE KENT CONTINUES CALLING FOR US MILITARY WITHDRAWAL FROM MIDDLE EAST

U.S. President Donald Trump motions to reporters after getting off Air Force One on July 22, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"The Israelis know they can’t fight this war without the U.S., so their goal is to get us on board with more strikes, ground troops, etc., in the hopes that American causalities will sway public opinion enough to escalate into a chaotic, drawn-out war," Kent wrote in part of a Sunday post on X. "Our only viable option is to leave now—President Trump should use this pause in fighting to get our troops out & use quiet economic diplomacy to reopen the SOH & BAM."

The Trump administration has defended the military campaign as necessary to destroy Iran’s missile capabilities, cripple its navy, sever its support for terrorist proxies and prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The White House has also credited what it called "decisive American strength" with producing an agreement intended to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Burnham says there are ‘big decisions’ ahead on making council tax fairer – UK politics live
excerpt:
Labour’s 2024 manifesto did not include any specific commitments on council tax but two models are being floated

Andy Burnham has said there are “big decisions” ahead of his government on council tax...
body_text:
Labour’s 2024 manifesto did not include any specific commitments on council tax but two models are being floated

Andy Burnham has said there are “big decisions” ahead of his government on council tax, as he criticised the unfairness of the current system for making some people pay higher rates than are levied on more expensive homes in London.

In his interview with Laura Kuenssberg for the BBC’s Panorama programme, Burnham said:

double quotation markThere are people here in Greater Manchester who pay a much higher council tax than people living in much larger homes in London.

So the chancellor before, Rachel Reeves, was right to start to reform council tax to create some fairness there in relation to people in homes that are of much greater value, who haven’t seen their council tax go up over the years because of the failure to revalue the banding.

That’s an example of something that I think was right and fair.

double quotation markWe need to honour the manifesto upon which Labour was elected, and if I was to bring forward any changes, obviously people would rightly say, well, is this consistent with that manifesto? So there are big decisions ahead, you are right about that.

Labour’s 2024 manifesto did not include any specific pledges on council tax. But during the election campaign Labour ruled out changing council tax bands. This did not stop Rachel Reeves last year announcing a council tax surcharge on homes worth more than £2m – a policy that could be seen as a breach of those campaign promises.

In a story for the i today, Eleanor Langford says Burnham is considering options to replace council tax and stamp duty. She says:

double quotation markTwo models are competing for support: a proportional property tax, which would replace both council tax and stamp duty with a flat 0.48 per cent annual charge on a home’s current value; or a land value tax – an annual charge based on the value of the land a property sits on, rather than the building.

Government sources have played down this report. We should get a more formal response at the lobby briefing later.

Keir Starmer resisting calls to stand down was “selfish and stubborn”, according to the current sole Scottish Labour leadership contender, Monica Lennon.

As the Press Association reports, the earliest high profile call for Starmer to quit came from former Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar, who broke cover in February. Sarwar is now leaving Holyrood having been given a seat in the Lords and a job as a business minister by Andy Burnham.

Speaking to BBC Radio Scotland this morning, Lennon – a former MSP who will return to Holyrood to replace Sarwar under the regional list system – said Starmer was one of the main reasons why Scottish Labour won just 17 seats in the Holyrood election in May. She said:

double quotation markClearly, the focus is the May election and what’s happened in Scotland.

The party has had its worst election result ever in the history of the Scottish parliament – in fact we’ve been losing seats and votes since 1999, so there’s a downward trend that cannot be ignored.

There’s lots of reasons, but I think the primary reason was Keir Starmer.

We couldn’t get a proper hearing on the doorsteps or around the country because that was the first thing that was brought up.

People felt they saw Keir Starmer and his words and actions didn’t match – there was a deep disappointment.

double quotation markI think, on reflection, Keir Starmer should have read the room, I think he was selfish and stubborn and I think that’s been a big part of our problem.

That has contaminated people’s view of Scottish Labour.

While the party is at its lowest ebb since the creation of the Scottish Parliament in terms of MSPs, Lennon warned: “It can get worse”.

The soon-to-be Glasgow MSP is the first to throw her hat in the ring to replace Sarwar, but has encouraged others to do so. She said:

double quotation markScottish Labour’s got some serious decisions to make, and it’s really important that our members have their say, that they’re heard.

I hope that other colleagues do come forward because I would welcome a debate, a discussion and a contest, because I think we really need to have that.

Denis Campbell is the Guardian’s health policy editor.

Andy Burnham must convince voters of the “moral” and “positive” case for reforming social care, not just that it will help the NHS, health thinktanks said today.

The practical benefits that an overhaul of the system would bring for millions of older and disabled people and their families are also a strong argument the prime minister should make, not just less pressure on overcrowded hospitals, they believe.

Natasha Curry, the Nuffield Trust’s deputy director of policy, said:

double quotation markIt is right to recognise that the NHS and social care are deeply interconnected but the case for fixing social care extends far beyond protecting the NHS. There is a moral imperative to ensure older and disabled people can live independently with dignity and a compelling economic case too.

Millions of people have unmet care needs, while unpaid carers and disabled adults are too often prevented from working, participating in their communities and planning for their futures because the support they need simply isn’t there.

While it would help, reducing the number of people who get stuck in hospital despite being medically fit to leave – delayed discharges - won’t on its own get the NHS back to functioning smoothly, she added.

double quotation markBetter social care would undoubtedly help some patients leave hospital more quickly but we should avoid suggesting that fixing social care alone will fix the NHS.

Sarah Woolnough, the chief executive of the King’s Fund, welcomed Burnham’s determination to transform social care after successive governments “consigned [it] to the politically ‘too difficult’ box”.

His efforts to build public support for radical change must go beyond rhetoric about the NHS, she said.

double quotation markDebates about social care are too often haunted by ‘death tax’ rhetoric and the costs of improving the system rather than focussed on the tangible benefits reform could bring for people and families.

If the prime minister wants to succeed where previous governments have failed, he must make a positive case for reform and build a shared understanding of why change matters.

The Casey commission’s already-planned engagement with the public is an “opportunity to build understanding of social care and what reform could mean for people and their families”, added Woolnough.

As I explained earlier this month, we are no longer having comments open regularly below the line (BTL) on this blog. We are sorry about that, and the views of readers who complained about this BTL last week were noted.

I was away for most of last week, but I was reading the blog and the comments and I am grateful to everyone who made a point of saying how much they appreciated the blog. And I particularly enjoyed the poetry tributes, like the My Way version from Hesfalleninthewater and the Cole Porter one from AverageObserver, which was so lovely I’m tempted to quote it on my CV. Thank you.

The fact that we are closing comments does not mean we want to stop hearing from you.

From today, if you want to contact me, or anyone else writing the blog when I am not here, please email politics.live@theguardian.com.

You can email about anything but I am hoping that readers will use this email address for four things in particular.

1) Corrections. If I make a mistake, please flag it up and I will correct it. Blog posts are written and published quickly, and some errors do get through. It is even helpful to have typos pointed out; no mistake is too small to correct.

2) Comments (for publication). When we announced that we were closing comments BTL, many of you said you greatly value hearing what other readers think about the politics stories of the day. I would like to let this carry on by using some comments ATL. In particular, I would welcome comments that: contain new information about a story being covered ATL (ideally with links); contain comments or arguments about those stories that readers may find original and interesting; or signpost readers to other stories or articles they may find interesting (again, with links please).

It may take a while before I work out how best to mix comments with all the other material used ATL. I’m sure I will end up only using some of the comments submitted. But it is important and helpful to me to know what you think about what is in the news, so do please send in your thoughts anyway.

When I do include comments, I am less likely to quote in full anything longer than about 150 words.

And I will assume that readers are happy to be quoted by name unless they say otherwise.

3) Questions. If you have a question, do email. If I think readers generally may be interested in the answer, I will post the Q&A ATL (as I used to do when comments were open BTL.)

4) Complaints. If you don’t like the way I am covering anything, or not covering something, do say. I don’t have any control over other aspects of the Guardian’s reporting, but I always want to know if people have concerns about what I am writing.

All emails will get read, and I will try to reply to most or all of them too. But it is hard to know how many will come in.

If you want to contact me very quickly, I will probably see your message sooner if you use social media. You can reach me on Bluesky at @andrewsparrowgdn.bsky.social or, if you still use X, at @AndrewSparrow.

Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, has said that he hopes MPs can find “a real and lasting consensus” on social care.

In a statement issued in response to Andy Burnham’s comments on the topic (see 9.03am), Davey said:

double quotation markI know for a fact this morning that carers I know will feel a sense of hope that politicians may finally do something serious to fix care in our country.

I am ready to roll up my sleeves and do whatever I can to find a real and lasting consensus on social care.

Family carers must be at the heart of any new system, everyone must get the care they need and no one should lose their home as a result.

Good morning. Yesterday Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told Sky News that, while Andy Burnham spent his first week as PM focusing on cost of living issues, this week the public would see “a prime minister that runs towards big and difficult issues rather than runs away from [them]”. Those challenges include reforming social care and, as Peter Walker reports, Burnham has pledged to use “whatever political capital I have” to finally fix the crumbling social care system in England, saying that without rapid action the NHS could effectively collapse.

Burnham was speaking in a 30-minute interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg going out on Panorama tonight. The BBC put the full interview on iPlayer at 6am this morning, and there is a write-up on the BBC’s website here.

Burnham is due to give a speech on social care on Wednesday, but he is due to be addressing other problem issues this week as well. According to Andrew McDonald and Megan McElroy in their London Playbook briefing for Politico, tomorrow we are getting some announcement on getting young people back to work, on Thursday a defence-related announcement is due, and on Friday Burnham is expected to unveil plans (first reported in the Sunday Times) to give more control over how government money gets spent in their areas.

In his interview with Kuenssberg, Burnham was asked if he would put a new social care system in place before the next election. He did not make that commitment; he has only got three years at best, and full reform could take the best part of a decade. But he did say that he wanted to go “as quickly as I can on the reform” and that there were “major changes you can make before the next election”.

Burnham does not need Tory votes to pass legislation to reform social care in the Commons because he has a working majority of 166. But Burnham’s plans won’t survive if the next election results in Labour being replaced by a government committed to ripping them up. Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, has indicated that he hopes Burnham will produce plans that the Liberal Democrats can support. But Reform UK and the Conservatives have both signalled that they might use their opposition to the Burnham plan. When Burnham was health secretary before the 2010 general election, he floated a proposal to fund better social care through a levy on inheritance. The Tories immediately labelled this a death tax, it became hugely unpopular, and Labour had largely dropped the idea even before they lost the election.

We don’t know what Burnham will propose this time; the veteran Whitehall fixer Louise Casey is leading a review, and Burnham is expected to ask her to produce a final report soon, instead of waiting until 2028 as originally planned. But Burnham has talked about the case for a “care levy”.

In an article for the Sunday Telegraph yesterday, Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson, said his party would oppose anything that amounted to a “radical tax grab”. He said voters “rightly want meaningful efficiency savings, not another tax assault”, and he challenged Burnham to hold an election on this issue. He has been repeating this message on GB News.

This morning, in an open letter to Burnham, Kemi Badenoch has implied that she is willing to work with Labour on this. “The Conservatives are happy to work with you and other parties on reforming social care,” she says. But she also makes it clear that she will fight like fury any plan Burnham is realistically likely to propose.

double quotation markBut we will only support a solution that abides by two core principles.

First, any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives.

Second, the money must be found by reducing current spending. You must rule out any tax rises, or increased borrowing that will ultimately fall on the next generation to pay for.

Compared to the last Conservative government’s budget plans, spending in 2028/29 alone will be £152bn higher (that’s 11% above what was planned in that year under the Conservatives). As a result, taxes will be £105bn higher (up 8%) and borrowing will be £47bn higher (more than double previous plans).

The tax burden has risen to a record high under Labour, and there is already speculation that you will increase taxes further at the budget this autumn in order to pay for all the things you have announced in your first week, plus the outstanding gaps in funding for the defence investment plan.

(Labour is spending a lot more than the last Conservative government budgeted for the second half of this decade. But the Tory long-term spending projections were widely criticised at the time by economists as unrealistically low.)

I will post more on Burnham’s BBC interview soon.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Afternoon: Andy Burnham meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, at a naval base in the UK.

As I explained earlier this month, we are no longer going to have comments open below the line on this blog. From today, if you want to contact me, or anyone else writing the blog when I am not here, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. I will post a bit more on how we hope to use this email system a bit later.

title: Prince William likely 'livid' over Meghan Markle's 'tasteless' photos at Princess Diana's home: expert

Meghan Markle shared photos of her children, Prin...
body_text:
Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," recounts how Kate Middleton rebounded after her 2007 breakup with Prince William before the couple reunited.

Meghan Markle shared photos of her children, Princess Lilibet and Prince Archie, frolicking around the late Princess Diana's childhood home and experts are calling Markle's move "tasteless."

This week, Markle crafted an Instagram post from the family's recent U.K. visit. She captioned her post, "Summer Holiday," and one of the images shows Prince Harry with his kids walking on a grassy path with hedges and large trees. The photo is believed to be taken at Althorp, the Spencer family’s ancestral estate.

In the photo, Archie and Harry are carrying bouquets, which seemingly suggest that they visited Diana's burial site, which is on an island in the middle of her family's estate.

A royal expert says Prince William is likely "livid" that Meghan Markle shared photos from Princess Diana's ancestral estate. (Getty Images)

Hilary Fordwich, British royals expert, told Fox News Digital that Prince Harry's oldest brother, Prince William, is likely "livid" by Markle's photos.

KING CHARLES KEPT PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON IN THE DARK ABOUT SECRET HARRY AND MEGHAN REUNION: REPORT

"Not only is Prince William likely to be livid regarding such commercialization of Althorp in such a tacky tasteless media post, it’ll fuel his disgust so he shall thwart any major re-entry," she began. "Likewise,  Camilla, courtiers, palace aides, security officials & other institutional gatekeepers who are duty bound to protect the monarchy, will all do their utmost to thwart MM & H’s attempts."

"Not only is Prince William likely to be livid regarding such commercialization of Althorp in such a tacky tasteless media post, it’ll fuel his disgust so he shall thwart any major re-entry."

Richard Fitzwilliams, royal expert, pointed out that the Spencer's must have given the Duke and Duchess of Sussex permission to visit Althorp, therefore her post is "permissible."

PRINCE HARRY LONGS FOR HIS OLD ROYAL LIFE AS AMERICA ISN'T WHAT HE EXPECTED, EXPERTS SAY

"Meghan shared pictures of their children on what is assumed is Althorp, home of the Spencer family. That would have been allowed by the Spencer's and is therefore permissible," he told Fox News Digital.

Fitzwilliams continued, "What is important is the silence Harry and Meghan have somehow managed to maintain after seeing King Charles and Queen Camilla in contrast to what has happened previously. It will have been made clear that there would be no future meetings if they had talked to any of the media."

An aerial view shows the burial site of Diana, Princess of Wales, at the Althorp Estate in Althorp, United Kingdom. (David Goddard/Getty Images)

Helena Chard, British broadcaster and photographer, called Markle's decision of sharing a private family moment publicly "predictable."

"As for Meghan posting photos of the children at Diana’s family home. It is a predictable move. It ties them to history without using a title. However it also shows a slight tension, wanting the Royal story when it helps, while keeping distance when it doesn’t," Chard said.

"The public understands Peace in Private but basically the Crown has to come first," she concluded.

A photo of Kate Middleton, Prince William, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Chris Jackson/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

On Harry and Meghan's recent trip to the U.K., they were reportedly reunited with King Charles and Queen Camilla. Charles had not seen his grandchildren since 2022.

"She is being predictably provocative & tasteless since Princess Diana’s resting place is purposely at Althorp, a most private family mourning location & deeply symbolic being Princess Diana’s ancestral home."

Princess Diana died in 1997. She was photographed here in 1983. (Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty Images)

Chard is highly doubtful that Charles' visit with his estranged son means Harry will be accepted back into the "royal arena."

"I doubt Charles will just let the Sussexes back into the Royal arena, especially as there has been no genuine contrition. A family reunion is one thing. A return to royal life is another," she said.
