title: 'Shark Week' host Forrest Galante explains why crushing beers in the ocean is a bad idea
excerpt:
Fox News host Jesse Watters speaks to OCEARCH founder Chris Fischer about shark safety on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

It’s the most wonderful time of the year: "Shark Week."

That annual stretch when ...
body_text:
Fox News host Jesse Watters speaks to OCEARCH founder Chris Fischer about shark safety on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

It’s the most wonderful time of the year: "Shark Week."

That annual stretch when Americans collectively gather around their TV sets to learn everything there is to know about the ocean’s apex predators and to ask ourselves why we are dumb enough to swim in the ocean in the first place.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

But lucky for those of us who don’t want to end up the subject of a future "Shark Week" documentary, wildlife biologist, conservationist and TV host Forrest Galante has some simple advice.

Forrest Galante has come face to face with some of the ocean's most insane predators. (Forrest Galante)

Galante recently joined OutKick Outdoors to talk about shark attacks, shark behavior and his upcoming Discovery special, "Alien Sharks: Untamed America." And while he stressed that the chances of having a negative shark encounter are already extremely slim, he said beachgoers can make those odds even better by using some common sense.

"You know, the best thing you can do is educate yourself," Galante said. "Think about where you're going. Learn what the species are."

If you are looking for some blanket rules before your next beach trip, Galante offered a few.

"Don't go in the water at dawn or dusk," Galante said.

Sharks are crepuscular, meaning they are most active at dawn and dusk. That is when they are more likely to be feeding closer to shore, which is also exactly where people tend to be splashing around during summer vacation.

Even in waters where sharks are frequently found, experts noted that human encounters rarely lead to bites. (iStock)

"Don't swim near river mouths," Galante said. "That's when sharks are feeding."

River mouths can attract baitfish and other food sources, which can also attract sharks. If there is a place where sharks are naturally more likely to congregate, that is probably not the spot to float around with a drink in your hand and your guard down.

"Don't go swimming by yourself," Galante said.

This is one of those tips that applies to pretty much every outdoor activity. Hiking alone, boating alone, swimming alone — all of it adds risk.

Palm Beach closed as beaches in Sydney's north have been closed since Tuesday due to shark attacks and dangerous currents during summer in Sydney on January 22, 2026 in Sydney, Australia. (Corbis via Getty Images)

And Galante said there is another simple clue beachgoers should pay attention to.

"If you see no one on the beach, that's usually not a good place to go swimming," he said.

"On the flip side of that, don't go swimming where people are fishing and throwing bait in the water and things like that," Galante said.

This one should be obvious, but apparently we need to say it anyway. If people are actively tossing shark food into the water, you can probably bet sharks will be there, too.

Sharks are not hunting humans, but they are curious predators. And sometimes, something as simple as a flash of light can get their attention.

"Wearing something highly shiny, like jewelry or sequins or anything with those little mirrors that put out light, can look like a school of bait fish," Galante said.

That matters because, according to Galante, shark attacks on humans are usually because the shark thinks you're something else.

"They say that something like 99% of shark bites are a case of mistaken identity," he said. "You see a flash from a sparkly bit of jewelry or something, and the shark goes, ‘Oh wow, is that food?’ Unfortunately, when a shark asks the question, ‘Is that food?’ they do so by taking an investigative bite."

FORREST GALANTE SAYS MOST SHARK BITES ARE A CASE OF MISTAKEN IDENTITY AS FLORIDA ATTACKS LEAD THE US

And that is where things can go very wrong.

"They don't have hands," Galante said. "They can't feel it, so that investigative bite can be very, very damaging and, in some cases, fatal."

This is the one that might surprise people. According to Galante, even certain sounds can draw a shark's attention.

"The crackling of a water bottle, or even the crunching of a beer can, sounds a lot like the crunching of fish bones to a shark, and it can make them come and investigate," he said.

Friends take a selfie on a beach during summer vacation while enjoying holiday together and drinking beer by the ocean. (Getty Images)

Galante made it clear that most sharks are not looking for humans as prey.

"Most of the time, we're not even on the menu," Galante said. "They're just trying to figure out if we are."

So no matter what horrors you see on your TV screen this week, there is no need to cancel your beach trip.

"Just taking a few very simple precautions can greatly reduce your already very slim chance of having a negative encounter," Galante said.

Galante’s Shark Week special, "Alien Sharks: Untamed America," premieres Wednesday on Discovery and Max. The special follows him across the United States in search of some of the strangest and least-known shark species living in American waters — including glow-in-the-dark swell sharks, seagrass-eating bonnethead sharks, massive basking sharks and sawfish that look like something out of Star Wars .

In his new special, Forrest Galante scoured U.S. waters searching for rare species of sharks, including off the coast of Massachusetts (seen here). (Forrest Galante)

"We have some of the coolest, the largest, the smallest, the weirdest and the most bizarre and incredible sharks right here in the United States," Galante said.

Just maybe don’t go looking for them at dusk while wearing sequins and crushing a beer can.

Love all things wildlife and outdoors? Follow OutKick Outdoors on Instagram and TikTok!

title: Darfur: Weaponising Identity
excerpt:
How land conflict, state neglect and racist ideology have driven Darfur towards alleged genocide.

This episode examines how mass violence in Darfur has been constructed over time and why many activis...
body_text:
How land conflict, state neglect and racist ideology have driven Darfur towards alleged genocide.

This episode examines how mass violence in Darfur has been constructed over time and why many activists, governments and courts have labelled it genocide, even as that term remains politically contested. It traces how environmental stress, neglect of the peripheries and competition over land fed grievances between communities. It shows how Khartoum armed and mobilised militias, how racialised language framed “Arabs” and “Africans” as enemies and how aerial bombing, burning of villages and mass displacement became tools of policy. Through survivors’ testimony and legal analysis, the film follows the path from counterinsurgency to crimes against humanity and alleged genocide and asks what justice has – and has not – been delivered for Darfur.

title: Who is India’s new education minister Pralhad Joshi?
excerpt:
Pralhad Joshi has been appointed as India’s education minister after weeks-long protests over an exam leak scandal led to the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan.

Pradhan’s departure, which came on Sat...
body_text:
Pralhad Joshi has been appointed as India’s education minister after weeks-long protests over an exam leak scandal led to the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan.

Pradhan’s departure, which came on Saturday, was one of the main demands of the youth-led demonstrations that in recent weeks had spread across India into a major challenge for Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The 63-year-old Joshi is already the minister of new and renewable energy and consumer affairs, food and public distribution but will now also handle the education portfolio, a task political analysts said is likely to prove challenging amid increased scrutiny over the education system.

As one of the Modi government’s longest serving ministers, Joshi is seen as close to the powerful prime minister.

After being appointed to lead the Ministry of Education, Joshi wrote on social media that he was “grateful” to Modi “for placing his faith” in him and “entrusting” him with responsibility.

“I accept it with humility and a deep sense of duty,” he said.

Joshi was born in 1962 in Bijapur in the southern Indian state of Karnataka. He graduated with a bachelor’s degree in arts from the KS Arts College, Hubballi, which is affiliated with Karnataka University.

He cofounded a chemicals business after graduation. However, he was interested in politics from a young age and associated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a right-wing Hindu volunteer organisation founded in 1925 by physician and Hindu nationalist Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in Nagpur in modern-day Maharashtra.

The RSS is often described as the ideological mother of the BJP.

Joshi’s political career officially began in the early 1990s during the Hubballi Idgah Maidan issue, a major political and religious conflict in Karnataka primarily centred on land usage by Muslims and Hindus, during which the BJP and RSS also demanded the Indian national flag be flown on the disputed land.

In 2004, Joshi was appointed as a BJP member of parliament from the Dharwad district. He  has since won five straight parliamentary elections.

In 1998, Joshi was appointed president of the BJP in the Dharwad district and in 2014 rose to become the state of Karnataka’s BJP president.

In May 2019, he was appointed to Modi’s cabinet as minister of parliamentary affairs, coal and mines. In 2024, Joshi introduced several reforms to increase production of coal to meet growing energy demands.

He faced criticism from climate activists and local communities for championing coal production amid climate change concerns. In 2025, he became minister of new and renewable energy and consumer affairs, food and public distribution.

According to the government, this portfolio involves “working towards a cleaner and sustainable future of the country, achieving 500 GW through renewable energy and non-fossil energy sources by 2030 and net-zero target by 2070, which are essential for India’s economic development and national security”.

One of the key challenges Joshi will face is addressing the concerns young people in India have about the education system, especially after a scandal involving the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance examinations.

NEET scores determine whether aspiring doctors are eligible to join undergraduate medical colleges and, if so, which schools they qualify for.

Nearly 2.3 million test takers across India as well as at examination centres in Doha, Dubai, Singapore and Kathmandu, appeared for the NEET this year on May 3, battling it out for fewer than 130,000 spots in medical colleges.

After allegations of a leak of the examination paper, the Indian government announced on May 12 that the examination was voided, and another test would be held.

Disillusioned and frustrated, thousands of students protested.

On Sunday, Joshi held his first meeting as education minister to assess the situation and implement new schemes.

title: Melissa Gilbert, Michael Landon and more: Where the original 'Little House on the Prairie' cast is now
excerpt: Sidney Greenbush recalls behind-the-scenes memories with the "Little House on the Prairie" cast and explains why she stepped away from acting. Greenbush is the author of a new children's book, "Seven ...
body_text:
Sidney Greenbush recalls behind-the-scenes memories with the "Little House on the Prairie" cast and explains why she stepped away from acting. Greenbush is the author of a new children's book, "Seven Sisters – The Lantern of Humanity."

The popular new adaptation of "Little House on the Prairie," which began streaming on Netflix earlier this month, has caused a resurgence of interest in the original 1974 television series starring Melissa Gilbert and Michael Landon.

The cast of "Little House on the Prairie" is seen in a promotional photo. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

Melissa Gilbert played Laura Ingalls on "Little House on the Prairie."  (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images; Stephane Cardinale - Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images)

Melissa Gilbert is best known for her portrayal of Laura Ingalls in the original series, which she began in 1974 at just 9 years old.

The 62-year-old had already been on shows like "Gunsmoke" and "Emergency" when the show started.

Also serving as the narrator of the show, Gilbert stayed on "Little House on the Prairie" for all nine seasons, until 1983.

BELOVED 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' FACES WAGONLOAD OF 'WOKE' ALLEGATIONS OVER NETFLIX REBOOT

During her time on the show, she made several TV movies, including "The Miracle Worker," "The Diary of Anne Frank" and "Splendor in the Grass."

She also reprised her role in the TV movies "Little House Years," "Little House: Look Back to Yesterday," "Little House: The Final Farewell" and "Little House: Bless All the Dear Children."

Gilbert continued to act after the show ended on dozens of TV movies and she also voiced Barbara Gordon on "Batman: The Animated Series" from 1992 to 1994.

Gilbert also made TV appearances on shows like "Touched by an Angel," "Providence," "7th Heaven" and "Nip/Tuck." She had a recurring role on Hallmark’s "When Calls the Heart," but recently revealed in an Instagram post that she would not be returning to the show. She said she was told that was due to "budget issues."

The news came after her husband Timothy Busfield, who she married in 2013, was charged with two counts of criminal sexual contact of a minor and one count of child abuse in January. He was indicted by a federal grand jury in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a minor.

Busfield has denied the charges and Gilbert has continued to support him, telling ABC in April that he is the "last person in the world who would hurt a child."

"I trust him with my children's lives, with my grandchildren's lives, my nieces and nephews," she added. "He is an honorable, caring, generous human being."

ORIGINAL 'LITTLE HOUSE' VILLAIN RETURNS FOR REBOOT WITH WARNING FOR NEW NELLIE

Gilbert also defended the new reboot after she said she’d seen fans debating on social media whether the new version or the original were historically accurate and faithful to the books.

"The short answer is no, neither are entirely accurate to the times nor the books," she wrote in a Substack essay.

After giving several examples of inaccuracies, she wrote: "My hope is that folks realize that these are all perfect examples of dramatic license. Even the real Laura took dramatic license in writing her books. For example, in the book, ‘Little House on the Prairie,’ all three Ingalls girls are older than they were in real life."

She added, "So rather than getting all twisted up in what’s real and what’s dramatized, maybe just sit back and go for the ride the creative minds behind these shows want to take you on. If you like it, stick with it. If you don’t, you don’t have to watch."

Michael Landon is seen here on "Little House on the Prairie" and in 1990, a year before his death. (NBCU Photo Bank; Photo by Kypros/Getty Images)

Michael Landon, who played Laura’s father Charles Ingalls on the show, began acting in the 1950s, appearing on shows like "Cheyenne," "Suspicion" and "The Rifleman." He was also in the movie "I Was a Teenage Werewolf."

Landon directed many of the show’s episodes and wrote and produced the show.

Before "Little House," he starred as Little Joe Cartwright on the long-running series "Bonanza."

Landon continued to work on several TV movies after the show ended, and he starred as angel Jonathan Smith on the 1984 to 1989 series "Highway to Heaven."

He also reprised his role as Charles Ingalls in four TV movies.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Landon died at 54 years old in 1991, just months after he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.

Gilbert called Landon a "mentor and father figure" in a Fox News Digital interview in 2024. She said she saw her TV dad a week before he died.

"There were always funny moments with Michael," she said. "Even as sick as he was, he still maintained his incredible sense of humor."

Gilbert frequently posts memories of him on her Instagram, writing earlier this month, "I’ve always felt like the luckiest girl in the world because he chose me to be his ‘Halfpint.’ Working with him was more than formative. I learned most of what I know about our industry from him."

Karen Grassle seen as Caroline Ingalls on "Little House on the Prairie" and at an event in 2024. (George Hurrell/NBCU Photo Bank; Arnold Jerocki/WireImage)

Karen Grassle, who played Laura’s mother Caroline, was mainly a theater and Broadway actress before landing the role on "Little House."

After the show ended, the 84-year-old continued to act until 2021, starring in the movie "Not to Forget."

Grassle had a contentious relationship with Landon while on the show, which stemmed from a salary dispute in Season 2 and prompted her to leave a year before the show ended.

She formed a special bond with her onscreen children "so they felt comfortable doing scenes with me as their mother," but her relationship with Landon, whom she called an "amazing, multi-talented person," soured, according to People magazine.

"I felt insulted as his co-star on a hit series," Grassle told the New York Post about his refusal to grant her a raise, arguing she should be paid the same as her onscreen children. "I didn’t want to gouge anybody, but I expected a fair wage."

She said Landon also cut her onscreen time during the dispute and made sexist jokes on set.

The actress reconciled with Landon before his death, telling the Post: "I am very grateful that we mended our fences."

Grassle is also very proud of her time on "Little House," calling her character "an incredibly strong woman with a nature full of texture. Her spirit is one to live by."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Melissa Sue Anderson played Laura's older sister Mary Ingalls on "Little House on the Prairie." (Bruce Birmelin/NBCU Photo Bank; Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

Melissa Sue Anderson played Laura’s older sister Mary Ingalls on the show.

The 63-year-old was the only member of the cast to be nominated for an Emmy for an episode about her character going blind.

Two years older than Gilbert when she started on the pioneer show, Anderson had only done a little TV work — including as Bobby Brady’s first kiss — before "Little House."

Anderson made her film debut in the horror movie "Happy Birthday to Me" in 1981 and after the show ended, she made TV appearances on shows like "Hotel," "Murder She Wrote," "The Equalizer" and "The Love Boat."

She met her husband, Michael Sloan, while appearing in the 1980s reprisal of "Alfred Hitchcock Presents." The couple welcomed two daughters and Sloan died in 2025.

Anderson and Gilbert famously didn’t get along.

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' RETURNS AS NEW NETFLIX ADAPTATION AIMS FOR WHOLESOME ENTERTAINMENT

"We were very, very different," Anderson told the Atlanta Constitution-Journal.

Anderson also published a memoir about her time on the show called "The Way I See It: A Look Back at My Life on Little House."

Gilbert felt that Anderson acted like the boss on set.

"From the moment we walked onto that set, Melissa Sue Anderson was the boss of me," she said in an interview, according to Parade. "She took that absolutely seriously. She was two years older than me, which, you know, when you’re 9 and 11 is a big deal."

Gilbert added, "She was tough on me both off and on camera, but on camera especially."

Anderson explained that she was just very shy, telling Harry Brownstone on his podcast last year: "I wish I had been more outgoing so I could have enjoyed it more and been more easygoing about everything."

However, the pair reunited last year at Gilbert’s off-Broadway play "Pen Pals."

"Reconnection with a sister," Gilbert wrote. "Long, healing talks. Lots of reminiscing. Lots of catching up. Lots of laughter and a few tears."

MICHAEL LANDON'S 'LITTLE HOUSE' CO-STAR EXPOSES ACTOR'S WILD ON-SET PRANKS

"Just us Ingalls girls. The best part is, the past is now just that and we can move forward as the sisters/friends we always wanted to be," she wrote.

Sidney and Rachel Lindsay Greenbush both played younger sister Carrie Ingalls. (Gary Null/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images; David Livingston/Getty Images)

Twins Rachel Lindsay and Sidney Greenbush were just 3 years old when they were cast as younger sister Carrie Ingalls.

Sharing the role for eight years, they chose to leave after the eighth season when they were 12 years old.

"Everybody separated, and I didn’t see anybody," Rachel Lindsay said at a 50th anniversary reunion, according to Entertainment Weekly. "And that was really hard for me personally because I didn’t realize how connected I had been to everybody until years later."

"You make these really deep, intense bonds working with each other every single day, and then when it’s over, you’re just supposed to be like, ‘Okay, that was nice. Bye,’" she told the outlet. "And it’s really hard that way."

Both sisters retired from acting in 1983 to focus on their education.

In 2014, she married Daniel Sanchez, whom she first met when he lived near the set and used to sneak on to hang out with the cast and crew, according to People magazine.

She also has a grown daughter from a previous relationship.

Sidney acted in "Hambone and Hillie" in 1983 and Rachel Lindsay was in an episode of "Matt Houston."

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR REVEALS WILD FRIENDSHIP WITH JIM MORRISON BEFORE WHOLESOME TV FAME

Sidney just wrote a children’s book called "Seven Sisters: The Lantern of Humanity."

"I remember when they were making the movie 'Return to Oz.' My sister made it to the final three girls who were selected," Sidney told Fox News Digital last month.

"They all did screen tests, and for the silliest of reasons, they chose another girl over her," she said. "Of course, we all know there can only be one choice in the end, but it's a lot of pressure for children. So I decided I was going to explore other things because sometimes you go to what they call 'cattle calls,' where there are so many people competing for the same role. The casting directors aren't always nice."

The two sisters were credited as "Lindsay Sidney Greenbush" on the show.

Alison Arngrim played bully Nellie Oleson on "Little House on the Prairie." (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images; Arnold Jerocki/WireImage)

Nellie Oleson, the daughter of the mercantile store owners who bullied Laura, was played by Alison Arngrim.

The 64-year-old was just 12 when she began acting opposite Gilbert, saying at the 50th reunion the two of them were "like sisters" on set, according to People.

"It's so completely bonkers," Arngrim said. "Here's Melissa Gilbert and I playing mortal enemies, beating each other senseless all week. And then on the weekends, we'd go to each other's house for a slumber party, and we were hanging out."

She is also the author of "Confessions of A Prairie Bitch: How I Survived Nellie Oleson and Learned to Love Being Hated" and had a one-woman show called "Confessions of a Prairie Bitch."

In 2002, she was honored with the Young Artist Former Child Star Lifetime Achievement Award for her work on the show.

Aside from "Little House, Arngrim also made appearances on shows like "Fantasy Island," "The Love Boat," the TV movie "Life Interrupted" and she recently made a cameo on the "Little House" reboot.

Katherine MacGregor was gossip Harriet Oleson on the show. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

Katherine MacGregor played nasty gossip Harriet Oleson on the show.

After she died at 93 years old in 2018, Gilbert called her "outspoken and hilariously funny" in an Instagram post.

"A truly gifted actress as she was able to play a despicable character but with so much heart. Her Harriet Oleson was the woman our fans loved to hate. A perfect antagonist," she added.

"The thing people outside of our prairie family didn't know, was how loving and nurturing she was with the younger cast."

Before "Little House," MacGregor acted on shows like "Mister Peepers," "Mannix," "Emergency!" "All in the Family" and "Ironside."

NETFLIX'S 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' ACTOR HOPES NEW SERIES WILL UNITE OLD AND NEW FANS

She was also a successful Broadway actress and she returned to the theater after the show ended. She retired from acting in the early 2000s.

Richard Bull played Nels Oleson, Harriet's husband and Nellie's father. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

Richard Bull played Nels Oleson, husband to Harriet who, with her, owned the town mercantile store.

Bull began acting in the 1950s, landing parts on shows like "Perry Mason," "Highway Patrol," "The Virginian," "The Fugitive," "The Alfred Hitchcock Hour," "Gidget," "Gomer Pyle: USMC," "The Andy Griffith Show," "Bewitched," "Mission: Impossible" and "Bonanza" before the show’s run.

He also starred as the doctor on "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea" from 1964 to 1968.

He continued to act until 2011 on shows like "Lou Grant," "Knots Landing," "Hillstreet Blues," "Designing Women" and "ER."

He also reunited with Landon on three episodes of "Highway to Heaven."

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR SAYS CHILD ACTORS GET 'DROPPED' AFTER HOLLYWOOD FAME FADES

Dean Butler came onto the show later in the series to play Laura's husband. (NBCU Photo Bank; Albert L. Ortega/Getty Images)

Dean Butler played Laura’s eventual husband, Almanzo Wilder, who came onto the show in the sixth season.

He also appeared on shows like "CHiPs," "Fantasy Island," "Who’s the Boss?" "The Love Boat," "Hotel," and had a recurring role on "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."

From 1986 until 1988, he starred on "The New Gidget" as Jeff "Moondoggie" Griffin.

His last acting role was in 2008, and since then he has mainly worked behind the camera as a sports, entertainment and documentary producer, including a docuseries he narrated called "The Little House Phenomenon: A Place in Television History."

Butler, like Gilbert, commended the reboot, writing on Instagram earlier this month: "Something that I love about the program that I think would have been really fun in the original — which we did not do... is the family singing. Writers have rolled in songs that Pa played on his fiddle, and the family is singing along, and they’re doing it beautifully, and this really is the spirit of Laura’s books."

He added that the show is beautifully produced, saying "there is a lot of good stuff going on here."

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Water supply failure leaves Gatwick airport without working toilets
excerpt:
Airport’s bars and restaurants also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running water

A water supply failure at Gatwick left passengers without access to working toilets or bars a...
body_text:
Airport’s bars and restaurants also unable to serve drinks to passengers because of lack of running water

A water supply failure at Gatwick left passengers without access to working toilets or bars and restaurants.

Passengers posted online that they were unable to get hot drinks, wash their hands or fill up water bottles at the airport in Sussex.

The problem also had an impact in the wider Sussex and Kent area on Sunday, water suppliers said.

A statement from Gatwick said: “A water issue in the Horley area is causing disruption at the airport this morning. The problem is affecting water supply in both terminals and is currently under investigation.

“Bottled water is being made available to passengers and staff across the airport and other contingency measures are being put in place to ensure the welfare of our passengers. We will provide further updates and apologise for any inconvenience to passengers.”

Bottled water was being given to travellers at the airport and flights were not affected.

The utility company SES Water said there had been interruptions to water supplies in parts of the TN11, RH1, RH6 and RH10 postcode areas.

In its most recent statement at 2pm, the company said: “We are pleased to provide an update that our Bough Beech water treatment works are back up and running, we now need to treat the water before returning services to normal as quickly as we possibly can. We would like to thank customers and our partners at Gatwick airport for their continued patience, and we are sorry for the inconvenience this is causing. We will update you on the progress of the work as soon as we can.”

The TalkTV presenter Julia Hartley-Brewer posted on X: “If you’re on your way to Gatwick airport, it might be helpful to know that there is no running water across the entire airport. That means no coffees, no water fountains, no flushing toilets and no hand washing.”

On Facebook, one user posted: “Gasping for a drink & crossing my legs right now. This is ridiculous! Gatwick airport has shut all restaurants and most toilets due to a water outage. Not a great start to the holiday.”

The former MP and recently appointed government “music champion” Michael Dugher wrote on social media: “At least allow people to use the chairs in all the closed restaurants and bars. No water is one thing, but depriving people of somewhere to sit is another … Families are having to sit on the floor.”

Roger Wood, from Tunbridge Wells, Kent, arrived at Gatwick’s south terminal at about 11am on Sunday to fly to New York. He told reporters: “There was no communication. We arrived at 11ish and it had only started recently.

“We met friends at the bar but they couldn’t serve us as they were unable to wash their hands. I’ve never seen Wetherspoons empty. No idea when it’ll be resolved. The toilets also lacked water to wash hands.”

title: Berlin Pride van and knife rampage an ‘Islamist terrorist attack’, say German authorities
excerpt:
Police hunt for main suspect, named as Abdul Ballout, 21, after fatal attack in Tiergarten park close to LGBTQ+ event

A deadly van ramming and knife rampage near Berlin’s Pride festival was an Islami...
body_text:
Police hunt for main suspect, named as Abdul Ballout, 21, after fatal attack in Tiergarten park close to LGBTQ+ event

A deadly van ramming and knife rampage near Berlin’s Pride festival was an Islamist terrorist attack, German authorities have said as the hunt for the main suspect continues.

One person was killed and 29 others were injured after a man drove a minivan into a crowd of pedestrians, then attacked people with what appeared to be a machete. The attack took place in the Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate at about 10pm local time on Saturday, close to one of Europe’s biggest LGBTQ+ celebrations.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, named the chief suspect as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, and said Ballout was thought to have used a machete to attack people, leaving some victims with life-threatening injuries. “Everything we see here indicates that we are dealing with an Islamist terrorist attack,” Dobrindt said.

“We are dealing ​here with ‌a suspected ‌perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention ‌to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene,” Dobrindt told ‌a press conference near the site of the attack. He said Ballout had a criminal conviction and had been sentenced to a year and 10 months in prison, but that the sentence had been suspended.

German media reported that Ballout, a German national with Lebanese roots, was a supporter of Islamic State and last year travelled to the Middle East in a failed attempt to join the group. He was then convicted in Germany of “preparing a serious act of subversive violence”, the news outlets Bild and Der Spiegel reported.

Police and prosecutors have asked for help in finding Ballout, but warned the public to avoid “direct contact” with him, saying he may be armed and dangerous.

Ballout is described as thin, about 1.90 metres (6ft 3in) tall with black hair, and dressed in a black hoodie and white trousers.

Police searched an apartment in the Schöneberg district of Berlin in the early hours of Sunday, but said they had found no one there.

The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, urged Germany to avoid division and intimidation in the aftermath of the attack. “We ​will think ​about ​consequences, we ​will ‌defend ​our freedom,” he said in a news conference.

Earlier, Merz vowed to punish those responsible, describing the “heinous act” as an “attack on our society” in a social media post. The flag at the German Bundestag was ordered to be lowered to half mast.

The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and came as Germany remained on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks.

Hours after the attack many details remained unclear, but police said the vehicle had struck multiple ⁠people after being driven into the Tiergarten close to the Brandenburg Gate. Police said those hurt “included several with life-threatening injuries”.

The driver of the white minivan had swerved shortly before 10pm into the park, close to where the route of the Pride march had been earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree, police said.

“[The vehicle] was empty, which is why we are currently working intensively to track ​down the perpetrator or perpetrators,” police said. Bild cited a witness as saying that a man had emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot.

A hunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.

Emergency workers set up a helicopter landing pad near the Reichstag parliament building to transport the injured to hospitals.

Julian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a terrible day. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked,” he said.

Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in Berlin in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the Pride parade.

It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.

Berlin’s mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.

“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”

For the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally. Berlin will hold a state election in September.

The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “taking a stand is hot”, which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to LGBTQ+ people in Germany.

More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.

Earlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest.

Before last year’s parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisations sounded the alarm that attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat. Campaigners said a rise in hostility had accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.

European leaders offered solidarity, including heads of government in Belgium, the Netherlands and Sweden. “Italy firmly condemns and opposes all forms of hate and extremism,” the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, wrote on X, adding: “We stand with Germany and the German people.” The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said: “Faced with hatred and violence, our response will always be unity, freedom, and resolve.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, a German centre-right politician allied with Merz, sent her deepest sympathy to the victims of the attack, describing the CSD parade as standing for “freedom, dignity and equality – the fundamental values of the EU”.

Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said he was “horrified by the appalling attack in Berlin” and had spoken to his counterpart, Johann Wadephul, “to convey the UK’s solidarity: we stand with Germany”.

Far-right leaders were also quick to comment on the attacks. The co-leader of the AfD Tino Chrupalla wrote on X: “We will not allow religious extremists to divide our country with violence and intolerance!”

The president of France’s far-right National Rally, Jordan Bardella, wrote: “The Islamist threat remains a major issue in Europe and continues to target what they hate most about our civilisation – and what we cherish so much – freedom.”

title: Joy in Greece as Mount Olympus joins Unesco list of world heritage sites
excerpt:
Mythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in Normandy

After a 12-year wait, Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the ancient Greek gods, has been inducted ...
body_text:
Mythical home of the ancient Greek gods designated alongside the D-day landing beaches in Normandy

After a 12-year wait, Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the ancient Greek gods, has been inducted into a hall of more modern fame as Unesco announced it would be added to its world heritage list.

Greece’s highest mountain made the list alongside the second world war D-day landing beaches in northern France and the ancient Japanese capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara. South Sudan’s Boma-Badingilo landscape, host to one of the world’s largest land mammal migrations, also won a designation – a first for the east African country.

The nominations were among dozens reviewed at a Unesco committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, on Sunday.

In the case of Olympus, inscribed as a mixed world heritage site in recognition of its cultural and natural significance, the news was met with near euphoria in Greece.

Immortalised as the seat of Zeus, king of the 12 Olympian deities, the mountain rising 2,918 metres from a base near sea level had been on a tentative list of sites since 2014.

The head of Greece’s Unesco delegation in Busan, Georgios Koumoutsakos, hailed the decision as one that would ensure the site’s preservation.

“It reaffirms our unwavering commitment to safeguarding Mount Olympus for the benefit of present and future generations,” he said. “As Greek mythology wisely reminds us, it is always best to remain on good terms with the gods.”

The region’s mayor, Evangelos Geroliolios, said before the announcement that the site’s induction would “place greater responsibility on our part to protect the [local] environment”, not least its extraordinary biodiversity.

The committee’s annual meeting, which ends on Wednesday, is expected to examine about 30 nominations. Those successful will join 1,248 sites across 170 countries admitted to the world heritage list for their “outstanding value to humanity”.

Inscribed monuments can provide a vital boost for their preservation under an international convention overseen by Unesco, which also gives advice and financial support. Other world heritage sites include the Acropolis in Athens, the Great Wall of China, the pyramids of Giza in Egypt and the Taj Mahal in India.

As with Mount Olympus, efforts to get the D-day beaches in Normandy inscribed had gone back years.

Included in the French bid were all five of the beaches – Omaha, Utah, Sword, Gold and Juno – where more than 150,000 allied troops came ashore on 6 June 1944, and the Pointe du Hoc cliff that was also a focal point of the assault.

The largest amphibious operation ever mounted, in which 4,000 soldiers died, was decisive in the battle to liberate Europe from Nazi occupation.

France first nominated the 50-mile (80km) stretch of coastline in 2008. Reacting to the decision, the country’s permanent delegate to Unesco, Ahlem Gharbi, said the designation carried particular weight at a time of such international tensions.

The president of the Normandy region, Hervé Morin, who had championed the cause, maintained that inclusion on the list would represent “immense recognition” for the soldiers who had sacrificed so much to defeat Nazism.

Echoing Greek officials, he said: “This decision places a responsibility upon us. It compels us to preserve this site, to protect it, to cherish it even more, and to promote its value.”

The international council on monuments and sites, one of the bodies that recommends additions to the Unesco list, had previously warned of the threat posed to the Normandy sites by tourism, climate change, rising sea levels and nearby windfarm development, and had called for stronger monitoring and preservation.

The coastline is covered with extensive remnants of the time of the landings, including concrete German bunkers and gun positions, sunken vessels and allied installations.

Unesco said in a statement that the beaches formed an “exceptional cultural landscape shaped both by the events of 1944 and by their enduring remembrance”, all of which justified further protection. As with Mount Olympus, the landing points have attracted record numbers of tourists in recent years.

The agency’s move to include places associated with conflict has fuelled controversial debate over whether “sites of memory” are befitting of world heritage status and Unesco’s stated mission to “foster a world of greater equality and peace”.

Three sites used by Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge regime for torture and execution were inscribed last year.

After so many years of campaigning, Greek officials said Sunday’s decision had been made all the sweeter given signs of further delays.

In the draft agenda of this week’s meeting, Unesco had signalled the Mount Olympus file would be referred back to the country for further details, spurring fears that proved to be baseless when the nomination won unanimous support.

title: Fauci's newly released COVID diaries reveal bizarre fixation on fame as pandemic deaths mounted
excerpt: Senator Rand Paul forecasts Dr. Anthony Fauci's dishonesty in his upcoming Senate testimony regarding COVID-19 origins. Paul provides evidence of Fauci destroying records and actively funding dangerou...
body_text:
Senator Rand Paul forecasts Dr. Anthony Fauci's dishonesty in his upcoming Senate testimony regarding COVID-19 origins. Paul provides evidence of Fauci destroying records and actively funding dangerous gain-of-function research in Wuhan, China. He asserts that Fauci's support for such risky research, despite the potential for a pandemic, represents ‘the worst public health decision’ made in our lifetime.

Newly released diary entries reveal that as COVID-19 deaths mounted around the world, former White House COVID advisor Dr. Anthony Fauci became increasingly fixated on his newfound celebrity.

Released by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., the journals chronicle Fauci's day-to-day role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors and world leaders, media appearances, and his personal observations as the pandemic unfolded.

Paul, a longtime Fauci critic who frequently clashed with Fauci over the federal response and the origins of the virus, made the diaries public as part of the committee's ongoing oversight investigation. The release comes days before Fauci is scheduled to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Paul.

GABBARD SAYS DECLASSIFIED BIOLAB RECORDS VALIDATE CONCERNS PREVIOUSLY DISMISSED AS MISINFORMATION

Fauci served as chief medical advisor to President Donald Trump during the COVID-19 pandemic before later continuing in the role under President Joe Biden. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

A surprising recurring theme throughout the diaries is Fauci's growing awareness of his own public profile during the most intense months of the pandemic, which ultimately claimed more than 7 million officially reported lives worldwide, including roughly 1.2 million in the United States.

On April 7, 2020, after recording the latest pandemic developments, Fauci wrote: "Press still hot and heavy about me. Multiple stories per day directly or indirectly involving me."

SLACK MESSAGES RELEASED BY RAND PAUL APPEAR TO SHOW AUTHORS OF KEY COVID-19 ORIGIN PAPER HELD PRIVATE DOUBTS

Dr. Anthony Fauci, who led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, became a central figure in the federal government's response to COVID-19. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

By May 21, after recording the latest pandemic figures — nearly 98,000 global deaths and more than 27,000 U.S. deaths — and documenting the day's White House coronavirus task force meetings, Fauci wrote that his "national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable" and that it was "not hyperbole" to say he was "the most famous and talked about person in the country."

He added that Trump "seems to be enamored of me even though I am taking the spotlight away from him," writing that the two were developing "a very unique and interesting relationship." Fauci also noted that Secret Service agents had become so familiar with him they often waved him through White House security without checking his identification.

As the attention continued to grow, the diary increasingly documented how Fauci's prominence had expanded beyond public health. A month later, as the United States recorded what Fauci described as a record 40,000 new COVID-19 cases in a single day, he wrote that he had been invited to appear on "Dancing with the Stars."

LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS

Dr. Anthony Fauci emerged as a leading public face of the U.S. pandemic response, though his relationship with President Donald Trump grew increasingly strained as the pandemic wore on. (Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

The diaries also document Fauci's growing frustration with the Trump White House. On July 2, 2020, after warning that the country could be entering an "exponential" increase in COVID-19 cases heading into the Fourth of July weekend, Fauci wrote, "POTUS and his people have essentially dropped out and do not even recognize that an outbreak is ongoing."

He also complained that the White House was denying requests for him to appear on major television programs. Across multiple entries, Fauci criticized White House communications officials for restricting his television appearances, questioned the administration's public messaging and expressed frustration that media coverage increasingly portrayed him as being at odds with Trump.

ANTHONY FAUCI DELIVERED ONE OF THE WORST FIRST PITCHES IN BASEBALL HISTORY SIX YEARS AGO

Dr. Anthony Fauci throws out the ceremonial first pitch prior to the game between the New York Yankees and the Washington Nationals at Nationals Park on July 23, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

Fauci also repeatedly defended himself against what he described as the "countless" profiles written about him. He wrote that White House officials were upset because the coverage made it appear he was becoming "a star that outshines" the president.

He also insisted several of the profiles had been written without interviewing him and wrote that he had "no desire to conflict with, embarrass or show up the POTUS," later deciding to stop participating in profile interviews altogether.

Taken together, the entries offer an unusually personal account of Fauci's role during one of the most consequential public health crises in modern U.S. history, capturing not only the government's internal deliberations but also his private concerns about the pandemic, his increasingly complicated relationship with the Trump White House and the extraordinary public attention that followed.

title: ClickLock Mac malware locks apps until you give in
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A routine "verify you are human" page should never ask you to open Terminal, the Mac app used to run computer commands...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A routine "verify you are human" page should never ask you to open Terminal, the Mac app used to run computer commands. Yet that is how a new malware attack appears to get onto a Mac. The page tells you to copy and paste a command into Terminal. It then shows a convincing progress bar while the command quietly downloads malicious software in the background.

Next, a password box may appear that looks like a normal macOS request. If you cancel it, the malware can come back after you sign in again and repeatedly close Finder, your browser and other apps. Your Mac may feel almost impossible to use until you enter your login password.

The malware, called ClickLock, is built to steal personal information from your Mac. It searches for saved passwords, browser data and cryptocurrency wallet files. It can also install a hidden tool that lets an attacker reconnect to your computer later and control it remotely.

Researchers at cybersecurity company Group-IB discovered the malicious script on VirusTotal, an online service that checks files for threats. Someone first uploaded it there on June 9, 2026, yet none of the security tools on the platform detected it at the time of the researchers' report. Group-IB says the campaign has targeted at least 100 systems across 33 countries since May.

Here is how ClickLock takes over a Mac and what you can do to protect yourself.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

ClickLock may begin with a fake verification page that tells you to paste a command into Terminal. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

ClickLock is a set of malicious scripts designed to steal sensitive information from a Mac. The malware can collect your Mac login password and browser data. It also searches for cryptocurrency wallet files, password manager extensions and information stored in macOS Keychain.

One component installs a persistent backdoor. That hidden connection can allow an attacker to access your Mac remotely even after the other parts of ClickLock remove themselves.

ClickLock gets started without exploiting a known macOS flaw. It also does not need admin-level access at the beginning. Instead, the attack depends on convincing you to run the command yourself.

Group-IB believes ClickLock likely spreads through a tactic called ClickFix. ClickFix attacks show you a fake error or verification request. The page then gives you a command that supposedly fixes the problem.

In this case, the ClickLock script displays a fake Cloudflare verification sequence after you paste the command into Terminal. An animated progress bar cycles through reassuring messages about checking browser signals and confirming you are human.

Meanwhile, the script disables keyboard interruptions and hides the Terminal cursor. It then downloads several malicious components in the background. Researchers have yet to confirm the exact landing pages used in the campaign. They also do not know whether people reached them through malicious search results, compromised websites, phishing messages or social media. However, the script's design strongly points to a ClickFix-style lure.

After the malware begins running, it displays a fake macOS password window. The pop-up uses your real username and an Apple icon downloaded by the attacker. If you enter a password, ClickLock checks it against your Mac. When the password works, the malware records it and sends it to the attacker through Telegram.

An incorrect password brings up another request. If you cancel the window, ClickLock installs two LaunchAgents. A LaunchAgent is a macOS instruction that can automatically run software when you sign in. In this case, the LaunchAgents bring the password-stealing components back at your next login.

HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER

The malware can repeatedly close apps and pressure you to enter your Mac login password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

When the password-stealing module returns, it begins closing visible apps every 210 milliseconds. It targets Finder, the Dock and Terminal. It also shuts down Activity Monitor, System Settings, Spotlight and common web browsers.

The fake password window may remain as the only useful item on your screen. That can make your Mac look broken while pressuring you to enter your password. Group-IB found that the loop can run for about 83 hours. It stops earlier when the malware captures a valid password.

A second ClickLock component targets Chrome's Safe Storage key. Chromium-based browsers use this key to help encrypt passwords, cookies and autofill information stored on your Mac. An attacker with the key and copied browser databases may be able to decrypt that information offline.

This part of the attack triggers a genuine macOS Keychain authorization prompt. However, the malware caused the request. ClickLock then runs another process-closing loop while waiting for you to approve access. Researchers found that this loop repeats every 200 milliseconds and can continue for nearly 35 days. The script also suppresses macOS NotificationCenter for roughly six hours. That could hide warnings or notifications that might reveal the attack.

ClickLock searches for information across eight browsers. Those browsers include Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Vivaldi, Arc and Chromium.

The targeted browser information includes:

The malware also searches for desktop cryptocurrency wallets and encrypted wallet vaults. It can collect cached blockchain addresses across several networks. Other targets include macOS Keychain, Terminal command histories and FileZilla server details. The malware also records basic information about your Mac and its public IP address. ClickLock packages the collected information into a ZIP archive. It uploads that archive through Telegram's Bot API. Files larger than 40 MB get divided into smaller pieces, while retry code keeps trying after network failures.

If your Mac starts acting this way, shut it down and restart in Safe Mode before entering any password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

One ClickLock component uses a modified version of the open-source GSocket tool. The malware installs a reverse shell, which gives the attacker a command-line connection to your Mac. On macOS, it disguises the backdoor as an iCloud-related process.

ClickLock uses a LaunchAgent and scheduled commands to keep the backdoor running. It also changes shell configuration files. Most of the other ClickLock modules delete themselves after completing their work. The GSocket component remains installed, which means the attacker may retain access after your Mac appears to return to normal.

The original ClickLock script had zero detections on VirusTotal when Group-IB analyzed it. Security vendors may update their detection tools as they learn more about the threat. The attackers also stored payloads on compromised websites that previously had clean reputations. Some components run without saving a normal file to the drive. Others erase themselves after stealing data.

However, ClickLock still produces suspicious activity while it runs. Warning signs include nonstop app closures, repeated password requests and sudden access to multiple browser folders. Security tools may also detect unusual connections to Telegram's API. For you, the earliest warning sign is much simpler. A website tells you to paste a command into Terminal. Legitimate human verification happens inside your browser. It should never require you to run a Terminal command.

These steps can help you avoid the ClickLock trap and respond quickly if the password loop starts.

Leave the page when it tells you to open Terminal and paste a command. A polished design offers no proof that the request is safe. Familiar logos can also be copied. Group-IB warns that a website asking you to use Terminal for verification is attempting to compromise your system.

Terminal commands can download software and change important settings. Never run an unfamiliar command simply to see what happens. Ask a trusted technical professional to inspect it first.

Think about what you were doing when the password window appeared. A website verification should have no reason to ask for your Mac login password. It should also have no reason to request access to Chrome information stored in Keychain. Cancel the request when the timing feels wrong.

Install macOS updates and keep automatic security updates turned on. Apple builds malware protection into macOS through Gatekeeper, Notarization and XProtect. Apple updates XProtect automatically as it identifies new malware. However, no built-in protection can eliminate every risk when you manually run a malicious command.

Strong antivirus software can provide another layer of protection against malicious files and suspicious behavior. Still, a clean scan cannot guarantee that ClickLock left nothing behind. The backdoor persists after other components erase themselves. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Do not enter your password to make the pop-up disappear. Press and hold your Mac's power button for up to 10 seconds until the computer shuts down. On a MacBook with Touch ID, press and hold the Touch ID button. Group-IB recommends forcing a shutdown when your Mac becomes unresponsive and keeps requesting your password. The company then recommends starting the Mac in Safe Mode.

Mac with Apple silicon: Wait until the Mac shuts down completely. Press and hold the power button until "Loading startup options" appears. Select your startup volume. Hold the Shift key, then click Continue in Safe Mode.

Intel-based Mac: Turn on or restart the Mac. Immediately press and hold the Shift key until the login window appears.

Once Safe Mode starts, turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the Ethernet cable. Then contact Apple Support or a trusted cybersecurity professional. Removing a browser extension or clearing your history will not remove ClickLock's persistent backdoor.

Use a separate trusted device to change the password for your primary email account. Then secure your Apple Account and any financial accounts stored on the Mac. Change password manager credentials and review active sessions. Sign out of devices or sessions you do not recognize. Review the devices connected to your Apple Account and remove unfamiliar ones. Apple also recommends changing your Apple Account password when you suspect unauthorized access. After a professional cleans or resets the Mac, change its local login password. Assume the attacker received that password if you entered it into the ClickLock window.

ClickLock depends on one dangerous moment: convincing you to paste a command into Terminal. Once that happens, the malware can begin stealing information before the password pressure even starts. The biggest red flag is easy to remember. No trustworthy website needs Terminal to prove you are human. If your Mac starts closing apps and demanding a password, shut it down rather than giving in. Start in Safe Mode and get help checking for the persistent backdoor. Then use another trusted device to secure your most important accounts.

Have you ever seen a suspicious password prompt or fake verification page on your Mac? Tell us what it looked like and what you did next in the comments below. Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: 'Blue Lagoon' star Christopher Atkins says alcohol cost him iconic 'Footloose' role before getting sober
excerpt:
The actor, who was a sex symbol in the '80s, recalled playing the love interest of Brooke Shields and Linda Gray. Atkins now wants to work behind-the-scenes as a filmmaker.

Christopher Atkins claims ...
body_text:
The actor, who was a sex symbol in the '80s, recalled playing the love interest of Brooke Shields and Linda Gray. Atkins now wants to work behind-the-scenes as a filmmaker.

Christopher Atkins claims his drinking cost him the lead role in "Footloose," which ultimately went to Kevin Bacon.

The "Blue Lagoon" actor looked back at his career during a recent appearance at Fanboy Expo Knoxville in Tennessee, which celebrates pop culture and nostalgia, People magazine reported.

According to the outlet, the 65-year-old actor said filmmakers behind the 1984 classic wanted to meet with him before making their final casting decision, but he wasn't able to pull it off.

BRAT PACK ICON ANDREW MCCARTHY SAYS DRINKING 'DERAILED MY CAREER ENTIRELY'

Christopher Atkins (left), who starred opposite Brooke Shields (center) in 1980's "The Blue Lagoon," recently told a panel at the Fanboy Expo Knoxville that he lost the lead role in 1984's "Footloose" to Kevin Bacon (right) because his drinking cost him an important meeting with the filmmakers. (Sonia Moskowitz/Getty Images; CBS via Getty Images)

"I was a mess back then," he told the panel, as quoted by People. "I was partying it up way too much, and they called me in."

"I said ... 'I can't go in right now. I've been drinking and carrying on,'" Atkins recalled. "And they said, 'No, they need to see you.' And I went in, and I just blew that audition ... I mean, it wasn't even an audition — I had the part, but I was so messed up that they said, 'Yeah, we're going to have to pass on this guy.'"

Atkins was offered the role of Ren in "Footloose," after making his on-screen debut alongside Brooke Shields in "The Blue Lagoon." (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)

"And I'm almost 40 years sober, so there you go," Atkins added.

WATCH: CHRISTOPHER ATKINS LOOKS BACK AT ‘THE BLUE LAGOON’ AND ‘DALLAS’

The actor also reflected on his breakout role in "The Blue Lagoon" during the discussion. The former teen heartthrob was just 18 when he was cast in the 1980 movie opposite Brooke Shields.

"I'd never done anything before," Atkins explained. "Never wanted to be an actor — I only wanted to play baseball. That was my dream."

Kevin Bacon as Ren appears in a scene from the movie "Footloose." (CBS/Getty Images)

"I didn't know what a camera looked like. I had no idea what a mark was, and I knew nothing. And I had to jump on an airplane and fly all the way to Fiji," he said.

Actor Christopher Atkins attends CollectorFest New Jersey 2020 at Wayne P.A.L. in Wayne, N.J., on Oct. 18, 2020. (Bobby Bank/Getty Images)

"I ended up modeling for [the] Ford Modeling Agency in New York City and auditioned for 'The Blue Lagoon'... And I kept getting called back and called back and called back. And then [after] a couple of months, I didn't hear from them... And then all of a sudden, I got another callback."

The "Dallas" alum said his "whole life changed" after the movie's release.

Christopher Atkins went on to star in "Dallas" opposite Linda Gray. (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)

"We were young, and so you're constantly getting this notoriety," Atkins explained. "And the magazines need you to sell their magazines, and you're hot at that time. And so it does get overwhelming... There are times when you're doing interviews, and you have a line of people, and you have to say the same thing to each person because they have the same question."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Brooke Shields and "Blue Lagoon" co-star Christopher Atkins circa 1980 in New York City. (Sonia Moskowitz/IMAGES/Getty Images)

"But it changes your life, because all of a sudden you’re nothing and then you’re on every single grocery store magazine."

Back in 2025, Atkins told Fox News Digital he "didn't know that much" about Shields, then 14, before she joined him on the set of "The Blue Lagoon."

Despite the controversy, "The Blue Lagoon" became a major box office success and made Christopher Atkins an overnight star. (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)

"I lived on [a] boat off the island [where we were filming]... she hadn't come yet," he said at the time. "She had another week or so before she was going to get here. The director had put her picture up over my bed so that I could start falling in love with her before the movie started. That was my introduction to Brooke Shields."

Actors Christopher Atkins and Brooke Shields in the 1980 movie, "The Blue Lagoon," directed by Randal Kleiser. (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)

The movie was controversial for depicting the two young characters in a sexual relationship. Shields and the movie's crew have long maintained that she used body doubles for nude scenes and that her hair was glued to her body to avoid exposing her chest, People magazine reported.

"The crew was all Australian," Atkins said. "Back in the day, all the Australian beaches... were topless. It was very natural and freeing for the Australians... And being on a deserted island, there were no tourists, nothing. It was just us on this island... [And] these two kids, in a natural [and deserted] environment, they wouldn't wear clothes. It wouldn't be something that was in the forefront of their minds, that they needed to cover up."

Christopher Atkins and Brooke Shields attend an event celebrating their movie at the Cinerama Dome theater in Hollywood on June 19, 1980. (Robert Ware/WWD/Penske Media via Getty Images)

"As time went on, it just became more and more natural not to have clothes on," Atkins said. "The crew made it very, very easy. Randall [Kleiser], the director, made it very, very easy about it. [The scenes] were absolutely important for the film, but it wasn't grandiose. It wasn't something that was there for the exhibition of the film. He really wanted this to be as natural and as real as possible. I understood that and got that."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The Blue Lagoon" sparked controversy for its depiction of teenage sexuality and nudity, despite the filmmakers' use of body doubles and other techniques for certain scenes. (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)

"By the time I was done leaving that island four and a half months later, it [was] really hard for me to keep my clothes on at a beach," he joked.

People magazine noted that critics largely panned the movie. However, it was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Cinematography. The outlet reported that the movie grossed more than $58 million worldwide, making it the ninth-highest-grossing film of 1980.

Christopher Atkins recently told a panel at the Fanboy Expo Knoxville that he's nearly 40 years sober. (Sonia Moskowitz/Images/Getty Images)

Looking back at his Hollywood career, Atkins said he has no regrets.

Christopher Atkins attends a private screening of the Oculus Virtual Reality short film "Defrost" on Aug. 17, 2015, in Los Angeles. (Paul Redmond/Getty Images)

"I got to a point in my life where I married young," he said. "I wanted to be a dad more than chase the business... When I was 16, I used to teach sailing in Rye, New York, to little kids. From that measly paycheck that I was getting, I used to put a dollar away for someday when I had kids. That's how badly I wanted kids. When I had my two kids, I just did whatever came my way to put food on the table for them and keep working."

In this undated photo, Brooke Shields and Christopher Atkins attend a celebrity Halloween event at the home of Susie Field for the children of Los Angeles Children's Hospital in Beverly Hills. (SGranitz/WireImage)

"I've been blessed," he said. "I've done more than 100 movies and television shows at this point. Now my kids have their kids, and that's pretty remarkable... I've done everything in this business except make my own film. That's the last box I now want to check off... That's what I'm chasing right now, putting some really good projects together... So there are no regrets."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Too much screen time may trigger lasting brain delays, top health official warns
excerpt: Dr. Stephanie Haridopolos recommends creating a family screen plan, modeling healthy habits, redirecting kids to offline activities and disconnecting during meals, bedtime and car rides to build bette...
body_text:
Dr. Stephanie Haridopolos recommends creating a family screen plan, modeling healthy habits, redirecting kids to offline activities and disconnecting during meals, bedtime and car rides to build better connections.

As screens compete for families' attention, children's development is paying the price, top federal health officials warn.

Early and excessive screen time can trigger severe neurocognitive delays in young children, impacting attention spans, memory and language skills, according to Dr. Stephanie Haridopolos, interim surgeon general and principal deputy assistant secretary of health.

"Parents are now fighting for attention from the screens," Haridopolos told Fox News Digital.

DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

To help parents combat screen addiction, the U.S. Surgeon General's Office has released a targeted framework known as "the 5 Ds."

Don't wait for a conflict to establish boundaries, experts recommend. Sit down as a family to outline clear, age-appropriate rules regarding when, where and how long screens can be used throughout the day.

Setting explicit expectations ahead of time cuts down on daily arguments, experts say.

High screen exposure in young children threatens early brain tissue development, leading to delays in attention, memory and speech, experts say. (iStock)

Parents should model healthy screen habits themselves, Haridopolos said.

"If we're constantly on our screens, then perhaps our children will be, too," she said, encouraging adults to "be good role models and lead by example."

Rather than defaulting to giving children a tablet when they're bored, Haridopolos recommended steering them toward hands-on activities, such as doing arts and crafts or preparing a healthy meal together.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Breaks like summer and the holidays are critical windows for families to reset digital boundaries, the interim surgeon general suggested.

Scrolling while eating can lead to higher caloric intake and increased consumption of ultraprocessed foods, the interim surgeon general warned. (iStock)

Haridopolos encouraged families to build regular screen-free periods into their daily routines, including during meals, car rides and before bedtime.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As part of the "Delay" step, the program recommended putting off children's access to screens whenever possible.  (iStock)

As part of the "Delay" step, Haridopolos recommended putting off children's access to screens whenever possible. One way to do that, she said, is by requiring phones and other mobile devices to be charged overnight in a shared household space — like the kitchen or living room — rather than in children's bedrooms.

"Those are some simple activities that you can do that will make huge changes in the future," the interim surgeon general added.

Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Firefighters in France battle to prevent huge blaze from approaching Bordeaux
excerpt:
Efforts to contain wildfire that has consumed an area of four times the size of Paris impeded by windy conditions

Authorities are battling to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in south-west Franc...
body_text:
Efforts to contain wildfire that has consumed an area of four times the size of Paris impeded by windy conditions

Authorities are battling to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in south-west France that has consumed an area of land four times the size of Paris.

Efforts to extinguish the blaze in the Gironde region, where nearly 220,000 people have been evacuated, were hampered by windy conditions on Saturday night.

In Spain, fires west of Madrid were being brought under control, but the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez spoke of “difficult hours” ahead, saying the country was suffering the effects of the climate emergency.

Wildfires have forced more than 375,000 people to flee their homes in France and Spain.

Bordeaux’s mayor, Thomas Cazenave, described the Gironde blaze as being “at the gates of the metropolitan area”, between 15 and 20 miles (25 and 30km) from the city itself, which has a population of 268,000. An evacuation of the city was not on the cards, he said.

Nearly 260,000 people have been evacuated across France as a whole, including 36,000 ordered to leave another wildfire zone in the Landes region further south earlier this week.

The country’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Sunday that the previous night had been difficult and “the situation remains very unfavourable”. He said the Gironde fire had become “extremely virulent and unpredictable again” early on Saturday night, generating its own wind and spreading erratically towards the Bordeaux metropolitan area. It had become calmer by the end of the night, he said.

About 2,500 firefighters, including a Swiss team, 1,500 military personnel and about 1,200 police had been deployed to Gironde, Nuñez said, as he praised the contribution of 450 volunteers from civil security organisations.

He said another five Gironde municipalities had been evacuated overnight.

One firefighter told Agence France-Presse that the fire was so virulent it had formed a pyrocumulonimbus, a fire-generated thunderstorm that “creates its own wind, with whirlwinds, becoming erratic and uncontrollable”.

The French prime minister, Sébastian Lecornu, had warned late on Saturday that the coming hours would be difficult as the weather changed. “France is facing a historic situation,” he wrote on X. “Nearly 100,000 hectares have already burned, an unprecedented level and around thirty fires are simultaneously active across the territory.”

Three men were arrested in Gironde on Saturday on suspicion of endangering lives. Two of them were accused of setting off fireworks.

Authorities in Spain said major areas of fire near Madrid had been contained, but Sánchez said: “We’re facing some difficult hours, although it’s true that the latest update has shown that last night was very positive in terms of the fire’s evolution and efforts to control it.”

He said Spain and neighbouring Portugal were experiencing the varied consequences of the climate emergency, from fires and storms to heavy snowfalls. “The entire Iberian peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency in a very specific way,” he said.

Major areas of the fire near Madrid had been “contained and cooled down”, according to a senior officer with Spain’s military emergencies unit.

Lt Col Alfonso Arribas told the state broadcaster, RTVE, on Sunday morning that important strides had been made in containing the blaze.

While the fire near Madrid was being brought under control, emergency workers battled to extinguish a new fire near the Mediterannean port city of Valencia, where at least 15,000 people were evacuated. “The fire is beyond our capacity to extinguish, it has a perimeter of about 21 kilometres,” the Valencia region’s president, Juanfran Pérez Llorca, said late on Saturday.

Authorities also ordered the evacuation of eight more municipalities near Toledo south of Madrid on Saturday, bringing the number of people forced to flee their homes by wildfires in Spain in recent days to 116,000. The situation prompted the government to declare a national emergency over a wildfire for the first time.

Spain’s interior ministry said on Saturday evening that a man had died in a fire in the Valencian town of Manises. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said.

The blazes are the latest episode in a summer of wildfires that threaten to burn an unprecedented expanse of land. Europe has endured a series of heatwaves since the spring, fuelled by the climate crisis, including the hottest-ever June, leaving vegetation tinder dry.

The EU commissioner for crisis management, Hadja Lahbib, told the BBC it was likely that damage from wildfires would exceed previous records. “Last year, one million hectares burned during the summer and so we are expecting to face another historical, sad record because the season has started earlier in the year,” she said.

“Forecasters are predicting, unfortunately, another heatwave so we can expect other wildfires.”

Spain’s environment ministry said 32 major fires affecting 152,678 hectares had been recorded so far in 2026, compared with seven affecting 24,133 hectares in the same period in 2025.

The Gironde fire in France has so far burned 42,000 hectares, an area four times the size of Paris and one of the biggest devastations of land since the second world war.

At least 240 homes had been destroyed and many more damaged, a gendarme told BFMTV.

Firefighters are battling to slow the fires progression toward Bordeaux from the on the ground and air, with planes dropping water and retardants. Jérôme Steffe, the mayor of Cestas commune, 10 miles from Bordeaux city centre, told French media: “We are working together to put in place a firewall to block the advance of the flames.”

An exhibition centre in Bordeaux has been turned into an emergency shelter, providing camp beds and food for thousands of people, including hundreds of older people evacuated from care homes.

Cazenave said he had asked the central government for an economic crisis plan for the area because many businesses and workers had been evacuated from areas west of Bordeaux and the tourism industry had been heavily affected. He said it was impossible to say when people evacuated as a precaution could return to their homes.

“We don’t know how long this crisis will last, whether several days or several weeks,” he said.

The Landes fire has consumed 3,600 hectares and a rekindling of flames on Saturday had to be tackled from the air Nuñez said. French authorities are also dealing with wildfires in the south-eastern Var region, where 3,000 people have been evacuated, as well as the High Alps and Corsica.

title: President Ahmed al-Sharaa: Syria seeking security deal with Israel
excerpt:
