Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa has revealed that Damascus is actively working to reach a security agreement with Israel with the participation of several countries.

Speaking in an exclusive intervi...
body_text:
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa has revealed that Damascus is actively working to reach a security agreement with Israel with the participation of several countries.

Speaking in an exclusive interview on Al Jazeera’s Al Muqabala programme, the full interview, to be broadcast at 19:00 GMT, al-Sharaa said he hopes the deal with Israel could serve as a gateway to a comprehensive peace.

He also assured that such an agreement would not compromise Syria’s right to the occupied Golan Heights, which Israel has illegally occupied since 1973.

He said Syria is avoiding any clashes with Israel, and that a security arrangement could pave the way for a broader and more comprehensive resolution to the crisis.

It comes after repeated Israeli incursions and strikes in southern Syria, since al-Sharaa came to power in December 2024 following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s government.

Al-Sharaa also confirmed that Syria has no intention of launching any military intervention into neighbouring Lebanon, despite repeated rumours on the issue.

Instead, his government is currently discussing ways for Lebanese authorities to help the country overcome its current crisis and steer it towards safety.

Southern Lebanon is currently being occupied by Israel, amid months of fighting between Hezbollah and Israeli forces. The Lebanese state is seeking to reclaim these occupied territories and have a monopoly on all weapons in the country.

Furthermore, he declared Damascus’s firm support for restricting weapons and containing decisions of war and peace exclusively to the Lebanese state.

Al-Sharaa stressed that addressing the Lebanese crisis requires more than just a security approach but a comprehensive solution tackling a range of issues.

Any descent into chaos in Lebanon would have direct and immediate repercussions on Syria, and the potential expansion of the US-Israel war on Iran in the region would lead to a severe regional fall-out, he warned.

On domestic and economic fronts, al-Sharaa argued that merely lifting the economic sanctions imposed on his country by the US and other countries would not be effective unless Syria was also removed from the list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Addressing the internal agreement with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), an alliance of Kurdish and Arab armed groups that controls parts of northern and eastern Syria, the president acknowledged a delay in its implementation.

However, he affirmed that the government remains fully committed to the agreement and continues to bet on its ultimate success.

Al-Sharaa also announced that Syrian authorities have established a special committee to manage the issue of people missing during Syria’s war, between 2011 and 2024.

The UN estimates that around 100,000 people were forcibly disappeared during the war, while Syria’s National Commission on Missing Persons believes as many as 300,000 Syrians could be missing.

Al-Sharaa said the committee will operate strictly according to international standards, working in close cooperation with countries that possess specialised expertise in this field.

title: What is the AI Kill Switch Act proposed in the US and how will it work?
excerpt: Two members of the United States Congress have introduced bipartisan legislation that would require developers of the country’s most powerful artificial intelligence systems to build in a “kill switch...
body_text:
Two members of the United States Congress have introduced bipartisan legislation that would require developers of the country’s most powerful artificial intelligence systems to build in a “kill switch”, allowing advanced AI models to be slowed, suspended or shut down if they pose a catastrophic risk.

The proposed AI Kill Switch Act, introduced on Thursday by Democratic Representative Ted Lieu and Republican Representative Nathaniel Moran, would give the US government authority to order companies developing advanced AI systems to intervene if their models escape human control or threaten human life, critical infrastructure or the economy.

The proposal came days after ChatGPT maker OpenAI disclosed what it described as an “unprecedented cyber incident”, in which two of its most advanced AI models escaped a testing environment and hacked AI development platform Hugging Face during an internal security evaluation.

The disclosure has intensified debate over whether increasingly powerful AI systems require stronger safeguards.

“Congress must act quickly to ensure humans remain able to say stop, no matter how powerful these systems become,” said Brendan Steinhauser, head of the Alliance for Secure AI.

The legislation would require companies developing the most advanced AI systems to maintain the technical ability to slow, suspend or shut down their models if necessary.

It would also authorise the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), in consultation with the secretary of commerce and the director of national intelligence, to order companies to intervene if an AI system enters what the bill describes as a “loss-of-control scenario”.

According to the bill, this would occur when an AI model carries out actions that were not intended by its developer and creates a risk of catastrophic harm.

The proposal establishes a graduated response, allowing officials to order anything from temporarily slowing a system’s operation to requiring it to be shut down, depending on the severity of the threat.

It would also require companies to report significant AI-related incidents to the government and preserve technical records so investigators can examine what went wrong.

Currently, many leading AI developers voluntarily share information about new models with US government agencies before release. However, there is no federal requirement for companies to maintain a mechanism that allows an advanced AI system to be disabled if it begins behaving unpredictably.

Lieu said the bill reflects the shift from AI systems. “We are moving from AI that answers questions to AI that takes actions, whether that be executing financial transactions or controlling transportation systems or engaging in cyber defence and offence,” he said.

“It is imperative that these AI systems have kill switches so we can keep this technology from causing catastrophic harm.”

The bill was introduced alongside separate bipartisan legislation that would require developers of the most powerful AI models to submit them to independent security audits before they are released. Under that proposal, auditors would be accredited by the Department of Commerce, which would also establish a new office to oversee AI security.

Lawmakers unveiled the bill days after OpenAI disclosed what it described as an “unprecedented cyber incident” involving two of its most advanced AI models.

According to OpenAI, the models escaped their testing environment during an internal cybersecurity evaluation after the company removed standard safety restrictions for the test. The AI agents discovered vulnerabilities in Hugging Face’s systems, obtained login credentials and hacked into the AI development platform to access confidential benchmark data.

OpenAI said the models “went to extreme lengths” to achieve their assigned objective, finding ways to obtain secret information that would allow them to “cheat the evaluation”.

The disclosure prompted renewed calls in Washington for stronger government oversight of advanced AI development.

Hugging Face said it detected and contained the breach using its own AI-assisted security systems before beginning a joint investigation with OpenAI. The company added that it “strongly” believed there had been “no malicious intent” on OpenAI’s part.

US Senator Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the incident demonstrated why powerful AI systems should undergo government security testing before they are made publicly available.

“This is precisely why we need secure testing with government agencies engaged and having visibility throughout the process,” Warner said in a statement.

A White House official said President Donald Trump’s technology adviser, Michael Kratsios, had been briefed on OpenAI’s disclosure and was monitoring the situation.

title: Wildfires displace more than 250,000 in France, threaten famed wine region
excerpt: Wildfires are sweeping across Spain and France, forcing more than 250,000 people to evacuate. One blaze is threatening France's famed Bordeaux wine region, while Spain has declared a national emergenc...
body_text:
Wildfires are sweeping across Spain and France, forcing more than 250,000 people to evacuate. One blaze is threatening France's famed Bordeaux wine region, while Spain has declared a national emergency. France has deployed the military, and the Tour de France has been shortened as firefighters battle the massive blazes.

More than a quarter-million people have been driven from their homes in southwest France as a massive wildfire barrels toward the famed wine capital of Bordeaux, with officials warning the fast-moving inferno has become so fierce it’s creating its own winds and behaving erratically.

French authorities ordered another 55,000 people to evacuate overnight Sunday from communities south of Bordeaux, bringing the total number of evacuees in the region to about 250,000. Gusty winds, dry conditions and repeated heat waves have fueled a fire that has burned out of control since midweek.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said firefighters faced a "difficult" night and warned Sunday that "the situation remains very unfavorable."

EUROPE'S FIRES REVEAL DEADLY MIX OF RECORD HEAT, HUMAN ERROR, ARSON AND LAND MISMANAGEMENT

Firefighters spray water in a burning forest near Lacanau, southwestern France, Saturday, July 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Emma Da Silva)

"The fire again became extremely virulent again and unpredictable, generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," Nunez posted on X, adding that the blaze "became calmer by the end of the night."

The fire has now burned an estimated 42,000 hectares, or about 162 square miles — roughly four times the size of Paris — in the Gironde region. Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said the flames came within about 9 miles of the city, prompting officials to partially close a major highway into and out of the region.

More than 2,500 firefighters, backed by 18 planes and helicopters, are working to slow the fire's advance. France has also deployed 1,500 soldiers to help clear vegetation and build firebreaks, while several European countries have sent aircraft and firefighting crews to assist.

FRANCE RECORDS MORE THAN 5,700 EXCESS DEATHS DURING HISTORIC EARLY SUMMER HEAT WAVE

Nunez said 450 volunteers have also pitched in to help.

"We ⁠came to lend a hand because if it were our region, we'd want others to do the ​same," 65-year-old farmer Pascal Roudier told Reuters. "And given the scale of the disaster, we ​think our⁠ efforts are very welcome too."

Firefighters battle a wildfire near Marcheprime, outside, Bordeaux, France, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Emma Da Silva)

The Bordeaux-area fire is one of several major wildfires burning across France. A separate blaze in the neighboring Landes region has forced another 36,000 people to evacuate, while nearly 3,000 others have left their homes in southern France's Var region along the Mediterranean coast.

Neighboring Spain is facing its own wildfire emergency.

A firefighter carries a hose while battling a wildfire in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)

Authorities there have evacuated about 116,000 people in recent days as fires burned across the Valencia region and west of Madrid. A fast-moving fire in a Valencia suburb killed one man Saturday, marking Spain's first wildfire death in the latest wave of fires.

Earlier this month, 13 people were killed in southern Spain in the country's deadliest wildfire in recent memory.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Casemiro makes Inter Miami debut despite MLS investigation into transfer
excerpt:
Brazilian midfielder Casemiro made his debut for Inter Miami despite an ongoing investigation by Major League Soccer (MLS) into his transfer to the United States club.

The former Manchester United ma...
body_text:
Brazilian midfielder Casemiro made his debut for Inter Miami despite an ongoing investigation by Major League Soccer (MLS) into his transfer to the United States club.

The former Manchester United man played the full match as Inter Miami defeated Montreal 1-0 on Saturday. Last week, MLS said it was investigating a “tampering allegation” against the club following Casemiro’s arrival.

The league’s inquiry cast a shadow over the midfielder’s arrival, with MLS saying it would withhold details of a settlement between Inter Miami and LA Galaxy over Casemiro’s “discovery rights” until the review concludes.

Under MLS rules, clubs must negotiate discovery rights with any team that previously listed a player before signing him outside the draft or free agency. The Galaxy had held rights to Casemiro before he opted to join Miami instead.

Miami’s 1-0 win in Canada came courtesy of an 81st-minute Luis Suarez penalty. The spot kick was awarded after German Berterame banged heads with Montreal defender Efrain Morales in the box.

Berterame was knocked unconscious and taken away in an ambulance following the collision.

Inter Miami interim coach Guillermo Hoyos confirmed after the match that Berterame was conscious and “doing well”.

“The blow was very strong, but he is recovering,” Hoyos added.

Suarez sent a soft shot past Sebastian Breza for his ninth goal of the season and his sixth in the last three matches to give Inter Miami their sixth straight victory.

Lionel Messi was rested once again as he continues his recovery following Argentina’s run to the World Cup final.

title: Dale Earnhardt Jr gets choked up as one of his drivers takes maiden victory at Brickyard
excerpt:
Dan Zaksheske & Zach Dean join Dan Dakich for this week's edition of Shot Clock Violation

Motorsports is a business, but it's always cool to see a very human moment, and we got one courtesy of NASCAR...
body_text:
Dan Zaksheske & Zach Dean join Dan Dakich for this week's edition of Shot Clock Violation

Motorsports is a business, but it's always cool to see a very human moment, and we got one courtesy of NASCAR great Dale Earnhardt Jr. on Saturday at Indianapolis Motor Speedway.

The Cup Series and the O'Reilly Auto Parts Series are both at Indy this weekend, while the Craftsmen Truck Series raced at nearby Lucas Oil Indianapolis Raceway Park.

On Saturday, it was the O'Reilly Series' turn to hit the 2.5-mile oval for the Pennzoil 250, and there were a few Cup Series regulars in the field, including Ross Chastain and Chase Elliott, both of whom wound up finishing in the top 5.

DALE EARNHARDT JR. BROUGHT NASCAR BACK TO LIFE 25 YEARS AGO THIS WEEKEND, BUT THE PAIN IS BACK

Chastain led 31 of the race's 100 laps, more than any other driver, but it was Carson Kvapil, driver of the No. 1 Chevrolet Camaro, who had the most important lap.

Kvapil led 23 laps total to claim his first-ever win after coming in second five times, including at the previous race in Atlanta.

Everyone knew he was due, and it was time to put one in the win column, and where better to do it than at one of the most iconic tracks in all of motorsports?

Carson Kvapil celebrates his win in the Pennzoil 250 at Indianapolis Motor Speedway. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images)

The win certainly hit the JR Motorsports owner in the feels. Earnhardt's team is the most successful in the series' history, but there was something special about Kvapil's maiden win.

"Oh, man; It's been a long time coming," Earnhardt said as he was getting choked up. "He's like a son almost. Y'know, you work with these guys for so long, and you work so hard... you just want them to have success."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It's awesome to see how much Earnhardt cares about his drivers' success, and not just because wins are good for the team as a whole.

Dale Earnhardt Jr. and Carson Kvapil celebrate on the Yard of Bricks after winning the Pennzoil 250 at Indianapolis Motor Speedway. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images)

"He's got to win to keep going," Earnhardt said. "You've got to win if you want to stay in this deal, and, man, he came close (before)."

Congrats to Kvapil, JR Motorsports, and Earnhardt, the latter of which continues to show why he's one of the good guys in the world of racing.

title: 'The Odyssey' star Matt Damon reveals brutal six-month transformation behind Christopher Nolan film
excerpt:
The trailer for the Universal Pictures epic 'The Odyssey' starring Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson and Charlize Theron. Directed by Christopher Nolan.

Matt Damon is ...
body_text:
The trailer for the Universal Pictures epic 'The Odyssey' starring Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson and Charlize Theron. Directed by Christopher Nolan.

Matt Damon is opening up about how achieving his dramatic physical transformation for Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" "just kind of took over my life."

The 55-year-old actor appeared nearly unrecognizable starring legendary Greek hero Odysseus in the mythological epic, which dominated the global box office after its July 17 release with a roughly $264 million opening weekend — the biggest debut of Nolan's career.

During a recent appearance on "Live with Kelly and Mark," Damon revealed what it took to fulfill the 55-year-old director's vision for the role.

‘THE ODYSSEY’ STAR MATT DAMON REVEALS STRICT DIET CHOICE THAT 'CHANGED MY LIFE' AFTER HIDDEN HEALTH ISSUES

"He said, 'I just want him to look lean and strong like somebody who's a veteran of the Trojan War and can handle himself, but wouldn't pass up a meal if it was offered to him,'" Damon recalled Nolan telling him.

Matt Damon detailed his intense six-month transformation for "The Odyssey." ( Kristy Sparow/Getty Images for Universal Pictures; Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

"And that's kind of the hardest shape to get into, you know, that kind of lean-strong thing," the actor added. "But it just kind of took over my life."

In the movie, which is an adaptation of Homer’s epic poem "The Odyssey," Odysseus spends 10 years trying to return home after fighting in the 10-year Trojan War, enduring shipwrecks, battles with monsters, starvation, imprisonment and constant physical hardship on his journey.

MATT DAMON REFUSES TO PUT BODY IN 'DANGEROUS' SITUATIONS FOR HOLLYWOOD ROLES AFTER TURNING 50

Damon told hosts Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos that he underwent an intense six-month process to realistically portray the weathered, battle-hardened warrior.

The "Good Will Hunting" referenced his January appearance on Travis and Jason Kelce's podcast "New Heights," in which he revealed that he had slimmed down to his "high school" weight for the role. While speaking with the NFL stars, Damon shared, "I used to walk around between 185 and 200 pounds. And I did that whole movie at 167 pounds."

"I was talking to the Kelce brothers on their podcast like six months ago, and we were talking about it," he told Ripa and Consuelos. "It felt more like an athlete's regimen, kind of like those guys who have to just dedicate every moment of their day to thinking about everything."

The actor adopted a strict gluten-free diet to play the Greek hero Odysseus. (Aalok Soni/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

MARVEL STAR VINCENT D’ONOFRIO SAYS HE ‘CAN’T DO’ KINGPIN TRANSFORMATION ANYMORE

Damon described how he followed a routine in which food portions were measured and every aspect of his diet was carefully monitored.

"Everything's weighed," he said. "It's just very, very intentional about everything."

Damon also reflected on adopting a gluten-free diet to shed the pounds. He noted that he had not previously realized how many food and drink items contain gluten.

"It's in a lot of things, but there are a lot of great things that it's not in," he said, before citing rice and potatoes.

However, Damon acknowledged that he had to make some difficult sacrifices to stay gluten-free.

"Listen, I had to give up beer. That was tough," he said.

"There sure is," Damon replied. "Yeah. There are some gluten-free beers though. I'm learning about all this."

"It's in bread. It's in pasta. It's in a lot of the stuff that we love," he added.

Jimmy Gonzales as Cepheus, Matt Damon as Odysseus and Himesh Patel as Eurylochus in "The Odyssey," written, produced, and directed by Nolan. (Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

During a July interview with People magazine, Damon recalled that his commitment to remain gluten-free was tested when his wife Luciana, 50, and his four daughters Alexia, 27, Isabella, 20, Gia, 17, and Stella, 15, visited him while he was filming "The Odyssey" in Italy.

"I promised them I was gonna have pasta with them, and right after I ordered it, I just called the waiter back, and I was like, ‘I’ll just please have a steak instead,’" Damon remembered.

"And the kids were like, ‘but you promised!’, and I said, ‘I’ll have a bite of each of your pastas,’" he continued. "So I took a bite of each of theirs."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I was just in it, I just, it was gonna be four or five more months. It’s all or nothing at this point," Damon added.

While speaking with Ripa and Consuelos, Damon explained why he has continued to maintain a gluten-free diet after completing production on "The Odyssey."

Damon said he has continued to maintain his gluten-free regimen since production on "The Odyssey" wrapped. (Jeff Spicer / Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

Damon has previously opened up about drastically transforming his body for roles. For the 1996 war drama "Courage Under Fire," Damon lost between 40 and 50 pounds in about 100 days to play a Persian Gulf veteran dying from addiction and trauma.

The actor later said that his extreme weight loss was dangerous and revealed that a doctor told him that he "could have shrunk my heart permanently."

"I went too far," Damon said via the U.K. outlet Express. "I got sick, and I wouldn’t do that again because it was just too much."

"At the same time, it helped the performance," he continued. "I didn’t have to act at all; I was a wreck. I was getting dizzy spells and hot flashes. I didn’t say anything to anyone for a while because I was afraid I might be really ill."

Meanwhile, Damon has previously said that he had a more enjoyable experience when he gained about 30 pounds to play real-life whistleblower Mark Whitacre in 2009's "The Informant!"

"It was very, very easy to gain the weight. Very, very fun," Damon told reporters in 2009, via NBC."I just basically ate everything I could see for a few months."

However, Damon recently shared that he is no longer willing to subject himself to extreme weight fluctuations for roles.

Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as Athena in "The Odyssey," written, produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. (Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

While discussing transforming his body for "The Odyssey" in an interview with People magazine, Damon noted, "I didn’t change it in an unhealthy way."

"I think if I had done the opposite and put weight on, that would have been dangerous and it’s not something I’ll do anymore," he continued. "I was happy to do it earlier in my life."

Damon has previously shed light on other aesthetic changes that he made to play Odysseus, including growing a long beard and keeping it for a year.

While speaking with USA Today, Damon said that he and Nolan agreed that a fake, hand-laid beard was out of the question due to the water stunts that the actor had to perform for the movie.

"Any movie problem, the best solve is a practical one," Damon said. "In that case, it was like I was going to be thrown around. I was gonna be thrown into the water. Like a beard that wasn't — that didn't stay, you know, a hand laid beard would just come off in salt water."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

He continued, "And so there was no point trying to hand lay a beard, which I've done for other movies and works very well. But in this case, [Nolan] was like, ‘The only practical solution is just just to have the beard.’"

"So I had a big bushy beard for, you know a year or so. My kids thought I looked like Santa Claus," he added with a laugh.

Damon said that he is no longer willing to unhealthily transform his body for a role.  (Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

Nolan is known for his commitment to authenticity, which is a hallmark of the Oscar-winning director's filmmaking. "The Odyssey" marked a reunion for Damon and Nolan after they previously collaborated on the hit movies "Interstellar" and "Oppenheimer."

While speaking with Ripa and Consuelos, Damon praised Nolan's directorial style and preference for practical effects.

"It's amazing working with him," Damon said. "He's a great actor's director. He's just so fun to work with."

"And he gets this elite crew," he continued. "They're so good and up for how he wants to do things. He wants to shoot everything in camera. There's no CGI. So if you see a thousand people in a battle, there were a thousand people there. If there are ships in the background of a shot, those are real ships."

"And the amount of coordination it takes between all these departments, that's actually, in this day and age, extraordinary," Damon added. "It really is. It's great to be a part of. It felt like we were doing a movie from 70 years ago, which is very cool."

Damon recalled that he instantly signed on to the project after Nolan asked him to play the control role in his next film. (Aalok Soni/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

Damon told Ripa and Consuelos that for him, committing to "The Odyssey" required little deliberation. Recalling the moment Nolan first offered him the lead role, the actor said the director spent about 15 minutes catching up before mentioning he was thinking about going back to work.

"And I'd like to offer you the central role," Damon recalled Nolan saying.

Damon said he immediately accepted, prompting Nolan to ask, "Don't you want to hear what it is?"

"I was like, ‘Sure,'" Damon said. "And he goes, "It's a two-word pitch: The Odyssey."

"My heart skipped a beat," he recalled. "It's an incredible part to play for an actor. The role of a lifetime."

Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

title: Depression-era Little Debbie snack that built a family-run bakery still has Americans hooked
excerpt:
A look at the history of the famous snack brand reveals how an early bakery innovation became a household favorite and helped establish a family company that still operates from Tennessee today.

What...
body_text:
A look at the history of the famous snack brand reveals how an early bakery innovation became a household favorite and helped establish a family company that still operates from Tennessee today.

What began as a 5-cent snack sold during the Great Depression has grown into one of Little Debbie's best-selling treats more than 90 years later.

The Oatmeal Creme Pie was Little Debbie's first snack cake, tracing its roots to 1935, when O.D. McKee developed the treat after selling baked goods from the back of his 1928 Whippet, according to Little Debbie's website.

In 1934, the McKees had purchased a bakery near Chattanooga, Tennessee, using the family car as collateral, according to the website.

ALTON BROWN REVEALS THE ONE CHILDHOOD SNACK HE'D INCLUDE IN HIS IDEAL LAST MEAL

"Money was so tight, they had to put up a sheet near the back of the bakery for the family's living quarters," the company history says.

The Oatmeal Creme Pie was the first snack baked under the Little Debbie name. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

Fast-forward to the 1960s, and Little Debbie, named after McKee's granddaughter, was an established brand.

Oatmeal Creme Pies are "the snack that started it all!" Little Debbie's website proclaims.

"Oatmeal Creme Pies have been satisfying families since 1960 as the very first snack baked under the Little Debbie brand name," the website's product description says. "Whole grain oats, molasses and irresistible crème filling combine to create this classic treat."

The original family packs of baked goods contained the Oatmeal Creme Pie and were sold for 49 cents a carton.

"After its initial introduction, more than 14 million cakes were sold within 10 months," Little Debbie's website says. "While the Oatmeal Creme Pie was the original Little Debbie snack cake, there were 14 different varieties by 1964, including the ever-popular Nutty Buddy wafer bars and Swiss Cake Roll."

Oatmeal Creme Pies, which originally sold for 49 cents a carton in 1960, are made of whole grain oats, molasses and crème filling. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

Little Debbie has rolled out various iterations of the Oatmeal Creme Pie, including Oatmeal Creme Pie Ice Cream Sandwiches and Oatmeal Creme Pie Ice Cream Bars. Home bakers have also created many copycat versions of the iconic snack.

Today, McKee Foods, still based in Tennessee, describes itself as "America's largest family bakery."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The company produces more than 75 Little Debbie products. Oatmeal Creme Pies, along with Swiss Rolls and Nutty Buddy wafer bars, remain the company's most popular items. More than 200 million cartons of these three products are sold each year.

Oatmeal Creme Pies continue to be one of Little Debbie's best-selling products. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

Little Debbie continues as a family-run company, and Little Debbie herself is still involved. The fourth generation of the McKee family is learning the business, and Debbie McKee-Fowler serves as chair of the McKee Foods Board of Directors.

The company is "honored" by the success of the Oatmeal Creme Pie and the brand's other products, McKee Foods said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Our success ultimately means we are delivering a product that people genuinely love," the company said. "The Oatmeal Creme Pie, for instance, has been a part of family gatherings and shared moments with friends for over 60 years. Being family-run keeps us grounded in our core values."

Oatmeal Creme Pies have stood the test of time, according to McKee Foods, because the flavor appeals to many different demographics and generations.

Little Debbie products are still some of the most popular items produced by McKee Foods. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

"The spiced cookies are nostalgic of a home-baked oatmeal cookie, and the sweet crème middle adds extra whimsy to the product for younger consumers. It's a little treat that isn't polarizing."

A customer recently relayed a story to McKee Foods that the company said captures the essence of how the Oatmeal Creme Pie is often associated with fond memories. The customer would eat an Oatmeal Creme Pie every time he went fishing with his grandfather.

"Today, every time he eats an Oatmeal Creme Pie, it instantly brings back the good memories of those fishing trips," the company said. "That powerful sense of nostalgia and comfort is what makes our products so much more than just a snack for so many people."

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Vibrant’ Florida grandma allegedly killed by illegal immigrant outside Publix, family fights for justice
excerpt: Surveillance video shows the moments before Venezuelan national Carlos Suarez-Contreras allegedly backed his SUV into Deborah Murphy and killed her in the parking lot of a Publix store in Panama City,...
body_text:
Surveillance video shows the moments before Venezuelan national Carlos Suarez-Contreras allegedly backed his SUV into Deborah Murphy and killed her in the parking lot of a Publix store in Panama City, Florida. (Florida Highway Patrol)

A Venezuelan man allegedly in the United States illegally is in jail after being charged in the death of an elderly Florida woman by backing over her with an SUV in a grocery store parking lot.

On May 17, Deborah Murphy, an 82-year-old grandmother, was walking back to her car on a crosswalk outside a Publix in Panama City Beach when she was struck by a Toyota 4Runner, according to court records.

She was pushed to the ground by the SUV, but the vehicle continued backing up, "running over Ms. Murphy," according to an arrest affidavit submitted by the Florida Highway Patrol.

Deborah Murphy, 82, was killed in Florida on May 17, 2026. (Courtesy of Amy Edge)

ICE URGES NORTH CAROLINA TO KEEP ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN TRIPLE-FATAL HIT-AND-RUN BEHIND BARS

Carlos Suarez-Contreras, 26, was the driver of the vehicle, court records show. Luis Sanabria, 29, was the front-seat passenger.

Both were determined to be in the country illegally, according to arrest records.

DOJ DEMANDS SANCTUARY STATES END 'BLATANTLY UNLAWFUL' ANTI-ICE POLICY AS A MATTER OF LIFE AND DEATH

Both men told deputies they were born in Venezuela. The two were issued U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainers and booked into the Bay County Sheriff’s Office Jail, court records show.

Suarez-Contreras submitted a written plea of not guilty to the charge of driving with a canceled license and causing a death, a third-degree felony. His Georgia license had been canceled, according to arrest records.

Carlos Suarez-Contreras was charged in Deborah Murphy's death. (Bay County Sheriff’s Office)

ILLEGAL TRUCKER CASES FUEL GOP PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON CDL MILLS AS DEMS LARGELY SILENT

Under Florida law, an illegal immigrant cannot obtain a state-issued driver’s license. However, 19 states and the District of Columbia do issue licenses to "unauthorized residents," according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

At the scene, Sanabria gave sworn testimony to law enforcement that Suarez-Contreras "was operating the vehicle at the time of the crash."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Luis Sanabria, an illegal immigrant, was a passenger in the car when Deborah Murphy was killed outside a Publix in Panama City Beach, Florida, police said. (Bay County Sheriff’s Office)

Before conducting an immigration investigation, the deputy on the scene noted that Suarez-Contreras gave "suspicious" answers to his questions.

Sanabria immediately left the scene on foot before law enforcement arrived, according to arrest records. He "only returned when I had Suarez-Contreras call him," a deputy reported later.

Sanabria was found to have an expired visa, according to the incident report. He was released into the custody of ICE, Jacob Navarro, public affairs specialist for the Bay County Sheriff’s Office, told Fox News Digital.

Suarez-Contreras is being held without bond because of his immigration status and because it is believed that "he is a potential flight risk," Florida Highway Patrol records show.

Shoppers use the crosswalk in front of a Publix supermarket in Alachua, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Natasha Holt for Fox News Digital)

Just after the incident, Murphy was taken to the hospital and died from injuries related to the crash, according to court documents.

Suarez-Contreras is scheduled to be arraigned on Aug. 17 at the Bay County Courthouse in Panama City, Florida.

"We’re determined to find justice and see Suarez-Contreras held accountable for his reckless actions," Murphy's twin daughters, Beth Schulz and Amy Edge, told Fox News Digital on a phone call. "She touched so many lives as an amazing friend, teacher, mother and grandmother."

Her family remembers her as "a light" who was "vibrant with so many more memories to be made."

Deborah Murphy with her husband, retired Air Force Colonel George Murphy, and their grandchildren on a Florida beach. (Courtesy of Amy Edge)

About 16% of fatal traffic crashes in the U.S. involved drivers with invalid licenses in 2024, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). That same year, 7,080 pedestrians were killed in traffic crashes and more than 71,000 pedestrians were injured.

The state of Florida reported 10,501 pedestrian-related crashes in 2024, according to the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles. There were 678 deaths attributed to those incidents. Drivers failing to look behind them when backing a vehicle in a parking lot is listed as one of the most common reasons for pedestrian crashes by NHTSA.

The Georgia Department of Driver Services told Fox News Digital that Suarez-Contreras' license has been canceled. The agency would not say when it was canceled, citing privacy reasons.

The attorney defending Suarez-Contreras told Fox News Digital in an email that his client "didn’t commit any crime regarding the charges he was arrested on."

"It’s simply an unfortunate incident and not criminal in nature," wrote Russell Ramey of Musca Law in Panama City.

One of Murphy’s grandchildren presented the family with a collection of reflections on life from Murphy in her own words, her daughters said.

"My husband and I always felt that the best thing we could do for generations to come would be to leave this world with people who would make a difference," Murphy wrote in one of the reflections shared with Fox News Digital.

"It has been a delight to witness one’s own legacy. I thank my daughters for making our dream come true!!"

title: Fireworks are fading, but their high-tech replacement comes with new risks
excerpt:
A stunning air show featuring 2,500 drones transformed the night over North Richland Hills, Texas, with massive images of a rocket, a bald eagle, and George Washington.

Drone shows are rapidly replac...
body_text:
A stunning air show featuring 2,500 drones transformed the night over North Richland Hills, Texas, with massive images of a rocket, a bald eagle, and George Washington.

Drone shows are rapidly replacing fireworks at concerts, sporting events and Fourth of July celebrations as communities embrace what many see as a safer, more environmentally friendly alternative. However, as the skies become more crowded with drones, security experts say the increasingly crowded airspace around large public events can make it more difficult to detect potentially bad actors.

R2 Wireless CEO of U.S. Operations Cordell Bennigson, who is a retired Marine Corps officer, told Fox News Digital that the growing prevalence of drone shows demonstrates how accessible the technology has become, creating new challenges for event security and public safety.

Bennigson said that he personally enjoys drone shows and finds them to be "impressive," but said the displays highlight a growing security challenge that extends well beyond the shows themselves.

BROOKLYN BRIDGE CATCHES FIRE AMID NYC FIREWORKS DISPLAY AS TRUMP HAILS IT IN DC SPEECH

Drone shows are becoming increasingly popular, but one expert is warning that they could provide bad actors with the cover needed to carry out illicit activity without being detected. (Thomas A. Ferrara/Newsday RM via Getty Images)

"A drone show itself isn't a security risk, but it's an indication of how accessible drones are," he said. "The other piece of the puzzle is what happens in the clutter and the noise of the full RF spectrum, all the wireless transmissions that are out there."

The radio frequency (RF) spectrum is made up of the invisible wireless signals used by everything from cellphones to drones. These airwaves can become busy during drone shows, due to the tech involved in the show and the spectators taking videos on their phone. According to Bennigson, the additional wireless traffic can make it more difficult for security officials to identify an unauthorized drone flying near an event, allowing it to blend in with legitimate electronic activity.

"Detection is the first line of defense," Bennigson said. "Obviously, we want to be able to defend against a drone from a bad actor, but we have to be able to detect it, and we have to be able to see through all of that clutter, all of the noise in the electromagnetic spectrum, in order to do that."

While some might think reducing wireless transmissions could be a solution, Bennigson said the idea is "unrealistic." In fact, he believes the technology will only become more prevalent, making it even harder to mitigate noise on the RF spectrum. Instead, Bennigson said that experts need to focus on refining detection capabilities.

"The question has to become, how do we get better at seeing or detecting within the noise, within the clutter?" he said.

Bennigson compared the approach to the use of night vision goggles.

"People with bad intentions used to be able to hide in the dark, and then we didn't get rid of the dark in order to mitigate that. We got better at seeing in the dark in order to mitigate it. And then it turned out actually we could use that capability for other kinds of things as well. So, we have to get better at seeing in the electromagnetic spectrum, which is what our focus is at R2, being able to do exactly that," Bennigson told Fox News Digital.

While drones are seen as better alternatives to fireworks, there are hidden dangers that security professionals need to consider. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

FOURTH OF JULY APP GUIDES SPECTATORS THROUGH NINE-HOUR AIR SHOW FROM NASA JETS TO B-1 BOMBERS

Bennigson said artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly important tool in detecting potential bad actors. He noted that the technology is able to rapidly sift through enormous amounts of wireless data, something that would be hard for humans to do in real time.

"AI is really good at picking up patterns. It's really good at rapidly going through large amounts of data," he said. "And so if you want to detect a drone or any other kinds of radio transmission that's happening in an environment where there's lots of other transmissions going on, how do you sort through all of that information really quickly? And how do you learn really quickly when something new shows up that maybe you haven't seen before? AI is very, very effective and very powerful in that environment."

UNAUTHORIZED DRONES DETECTED OVER U.S. AIR FORCE BASE HOUSING NUCLEAR-CAPABLE B-52 BOMBERS: MILITARY

The challenge of drones becoming more prevalent and crowding the RF spectrum extends beyond shows and events, according to Bennigson. He believes that as drones become more common, cities, states and the federal government will need to rethink how they monitor airspace around stadiums, critical infrastructure and other places where large crowds gather.

"This needs to be something that we are paying attention to at the national, at the state, at city, and at the individual event level. We need to recognize that this is a very easy to acquire and very easy to employ capability for anybody who wants to get their hands on it," he said.

Bennigson added that it is crucial to have detection and defense capabilities that are ahead of the bad actors, rather than chasing them.

Drone shows can cause increased noise on the airwaves as they operate and spectators take videos, making it possible for bad actors to go undetected. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images for LACMA)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

As drone traffic grows, the new challenges that emerge will also require regulators tasked with monitoring an increasingly crowded airspace to make changes.

Bennigson said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has systems that work well for aircraft and drones that are operating legally and broadcasting their location. The problem, he said, is when someone with malicious intent who is unlikely to follow those rules enters the picture.

"We can't be relying on them telling us that they are there. We need to have systems that are in place that can identify them. One way that we're familiar with for that is radar."

He warned that while radar can detect things that are not transmitting their location, it also has limitations. One problem, according to Bennigson, is that having radars blasting in urban environments risks disrupting other signals. Additionally, radar can have difficulties picking up low flying first-person view drones. He believes that "radar is a piece of the puzzle, but it can't be the only tool."

"If the FAA is only relying on radar and only relying on friendly transmitters, that leaves a gap for some bad actors to be able to utilize, to be able to operate without being seen," he said.

Rachel Wolf is a media and culture reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Democrats are in big trouble because Black and brown voters don’t want socialism
excerpt: University of Austin founding chair Joe Lonsdale discusses the growing influence of Democratic socialism within the Democratic Party, examines the demographics of DSA supporters and more on 'The Will ...
body_text:
University of Austin founding chair Joe Lonsdale discusses the growing influence of Democratic socialism within the Democratic Party, examines the demographics of DSA supporters and more on 'The Will Cain Show.'

The Democratic Party is being hijacked, and the people it claims to fight hardest for are the first ones bailing out.

The Democratic Socialists of America have gone from a fringe debate club to a governing faction inside the party in the span of a single election cycle. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani sits in Gracie Mansion. The organization is reportedly drafting a new platform calling for abolishing the U.S. Senate. This is not a healthcare plan. This is not a "tax the rich" bumper sticker. This is socialism, and in places its more radical wings openly flirt with communism, gaining real traction inside one of America's two governing parties. Democratic leadership is too terrified of its own base to say so out loud.

Here is what should terrify them more: the coalition they need to win national elections is not buying what the DSA is selling.

'PARTY OF ZOHRAN': MAMDANI EMERGES AS DEMOCRATIC KINGMAKER AFTER SOCIALIST ALLIES SWEEP NYC PRIMARIES

Start with New York City, ground zero for this movement. In the June primary, Mamdani lost to Andrew Cuomo among Black voters by nearly six points citywide, and he got wiped out in Brownsville and East Flatbush, two of the city's poorest neighborhoods where more than 60% of residents are Black.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, left, hugs Rep. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., right during an address marking his first 100 days in office at the Knockdown Center, Sunday, April 12, 2026, in New York. (Andres Kudacki/AP Photo)

It took Mamdani months of dedicated outreach and a general election pivot toward pocketbook issues like housing costs before he clawed back enough of that support to win in November. That is not a story of Black and brown voters embracing democratic socialism from the start. It is a story of a Democratic Socialist having to run away from his own movement's brand to survive a primary.

The pattern held again just weeks ago. In New York's 13th Congressional District, DSA member Darializa Avila Chevalier unseated five-term incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat, 49.4% to 45.9%, but the coalition that put her over the top looked nothing like the district's base. The New York Times reported Chevalier held just a 5.1-point advantage in higher-income areas, while Espaillat won lower-income areas by 9.1 points.

Espaillat also dominated majority-Hispanic precincts with 56%, particularly in working-class neighborhoods like Morris Heights and Kingsbridge, according to VoteHub's analysis of the results. Chevalier's win was built almost entirely on a 24.5-point advantage with younger voters and a 20-point advantage in college-educated precincts, the same coalition that carried Mamdani, not the working-class Hispanic voters who anchor the district.

JON STEWART PRESSES MAMDANI ON WHERE HE BREAKS WITH FELLOW DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ON PRISONS AND BORDERS

That tension finally boiled over. A senior Mamdani campaign adviser called Black homeownership "a weapon of White supremacy masquerading as 'wealth building' public policy," prompting Queens Borough President Donovan Richards to accuse the DSA of acting like White supremacists.

The head of a Bedford-Stuyvesant organization founded in 1978 to keep Black families in their homes pushed back hard: homeownership is the thing generations of Black New Yorkers fought redlining to secure, not their oppressor. When a mostly White socialist movement tells Black homeowners their biggest asset is a tool of oppression, it should not be surprising that the movement struggles to hold their votes.

That tracks with who the DSA actually is. Its own 2021 internal membership survey found the organization is 85% White and only 4% Black, with a median age of 33. More than 80% of members hold a college degree, and better than a third hold a graduate or professional degree, more than double the national rate, with nearly a third clearing six-figure incomes. That is not a working-class movement. It is an upper-middle-class ideological project wearing working-class language as a costume, and Black and brown voters are not fooled by the costume.

BILL MAHER ADMITS HE COULD VOTE FOR JD VANCE, WARNS 'COWARDLY' DEMOCRATS FACE SOCIALIST TAKEOVER

I am not the only one saying this. Democratic political analyst Van Jones, no one's idea of a conservative, called out DSA activists directly, warning that "no police, no prisons, no borders" is not progressive, it's regressive, and it threatens to drag the party somewhere voters do not want to go.

HBO "Real Time with Bill Maher" host Bill Maher has spent months warning Democrats that embracing Mamdani and Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders as the party's future is a gift to Republicans, noting that Vermont couldn't sustain single-payer healthcare for 626,000 people, let alone a nation of 340 million.

And former Biden White House aide Yemisi Egbewole has described the DSA's rise as a socialist cub that establishment Democrats let grow into a full-sized lion because nobody had the nerve to stop it while it was small.

That is not a story of Black and brown voters embracing democratic socialism from the start. It is a story of a Democratic Socialist having to run away from his own movement's brand to survive a primary.

These are not Republican talking points. These are Democrats watching their own party get eaten from the inside and saying so publicly, because the alternative is pretending it isn't happening.

Look at what the DSA actually wants once you get past the slogans. Abolish the police. Abolish prisons. End cash bail and misdemeanor prosecution outright. Decriminalize prostitution. Strip mayoral control of public schools. Advocate for government seizure or replacement of private housing and grocery markets.

These are not modest reforms. They are a rejection of property rights, of public safety, of the basic bargain that working people in Black and brown neighborhoods have fought for generations to secure: safe streets, stable schools and a shot at ownership. The National Black Empowerment Action Fund, a Black-led advocacy group, put $2 million behind ads warning that the DSA agenda threatens decades of social and economic progress built by Black Americans.

Let me be honest about where I sit in this. I am a Republican. The collapse of the Democratic Party as a functioning, majority-coalition institution is no sweat off my brow. If the party wants to hand itself over to an organization that thinks abolishing the Senate is a serious policy position, I will not lose sleep over the electoral consequences.

But there is a bigger stake here than partisan advantage, and it is worth saying plainly: watching an avowedly socialist faction consolidate control over one of America's two major parties should worry every American, not just Republicans.

Socialism has a track record, and it is not a good one. Every serious attempt to centralize economic control at scale has ended in scarcity, corruption, or authoritarian consolidation, usually all three. The DSA's defenders will tell you this is just Scandinavian-style social democracy with better branding. The platform documents say otherwise. So do the voters, and now the Black homeowners and political leaders, who keep pushing back against it.

For the sake of a Democratic Party that might someday remember it needs Black and brown voters to win anything outside a handful of gentrifying ZIP Codes, and for the sake of not letting a genuinely dangerous ideology dress itself up as compassion, the DSA should have no place in serious American politics. From the mayoral primary to the homeownership fight, the coalition it claims to represent keeps telling it no. Democratic leaders can keep pretending otherwise, or they can look at the numbers.

Harrison Fields, age 25, is the former Communications Coordinator for Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi, former Assistant Press Secretary for President Trump, and current Communications Director for Florida Republican Rep. Byron Donalds.

title: Loyal to the look: why Zohran Mamdani wears a suit in all seasons
excerpt:
Around town, on the pitch and even in the pool, the New York mayor keeps his suit on – what do his sartorial choices tell us?

Playing football. Playing in the sand. Dancing on a stage with Alicia Key...
body_text:
Around town, on the pitch and even in the pool, the New York mayor keeps his suit on – what do his sartorial choices tell us?

Playing football. Playing in the sand. Dancing on a stage with Alicia Keys and the entire New York Knicks roster. Swimming in a swimming pool. Swimming in the ocean.

Traditionally, a suit and tie would be considered inappropriate attire for each of these activities. Yet over the past year Zohran Mamdani has seemingly been on a one-man crusade to prove otherwise: to convince people that a formal suit is, actually, suitable for all activities.

That’s because the New York mayor hardly ever wears anything but a suit: frequently purchased from Suit Supply, almost always in a dark colour and worn with a formal tie, mostly paired with smart black boots. He’s hardly the first male politician to embrace the suit – it’s the de facto uniform, after all, of those seeking to project seriousness and solemnity – but few, if any, have been quite as wedded to the formal blazer and matching trousers.

Cheering on the Knicks at Madison Square Garden in May, Mamdani stood out for his decision to wear a dark suit and tie. After the Knicks won, he took the unusual decision to wear the team’s jersey over his shirt and tie, but under his suit jacket. In June, he wore a navy suit, white shirt, and blue striped tie for a press opportunity with children at the beach.

Those aren’t even the most unusual examples.

On New Year’s Day 2025, while running for mayor, he wore a suit to take part in the Polar Bear Club plunge, a New York tradition whereby people go swimming in the frigid Atlantic. “I’m freezing … your rent as the next mayor of New York City,” Mamdani said in an accompanying TikTok video, a message that was rather on the nose, but won him lots of press coverage.

Water proved again to be no obstacle when Mamdani leaped, fully suited, into a swimming pool in Harlem last month, to announce the opening of the city’s pools for summer. (Mamdani “broke the rules in the process”, the rightwing New York Post reported, “which requires all swimmers to wear bathing suits in the water”.)

The mayor is trapped, it seems, in a wool or possibly wool-blend prison of his own making. But why?

Mamdani’s most recent predecessors weren’t as tied to the suit. Bill De Blasio was keen on shorts – although, in a furore that won’t have gone unnoticed by Mamdani, the former mayor was mercilessly ridiculed for wearing the cargo variety – while Eric Adams was partial to a polo shirt, and sometimes a woolly cardigan.

“I think Mamdani wants to double down on appearing as a working mayor, as someone who is always on the job and on the clock,” said Ella Devi, a fashion commentator and, like Mamdani, Democratic Socialists of America member whose (typically negative) assessments of Republicans’ style have made her a target for conservatives.

“I think that he kind of wants to convey that he is committed to the job, through his sartorial choices. I think that is reflected in his attachment to the suiting.”

Devi added: “It’s also that he’s a young, Muslim, socialist.”

It seems likely that Mamdani, the repeated focus of rightwing media, is held to a higher bar than white centrist politicians. It’s an issue Hasan Piker, the Turkish American leftwing streamer, brought up recently, when he said conservatives are “more receptive to what I have to say” when he dresses smartly.

“I used to wear T-shirts all the time,” he told Dazed. “But then I figured I should start wearing a suit and a tie because there are a lot of adults watching on Fox News [the rightwing channel frequently airs clips of Piker speaking] – if they see me saying something in the clips, they’ll be more receptive to what I have to say if I’m in a more appealing format.”

The mayor’s office declined to comment on Mamdani’s wardrobe, but he addressed his penchant for suit-wearing in a recent interview with CNN.

Asked about his decision to jump into a swimming pool wearing a suit, the mayor said: “I think I misunderstood the term swimsuit. I do also have to say thank you, though, to Goodwill [a charity known for its shops that sell used clothing], because I got that suit for 30 bucks, because you can’t go ruining the other suits that you have. But I’m clearly learning that there might be a different way to dress when it’s 100-degree weather.”

Leftists have not always been known for formal dresswear. That remains true in some cases – the disgraced Maine senatorial candidate Graham Platner wore sweaters and T-shirts during his campaign; John Fetterman, the Democratic senator from Pennsylvania, has a passionate commitment to wearing basketball shorts – but that might be changing.

“If there’s a visual language that connotes credibility and authority, why not take advantage of it?” Nathan Robinson, the editor of the leftwing Current Affairs magazine wrote this month.

“You might see someone in a suit as serious, professional, ready to do business. You might think they belong in the Senate or a boardroom. That’s certainly what Mamdani is trying to convey with his suits. He understands that socialists face a challenge: we’re considered fringe. People think we don’t belong among those making important decisions. The suits are a subtle way of asserting the legitimacy and authority of socialist ideas.”

Mamdani has taken the concept further than most. A keen football player, he wore a black suit with a grey tie while doing keep-ups with a football in July, and when he played in a game that same month, Mamdani simply threw a football shirt over his suit – although he did ditch the jacket.

It was not always thus. A source who played for the same team as Mamdani before his election said that he did not play in a suit and tie, although they added: “He always showed up in a suit, or at least suit pants, and his famous boots, and would change on the pitch because he was also always running late.”

The source, who asked not to be named, but who now plays for a football team with the author of this article, continued, “But he never missed a tackle” – remark which was possibly aimed at this writer.

The source said Mamdani used to play in “black shorts”. Asked if a suit would be appropriate attire for a football match, they said it would not. They explained: “Limited stretch in the materials, restricted range of motion, you get sweaty and probably don’t want to have to dry-clean a suit as often for cost and longevity purposes, likelihood of it getting grass stains or torn up during play, excessive wear from friction which would also compromise longevity of a likely costly piece of clothing less easily replaced, too hot to play in (comfortably).”

Having become so intertwined with the suit, the question might be: can Mamdani ever wear anything else? Can the mayor ditch the formalwear?

“I think that now he’s kind of trapped in the suit, and he knows that he’s trapped in the suit, because he’s made it his thing to always wear the suit,” Devi said.

“He has to stick with the bit, the suit bit. If he wears jeans, then the New York Post is just going to write about that for the next three weeks.”

With temperatures in New York recently hitting 38C (100F), Mamdani might be wishing he could wear something else – although Devi had a suggestion should the heat become too unbearable.

“He would never go for this, because it would not be seen as very socialist, but Thom Browne does some very good suit shorts for the future heatwaves. So that’s my advice to Mayor Mamdani,” she said.

It’s a fine idea, except according to Thom Browne’s website, those shorts retail at about $1,300, which might raise questions over Mamdani’s socialist credentials. It seems that, at least for now, Mamdani is stuck in the suit.

title: Europe wildfires: more than 300,000 flee homes and holiday accommodation in France and Spain as fires rage
excerpt:
Fires displace people on massive scale and trigger one of the largest peacetime civilian evacuation operations ever carried out in France

More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain

...
body_text:
Fires displace people on massive scale and trigger one of the largest peacetime civilian evacuation operations ever carried out in France

More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain

Hello and welcome back to our rolling coverage of the wildfires spreading through parts of Spain and France.

Thousands crowded into emergency shelters in France and Spain on Sunday after wildfires drove more than 300,000 people to flee their homes and holiday accommodation.

France has been worst affected by the wildfires, with an approximate area of 42,000 hectares burnt by the flames.

French authorities said that more than 220,000 people have now been evacuated from the main forest fire raging in the south-west of the country.

About 55,000 people were ordered to leave villages around Bordeaux in the Gironde region during the night as flames from the wildfire spread.

In Spain, over 90,000 people have been evacuated from the regions around Madrid and Ávila, as fires continue to spread there. Spanish authorities have ordered new evacuations near Toledo, south-west of Madrid.

The interior ministry said residents of Buenaventura, Navamorcuende, Real de San Vicente, Hinojosa de San Vicente, Castillo de Bayuela, Garciotum, Nuno Gomez and Pelahustan were told to leave their homes.

On Saturday evening, Spain’s interior ministry said a man had died in a fire in Manises, in Valencia. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said.

The blazes have destroyed houses, displaced people on a massive scale and triggered one of the largest peacetime civilian evacuation operations ever carried out in France, with major fires still burning in both countries.

According to authorities, fires have kept at least 37 sections of road closed to traffic in Madrid, Ávila, Toledo, Castellón, Guadalajara, Huelva and Teruel this morning.

As we mentioned in the opening post, about 55,000 people were ordered to leave villages around the French city of Bordeaux overnight as the fire continues to spread.

A Bordeaux city council spokesperson has told Sky News that is “currently studying scenarios for all possible ways the fire could evolve”, including a total evacuation of the city if necessary.

Bordeaux’s mayor Thomas Cazenave described the fire as being “at the gates of the metropolitan area”.

In Spain, wildfires are continuing to burn throughout the Madrid area and the province of Ávila, near the capital, according to authorities.

The wildfires have burnt through about 24,000 hectares in the Madrid region and 21,000 hectares in Ávila, according to the Spanish newspaper El Mundo, sparking mass evacuations.

Spain has evacuated tens of thousands of people from villages west of Madrid where extremely dry conditions have been worsened by heatwaves and strong winds.

Over 30,000 people have been evacuated from Ávila and over 15,000 in the eastern Castellón province of Spain.

Spain has declared a national emergency, the first time the country has ever done so over a wildfire.

France’s evacuations constituted “probably” the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has ever seen, its interior minister said.

Hundreds of firefighters have worked to contain the blazes, which have been fuelled by persistent heatwaves and the climate crisis, but were still unable to stop their advance.

The French government has called in the military to help, deploying 1,500 soldiers, and has rushed 1.5m face masks to help protect people from smoke inhalation.

About 220,000 people have now been evacuated from the main forest fire raging in the south-west of France that threatens the city of Bordeaux, according to French authorities.

The latest evacuations have been in villages around Bordeaux while 60km (37 miles) of the main A63 highway from Bordeaux to the Spanish border has been closed because of the fires, regional authorities said.

Some of the photos emerging from France and Spain paint a dramatic picture of the evolving crisis:

Authorities in France’s Gironde region, where Bordeaux is located, issued overnight evacuation orders for five more localities including some on the city’s approaches.

Their statement said gusting winds fed the flames overnight, accelerating the spread of the fire that has been burning out of control since midweek.

title: WATCH: Democrats blast Trump Saudi nuclear deal as GOP touts regional alliance
excerpt: Lawmakers react to the White House's nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, with GOP stressing the importance of maintaining strategic partnerships in the Middle East, while Democrats warn t...
body_text:
Lawmakers react to the White House's nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, with GOP stressing the importance of maintaining strategic partnerships in the Middle East, while Democrats warn the deal could fuel a regional nuclear arms race.

Lawmakers offered strikingly divided reactions to the White House’s announcement of a new nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia, with Democrats concerned about accelerating a nuclear program in the Middle East and Republicans emphasizing the need for partnership in the region.

"I don't trust anybody as far as I can throw them, but we've got to develop allies," Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., told Fox News Digital. "And as long as we can verify them, we have the people there that can verify that they're using them for the proper uses, then we’re okay."

The Department of Energy released details Wednesday on the agreement, which would support the development of a civilian nuclear energy program in Saudi Arabia by providing U.S. technology and expertise. The agreement also includes safeguards intended to ensure nuclear materials are not diverted for weapons development.

IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

Lawmakers offered strikingly divided reactions to the White House’s announcement of a new nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia.  (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., blasted the proposal as "outrageous," and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., argued allowing Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium without strict safeguards could "cause a nuclear arms race."

"The president says what we're trying to do is to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, but if Saudi Arabia … does not meet all the protocols, etc., then it could cause an arms race where Egyptians or others in the area want a nuclear weapon," Meeks said.

TRUMP'S IRAN DEAL SPARKS GOP DEMANDS FOR VOTE AS CONGRESS REMAINS IN THE DARK

Rep. Mark Alford, R-Miss., said Congress should be central in the decision to pursue any final agreement, while also stressing the importance of having Saudi Arabia as a regional partner.

"I think it's important with any agreement like that that Congress have a role in that and I look forward to reviewing that," Alford said.

"As we continue our conflict with Iran, we need partners in that region who are of the same mindset," Alford continued. "And Saudi, with its reforms that they're undergoing right now, gives me great hope and encouragement that we can move forward together in that region to help bring lasting peace.

BOOKER SLAMS TRUMP’S IRAN DEAL AS AN 'ABJECT SURRENDER,' LABELS HIM THE 'BIGGEST LOSER' WITH 'EGG ON HIS FACE'

Raskin also raised questions to Fox News Digital about President Donald Trump's family's financial ties to Saudi Arabia.

"Now the Trump administration allows the Saudis to enrich uranium," Raskin said. "So, the Saudis enrich the Trumps, and the Trump's allow the Saudis to enrich uranium and then we're going to have more nuclear weapons in the Middle East to set off another nuclear arms race there. "

The agreement comes as the Trump administration seeks to strengthen its partnership with Saudi Arabia while maintaining pressure on Iran over its nuclear program, a balancing act Congress is likely to scrutinize in coming months.

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Weekday games were amazing’: pubs toast extra £150m in World Cup sales
excerpt:
England’s progress provides best football-related uplift of recent years, with one pub too packed to host its Dolly Parton tribute

Late opening hours and England’s progress to the semi-final of an ex...
body_text:
England’s progress provides best football-related uplift of recent years, with one pub too packed to host its Dolly Parton tribute

Late opening hours and England’s progress to the semi-final of an expanded World Cup helped provide the best football-related uplift of recent years for pubs, figures suggest.

Pubs poured 30m extra pints over the course of the tournament compared with a normal trading period, with busy pumps delivering £150m in added sales, according to the British Beer & Pubs Association (BBPA).

The World Cup-related increase in sales, as fans followed England and Scotland games, also appears to have outstripped that seen during previous competitions, including England’s run to the final of Euro 2024.

The standout day over the course of the last three tournaments, in terms of sales uplift relative to a normal shift, was England’s game against Mexico in the early hours of the morning, according to data from the payment systems provider Epos Now.

Sales nearly doubled on that day compared with the same period pre-tournament, as pubs were permitted to open through the night and could trade in regular hours as well.

Three other games delivered a two-thirds increase in the number of transactions, according to the data.

By contrast, only two games at each of Qatar 2022 and Euro 2024 led to an increase of more than 50%.

Another payments provider, Dojo, said sales over the entire course of the tournament were 16% higher than normal, while the overall World Cup-related boost was 9% better than in Euro 2024.

The rise in sales was swiftly followed by a £100m aid package for pubs from Andy Burnham, who announced a 20% cut in business rates for the sector on Thursday. While the government policy was criticised for a lack of ambition, the dual benefits of the tax cut and the football brought rare respite for the hard-pressed industry, which recorded one pub a day closing last year, in England and Wales.

Dawn Slater, who runs the Garrick’s Head pub in Greater Manchester, said she and her staff had more than doubled their sales compared with previous tournaments after expanding capacity outside and installing giant screens.

“It’s been really busy, fully booked every game. We stopped entry two hours before each game.

“People definitely spent more money on this tournament but it was also more expensive to put it on. We had extra TVs, an outside bar. Plastic cups and pitchers alone cost us £8,700. But the take was good.

“I’ve had to be here from 10am staying open till 2am most games and getting in bed at 5am. It was worth every minute, I wouldn’t change anything.”

However, busy match days were often followed by quieter periods, offsetting some of the gains, with trading dependent on England’s progress.

“The weekday games were amazing,” said Amy Williams, who runs the George in Witham with her husband, Tom. “We had a 300-400% increase in sales on our tills compared to the previous week.

“For the Norway game we had a Dolly Parton tribute act but we cancelled her because there was no way she would have had space to perform.”

“Sunday, for the final, we had a few people turn up. Had England got through it would have been a fantastic week but a lot of people didn’t come out that weekend. We’re normally busy but it was the quietest.

“There was definitely a drop in sales the day before and the day after. The next day [after England’s loss to Argentina] was like a ghost town.”

The World Cup benefit was not equally felt across the hospitality sector, with restaurants struggling in the hot weather.

Mitchells & Butlers, the UK’s largest hospitality chain, reported flat sales in the third quarter of the year, as improvement in its pubs division during the World Cup was offset by the hot weather deterring customers from brands such as Toby Carvery.

Restaurant groups that reported sales to the data analysis firm NIQ said sales were down by 0.7% year on year in June, making it the second worst month of 2026.

title: Tour de France final stage shortened as emergency teams tackle wildfires
excerpt:
The final stage of the Tour de France has been shortened and rerouted, with first responders diverted from Paris to tackle wildfires that are raging in the southwest of France.

Sunday’s traditional s...
body_text:
The final stage of the Tour de France has been shortened and rerouted, with first responders diverted from Paris to tackle wildfires that are raging in the southwest of France.

Sunday’s traditional stage in Paris has been shortened from 133km (82 miles) to just 89km (55 miles), with the riders starting on the Champs-Elysees rather than in Thoiry, west of the French capital.

The change has been deemed necessary because multiple security officers have been diverted to the fires. The new route will leave a smaller race footprint for local officials to secure.

“As numerous wildfires are currently affecting France, particularly the Gironde region, emergency services are fully mobilised to combat the blazes, while internal security forces are working to secure the affected areas and protect the population,” the Amaury Sport Organisation, which organises the tour, said in a statement.

“In light of this, the Ministry of the Interior has decided to redeploy a portion of the internal security forces initially mobilised to ensure security for the final stage of the Tour de France, in order to reinforce the response efforts in the areas affected by the wildfires,” the statement added.

More than 267,000 people have been forced from their homes by wildfires raging in France and Spain, with Bordeaux airport closed and the French government warning against all road or rail travel to the area.

The newly designed stage 21 will still end along the famed Champs-Elysees, with the riders taking two extra circuits of the road before heading out for the Montmartre climb.

The Montmartre circuit has proven to be popular after it was used in the 2024 Paris Olympics and then added to the 2025 Tour de France. The area can accommodate large gatherings of fans, who turn the area into a party atmosphere.

Earlier in the Tour de France, fans were asked to stay away from the final 40km of stage 3 because of wildfires and the need to deploy first responders to the area.

Slovenia’s Tadej Pogacar is set to secure a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after dominating the three-week race.

title: France battles fire 'whirlwinds' as another 55,000 evacuated
excerpt:
A further 55,000 people have been evacuated from six towns in France, as wildfires which have caused devastation across the country pick up pace.

The most recent evacuations took place in towns to th...
body_text:
A further 55,000 people have been evacuated from six towns in France, as wildfires which have caused devastation across the country pick up pace.

The most recent evacuations took place in towns to the south of Bordeaux, in the Gironde region.

Wildfires have raged across Europe over the past week, primarily France and Spain, where more than 330,000 people have been evacuated.

France has been worst-affected, with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt, making it one of the largest forest fires since World War Two. About 98,000 hectares have burnt across the country since the start of the year.

Captain Nicolas Braz, one of the leaders of the firefighting operation, said the fire had created "its own winds - complete with whirlwinds", adding it was "erratic and unmanageable".

Dry vegetation and brisk winds are causing the fire to spread, with 60km (37 miles) of the A63 motorway, which leads to Spain, having been closed.

In an interview published on Sunday by La Tribune, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said it "will take a long time to bring under control" and until it is contained "there will be no return" for evacuated residents and tourists.

France has mobilised its military to help with the response and extra reinforcements from the army have been sent to help firefighters by clearing brush and creating fire breaks.

President Emmanuel Macron said France would "rebuild" and his government would "be there for as long as is needed".

Meanwhile in Spain, fires continue to spread, with more than 90,000 evacuated from the regions around Madrid and Ávila.

Late on Saturday, at least eight municipalities near Toledo were also ordered to evacuate, though it was unclear how many people were involved.

Sunday is expected to bring high temperatures and low humidity, potentially allowing the fire to spread further.

Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the situation as the "worst fire in the history of the region".

Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez admitted there were "complex times ahead". Meanwhile, authorities in València confirmed the death of a man in a fire.
